pages.searchText: After a thorough deliberation, I persuaded Captain Murray, The Second Episode The Second Episode ... ; After a thorough deliberation, I persuaded Captain Murray, That he should allow me to go through his (Bootey Shah's) version. After a thorough perusal of his narration I told Captain Murray, That he had not given the whole truth about the Sikhs. (27) In this way, I developed a bond of friendship with him, And he invited me to express his desire. That I should get everything recorded to him, As to how the Khalsa originated and came into existence. (28) That he had reposed his faith in a Muslim. But there had been a life-long conflict between the Muslims and the Hindus, As they had been in continuous confrontation with each other. (29) The Muslims had been as much slandering the Hindus, As the Hindus had been condemning the Muslims. Hearing this, Captain Murray made a terse remark, That the Britishers were guite shrewd and sensible. (30) They were as capable of sifting facts from fiction, As a Swan? would separate the milk content from water. So he (the author) must state the facts unhesitatingly, Whenever the British had ventured into an alien land, They had always recorded the entire history of that region. Whatever they had found authentic and credible, They had despatched its contents to the king in London. (32) That I should disclose him this much of a mystery. How did the Sikhs acguire political power and statehood, And who bestowed sovereignty on the Sikhs? (33) Then, I answered Captain Murray in these words, The true Lord Divine has conferred sovereignty on the Sikhs. Captain Murray asked me who was their true Lord, I replied, Guru Nanak is their true Lord. (34) Murray said that Nanak was a mere mendicant, I remarked that Guru Nanak was the Lord of Lords, He was a Divine prophet and lord of the whole world. (35)

pages.title: The Second Episode
pages.episodeTitle: The Second Episode ... ;
pages.snippet: Many kings he turned into fakirs, and many fakirs he raised into leaders; Guru Nanak remained beyond worldly attachment, a sovereign among sovereigns. (36) Those who touched Guru Nanak’s feet gained such power that sparrows could strike haw
pages.searchText: The Second Episode The Second Episode The Second Episode ... ; Many kings he turned into fakirs, and many fakirs he raised into leaders; Guru Nanak remained beyond worldly attachment, a sovereign among sovereigns. (36) Those who touched Guru Nanak’s feet gained such power that sparrows could strike hawks and lambs could tear lions. (37) Those who sat upon royal thrones and commanded great armies became as servants before the power awakened by the Guru. (38) If a tyrant rose against them, he would quickly come to ruin. (39) So I told Murray that such sovereignty belonged to Guru Nanak’s house, and that one who came into the Guru’s refuge was protected while oppressors were struck down. (40)

pages.title: His reprimands turned many kings into paupers,
pages.episodeTitle: The Second Episode ... ;
pages.snippet: His reprimands turned many kings into paupers, And his blessings turned many paupers into kings. By keeping himself detached from politics and power, He came to acquire the status of a Lord of Lords. (36) Whosoever sought his Divine grace a
pages.searchText: His reprimands turned many kings into paupers, The Second Episode The Second Episode ... ; His reprimands turned many kings into paupers, And his blessings turned many paupers into kings. By keeping himself detached from politics and power, He came to acquire the status of a Lord of Lords. (36) Whosoever sought his Divine grace and blessings, They were imbued with power and sovereignty. His blessings made the timid sparrows pounce upon the hawks, And the meek lambs tear apart the lions. (37) Whose armies consisted of millions of horse riders, And whose eguipage consisted of thousands of canons. Who were the mighty occupants of royal thrones, They were annihilated by the descendents of Guru Nanak. (38) Intoxicated with a dose of Cannabis and the Name of the Lord, His followers (The Sikhs) charged at their adversaries with such ferocity, That their enemies could not bear the brunt of their attack, And they perished instantly under their mighty strokes. (39) How Guru Nanak was blessed with Divine power? Dear pious readers, I narrated him the following account: Responding to people's prayers, God Himself invited Guru Nanak, And made him a sovereign on His own behalf, And bestowed Nanak with all the Divine powers, Thereafter with a warm hug, God sent him to the world, Naming him Nanak, bade him to take birth in the Bedi dynasty. God instructed Guru Nanak to protect the meek and the humble, And crush all those who were evil and wicked. (40) Murray asked me to narrate all the events, Which led to the bestowal of Divine seal on Nanak/s house. I narrate it to my devout and dear readers, The whole account as I did to Captain Murray. (41) A lot of Chaos had come to prevail during the Kaliyuga, Corruption increased as religion and morality had declined. The rulers had turned greedy and avaricious, They had abandoned their moral duty of just governance. (42) The followers of the earlier religious sects who happened to be there, They had also gone astray (from their moral and religious path).

pages.snippet: Thus I told Murray that I would narrate everything: the year, the age, the land, and the place. (1) It was in Talwandi of Rai Bhoe near Lahore that Guru Nanak was born. (2) He was born in the Bedi Khatri lineage, in a family of deep piety.
pages.searchText: The Second Episode The Second Episode The Second Episode ... ; Thus I told Murray that I would narrate everything: the year, the age, the land, and the place. (1) It was in Talwandi of Rai Bhoe near Lahore that Guru Nanak was born. (2) He was born in the Bedi Khatri lineage, in a family of deep piety. (3) In Kaliyuga, when rulers had become butchers and righteousness seemed to fly away, the Guru took birth to restore the path. (43 and transition)

pages.title: The Episode About the First Sikh Guni
pages.episodeTitle: The Episode About the First Sikh Guni
pages.snippet: The greed for lucre had corrupted every section of society, Episode 3 In this dark age of Kaliyuga symbolised by a pair of scissors, The rulers have turned themselves into butchers. Dharma or Moral values have disappeared from public life.
pages.searchText: The Episode About the First Sikh Guni the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni The greed for lucre had corrupted every section of society, Episode 3 In this dark age of Kaliyuga symbolised by a pair of scissors, The rulers have turned themselves into butchers. Dharma or Moral values have disappeared from public life. The truth, symbolised by Moon, has been eclipsed in this darkest phase. Here I write the Legend of the First Mahal (Nanak) (How Nanak took Birth) That I must narrate the whole story (of Guru Nanak). With all the details of the year and the age of his birth, Along with the name of the place and the country of his birth. (1) Rattan Singh's version: Chaupai: The year of Guru Nanak's birth falls in the Bikrami Era?, Guru Nanak was born in the year 1526 (1469 CE). His birth place was Rai Bhoi Bullar's village of Talwandi, Which is situated in the vicinity of Lahore towards Kasur (Pakistan). (2) It was in the caste of Bedis, a subcaste of Kashtriyas?, That Guru Nanak took birth in this family of Bedis. It was a family of very religious and pious lineage, In which Guru Nanak took his human birth. (3) It was under the constellation of auspicious stars in Satyuga*, That the Prophet Narsimanh had taken human birth. In the age (yuga) of Treta? under a similar constellation of stars, Lord Rama had taken a human birth in that age. (4) As Lord Krihna was born under a similar dispensation in Duapar °, So was Guru Nanak Born in Kaliyuga in the same order. Guru Nanak's father was known by the name of Kalu Das, And his mother was known by the name of Tripta. (5) Guru Nanak's family was perfect in piety and moral virtues, Although it was not so rich and sound in affluence.

pages.title: Guru Nanak’s Birth and Destiny
pages.episodeTitle: The Episode About the First Sikh Guni
pages.snippet: In that age religion had grown thin while greed for wealth had become a form of deceit. Yet in that family a great one was born. (6) The hour, the house, the constellation, and the conjunction were all auspicious. (7) From the very moment of birth the parents felt a great radianc
pages.searchText: Guru Nanak’s Birth and Destiny the First Sikh Guni In that age religion had grown thin while greed for wealth had become a form of deceit. Yet in that family a great one was born. (6) The hour, the house, the constellation, and the conjunction were all auspicious. (7) From the very moment of birth the parents felt a great radiance, as if wealth, siddhis, and divine favor had entered the house. (8) The family rejoiced and summoned a learned pandit to examine the child’s destiny. (9–10) The pandit declared that this child was no ordinary being but one destined to guide the world. (11)

pages.title: Partly because of his family's piety and partly of his own volition,
pages.episodeTitle: The Episode About the First Sikh Guni
pages.snippet: Partly because of his family's piety and partly of his own volition, Guru Nanak was born here on the auspicious night of the full moon. (6) It was the most auspicious moment and under the most auspicious Zodiac sign, The most ideal constell
pages.searchText: Partly because of his family's piety and partly of his own volition, the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni Partly because of his family's piety and partly of his own volition, Guru Nanak was born here on the auspicious night of the full moon. (6) It was the most auspicious moment and under the most auspicious Zodiac sign, The most ideal constellation of auspicious stars. The most auspicious Zodiac sign and the most auspicious planet, And the most auspicious constellation of mellifluous planets. (7) Guru Nanak's birth ushered an era of name and fame for his family, Their fame and reputation spread manifold and wide. It marked a manifold increase in family's fortunes and influence, And God blessed the family with wealth and landed property. (8) When the earth was dug to bury his mother's post-natal placenta, Gold coins were sighted underneath the dug up earth. Feeling highly delighted and excited by this good omen, Guru Nanak's parents summoned the most learned pundit? of their area. (9) The Pundit cast a horoscope of Guru Nanak's Nativity, He felt extremely pleased with his tabulation. He cast a glance at the child's (Guru Nanak's) face spell bound, And a gentle smile ran all over his face. (10) Making a thorough interpretation of Guru Nanak's horoscope, The Pundit gave instructions to the parents of Guru Nanak. He predicted that a perfect prophet had taken birth (in their family), And that they must pay obeisance and show reverence to the child. (11) Since this new-born was a child without any blemish, His fame was likely to spread far and wide. He gave him a name beginning with the letter N, And named him Nanak after the prophet Narsimanh. (12) Whosoever came to have a glimpse of his face, Became fascinated with his charismatic appearance. Even after having repeated glimpses of his pious face, The onlooker was never satiated with his glimpse. (13) Some predicted that he would be a Sidh, Others predicted that he would be a prophet. Still others made predictions about his being a King, With all the regalia of an enthroned sovereign. (14).

pages.title: Guru Nanak’s Childhood Wonders and Balwand’s Devotion
pages.episodeTitle: The Episode About the First Sikh Guni
pages.snippet: This page turns from simple childhood admiration to the first public signs of Guru Nanak's spiritual mission. Guru Nanak teaches Satinam and Kartar Purakh to those around him, shaping devotion through speech, song, and the companionship of
pages.searchText: Guru Nanak’s Childhood Wonders and Balwand’s Devotion the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni This page turns from simple childhood admiration to the first public signs of Guru Nanak's spiritual mission. Guru Nanak teaches Satinam and Kartar Purakh to those around him, shaping devotion through speech, song, and the companionship of Mardana. The narrative also gathers stories of wonder and affection that make nearby people recognize his distinct greatness before his wider journeys begin. Balwand's reverence and hospitality fit into that pattern, showing how devotion formed around the young Guru even before formal preaching expanded outward. Read together with the adjacent readable page, the passage belongs to a sequence of early marvels, song, and recognition. It presents Guru Nanak's childhood as already charged with the teaching and charisma that later travels will reveal more fully.

pages.episodeTitle: The Episode About the First Sikh Guni
pages.snippet: Chaupai: The affluent wished to make an offering of their wealth to him, And the poor too wished to contribute money to his service. Some wished to test the effect of his blessings after making their offerings, Others made promises of offer
pages.searchText: Chaupai: The affluent wished to make an offering of their wealth to him, the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni Chaupai: The affluent wished to make an offering of their wealth to him, And the poor too wished to contribute money to his service. Some wished to test the effect of his blessings after making their offerings, Others made promises of offerings after the fulfilment of their wishes. (15) As Guru Nanak's fame and reputation spread in the Kaliyuga, More and more people flocked to have a glimpse of him. Whosoever visited him, shared his heart's desires with him, And listened to his discourses about the unknown and the future. (16) The father Kalu Das, impressed by his son's personality, Thought of a business proposition for his illustrious son. And went on any errand that his father sent him to. (17) He kept on meditating on the sacred Name of God, And began his conversations with the invocation of God's Name. He rendered the same advice to his fellow playmates, And made them recite the name of the True God. (18) Dohra: He improvised a musical string instrument out of a dry reed, And handed it over to his companion Mardana. He sang the sacred hymns to the accompaniment of music, And all his playmates joined to sing in a chorus. (19) Chaupai: If I narrate all the details of his childhood, Even a big volume would fall short to record his deeds. So restricting myself to the essentially core incidents, I wish to synopsize a few anecdotes from his childhood. (20) How he once engaged his fellowmates in a game, And how he restored a grazed crop to its original luxurious state. How Balwand once saw Baba Nanak's face with his own eyes, Being shaded with the spread out hood of a snake. (21) How did many other miracles come to light, This is how he developed a great reverence for Nanak, And honoured him after inviting him to his palace. (22) Dohra: Thus, Balwand invited and honoured Guru Nanak, And himself sat at his feet like an obedient son. And allowed him access to play in every comer of his palace, Inside, outside as well as his private bed chambers. (23).

pages.searchText: Guru Nanak’s Learning and Detachment the First Sikh Guni The child’s greatness became known to many, and the news reached even the ministers in Delhi. (24) When Baba Ji grew older, he was sent to a teacher so that he might be instructed according to custom. (25) Many marvels were seen in his learning, and the account of them spread everywhere. (26) When he came of age and entered household life, he still remained inwardly detached. (27) He worked in the storehouse, yet did not cling to profit; with Mardana beside him, he sang the Shabad on the rabab. (28)

pages.searchText: As iron turns into Gold with the touch of Paras, the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni As iron turns into Gold with the touch of Paras, Rai Balwand also gained in reputation with the touch of Nanak's feet. He also got promoted to the ministerial position at Delhi. (24). When Guru Nanak grew and gained more awareness, He was sent for getting education to a priest. How Guru Nanak taught his priestly teacher instead, I narrated that account to Captain Murray. (25) How Guru Nanak accomplished many other miracles, Which I did not narrate so as to restrict the size of this epic. How after Guru Nanak's marriage was solemnized. He named his two sons who were born to him. (26) How his father Kalu Das wanted his son to do business, And Wished his son to earn a fortune for himself. How Guru Nanak refused to toe the family line, And how his disobedience irked his parents. (27) How he paid no heed to the family's business line, And instead started reciting hymns with a Rabab. How he passed most of his time with companion Mardana, And took no interest in the business dealings. (28) Guru Nanak at Modikhana!? and A Dip in River Waiyeen Guru Nanak came to be known as a careless romatic, Following his total lack of interest in worldly affairs. Hearing this news, Guru Nanak's brother-in-law Jai Ram, A resident of Sultanpur, came to verify this news. (29) He took away Guru Nanak to Daulat Khan, Who was the Mulk Umrao!* of the territory of Sultanpur. He introduced Guru Nanak to the Sultanpur's Nawab, And got him appointed as incharge of his warehouse. (30) All those who are interested in knowing a detailed account, Those who wish to listen to various other episodes during this period, I have given only a very brief account of these incidents, Exactly as I had narrated these to Captain Murray.

pages.searchText: Guru Nanak Enters the River the First Sikh Guni As I heard it, I now tell it: Baba Ji became inwardly detached and turned toward udasi. (32) Going to the river with a companion, he entered the waters and did not emerge for a watch of the day. (33) An alarm spread everywhere: people cried that he had drowned, and Daulat Khan came running. (34) Search was made by every means, but he was not found. People said he had crossed beyond the visible shore. (35–36)

pages.snippet: Then Baba!* entered into a very contemplative mood, And became totally disinterested and detached from every affair. (32) He used to go to a river for his daily morning ablutions, Where he was always accompanied by a servant. One day, he di
pages.searchText: Then Baba!* entered into a very contemplative mood, the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni Then Baba!* entered into a very contemplative mood, And became totally disinterested and detached from every affair. (32) He used to go to a river for his daily morning ablutions, Where he was always accompanied by a servant. One day, he dived deep into the river, And did not come out for a very long time. (33) The servant, losing all hopes of Guru Nanak's survival, Raised an alarm and a lot of hue and cry. Hearing these cries that Guru Nanak had drowned, He ordered the nets to be cast in the river to trap his body, But had Nanak been there, then alone could he be traced. A thorough search was carried out across the other end. (35) When the foot-tracers and astrologers failed to trace him, The people felt that the current must have carried him away. There was much grieving and mourning at Jai Ram's house, And Daulat Khan also felt dumbounded and suspicious. (36) While this suspense continued for one or two days, Guru Nanak emerged out of the river on the third day. With a rag wrapped round his waist and a towel on his shoulders, He stood still and silent like a scarecrow in a field. (37) Hearing this news, people rushed to the spot, And started rallying round Guru Nanak. Daulat Khan also arrived at the scene, But Guru Nanak remained completely silent and detached, Daulat Khan summoned the services of Hakeems!, For Nanak must be afflicted with some serious disease. When Baba Nanak explained the psychic cause (of his silence) to the Hakeem, Daulat Khan felt relieved of his tension and fears. (40)

pages.searchText: Baba Nanak Becomes a Teacher of Truth the First Sikh Guni Mullahs and qazis said that Baba Ji had broken the ordinary bounds of religion, and many became intensely curious about him. (41) People began to say that he was a perfect, God-realized person and that whole households were becoming his disciples. (42) To both Hindus and Muslims he became a teacher of truth, restraining oppression and guiding people toward justice. (43)

pages.searchText: There were daily confrontations between Guru Nanak and Muslim Kazis!8, the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni There were daily confrontations between Guru Nanak and Muslim Kazis!8, Some even branding him a magician or a necromancer. But Daulat Khan did not agree with any of their opinions, As he came to repose his complete faith in Baba Nanak. (41) He believed him to be a supreme prophet of his age, And his whole family became followers of Guru Nanak. Baba Nanak treated both the Hindus and the Muslims without any discrimination, Whosoever came to him became Guru Nanak's follower. (42) He gave a message of truth to both the communities, And restrained both from indulging in acts of oppression. As he became more and more famous and popular, People came to seek his blessings from far and wide. (43) But both the wives had no issues. After paying obeisance to Guru Nanak, both of them were blessed, With two sons each, who grew to be as brave as lions. (44) Their names were Gazi Khan, Gazi Mast Khan, The other two being Mir Khan and Zolakh Khan. The two mothers made a public declaration that they were, Blessed with a Couple of sons each, with the grace of Baba Nanak. (45) Baba Nanak was contemplating over the issue, How to remain detached from the world. Since the world had already come to know of his presence, So he thought of getting away from the world. (46) How can the sun remain eclipsed forever Even if the sky is overcast with myriads of dark clouds? His fame spread far and wide in a very short time (47) How can a person resist shifting towards fire, Who had been under a severe grip of cold? Who were severely affected with pain and sorrow? (48) All the Hindu and the Muslim Saints and Sidhas, Came to see Baba Nanak after hearing of his fame, All of them went back acknowledging his spiritual supremacy. (49)

pages.searchText: Guru Nanak Sets Out with Mardana the First Sikh Guni The fame of Baba Ji’s greatness spread among saints, pirs, and seekers; each received an answer according to the state of his own heart. (50) Then Baba Ji set out upon udasi, taking Mardana with him and carrying the rabab upon his shoulder. (51) Wherever Baba Ji felt joy, there he would sing the Shabad with the rabab. (52) Saints, siddhs, pirs, and disciples came before him in wonder; wherever he went, he spread the remembrance of the True Name. (53–54)

pages.snippet: He blessed those with Knowledge who sought knowledge. With whatever desire one sought his grace, Undertook Udasees!? and Held Discussions with Sidhas Chaupai: Being overtaken by a sense of detached aloofness, Baba Nanak thought of traveling
pages.searchText: He blessed those with Knowledge who sought knowledge. the First Sikh Guni The Episode About the First Sikh Guni He blessed those with Knowledge who sought knowledge. With whatever desire one sought his grace, Undertook Udasees!? and Held Discussions with Sidhas Chaupai: Being overtaken by a sense of detached aloofness, Baba Nanak thought of traveling to other lands. Who followed Baba Nanak with his Rabab?!. (51) He would recite hymns to the accompaniment of music. Sidhas, Saints, Pirs? and their followers rallied round him, Delivering his message, he proceeded further on his travels. (52) To whatever country Baba Nanak paid a visit, He sermonized people to dwell on God's name. He eradicated the idol worship of all kinds, The worship of Pirs, Prophets, gods and goddesses. (53) He dispelled people's faith in all kinds of exorcism, Such as in various kinds of talismans, tantric rituals and occult powers, Such as various kinds of ghosts, spirits and Gugapir2. (54) Dohra: Whichever country Baba Nanak paid a visit to, Whether inhabited by the Hindus or the Muslims, He advised the Muslim's to shun others belongings as they shunned Pork, And preached the Hindus to shun others share as they shunned cow's meat. (55) Chaupai: Delivering a message of truth in this way, He explained the true import of the Koran to the Muslims, And explained the real essence of the Vedas to the Hindus. (56) Once Baba Nanak paid a visit to the town of Achchal Batala, Where Sidhas were holding their annual congregation. He entered into a debate with the Sidhas, But, the Sidhas, despite their spiritual powers, paled in argument. (57) Against Guru Nanak to another Sidha known as Bal Gudai.

pages.searchText: Transition from the Dialogue with Kaliyuga to the South Udasi the Dialogue Between Baba Nanak and Kaliyuga The Episode About the Dialogue Between Baba Nanak and Kaliyuga The page finishes the dialogue with Kaliyuga by contrasting destructive desire with the Guru's saving intent. Where the age wishes sinners to sink, Baba Nanak resolves to ferry the world across and refuses to abandon creation to corruption. That conclusion immediately becomes a journey outward as the narrative opens the southern udasi. The page therefore serves as a hinge from debate into travel, showing that compassion must move from speech into pilgrimage and instruction. The surviving text and neighboring pages make the movement clear. A world in moral decline is answered not by withdrawal, but by Guru Nanak's decision to go forth and redeem.

pages.title: Transition from the South Udasi to the East Udasi
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Udasi to the South
pages.snippet: This transition closes the southern travel materials and turns decisively toward the next itinerary. After the southern sequence concludes, the eastern udasi begins and the Guru's route opens through major places of pilgrimage and renuncian
pages.searchText: Transition from the South Udasi to the East Udasi Udasi to the South Episode About Udasi to the South This transition closes the southern travel materials and turns decisively toward the next itinerary. After the southern sequence concludes, the eastern udasi begins and the Guru's route opens through major places of pilgrimage and renunciant practice. The page uses that travel shift to sharpen a moral contrast as well, because the Guru encounters outward holiness mixed with confusion, hypocrisy, and spiritual pretension. The journey east is therefore not scenic movement alone but a new field for testing and teaching. Together with the adjacent readable pages, the passage works as a clean hinge between two udasis. It closes one circle of travel and launches the next phase of Guru Nanak's corrective wanderings.

pages.searchText: Episode About Udasi to the East Udasi to the East Episode About Udasi to the East Episode 6 Episode About Udasi to the East (The Eastern Udasi) Thereafter, Guru Nanak nursed another desire in his heart, That they should undertake another excursion to the east. He must endeavour to expose it. (1) First Satguru (Baba Nanak) had a dip in the Ganga, Then visited Rishikesh, the seat of the ancient rishis. He visited the place of Vallabh! across the river, Where all the residents were dressed like yogis?. (2) This region was a seat of eighty four Sidhas, It was known by the name of Gorakh Matta?. The Kaliyuga had spread its tentacles here widely, As the Sidhas displayed many kinds of their magical feats. (3) Here Baba Nanak recited and preached the Name of true God, And thereafter the place came to known as Nanak Matta. He visited Badri Nath*, Kedar Nath and the State of Orissa, And went further east even beyond the holy city of Jagan Nath. (4) As the artificial odour of a leather packing conceals Asafetida's real flavour, And the real flavour of Asafoetida gets obliterated by the leather stink. And they fleeced the people in the guise of saints. (5) And made them follow the path of truth and virtue. How innumerable was the number of such followers, No body can keep an exact count of them. (6) And brought back the prodigals to the path of virtue. He made them the followers of the true word of God, And established many centres of devotional congregations. (7) He organised many congregations of his followers, And induced them to meditate upon the name of God. He inculcated the virtue of feeding others before feeding themselves, And made them follow the path of compassion and righteousness. (8)

That they should proceed on a long excursion, And that he had never gone on a pilgrimage to the Kaaba. (1) Why did he not mention his desire earlier. Why did he take it so long to express that desire, As he could fulfill his desire much earlier. (2) Then Baba Nanak asked him to close his eyes, They had reached Kaaba for Haj* when he made him open his eyes. First he made Mardana to make obeisance at Kaaba, Then he took Mardana to other places of pilgrimage. (3) After that Baba Nanak laid down at the back of Kaaba, Where the enterance from the backside was locked and closed. It was locked and kept closed deliberately so that, Whenever a great Prophet approached, it would open automatically. (4) There happened such a miracle with the grace of Guru Nanak, That the gate opened automatically without a key. When this miracle came to the notice of the Shrine In-charge, He understood that a great prophet had arrived. (5) First It came to the mind of the shrine Incharge, That some great prophet must have arrived at the shrine. That was how the heavily locked door had opened. So they should go and look out for such a prophet. (6) They searched all around to find such a prophet, By making everyone touch the (earlier) locked and barred door. Even as all of them were trying together to close the opened door, The remaining doors to the shrine also got enclosed. (7) After that Guru Nanak's presence came to be realised, When all the closed doors opened on their own. At this, all the shrine-incharges felt extremely concerned, That yet another new miracle had taken place. (8)

pages.searchText: Guru Nanak at the Mecca Shrine Doors Udasi to the West At Mecca the shrine keepers first suspected that a Hindu ascetic had entered and dishonored the place, but when they dragged Guru Nanak away the doors themselves answered the insult by opening and closing in startling ways. (9–12) Punjabi haj pilgrims then identified him as Nanak Fakir, a prophet of both the Hindus and the Muslims, one who had taught haqq-nam and the discipline of truthful living to both communities alike. (13–14) Ashamed that all their effort had failed, the shrine officials resolved that if the doors opened at his touch they would accept him as a true pir and become his followers. (15–17)

Who had exhorted both the Hindus and the Muslims to pray and meditate, Who had weaned both the communities from non-belief and arrogance? (14) Did they not observe the phenomenon of doors having closed, The moment his feet were turned in another direction? There upon, all the shrine in-charges deliberated upon the whole issue, That they had used their whole strength to open the shrine doors, But having failed in all their attempts to open the gates, They had lost all their prestige and status. (16) So all the Shrine in-charges reached a unanimous resolution, That they should get the shrine doors touched by Guru Nanak. If the doors get opened with the touch of his hands, Then they should accept him as their prophet and become his followers. (17)

pages.snippet: The northern udasi carries Guru Nanak into the mountainous northern regions, lands imagined as filled with siddhas, ascetics, devas, and sacred heights where truth and falsehood had to be weighed carefully. (1–2) The poet pauses to admit that these journeys are too numerous to na
pages.searchText: Guru Nanak Challenges Empty Ritual in the North Udasi to the North The northern udasi carries Guru Nanak into the mountainous northern regions, lands imagined as filled with siddhas, ascetics, devas, and sacred heights where truth and falsehood had to be weighed carefully. (1–2) The poet pauses to admit that these journeys are too numerous to narrate in full, since many details already live in janam-sakhi traditions and a complete retelling would swell the book beyond measure. (3, 8–10) Even so, he stresses one constant: wherever Guru Nanak went in those northern regions, he challenged empty ritual and stone worship, and established the remembrance of the true Name through clear teaching. (4–7)

pages.searchText: These regions were supposed to be inhabited by, Udasi to the North Episode About Udasi to the North These regions were supposed to be inhabited by, Many Sidhas, Saints, Gods, Goddesses and chiefs of gods. (1) Guru Nanak went on a journey to these regions, To see the merits and demerits, to sift truth from falsehood. And then proceeded towards the snow-covered higher regions. (2) I restrain myself from giving all the minute details of this journey, In order to restrict the size and volume of this epic. Whosoever is interested in knowing all these details, When Guru Nanak visited these mountainous regions, He did not approve of the practices in these regions. He noticed several Maths! and monasteries of many gods and goddesses, Where the inhabitants were worshippers of phallic stone idols Shivling?. (4) Whichever region, Baba Nanak paid a visit to, He preached the true Name of God to the inhabitants. How innumerable are the episodes related to Guru Nanak (5) The number of episodes about Guru Nanak are innumerable and profound. The Sidhas, Saints and prophets have failed to keep a Count of these. That I cannot narrate all those travels and episodes. (6) Guru Nanak has traveled all the regions in the space, He has also traveled all over the various lands as well. He alone knows his powers and his worth, Or else his companions who travelled along with him know him. (7) If I narrate all the episodes about his travels, The present epic will become too large and voluminous. Had these details not been recorded in other epics (Janam Sakhees), I would have certainly laboured to write all the details. (8) Had there not been any earlier records of these events, I would have certainly taken more pains to give all the details. Whatever has not been mentioned earlier, I have endeavoured to narrate only those events. (9)

pages.searchText: From Northern Travels to Delhi Oppression Udasi to the North The poet closes the northern-travel account by saying he has only drawn forward what seemed most necessary, leaving fuller material to other tellings. (10) The narrative then turns sharply to the Delhi emperor: under the Pathan ruler, saints and pirs are humiliated, forced into grinding labor, and the age waits for Guru Nanak to overturn that oppression. (Episode 9, 1–2) Hindu and Muslim holy men alike appeal to the Guru as the one who can defend their dignity, while he answers with calm assurance that by the next day matters will turn in a better direction. (3–5)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Delhi Emperor
pages.snippet: Whatever has been narrated in great detail earlier, I have only made a mention very briefly. I have given expression to those events. (10) Episode 9 Now Follows the Episode of Delhi's Emperor Now, my dear readers, listen to the narration fu
pages.searchText: Episode About the Delhi Emperor the Delhi Emperor Episode About the Delhi Emperor Whatever has been narrated in great detail earlier, I have only made a mention very briefly. I have given expression to those events. (10) Episode 9 Now Follows the Episode of Delhi's Emperor Now, my dear readers, listen to the narration further, When Delhi was being ruled by the Pathan emperor. How he invited Guru Nanak's wrath on himself, And how his reign was replaced by the Mughal rule. (1) Brahm Khan Lodhi! was the ruler of Delhi at that time, Who fell on bad days during his reign. He ordered all the Sidhas, Saints and prophets to be arrested, And made them grind corn with the manually operated Chakkis?. (2) He declared all of them as fraudulent exploiters of the masses, Since they had failed to demonstrate any kind of miracles. Then all the Muslim and the Hindu saints agreed unanimously, That Guru Nanak alone was capable of getting them released. (3) He alone could protect their dignity and honour, He alone could preserve the sanctity of their sacred robes. As everyone is not the bravest amongst a battery of armed troops, As every animal is not as brave as a lion in the whole forest. (4) Hearing their petition, Guru Nanak remarked smilingly, That all the saints and prophets were equally empowered. That they were unnecessarily giving him that credit, And assured them that everything would turn out well the next day. (5) And made all the debris-loaded baskets rise above the heads of labouring saints. As he protected the honour of their sacred robes, His fame and reputation spread far and wide. (6) An elephant belonging to a gardener had died, Satguru Guru Nanak brought this dead elephant back to life.

pages.title: Transition from the Delhi Emperor Episode to the Episode of Emperor Karon
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Delhi Emperor
pages.snippet: The page closes the Delhi emperor material by showing that royal anger cannot finally prevail over prophetic truth. Guru Nanak warns that the Delhi sovereignty would not endure, turning the emperor's hostility into a sign of political imper
pages.searchText: Transition from the Delhi Emperor Episode to the Episode of Emperor Karon the Delhi Emperor Episode About the Delhi Emperor The page closes the Delhi emperor material by showing that royal anger cannot finally prevail over prophetic truth. Guru Nanak warns that the Delhi sovereignty would not endure, turning the emperor's hostility into a sign of political impermanence rather than lasting triumph. At the same time, the text begins opening a new discussion about the so-called episode of Emperor Karon. That shift is important because the book moves from courtly confrontation into reflection on how later writers handled older traditions and disputed dialogues. As a transition page, it therefore performs two jobs at once. It seals the Delhi warning and starts the textual argument that will dominate the next episode.

pages.searchText: Episode About the Emperor Karon the Emperor Karon Episode About the Emperor Karon Since this gardener used to provide food and shelter to the saints, He became worthy of Guru Nanak's grace for his acts of service. (7) The emperor felt extremely offended after hearing about these events, He felt that this Hindu (Guru Nanak) had displayed magical feats. He ordered/proclaimed that Guru Nanak be turned out of Delhi, And He must not be allowed to enter Delhi again. (8) Guru Nanak retorted that he would enter Delhi again and again, And predicted that another king would henceforth rule Delhi. Guru Nanak also predicted the end of Lodhi Dynasty's empire, And said that their royal writ would cease to run by 1878 (B.S.). (9) Thus Sri Guru Nanak inflicted his curse on him, And he died of gastroenterological disorder. And Delhi was occupied by the Mughal king, Who became a devout follower of Guru Nanak. (10) Episode 10 An Episode of Emperor Karoon (There was one Emperor Karoon) That all his doubts about Guru Nanak had been removed. But how did Baba Nanak hold a discussion with Emperor Karoon, He had certainly his doubts about that dialogue. (1) The Emperor Karoon's empire existed thousands of years ago, How could Baba Nanak have a dialogue with that emperor. Then I gave an explanation to David Murry, That there was an anomaly about this dialogue. (2) Baba Nanak himself never narrated this episode in his own words, But some foolish chronicler had written it as a dialogue. Later on another more irresponsible writer further expanded it, And made further interpolations into this episode. (3) They neither tallied the chronology of years between the two personages, Nor did they calculate the time lag between the two events. Since such discussions between saints were guite prevalent in those days, 53 Some odd writer had recorded it as a discussion (between Karoon and Nanak). (4)

pages.title: Transition from the Episode of Emperor Karon to the Lineage of the Sikh Gurus

pages.searchText: Transition from the Episode of Emperor Karon to the Lineage of the Sikh Gurus the Emperor Karon Episode About the Emperor Karon This page continues the criticism of corrupted storytelling by arguing that later writers had confused sakhi with gosht and mixed chronology with legend. The complaint is not minor, because it affects how readers understand what belongs to Guru Nanak, what belongs to older prophecy, and what belongs to careless retelling. After exposing that confusion, the book turns toward firmer ground by opening the lineage of the Sikh Gurus. The movement from disputed anecdote to ordered succession gives the reader a more stable framework for sacred history. In that sense the page is editorial even within the original text itself. It rejects muddle, then prepares the careful sequence of Gurus that follows.

pages.searchText: Transition from the Lineage of the Sikh Gurus to Aurangzeb’s Tyranny the Lineage of the Sikh Gurus Episode About the Lineage of the Sikh Gurus The lineage page advances through the Gurus in order and emphasizes the lamp-to-lamp succession of the Gurus as the proper image for transmission. Each Guru lights the next without rupture, so continuity rather than competition defines the line from Nanak to Gobind Singh. From that ordered lineage, the narrative pivots toward the age of Mughal oppression and the questions raised by David Murry about conflict with the empire. The shift matters because the serene continuity of succession now meets the violence of Aurangzeb's reign. This page therefore bridges doctrinal order and political crisis. It closes the succession list and opens the conditions under which martyrdom and resistance will have to be explained.

pages.snippet: The opening of this episode contrasts imperial ambition with moral refuge. Aurangzeb hardens his rule into forced Islamization, while Guru Tegh Bahadur emerges as the defender to whom the distressed and threatened turn for protection. The page gathers the pressure of the age by d
pages.searchText: Guru Tegh Bahadur Becomes a Refuge Aurangzeb's Tyranny The opening of this episode contrasts imperial ambition with moral refuge. Aurangzeb hardens his rule into forced Islamization, while Guru Tegh Bahadur emerges as the defender to whom the distressed and threatened turn for protection. The page gathers the pressure of the age by describing how coercion expands and how Hindu communities feel the tightening force of Mughal authority. In that atmosphere, Guru Tegh Bahadur's presence becomes not merely respected but necessary. Read with the following page, this passage is the doorway into a larger martyrdom narrative. It establishes Aurangzeb's tyranny as the condition that will make spiritual courage, consultation, and sacrifice central to what follows.

(18) The Brahmins from all the nooks and comers of the country, From Kashi (Benaras), Gangetic plains, Kurukshetra and other places. pages.searchText: Guru Gobind Singh’s Sacrifice for the Panth the Tenth Sikh Guru The argument turns to the tenth Guru: as Mughal clerics and rulers forgot older bonds and set themselves against the Gurus, Guru Gobind Singh answered in anger and founded the Panth to confront tyranny directly. (2–3) The passage frames the Guru’s loss of his four sons not as defeat but as a deliberate offering made for the life of the Panth, and asks why lineage was not preserved alongside mission. (3–4) In reply, the poet compares Guru Gobind Singh with earlier founders and prophets, insisting that for the sake of the Panth he accepted blame, sacrifice, and conflict so that Sikhs might be preserved and the wicked destroyed. (5–9)

pages.title: Denying that the Hindus (Guru Nanak! ) had bestowed the sovereignty on Mughals,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Tenth Sikh Guru
pages.snippet: Denying that the Hindus (Guru Nanak! ) had bestowed the sovereignty on Mughals, They claimed that their prophet Mohammad had bestowed sovereignty on them. (2) Guru Gobind Singh felt outraged (at this travesty of truth), And he created the K
pages.searchText: Denying that the Hindus (Guru Nanak! ) had bestowed the sovereignty on Mughals, the Tenth Sikh Guru Episode About the Tenth Sikh Guru Denying that the Hindus (Guru Nanak! ) had bestowed the sovereignty on Mughals, They claimed that their prophet Mohammad had bestowed sovereignty on them. (2) Guru Gobind Singh felt outraged (at this travesty of truth), And he created the Khalsa Panth? to destroy the Mughals. He sacrificed his four sons for this cherished cause, As he lost his own progeny for nurturing the Khalsa Panth. (3) Then David Murry asked me to resolve this paradox, Why did the Guru not preserve both his progeny as well as his ideology. All the ancient Sidhas and saints like Datta Tray? and Gorakhnath, Also had not raised any family to promote their ideological orders. The Muslim's prophet Mohammad? had also sacrificed his progeny, Sparing only the best among his progeny to promote his cause. (5) When Guru Gobind Singh had adopted the same strategy for the same purpose. To this query of Captain Murry, I offered the following explanation: The Muslims were cursed because of the cold-blooded murder of Sahibzadas°. (6) Guru Gobind wished to destroy the Mughals for this grave injustice, And the blame went to the Mughals mainly for shedding the blood of innocents. He created the order of the Khalsa Panth with the sole motive, Of strengthening the Sikhs and for destroying the wicked Mughals. (7) He also attributed the blame for his own sacrifice to the Mughals, And wished to promote his own ideological order, the Khalsa Panth. It is not possible to promote One's family and one's ideology simultaneously, As even Lord Rama and Lord Krishna® could not promote the two together. (8) Both Rama and Krishna kept their own nearest kins deprived of power, They handed over power to others to uphold that tradition. Satguru Gobind Singh handed over power to his followers, the Sikhs, For further strengthening the same old great tradition. (9) One can not preserve and promote one's own ideology. Much as an agricultural piece of land over grown with weeds, Cannot give a wholesome yield of grains. (10)

pages.title: The Khalsa Appears Openly
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Tenth Sikh Guru
pages.snippet: Continuing the explanation, the poet says the Khalsa Panth was never hidden after its creation; it was formed openly by the Satguru and could not remain concealed once it had taken its own shape. (1, 6) The Mughal empire may have seemed vast, yet its commanders, populations, and
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Appears Openly the Tenth Sikh Guru Continuing the explanation, the poet says the Khalsa Panth was never hidden after its creation; it was formed openly by the Satguru and could not remain concealed once it had taken its own shape. (1, 6) The Mughal empire may have seemed vast, yet its commanders, populations, and informants failed to grasp in time how widely the Sikhs had spread, whether through ignorance, misreading, or political blindness. (2–5) The answer given is that the Khalsa was born for visible struggle: Singhs were armed from the beginning, marked by khande-di-pahul, steel, and martial bearing, and therefore the Panth announced itself publicly rather than surviving as a hidden sect. (7–8)

pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode
pages.snippet: Episode 14 The Khalsa Must Be Autonomous And Self-Respecting That I must narrate the account of the Sikhs in minute detail. How did the Tenth Guru create the order of the Khalsa Panth? What kind of strategies did he employ to promote this o
pages.searchText: Another Episode Additional episode: Another Episode Episode 14 The Khalsa Must Be Autonomous And Self-Respecting That I must narrate the account of the Sikhs in minute detail. How did the Tenth Guru create the order of the Khalsa Panth? What kind of strategies did he employ to promote this order? (1) The Mughal empire was very vast and mighty, With their writ running all over the twenty two provinces. It stretched upto various islands in the midst of ocean, Over the mountaneous regions both in the East and the South. (2) When the whole populace of India constituted their subjects, How did the Sikhs manage to expand their influence? How did the subjects of this region (Punjab) put up a defiance to their rule? Where had the Mughal's Army disappeared to allow this defiance? (3) Were the Mughals not well informed about the Sikhs? Were they ignorant about the hostility between them and the Sikh Gurus? Had they reached some kind of settlement with the Sikhs? Had they accepted the Sikhs as the third religion!? (4) Wasn't there any politically shrewd person among the Mughals, Who could pinpoint the rising power of the Sikhs? Did the Khalsa Panth not stake their claim to sovereignty? Did the Khalsa Panth remain unnoticed by the Mughals? (5) The way I answered these guestions put forth by Captain Murry, My Gursikh readers must listen to the same account. The Khalsa Panth was as sharp and marked since its inception, As tender thorns are sharp and pointed from their budding stage. (6) How could the Khalsa Singhs? remain existent in isolation and secrecy? How could the Khalsa Panth remain hidden from the public gaze? The Singhs organisation was created to wage a war, As the Khalsa Panth was anointed with the touch of weapons. (7) The Khalsa Panth was initiated (Baptised)? with the ceremonial sword as, 75 The Khalsa Panth was administered the first draught of the sword immersed in elixir. With steel rings and sword on their headgear and slung across the shoulders, How could they remain unnoticed like the sharp-nailed lions in a jungle? (8)

pages.title: Another Episode
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode
pages.snippet: Guru Gobind Singh is presented as concluding that the Panth had to be fashioned for open struggle, because sovereignty would never come without war and the sacrifice of Guru Tegh Bahadur had already made peace with Mughal domination impossi
pages.searchText: Another Episode Additional episode: Another Episode Guru Gobind Singh is presented as concluding that the Panth had to be fashioned for open struggle, because sovereignty would never come without war and the sacrifice of Guru Tegh Bahadur had already made peace with Mughal domination impossible. (9–11) The empire is described as an old tree whose roots were already rotten; now, the Guru thought, the time had come to strike with the sword and bring its fall to completion. (12–13) Yet he did not desire kingship for himself. Instead he began to think about lifting up others, raising the lowly, and creating a new martial order answerable to the house of Nanak rather than to worldly rulers. (14–16)

pages.title: The perfect Guru the Tenth created the Khalsa Panth in this manner,
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode
pages.snippet: The perfect Guru the Tenth created the Khalsa Panth in this manner, So that they must wage a war against oppression. The Tenth Guru had decided this strategy from the very beginning. (9) There had developed a great hostility and conflict, B
pages.searchText: The perfect Guru the Tenth created the Khalsa Panth in this manner, Additional episode: Another Episode The perfect Guru the Tenth created the Khalsa Panth in this manner, So that they must wage a war against oppression. The Tenth Guru had decided this strategy from the very beginning. (9) There had developed a great hostility and conflict, Between the Sikh Gurus and the Mughal emperor. Since Guru Tegh Bahadur had sacrificed his life for this reason, How could the Sikhs let the Mughals get away with it? (10) Guru Tegh Bahadur, by making the Supreme sacrifice at Delhi, Had uprooted the Mughal Emperor's roots from Delhi. Guru Gobind Singh had made a proper assessment that, The roots (foundations) of the Mughal empire's had completely withered. (11) Or else a mighty storm could bring it tumbling down. Now the Mughal empire needed to be stormed with an armed attack, This was the only way to bring this crumbling empire down. (12) So Satguru Guru Gobind Singh himself decided to pick up the sword, And bring about the destruction of the Mughal empire. But then Guru Gobind Singh felt in his heart of hearts, That he himself had no need for a worthless royal power. (13) Sri Guru Nanak had blessed him with such a great divine seat, That all of Temporal royal power was subservient to it. Since he did not care for such an inferior temporal power, He must pass on this kind of political power to his subordinates. (14) Thereafter it occured to Satguru Guru Gobind Singh's mind, That the reign of Mughal rulers must be replaced. For this purpose, all the chiefs of the hill states, Must be made to pick up the sword against the Mughals. (15) But then on a second thought, Guru Gobind Singh thought, That these hill chiefs had never been his followers. Why should he embrace these outsiders at the cost of his own followers? (16) They are as indifferent as the stone idols that they worship, And they had always been ungrateful to the House of Nanak. As they called themselves soldiers and as belonging to martial races,

pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode
pages.snippet: The Guru’s reasoning turns explicitly toward the poor and marginalized communities: power should not be handed to those already enthroned, but to the neglected people whom the house of Nanak had always sheltered. (18–19) The passage lists p
pages.searchText: Another Episode Additional episode: Another Episode The Guru’s reasoning turns explicitly toward the poor and marginalized communities: power should not be handed to those already enthroned, but to the neglected people whom the house of Nanak had always sheltered. (18–19) The passage lists peasants, artisans, laborers, service castes, traders, and other socially disregarded groups as the ones who would receive dignity, brotherhood, and a claim to sovereignty through the Guru’s favor. (20–22) When Guru Gobind Singh calls such followers to take up arms against the Mughals, many shrink back in fear before imperial power, still imagining themselves as sparrows and lambs before hawks and lions. (23–25)

pages.title: They would never acknowledge that the Guru had conferred power on them.
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode
pages.snippet: They would never acknowledge that the Guru had conferred power on them. He would confer power and sovereignty on the poor people, The needy alone deserve to be endowed with rare gifts, What is the use of empowering those who are already pow
pages.searchText: They would never acknowledge that the Guru had conferred power on them. Additional episode: Another Episode They would never acknowledge that the Guru had conferred power on them. He would confer power and sovereignty on the poor people, The needy alone deserve to be endowed with rare gifts, What is the use of empowering those who are already powerful. The House of Nanak is known for its compassion and generosity, And known as the saviour and protector of the poor. (19) Those who belong to the various offshoots of lowly twelve sub-castes, And who know nothing about the game of power politics. Who are contemptuously known as rustic peasants, in the society, OR known as traders, small time shopkeepers and petty fighters. (20) Those who belong to the low castes of blacksmiths and carpenters, And the lowly placed tailors and wine-venders would receive his benediction. And the ignoble vegetable growers (kambojs) and scheduled castes. (21) Sainis, goldsmiths, sweepers and cobblers will form a part of this brotherhood. Ballad-singers, priests, and mendicants will also be the alliance partners, I shall confer sovereignty on these poor and needy gursikhs, So that they may remember my patronage and benediction. Saying this Guru Gobind Singh challenged his followers, That they should pick up swords and attack the Mughals. (23) The Sikhs did not agree to Guru Gobind Singh's proposal, Since they were highly scared of the Mughal empire's power. The Mughals had a large and powerful army, So the Sikhs did not accept Guru Gobind Singh's advice, As they felt that they would not be able to defeat the Mughals. The Sikhs were just timid sparrows as compared to the Hawk like Mughals, Or The Sikhs were just lambs against the lion like Mughals. (25) How could the Guru expect deer-like Sikhs to vanquish the lion-like Mughal forces? How could a downward flowing rivulet flow back towards the high-sloped mountains? Their forces consisted of veteran soldiers and warrior Pathans. While the Sikhs Constituted poor unskilled rustics, barbers and carpenters. (26)

pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode
pages.snippet: The Sikhs protest that the Guru has chosen humble, unarmed people rather than royal warriors, but Guru Gobind Singh recognizes in that very hesitation the old psychology he now has to transform. (27–29) He resolves to change both inner disp
pages.searchText: Another Episode Additional episode: Another Episode The Sikhs protest that the Guru has chosen humble, unarmed people rather than royal warriors, but Guru Gobind Singh recognizes in that very hesitation the old psychology he now has to transform. (27–29) He resolves to change both inner disposition and outer form: the old soft habits must give way to a martial bearing, new names, and khande-di-pahul so that the community can learn courage, sovereignty, and visible resolve. (30–34) The goal is not merely military efficiency but a self-respecting Khalsa that bows to no earthly throne, carrying divine autonomy in its very appearance and conduct. (35)

pages.title: They told the Guru that he had selected all the low-caste people,
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode
pages.snippet: They told the Guru that he had selected all the low-caste people, Who were completely defenceless and unarmed. He should throw this challenge before the martial royal chiefs, As they were the right persons who could serve his purpose. (27)
pages.searchText: They told the Guru that he had selected all the low-caste people, Additional episode: Another Episode They told the Guru that he had selected all the low-caste people, Who were completely defenceless and unarmed. He should throw this challenge before the martial royal chiefs, As they were the right persons who could serve his purpose. (27) Then Sri Guru Gobind Singh felt anguished and thought, That his followers did not wish to achieve anything in life. He had wished to confer power and sovereignty on them, But they were repeatedly refusing to accept this honour. (28) Sri Guru Gobind Singh, being an expert omniscient psychoanalyst, Had diagnosed the root cause of his Sikh's psychic malady. Since these Sikhs had been peaceful followers of a Charan Pahul* tradition, There was no spark of self-assertion and retaliation in their psyche. (29) They had been used to wearing a black woolen silken cap as head cover, As they had been indoctrinated to call themselves as servants or slaves, They being grounded in excessive compassion and humility, It would be futile to ask them to pick up swords. (30) He should first bring about a transformation in their character, And make their appearance formidable that evokes fear and awe. He should give his organisation a charismatic nomenclature, And administer a heavy dose of heady elixir to them. (31) So Satguru Sri Guru Gobind Singh arrived at a firm resolution, And made efforts to implement it after deep contemplation. They must adopt the dress code of a martial warrior race, And grow hair and wear turbans on their heads. (32) The warrior Kshtriyas had been suffixing the epithet Singhs The same suffix Singh would suit his followers names as well. He resolved to administer them the Khandey-ki-Pahul?, In order to make the Khalsa formidable and resolute. (33) In this way, they would learn the art of wielding power, And develop a feeling of having become rulers and sovereigns. From people weak as straw and reeds, he would turn them into men of steel, After partaking of sword-initiated elixir, they would not be scared to pick up swords. (34) The Khalsa must be as autonomous and self-respecting, As embodiment of all the Divine attributes in plenty. Never submitting to the sovereignty of anyone else, Except the sovereignty and autonomy of God alone. (35)

pages.searchText: Another Episode Additional episode: Another Episode The argument culminates in the rejection of older markers, shrine cults, and submissive habits, and then turns into a new sakhi of origin at Kesgarh about the birth of the Khalsa Panth. (36; Episode 15, 1) At Kesgarh Sahib the Guru consults learned men, fixes the undertaking, and selects five youths drawn across caste lines, making visible a new brotherhood rather than a continuation of older hierarchy. (2–5) These first Panj Pyare are gathered for the preparation of amrit, with water, sweetness, and the double-edged sword brought together under the Guru’s direction to begin the new initiation. (5–6)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth
pages.snippet: Hence forth, the Khalsa would not worship any spirits and graves of Pirs, Nor would they be worshippers of Gugapir Sultan*, Episode 15 Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth (The First Five Beloved Initiated Sikhs) After thoroughly del
pages.searchText: Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth Creation of the Khalsa Panth Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth Hence forth, the Khalsa would not worship any spirits and graves of Pirs, Nor would they be worshippers of Gugapir Sultan*, Episode 15 Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth (The First Five Beloved Initiated Sikhs) After thoroughly deliberating over the whole situation, Guru Gobind Singh arrived at a firm resolution. He started making endeavours to implement his resolution. (1) He summoned the services of learned Brahmins and great astrologers, To make a prediction about the auspicious moment for launching his mission. He made a selection of five sprightly youths, One each out of the five Indian castes. (2) By selecting these five youths from the five different castes, Guru Gobind Singh created a common brotherhood of all the four main castes. S. Daya Singh Sobti was the first to be selected from the Kshtriya caste, Who was a prominent inhabitant of the city of Lahore. (3) Dharam Singh from Hastinapur? was the second to be chosen, Who happened to be a Jat* with flowing Shiva like locks of hair. Mohkam Singh was the third, born and bred at Dwarka, Sahib Singh, a barbar by caste, was the fourth from a place, Which was also the abode of Bhagat/Saint Sain. Himmat Singh, the water-carrier, was the fifth chosen, Thus, the five youths from the five castes were identified. (5) Thereafter, Guru Gobind Singh got the Khandey ki Pahul® prepared, By mixing sweet-candies in a bowl of water. He stirred the sweetened solution with a double-edged sword, Satguru Guru Gobind Singh kept on chanting the true name of God, And kept on reciting the name of God, The Creator.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth
pages.snippet: Guru Gobind Singh prepares the amrit while uttering the divine Names, reciting martial bani, and binding the new ceremony to both remembrance of Akal Purakh and the line of the ten Gurus. (7–10) The initiation is then given to the first five, the Panj Pyare, through one bowl and
pages.searchText: Amrit and the Panj Pyare Creation of the Khalsa Panth Guru Gobind Singh prepares the amrit while uttering the divine Names, reciting martial bani, and binding the new ceremony to both remembrance of Akal Purakh and the line of the ten Gurus. (7–10) The initiation is then given to the first five, the Panj Pyare, through one bowl and one discipline, making the new order an embodied brotherhood rather than a symbolic gesture. (11–12) The page presents the amrit ceremony as both liturgical and martial: prayer, steel, shared draught, and collective rebirth are fused into a single founding act. (overall)

pages.title: He continued meditating on the timeless eternal God,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth
pages.snippet: He continued meditating on the timeless eternal God, In order to invoke His grace for the success of his mission. (7) First, Guru Gobind Singh recited the ballad consecrated to Bhagwati? (the primal force), He himself had composed this ball
pages.searchText: He continued meditating on the timeless eternal God, Creation of the Khalsa Panth Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth He continued meditating on the timeless eternal God, In order to invoke His grace for the success of his mission. (7) First, Guru Gobind Singh recited the ballad consecrated to Bhagwati? (the primal force), He himself had composed this ballad for the first time. And beseeched them to bestow their blessings on the Tenth Guru. (8) Which also came out from his own sacred lips. This war ballad Chandi-di-War!2 was a very inspiring composition, The recitation of which was also made mandatory during initiation ceremony. (9) O/ the primal force/Bhagwati/the Sword Which is capable of making a mince-meat of the wicked; Which is capable of decimating the forces of ignorance; Which is capable of waging a mighty war in the field; Which bestows its blessings on the mighty warriors. Which protects the mighty arms from being broken; Which ignites and illuminates the whole environment; Which emanates an ever-steady and undiminished brilliance, Which shines and illuminates as brightly as the sun. Which brings about peace and comfort for the saints; Which annihilates all kinds of evil and the wicked; Which eliminates all kinds of sins and strife; I have sought the protection and blessings of that Divine Power. Praise be to that creative Force of the Universe; Which sustains and preserves the whole creation; Which shields and protects me as well; Praise be to that sword, the emblem/incarnation of Bhagwati. Filling his cupped hands with the prepared Amrit Pahul (elixir) Satguru exhorted the five chosen ones to present themselves. Instructing them to face him with their eyes open wide, He sprinkled the cupped elixir into their eyes. (10) He made them recite and repeat the name of the timeless/eternal, And bade them shout the slogan, Victory be to God. As well as made each one of them drink five draughts of this elixir. (11) In order to eliminate all distinctions of caste and race.

pages.title: The Khalsa Receives Its Discipline
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth
pages.snippet: The newly initiated Khalsa is instructed to erase divisions of caste and old religious rank, to live under one visible code, and to leave behind alliances with sectarian intermediaries and rival claimants. (12–15) The discipline expands into daily conduct: kachh, turban, bani, re
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Receives Its Discipline Creation of the Khalsa Panth The newly initiated Khalsa is instructed to erase divisions of caste and old religious rank, to live under one visible code, and to leave behind alliances with sectarian intermediaries and rival claimants. (12–15) The discipline expands into daily conduct: kachh, turban, bani, repeated remembrance, and readiness in arms become part of the same shared bowl and one discipline. (14–17) Food, hunting, bodily conduct, and attachment to older rites are all reworked so that the first initiates receive a distinct collective rule from the Guru himself. (18–20)

pages.title: He instructed them to discard the four distinctions of caste,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth
pages.snippet: He instructed them to discard the four distinctions of caste, As well as their symbolic emblems such as the thread! and saffron mark. (12) Thereafter, Satguru bade them to obey the following injunctions: They would neither have any dealings
pages.searchText: He instructed them to discard the four distinctions of caste, Creation of the Khalsa Panth Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth He instructed them to discard the four distinctions of caste, As well as their symbolic emblems such as the thread! and saffron mark. (12) Thereafter, Satguru bade them to obey the following injunctions: They would neither have any dealings with the Masands!?, Nor with those indulging in female foeticide or smoking or being the followers of Ram Rai5, For whosoever dealt with them was bound to come to grief. (13) They must also contribute to Guru's House as per their financial capacity, As well as offer sacred karah Parshad! to the Khalsa fraternity. They must wear the Sikh undergarment!* and a turban on their heads, And follow the teachings of Sri Guru Granth Sahib. (14) Satguru, after delivering these instructions to the chosen five, Made them sling a sword from their shoulders. In the midst of chanting the name of eternal God. (15) Guru Gobind Singh further instructed them to read Gurbani, And meditate on God's name both in the morning and evening. As well as recite the text of Chandi-di-Var*!. (16) They must wear a turban twice a day on their heads, As well as wear the ordained arms round the clock. They should go on hunting expeditions after partaking Amrit, So that they might become well-versed in handling of arms. (17) They should eat mutton only after slaughtering the animal with one stroke, And desist from eating the meat of dead animals, They must clean and nourish the hair on their heads and their beards, And desist from shaving their hair with a blade. (18) They must discard the rituals associated with their dead ancestors, And concentrate and meditate on Guru-ordained teachings. They must remain vigilant against those going astray from the prescribed regimen, And award them suitable punishment for their acts of misdemeaneur. (19) He begged to be initiated himself in the same manner, From those five chosen ones whom he himself had initiated. (20)

pages.title: Guru and Khalsa Share Authority
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Creation the Khalsa Panth
pages.snippet: The Guru and the initiated five mirror one another in a new exchange of authority, and the poet compares this mutuality to the succession from Guru Nanak to Guru Angad. (21–22) With the amrit received, the Khalsa is said to arise as a formidable order, and from that day the Khals
pages.searchText: Guru and Khalsa Share Authority Creation of the Khalsa Panth The Guru and the initiated five mirror one another in a new exchange of authority, and the poet compares this mutuality to the succession from Guru Nanak to Guru Angad. (21–22) With the amrit received, the Khalsa is said to arise as a formidable order, and from that day the Khalsa spread quickly through expanding circles of Singhs and local centers. (22; episode 16, 1–3) Authority is distributed outward: wherever the Panj gather, khande-di-pahul may be given, ardas may be made, and the Khalsa acts with delegated responsibility rather than waiting on a distant center. (4–5)

pages.title: Episode About the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth
pages.snippet: After being initiated by the five initiated ones in the same manner, He came to be known as Teacher-disciple rolled into one. This has been the tradition from the very beginning, As Guru Nanak had also accepted Guru Angad as his Guru. (21)
pages.searchText: Episode About the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth Episode About the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth After being initiated by the five initiated ones in the same manner, He came to be known as Teacher-disciple rolled into one. This has been the tradition from the very beginning, As Guru Nanak had also accepted Guru Angad as his Guru. (21) After taking of Pahul-Amrit as per Guru's instructions, The Khalsa Panth flourished and went from strength to strength. It was in the year of seventeen hundred and fifty two, That the Khalsa Panth was founded on Wednesday in the month of Vaisakh. Episode 16 The Episode of Khalsa Panth's Expansion (This is How the Khalsa Originated) (Just after the Vaisakhi Day of 1699), the day of Khalsa's initiation, The Khalsa Panth started increasing and expanding. From the initial five, people in the bands of fifties and hundreds, Kept on joining its ranks after gueueing up for initiation. (1) Guru Gobind Singh decentralised and delegated his powers to the Khalsa, And put them on positions of responsibility in every sphere of activity. He sent his appointed emissaries to the South, the East and the North, As well as his representatives to the West and the mid-west. (2) Small bands of initiated Sikhs were sent to Amritsar and Patna, As well as several other places of Guru's influence. These young Singhs were sent with full powers to initiate others, After assuring them of his full backing and guidance. (3) He gave permission to his appointed Sikhs at various places, That they themselves should conduct the initiation ceremony. Wherever there was an assembly of five initiated Singhs, They would assume an equivalent status of Guru's congregation. (4) They were, undoubtedly, empowered to administer Amrit to others. These five initiated Singhs were to be asked to perform the lead prayer, Where all the congregated Sikhs would receive Guru's blessings. (5) They would be entitled to utilise the offerings made at a gurdwara, And remit the balance of offerings if any to the Guru.

pages.searchText: Letters Summon the Sangat to Pahul the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth The Guru sent letters to the sangat, asking them to come and receive the khande-di-pahul. (6) Whoever drank the pahul was to become filled with new radiance and turn fearlessly against tyranny. (7) Those who accepted the Guru’s command in Majha were blessed, and the Khalsa Panth emerged while the Satguru looked upon it with deep joy. (8–9)

pages.searchText: The Guru also wrote letters of instructions to other congregations as well, the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth Episode About the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth The Guru also wrote letters of instructions to other congregations as well, Asking his followers to come to him and get initiated. (6) In order to give a crushing defeat to the ruling Mughals. He had invested the Amrit with such mircalous powers, That it would uproot the Mughals and entrench the Khalsa Panth permanently. (7) Whatever instructions were issued by the Tenth Guru, These were accepted and followed by Majhail Singhs. This is how the Khalsa Panth came into existence, At whose origin the Guru felt extremely delighted. The Guru now ventured to eguip the Khalsa with arms, And prescribed various kinds of uniforms for them. (9) The tenth Guru started sitting on a raised dais in the centre, With armed Singh? guards all around his seated position. As Lord Krishna used to be surrounded by his consorts, So Guru Gobind Singh started sitting majestically among his bodyguards. (10) He would order his Singhs to exercise and run races, And inspect them from all sides in a standing position. While asking still others to get up and run a race. (11) And engage themselves in fighting mock duals of two each. Sometimes, the Guru would stand in the midst of a ploughed up field, And ask his Singhs to hit each other with pieces of solid earth. (12) Sometimes, the Singhs would play a game of Sonchi?, OR engage themselves in boxing and wrestling bouts. Guru Gobind Singh felt so much delighted at these adventurous bouts, That he wished to confer landed property awards on his brave Singhs. (13) The Guru asked his Singhs to ask for any kinds of territorial awards, Whatever kinds of material assets they aspired to possess, He would ensure to make those assets available to them. (14)

pages.searchText: Singhs Debate Dominion in Punjab the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth Some Singhs wished to rule in Punjab itself, while the Guru told them to ask for vast dominion — to the south, the hills, the east, and the west. (15) But the Singhs replied that if each asked for Punjab separately they would only end up quarrelling among themselves. (16) The Guru then urged them to seek broad jagirs and authority, while they answered that each desired only the country nearest his own home. (17–18)

pages.searchText: However, Singhs limited imagination could not grasp the extent of Guru's assurances, the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth Episode About the Expansion of the Khalsa Panth However, Singhs limited imagination could not grasp the extent of Guru's assurances, The Guru asked them to aspire for territorial rights over the superior Southern region, As well as the mountainous regions of the East and the West. (15) Instead of living and ruling over their homeland of Punjab. They asked repeatedly for their sovereignty over Punjab alone, While the Guru exhorted them to aspire for a very large territory, And exhorted them to occupy as much territory as they wished, But the nit-witted Singhs preferred to remain confined amongst their own kin, And aspired to settle scores with their own fraternal adversaries. (17) They preferred to settle in the vicinity of their own home, And wished to occupy the home land territory alone. These Singhs being the offsprings of the poor impoverished parents, How could they envision on a large vision and imagination. (18) The Singhs, demanded to get settled in the vicinity of Punjab. Although the Guru, wished to grant them sovereignty over distant lands, They lacked the imagination to aspire for a greater sovereignty. (19) Chaupai: Finally, the Guru told them in clear unmistakable terms, That they would remain confined to Punjab in fratricidal brawls. But the Singhs who had joined the ranks a little later, They were directed to settle in other distant lands. (20) Dohra: Whole of this account has been recorded in the epic Gur Bilas, Which I have summerised for the sake of economy. Whatever has been recorded by author Sukha Singh, I have endeavoured to give expression to those facts. (21) Chaupai: Whosoever wishes to read about this topic in more detail, He should search for those details in the epic Gur Bilas. How the chiefs of hill Principalities fought against the Guru, And earned a bad name for themselves by their misdeeds. (22) The author of Gur Bilas has mentioned all these in his epic, I have narrated what has been omitted there by its author. This history is both very lengthy and unlimited,
