Sham Singh had the distinction of collecting a ransom of seven lakh rupees from the powerful jat ruler of Bharatpur just for honouring the jat ruler with an embrace symbolic of jat's allegiance with the Khalsa Panth. He distributed this amount among the ten Sikh Misls in proportion to their respective strength. In fact, S. Sham Singh and Nawab Kapoor Singh formed the twin pillars of Khalsa Panth under whose joint command the ten Sikh Misls functioned and carried on the struggle for achieving complete Sikh sovereignty. Rattan Singh Bhangoo brings out the glorious achievements of these ten Sikh Misls through the epic simile of Lord Krishna and his ten Yadava contingents over the evil Jamankal from the Hindu mythology. Dohra: As there were ten Misls of the Yadav clan, So there were ten Misls in the Khalsa Panth. As Lord Krishna commanded the ten Yadav Misls, The tenth Sikh Guru directed the Khalsa Misls. (20) Chaupai: As the Yadavs escaped Kaljaman's onslaught, The number of times Jamankal invaded the Yadavs, The same number of times Abdali invaded the Singhs. (21) As Lord Krishna got Kaljaman destroyed by the Yadavs, So did the tenth Guru get Abdali decimated by the Khalsa. As all the Muslim rulers were annihilated by the Khalsa, The Khalsa Panth shouted slogans of Guru's victory. (22) The portrait gallery of eighteenth century Sikh martyrs and warriors will not be complete without mentioning the glorious contribution of S. Baghel Singh and S.Charat Singh. S. Baghel Singh, commanding the Kroressinghia Misl, not only burnt alive the wicked Sayyad abductor and hanged his Ahluwalia procurer of Luhari Jalalabad both of whom had kidnapped the daughter of a helpless Brahmin from the distant trans- Yamuna region but also rehabilitated her in the house of her would-be inlaws by solemnising her marriage as a daughter of the Khalsa Panth, giving a handsome amount in dowry as well. He extended not only the frontiers of territorial occupation of the Khalsa Panth in the East but also occupied Delhi for ever a year in 1783. He not only demarcated and constructed the seven sacred shrines associated with the Sikh Gurus in Delhi, but also levied and collected 38% share out of every rupee (Six annas out of a rupee) that came to the Delhi state treasury as octroi for the construction and renovation of dilapidated Sikh shrines. His brave exterior and charismatic personality created a terror among the Muslims. He went to see the Delhi's emperor Shah Alam II at the latter's invitation without bowing his head before the emperor as was the custom. S. Charat Singh has been portrayed as the bravest among the brave in this epic. If Baba Banda Singh Bahadur is the hero of the first part of this epic, S. He is portrayed as an epitome of Khalsa grit and dare devilry. S. Charat Singh's mettle as a Sikh warrior with a superhuman skill and bravery comes to the fore during the most fierce battle between Khalsa forces and those of Ahmad Shah Abdali that took place around the villages of Kup and Poheer near Malerkotla. This battle is also known as the greatest massacre or Wada Ghallughara in Sikh history. S. Charat Singh is the hero of this unequal battle between the Sikhs and the Mughals. He proves to be the saviour of many a Sikh lives in this battle. His heroic deeds of offence and defence are the ultimate in Sikh war history. Rattan Singh Bhangoo has delineated his warrior profile in the most sublime Chaupai: Uncountable was the number of wounds which S. Charat Singh received, Innumerable were the arrows, lances and swords which hit his body. His every blow resulted in wounding his adversary in fight. (148) Dohra: From the concluding day of this massacre of the Sikhs, Many a life of Sikhs in the caravan had he saved, Putting his own life at a great risk determinedly. (149) Chaupai: Praise be to S. Charat Singh said each member of the caravan, Undoubtedly would he be a chief among the Singhs. May he become a chief among the Khalsa Panth, Unitedly did they shower their blessings on this great Singh. (151) From Delhi to the South to the mountains in the East, Definitely would his writ run in all directions. Thus did the whole caravan pray for S. Charat Singh, That the entire Khalsa Panth might accept his leadership. (153) S. Bota Singh calls the bluff of Mughal Nawab of Lahore of having exterminated every Sikh in the State, by putting up a toll tax barrier on the highway to Lahore in a broad day light

pages.searchText: and sacrifices his life fighting against the battery of Mughal soldiers who had come to arrest and sacrifices his life fighting against the battery of Mughal soldiers who had come to arrest him. S. Hatthoo Singh Majhail, after his arrest by the Mughal authorities, achieves martyrdom when his body is torn into two parts by tying his two legs to two elephants pulling in opposite Singh of village Dalwan achieves martyrdom while fighting against the mighty Moman Khan and his most muscular Mughal warriors like Taki Khan, Mansa Ram and Daya Ram. He is one of those Sikh warriors who upheld the principle of Sikh honour and dignity at the cost of their Thus, S. Tara Singh accomplishing a legendary deed, Became famous (as a martyr) in the whole world. Following the great Guru's words in letter and spirit, He sacrificed his life rather than compromising his dignity. (50)*° and recording the glorious deeds of sacrifice and martyrdom of prominent Sikh warriors, is also an authentic social chronicle of some of the major upheavals, cultural and cross-cultural currents in the contemporary Sikh and Indian society. Prominent among these movements are the two massacres of the Sikhs-one in the swamps of Kahnuwan, District Gurdaspur and the second near the villages Kup and Poheer on the Ludhiana Malerkotla highway. Nearly one lakh militant Sikhs and their families perished in these two massacres. These are known as Chhota Ghallughara and Wada Ghallughara respectively. The first massacre was the result of an encounter between the Khalsa force and the Mughal forces together with the forces of Dewan Jaspat Rai was killed by the Singhs in an earlier encounter near Eminabad. The second massacre of the Sikhs on a much larger scale occurred during the Khalsa carvan's escape towards the Malwa region after the devastation of Majha including the nearly complete destruction of Harmandir Sahib by Abdali's forces. As the retreating Khalsa had ransacked Sirhind, its governor Jain Khan and Pathan rulers of Malerkotla conspired to block the Khalsa passage as Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces were invited to attack the Khalsa force from the rear. In the battle that ensued, the Khalsa force, being outnumbered and encircled from all sides, fought bravely but the Sikh casualties ran into several thousands. This was the worst massacre of the Sikhs in their entire history. As Rattan Singh Bhangoo's father and uncle had both participated in this fierce battle, his account of this massacre seems to be quite reliable. While many others died or got scattered from the caravan. The eye-witnesses reckoned that there were one lakh Singhs, Fifty thousand of whom survived, the rest having perished in this massacre. (143) My father (S. Rai Singh) put the figure at thirty thousand Singhs, Who perished in this crusade, the rest having returned safe.

pages.snippet: As both my (author's) father and uncle were part of this crusade, I have narrated this episode after listening this account from them. (144)*! Among the other episodes about Khalsa encounters and achievements are those of the slaughter of J
pages.searchText: As both my (author's) father and uncle were part of this crusade, As both my (author's) father and uncle were part of this crusade, I have narrated this episode after listening this account from them. (144)*! Among the other episodes about Khalsa encounters and achievements are those of the slaughter of Jain Khan, Nawab of Sirhind and destruction of Sirhind for the second time; massacre at Morinda and slaughter of Muslim converts families who were instrumental in arresting of younger Sahibzadas and handing them over to the Nawab of Sirhind, the sacrifices of Sikh martyrs belonging to Randhawa clan of villages Chamunday and Kairon Nanglia, the love-hate relationship between the Malwai Brars and Majhail Singhs; the siege of Jat rulers fortress at Deegh and Ghumer and the rapprochement between the Khalsa and the Jats, the the cultural currents that this social chronicle depicts are the emergence of some splinter Sikh groups such as Chandialias, Jandialias Niranjanias who, having originated from the Sikh Panth, came into conflict with the Khalsa Panth for purely mercenary reasons and causing a considerable damage to the Khalsa movement. Another sect that caused the maximum damage to the Khalsa Panth was that of the Sultanis. Members of this sect, though they dressed and lived like the Hindus, professed their faith in a Muslim Pir known as Sakhi Sarvar. The members of all these sects turned informers and collaborators with the Mughal and Afghan rulers and were instrumental in getting many Sikh martyrs like Bhai Taru Singh, Mehtab Singh and others arrested and executed. For instance, it was Harbhagat Niranjania who led a Mughal raiding party to invade S. Mehtab Singh's village of Mirankot. It also records the crumbling of the mighty Mughal empire and the subsequent internecine war Shah Abdali. The epic writer says that as a thorn is used to take out another thorn from the human flesh, the Divine power willed to get the tyrannical Mughals decimated by the Afghans as it had earlier ordained the Mughals to replace the despotic Lodhis. Finally, it was given to the Khalsa panth to hit the last nail in the coffins of both the Mughals and the Afghans: It was Nadir Shah who had capatured Delhi, The warrior who had killed the mighty Nadir Shah, The same warrior had tasted defeat at the hands of the Singhs. (48) As Nadir Shah had come to be known as Delhi's destroyer, So had Ahmed Shah come to be known as Nadir Shah's destroyer, So had Khalsa panth come to be known as Ahmed Shah's destroyer, Who had forced (the mighty) Ahmad Shah Abdali to flee. (49) The epic records two other events of his times. These are the invasion of Babur at the persistent request of Daulat Rai Lodhi of Sultanpur to seek blessings of Guru Nanak for the extinction of the Mughal empire, and demarcation and construction of a symbolic platform

pages.title: at Sirhind at the place of Sahibzada's execution by the repentant Wazir Khan, Nawab of
pages.snippet: at Sirhind at the place of Sahibzada's execution by the repentant Wazir Khan, Nawab of Sirhind. While both these are facts of history, much of the mythological baggage with which the epic writer has loaded these two incidences does not appe
pages.searchText: at Sirhind at the place of Sahibzada's execution by the repentant Wazir Khan, Nawab of at Sirhind at the place of Sahibzada's execution by the repentant Wazir Khan, Nawab of Sirhind. While both these are facts of history, much of the mythological baggage with which the epic writer has loaded these two incidences does not appeal to the sensibility of a modern reader. In the second incident, Bhangoo's version differs from the centuries-old Sikh belief, and perhaps historical records as well, when he states that the two younger Sahibzadas were beheaded instantly by a butcher with a sickle inside Wazir Khan's court after they refused to covert to Islam. It was many years after their execution that a platform was raised with the Nawab's permission at state expense on the advice of his Muslim clerics to rid the Nawab of several bodily ailments, which in their opinion, were a consequence of his sinful act of killing Guru's two innocent sons. This version runs counter the age-old belief that the younger Sahibzadas were bricked alive and finally beheaded. In Babur's case, Bhangoo depicts Guru Nanak blessing Babur and his dynasty to rule for seven generations by putting seven handfuls of connabis leaves in Babur's lap indicating that his dynastic rule at the end of his seven generations will be uprooted by the followers of Guru Nanak at the cost of great sacrifices, because Babur's descendents would have turned tyrants and oppressors like his predecessors the Lodhis. Although, it is historically true that the Mughals ruled effectively for seven generations, but the myth of Guru Nanak's blessings on Babur and sending the latter to heavens riding on Guru Nanak's wooden staff and showing him the highly subordinate position of prophet Mohammad among the hierarchy of world's prophets in the Divine Court and Guru Nanak's splendid position and closest proximity with the Divine seem more to be flights of his poetic fancy rather than incidents based on hard historical facts. Nevertheless, these two myths also highlight the sanctity of Sahibzada's sacrifice and Guru Nanak's divinity which fit into the overall design and scheme of this epic, though the excessive exaggeration and their mythological dimension somewhat blunts the modern readers sensibility. On the whole, his liberal use of mythology, especially of the Hindu mythology, has been very successfully and skillfully employed as has already been pointed in the introduction to the first volume of the translated version of this epic. The Hindu myths about Nehkalank Bhassmantar, Kaljaman, have been used so dexterously to emphasize the authenticity and inevitability of Sikh Sovereignty having a divine sanction that their use places Rattan Singh Bhangoo among some of the best modern Western and Eastern poets who have used myths from the ancient Greek and Hindu fertility cults to bring about the decadent aspects of their contemporary cultures and civilizations. As we analyse this aspect of Bhangoo's epic, he seems to be a man of vast erudition and scholarship, his doggerel colloquial verse covering the bulk of his epic notwithstanding. Taking into account his repeated references to appropriate hymns from the Adi Granth, Ramayan, Mahaabharata, Tantric Lore Chandi Astotar and Zafarnamah, it appears he was quite conversant with the ancient Indian classics and common beliefs and opinions of his contemporary society, though bulk of his information came through oral and traditional resources. To conclude in the words of Dr J.S. Grewal, There is some hearsay, which the author (himself) points out and there is much graphic detail which could come ultimately from first hand observation. Not only actions, but also sentiments, beliefs, ideas and emotions come into play to make the Prachin Panth Prakash arare kind of document. It embodies an understanding of the Khalsa tradition by a respectable member of the Khalsa who was deeply religious in his feelings and acutely political in his outlook on the world. This, in itself, is a telling comment on the Khalsa of his times and of the days of his ancestors.

pages.title: Apart from being a social chronicle of the contemporary times and an epic projecting a vision
pages.snippet: Apart from being a social chronicle of the contemporary times and an epic projecting a vision of Khalsa's sovereignty and its inevitable realization due to Sikh Guru's prophetic sanction together with the portrayal of legendary Sikh warrior
pages.searchText: Apart from being a social chronicle of the contemporary times and an epic projecting a vision Apart from being a social chronicle of the contemporary times and an epic projecting a vision of Khalsa's sovereignty and its inevitable realization due to Sikh Guru's prophetic sanction together with the portrayal of legendary Sikh warriors and martyrs, this work contains rare insights amounting to value judgements. For instance, in the first part, its author had dwelt from both Hinduism and Islam and the need to sacrifice one's progeny, if need be, to uphold One can not preserve and promote one's own ideology. Much as an agricultural piece of land over grown with weeds, Cannot give a wholesome yield of grains. (10) In the second part of this epic Bhangoo, being a direct descendent of those Sikh warriors who belonged to the Tat Khalsa (Majhail) faction of the Khalsa force, after the latter's rift with Banda Bahadur faction, has been found to be somewhat biased by some readers in favour of the faction consisting of warriors from his own stock. His deriding and debunking of Banda Bahadur, just before his defeat and death after his extreme glorification bordering almost on deification earlier, seems to confirm this impression. However, Bhangoo's catholicity of vision and impartial outlook towards personages and events comes out here as well. In a few lines of rare insight and a philosophical observation, he looks up on the miserable plight of the Tat Khalsa Singhs as a consequence of their betrayal and desertion of Banda Bahadur and his companions who were being held under seige by the Mughals at Gurdas Nangal. This reflection makes Bhangoo, not only an impartial observer of the two warring factions but also a poet with a deep analytical mind who was capable of making an indepth study of the strengths and weaknesses of the contemporary Khalsa Panth organization and presenting a balanced opinion on the whole situation. While SGPC approved version edited by Dr. Jeet Singh Seetal has given only two lines about this observation and deleted the rest of the four lines, Dr Balwant Singh Dhillon's edited version (Singh Brothers 2004) has retained the complete text of this observation. SGPC version reads: Sortha: Banda Singh had let out a curse on the Khalsa Panth, When he had to confine himself in the fort (at Gurdas Nangal). The Khalsa Panth had to bear the conseguences of their sinful act, Of not reaching out to the support of Banda Singh. (5)5 Dr B.S. Dhillon's version, however, carries the full text of this observation in continu- ation with above-mentioned lines which reads as follows: Dohra: Thereafter the scatterd Singhs hid themselves in the wilds, As in whatever little strength had they been left behind.

pages.title: Repentant did these Singhs feel at that time,
pages.snippet: Repentant did these Singhs feel at that time, As they remembered Banda Bahadur at that moment. (6) Chaupai: Truly was Banda Bahadur given to Khalsa Panth (by the Guru), Had we attempted to stand by Banda Bahadur, Definitely could he not be
pages.searchText: Repentant did these Singhs feel at that time, Repentant did these Singhs feel at that time, As they remembered Banda Bahadur at that moment. (6) Chaupai: Truly was Banda Bahadur given to Khalsa Panth (by the Guru), Had we attempted to stand by Banda Bahadur, Definitely could he not be killed by the Mughals. (7) Certainly could we have decimated the Mughals by now, Nor would have we been harassed as much. Truly had his curse fallen upon us (the Khalsa Panth), As he had already let out such a curse. (8)*° All these insights and observations reflect Bhangoo's vision matching that of a great epic writer, and reflect his sound knowledge of Sikh history, his erudition and scholarship and his profound thinking. In the editorial written in Punjabi by Giani Gurdit Singh the Prachin Panth Prakash issue of Singh Sabha Patrika, he states, S. Rattan Singh was an educated aristocrat. He could read and analyse epics written in Persian. He also had a knack for composing poetry. Above all, whereas his family lineage belongs to family of the martyrs of village Mirankot, his educational background is linked to the poet Sainapat, a court poet of Guru Gobind Singh. Rattan Singh Bhangoo himself has referred to this link in one of his other compositions. [Translation mine) Giani Gurdit has come across the manuscript of another composition written by Rattan Singh Bhanoo which is known as Hanuman Natak. In the preamble to this dramatic verse, Bhangoo has stated his educational background. Translated into English this Dohra: Praise be to Sri Guru Gobind Singh Who is worthy of great name and fame. Fifty two poets had he kept in his court, Who remained immersed in the nectar (or Knowledge). (13) In this sacred pool of nectar full of knowledge, Among them was included (the poet) Sainapat, Who hailed from a Jat stock from Majha. (14) Amanuensis had he been to the (tenth) Guru, And a composer of innumerable melodies. Initiated was he by administering Khandey-ki-Pahul, As he endeared himself to the Divine Guru. (15)

pages.searchText: Thereafter proceeding to the region of Majha, Thereafter proceeding to the region of Majha, Did he found a village in that region. It was in the vicinity of village Jagatpura, That he had set up his household there. (16) Dohra: Whosoever was fortunate to have his company, Chandan Saina Singh was one of these disciples, To the forested region Majhori Dhan did he belong. (17) One of them was a Brahmin, By the name of Punjaba was he known. At the village of Mirankot did he settle, Kaur Singh did he (the Brahmin) teach, Who happened to be my (Rattan Singh's) elder brother. Of S. Mehtab Singh were they grandsons, S. Mehtab Singh being the father of Rai Singh. (20) From this brother of mine did I receive education, With this sort of grace of the True Guru, I (Rattan Singh) also got blessed with education. (21) This poetic work was composed by Rattan Singh Bhangoo in the year 1881 B.S. or 1834 A.D. whereas Sri Gur Panth Prakash was composed in 1898 B.S. or 1841 A.D. I hope this documentary evidence about Rattan Singh Bhangoo's educational background meets the demand of section of the readers of the first part of the translated version of Sri Gur Panth Prakash by the author, who had pointed out that the translator had taken no pains to provide any information about the author's credentials for being an epic writer. The same section while acknowledging that Rattan Singh Bhangoo's verse being a hybrid language of Gurmukhi despite being colloguial Punjabi, is arduous in reading, has also faulted the translator for making his translation explicatory, while admitting at the same time that the translator has extended its reading range. It is precisely for this so-called explicatory stance of translation of this work of otherwise archaic idiom that innumerable number of readers, both in India and abroad, have commended this monumental effort on the part of the translator by way of a positive feedback both to the translator as well as to the Institute of Sikh Studies. Rattan Singh Bhangoo's major source of 18th century Sikh history being oral and traditional form of listening to the Sikh sagas from his elders, there are a few differences in the dates of certain historical incidences. For instance, he mentions the year of Bhai Mani Singh's martyrdom as 1794 B.S. as he heard it from his father but the writer of Shaheed Bilas

Mir Mannu's death is mentioned as 1823 B.S. or 1766 A.D. but, as per historical records, Mir Mannu died in November 1753. Similarly, the year of Ahmad Shah Abdali's death is recorded in Bhangoo's epic as 1823 B.S. or 1766 A.D., but historical records place it on October 23, 1772 A.D. Certain names such as those of Jassa Singh Ahluwalia's father's name, Nawab Aslam Khan in place of Zakaria Khan and Abdul Samad Khan in place of Zakaria Khan in episodes 90 and 91 have been wrongly recorded. But for these variations in dates here and there, there is hardly any variation between his version and historical records in the sequence and chronology of major events. That speaks volumes for the credibility of this epic as a social chronicle of the times as well as Bhangoo as chronicler and epic writer. We hope that this second volume improves upon the first volume so far as the quality of translation is concerned and makes up all the deficiencies which have been pointed out by the readers and reviewers of the first volume. pages.title: The Sangat Seeks a Written Assurance for the Panth
pages.snippet: The sangat receives the Granth's answer as a victorious and consoling command. Drums of joy are imagined, and the congregation turns from relief to responsibility by asking how the Khalsa is to endure and expand in the world. The surviving
pages.searchText: The Sangat Seeks a Written Assurance for the Panth The sangat receives the Granth's answer as a victorious and consoling command. Drums of joy are imagined, and the congregation turns from relief to responsibility by asking how the Khalsa is to endure and expand in the world. The surviving lines read as a collective prayer for the future of the community. The Singhs ask for a written assurance for the Panth so that those who try to diminish it will fail while the Guru's design remains protected. The page closes in the tone of ardās rather than argument. It presents the Panth as something sustained not by worldly cunning but by the Guru's foreknowledge, shelter, and explicit promise.

pages.title: Prophecy of Khalsa Triumph After Hardship
pages.snippet: The passage answers persecution with prophecy. It says that the power which inflicted so much suffering on the Khalsa would not stand, and that Punjab would come into the hands of the Singhs after this season of trial. The page then turns t
pages.searchText: Prophecy of Khalsa Triumph After Hardship The passage answers persecution with prophecy. It says that the power which inflicted so much suffering on the Khalsa would not stand, and that Punjab would come into the hands of the Singhs after this season of trial. The page then turns to scriptural reinforcement, drawing on saint-centered wisdom to argue that those who attack the holy ultimately lose all refuge. In that frame, the enemies of the Panth are not merely political rivals but offenders against a divine order already moving toward judgment. Even in this brief passage, the movement is clear: hardship is temporary, while the Guru's community is being prepared for visible ascendancy. The tone is meant to steady morale, not simply to predict victory.

pages.title: Guru Succession and Nadir's Question About the Sikhs
pages.snippet: A listener asks for an account of the line of Gurus after Guru Nanak, and the reply moves briskly through the succession from Guru Angad onward. The summary highlights the transmission of spiritual authority, the miri-piri ideal, martyrdom,
pages.searchText: Guru Succession and Nadir's Question About the Sikhs A listener asks for an account of the line of Gurus after Guru Nanak, and the reply moves briskly through the succession from Guru Angad onward. The summary highlights the transmission of spiritual authority, the miri-piri ideal, martyrdom, and the culmination of sovereignty in the Guru's final shaping of the Khalsa. This condensed rehearsal of Sikh history is not ornamental. It explains why the Panth acts with such independence: its political courage is presented as the outcome of a sacred lineage rather than a sudden rebellion. By the end of the page the narrative pivots back to imperial bewilderment. Nadir Khan asks who these raiders are, so the historical survey becomes the setup for the coming description of Sikh character and warfare.

pages.title: Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Subdued
pages.snippet: The answer to Nadir's inquiry describes the Sikhs as a people who live lightly, move constantly, and refuse the comforts by which ordinary armies are tamed. They sleep with weapons near them, endure hunger without complaint, and treat hards
pages.searchText: Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Subdued The answer to Nadir's inquiry describes the Sikhs as a people who live lightly, move constantly, and refuse the comforts by which ordinary armies are tamed. They sleep with weapons near them, endure hunger without complaint, and treat hardship as part of their discipline rather than as a cause for surrender. The page insists that persecution has trained the Khalsa into unusual cohesion: where one Sikh appears, many more seem ready to rise. Its argument climaxes in the claim that people sheltered by such a Lord cannot be defeated, because their courage is understood as a gift of divine protection rather than mere stubbornness. That logic also turns history into proof. Those who opposed the Guru's light are remembered as fading away, while the Panth survives precisely because its confidence is tied to the Guru and not to possession of territory alone.

pages.title: The Khalsa Rejects Nawabi and Claims Patishahi
pages.snippet: The Singhs answer worldly offers with a sharper doctrine of sovereignty. They say the Guru had already granted them patishahi, so a subordinate nawabi is too small a thing to desire or accept. From there the page imagines royal authority as
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Rejects Nawabi and Claims Patishahi The Singhs answer worldly offers with a sharper doctrine of sovereignty. They say the Guru had already granted them patishahi, so a subordinate nawabi is too small a thing to desire or accept. From there the page imagines royal authority as something carried by the Panth itself. Wherever the Khalsa gathers in fidelity, a throne may be raised, because the Satguru's promise is portable and does not depend on the sanction of a court. The rhetoric binds political confidence to revelation. The Guru's word does not fail, and so the Khalsa treats power not as borrowed favor but as a trust already lodged within its collective discipline.

pages.title: Khalsa Authority Compared to Guru Nanak Establishing Angad
pages.snippet: This page makes the transfer of authority visible through insignia and dress. The preserved lines describe the plume and garments being bestowed in a scene explicitly compared to Guru Nanak establishing Angad, so the Panth's honor is shown
pages.searchText: Khalsa Authority Compared to Guru Nanak Establishing Angad This page makes the transfer of authority visible through insignia and dress. The preserved lines describe the plume and garments being bestowed in a scene explicitly compared to Guru Nanak establishing Angad, so the Panth's honor is shown as a continuation of the Guru lineage rather than a break from it. The page also stresses that the trust has been handed over to the Khalsa as a body. Counsel, prayer, companionship, and discipline are presented as the proper means by which that authority is exercised and preserved. Its closing movement turns toward martyr resolve. The one who has received the Guru's charge must be ready to give his head without betraying the Panth, because delegated sovereignty is inseparable from sacrificial responsibility.

pages.title: Introduction Notes: Martyrdom Quotations and References
pages.snippet: This scholarly-notes page gathers quoted verses where Sikh speakers reject dying in flight, remember sacrifice for the Panth, and praise those who gave their heads or families for Sikhi. The quoted examples honor Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Dyal
pages.searchText: Introduction Notes: Martyrdom Quotations and References This scholarly-notes page gathers quoted verses where Sikh speakers reject dying in flight, remember sacrifice for the Panth, and praise those who gave their heads or families for Sikhi. The quoted examples honor Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Dyal Singh, Subeg Singh, and Subeg Singh’s son as martyrs who kept faith under torture. Their function is to support the introduction’s argument about Panthic sovereignty and sacrificial responsibility. The lower part records sources rather than episode action: J. S. Grewal’s Valorizing the Traditions, Karam Singh, Hari Ram Gupta, Ganda Singh, G. C. Narang, Indu Bhushan Banerjee, Sirdar Kapoor Singh, and M. H. Abrams are listed as references.

pages.title: Bhai Mani Singh as the Model Sikh and Teacher
pages.snippet: The fragment becomes a sustained praise-portrait of Bhai Mani Singh as the model Sikh. He is remembered as disciplined, learned, devout, and steady in judgment, with saintliness and organizational authority held together in one figure. The
pages.searchText: Bhai Mani Singh as the Model Sikh and Teacher The fragment becomes a sustained praise-portrait of Bhai Mani Singh as the model Sikh. He is remembered as disciplined, learned, devout, and steady in judgment, with saintliness and organizational authority held together in one figure. The page emphasizes that his excellence is not private holiness alone. He strengthens the Panth by teaching Sikhi widely, recounting sacred history, guiding conduct, and giving ordinary Sikhs a living image of fidelity joined to intellect. In that sense Bhai Mani Singh stands here as a standard for communal leadership. He embodies the kind of character by which the Khalsa preserves doctrine, memory, and discipline under pressure.

pages.title: Martyr Fidelity and the Ideal Nihang
pages.snippet: The page continues a martyrdom-inflected dialogue about the head, uncut hair, and the refusal to yield Sikh identity under coercion. It treats bodily suffering as secondary to keeping faith, so outward signs become part of an inward covenan
pages.searchText: Martyr Fidelity and the Ideal Nihang The page continues a martyrdom-inflected dialogue about the head, uncut hair, and the refusal to yield Sikh identity under coercion. It treats bodily suffering as secondary to keeping faith, so outward signs become part of an inward covenant rather than mere custom. From that debate the text broadens into a warrior ideal, praising the ideal nihang as fearless in battle and first to step forward wherever the Panth is endangered. Courage, austerity, and readiness for sudden combat are all folded into the same religious temperament. The effect is to join martyrdom and militancy instead of separating them. The Sikh warrior is admirable not because he loves violence, but because he has already accepted loss and therefore cannot be frightened away from duty.

pages.title: Martyrdom, Satnam, and the Unity of Guru and Sikh
pages.snippet: This page develops a theology of witness by insisting that Guru and Sikh cannot be separated. Martyrs accept the Guru's word as life itself, so their steadfastness is presented as proof that Panthic courage comes from grace and not from emp
pages.searchText: Martyrdom, Satnam, and the Unity of Guru and Sikh This page develops a theology of witness by insisting that Guru and Sikh cannot be separated. Martyrs accept the Guru's word as life itself, so their steadfastness is presented as proof that Panthic courage comes from grace and not from empty bravado. The fragment then shifts into confrontation with political authority. Demands for submission or conversion are answered with calm refusal, because the Khalsa understands its true command as already received from the Guru. In the final movement, even a child is imagined answering the challenge with Sikh certainty. The genuine kalma here is rendered through Satnam and Vahiguru, making verbal confession itself an act of unbroken allegiance.

pages.searchText: Introduction Notes: Khalsa Authority and Kapoor Singh This front-matter note preserves quoted evidence about Khalsa authority and recognition rather than a direct page of narrative. Its first quotation describes a power that had devastated Delhi and names Nadir or Ahmad Shah as enemies, but says the Khalsa forced Ahmad Shah’s side to flee. The second quotation turns to Kapoor Singh. It shows him humbly serving the Singhs, then records an Akal command received by the Panth to honor him with a robe of honor because his service had reached the proper station. The final citation from Episode 90 describes arranging five camps or standards and bringing Nishan flags from Sri Akal Bunga, so the page reads as a citation cluster about Khalsa authority and recognition.

pages.title: Early Martyrs and Ahmad Shah's Search for the Sikh Raiders
pages.snippet: The page first honors a lineage of five early martyrs and nihangs whose memory frames the Khalsa as a community already tested by sacrifice. That commemorative tone matters because it turns the narrative from names of the dead toward the li
pages.searchText: Early Martyrs and Ahmad Shah's Search for the Sikh Raiders The page first honors a lineage of five early martyrs and nihangs whose memory frames the Khalsa as a community already tested by sacrifice. That commemorative tone matters because it turns the narrative from names of the dead toward the living reputation their courage created. From there the focus shifts to the enemy court, where Ahmad Shah asks who plundered him and why his forces cannot catch the raiders. The answer presents the Singhs as austere fighters who have no fixed territory, move lightly, and refuse the settled habits that imperial power knows how to punish. In effect, the page lets even the adversary testify to Sikh resilience. The Khalsa appears not as a conventional kingdom but as a disciplined and elusive force that survives by mobility, hardship, and collective purpose.

pages.title: Epic Praise of the Panth and the Rise of Charhat Singh
pages.snippet: The Panth is praised in epic language that compares the Sikhs to the Yadavas and treats Guru-guided struggle as the power that breaks the Giljis and humbles arrogant Turks. The page uses that elevated frame to argue that Sikh victories belo
pages.searchText: Epic Praise of the Panth and the Rise of Charhat Singh The Panth is praised in epic language that compares the Sikhs to the Yadavas and treats Guru-guided struggle as the power that breaks the Giljis and humbles arrogant Turks. The page uses that elevated frame to argue that Sikh victories belong to a sacred historical pattern rather than to chance alone. It then narrows from the collective to a single rising leader, celebrating Charhat Singh for the wounds and hardships he has already endured in battle. His renown grows precisely because his body shows the cost of struggle instead of the comfort of easy command. By the end, admirers speak blessings that he would become sovereign over a wide dominion. The page therefore works as both praise-poetry for the Panth and a political anointing of Charhat Singh's future stature.

pages.searchText: Introduction Notes: Martyrdom and Citation Spillover This page is not continuous narrative; it is a citation spillover from the introduction and references. It quotes a short remembrance of Tara Singh’s martyrdom, saying his deed became famous and that he offered his head for the Guru without surrendering his Sikh resolve. The next citations collect casualty memories and anti-imperial praise: one reports enormous losses and a survivor’s family testimony, and another says the force that ravaged Delhi and was linked to Nadir or Ahmad Shah was eventually routed by the Khalsa. The lower lines turn back to bibliography, naming J. S. Grewal’s edited Khalsa perspectives volume, another Ibid. note, an Episode 13 citation, and a Dhillon edition reference for Episode 82. These entries identify the page as scholarly notes rather than an episode.

pages.searchText: Chandialias and Jandialas Introduced as Betrayers Chandialias, Jandialas And those who harmed This page opens a denunciatory episode about Chandialias, Jandialas, and others remembered as enemies of the Guru and the Panth. The tone is moral from the start, presenting these figures as examples of how treachery can arise even around sacred institutions. The first concrete case is a poor man who comes to the Guru's langar, eats there, and serves there, yet fails to absorb the discipline and gratitude that should have followed such grace. The poor man comes to the Guru's langar in need, but the page insists that receiving food and favor is not the same thing as inward transformation. As a result, the episode begins by contrasting outward proximity with inward failure. What should have become loyalty instead becomes the groundwork for later corruption and hostility.

pages.searchText: Hindal’s Reverent Bow in the Langar Chandialias, Jandialas And those who harmed Episode About Chandialias, Jandialas And those who harmed One day Guru Amar Das went from his seat to the langar. As Sikhs bowed at the Guru’s feet, Hindal also hurried forward, but his hands were covered with wheat flour from kitchen service. Afraid of soiling the Guru’s feet, Hindal folded his hands behind his back and bowed with his head instead. The Guru recognized the care in his heart, looked on him with kindness, and blessed him for that small act of thoughtfulness. The page then turns into the next shocking episode by warning that a freely given blessing can be kept only by a deep and worthy vessel. Like water in an unbaked clay pot, grace will not remain where character cannot hold it.

pages.searchText: Episode 83 — Hindal Squanders the Guru's Grace The Guru's Cause and the Sikh Panth And those Given to Debauchery and Irascibility The episode turns from remembered grace to remembered failure. He could not preserve the Guru's rare gift, so the blessing that should have deepened humility instead feeds imitation, vanity, and spiritual ambition. The page condemns Hindal for copying the Guru's institutions while draining them of obedience. He builds rival structures, cultivates followers around himself, and begins to treat borrowed sanctity as if it were his own inheritance. What began as proximity to the Guru is therefore rewritten as a cautionary tale. The deeper charge is not mere error but the deliberate squandering of a gift that should have produced devotion and truthful service.

pages.searchText: Episode 83 — Jinda Pir Claims and the Niranjania Heirs The Guru's Cause and the Sikh Panth And those Given to Debauchery and Irascibility The Guru's Cause and the Sikh Panth And those Given to Debauchery and Irascibility The indictment grows sharper as Hindal's circle begins to make extravagant religious claims and to rewrite sacred memory around itself. False assertions about living sainthood and fabricated lineage are presented as signs that ambition has overtaken reverence. The corruption does not stop with one man. Later heirs repeat the pattern and eventually declared themselves to be Niranjanias instead of Guru's Sikhs, turning inherited association into open distance from the Guru's path. The page therefore moves from personal arrogance to sectarian degeneration. Even external markers remain, but the inner practice of Waheguru-centered devotion is shown as having been hollowed out.

They are described as wavering between claiming Nanak’s Panth and Jinda Pir, while keeping close relations with Muslim and Sultani groups. Har Bhagat is singled out as especially destructive. According to the source, he denounced Sikhs, cooperated with Mughal forces, had Sikhs seized from their homes and sent to Lahore for rewards, and twice caused the author’s own village to be plundered. The account then names Kirpal and Dyal as successors who guided Ahmad Shah’s forces and contributed to the massacre near Malerkotla, where many Sikhs were killed. The page ends by saying Sikh pressure later drove them back and that quarrels within the line led to Kirpal’s death and Dyal Das’s succession.

pages.searchText: Episode 83 Ends; Episode 84 Begins — From Sharan Dass to Tara Singh The Guru's Cause and the Sikh Panth And those Given to Debauchery and Irascibility The page closes the corrupt line by describing Sharan Dass and related figures as morally rotten, exploitative, and unworthy of continuation. The denunciation is final in tone, as if the text means to sever the reader completely from that lineage of fabrication and abuse. Then the narrative deliberately turns toward a better exemplar. The call to listen to the episode of Tara Singh marks the hinge, introducing a Singh whose courage and discipline will answer the decay just condemned. Because of that transition, the page functions as more than an ending. It is a moral reset in which false claimants fade out and a martyr-hero enters to restore the reader's attention to Sikh steadfastness.

The crops which the two Singh farmers had raised, Were these lapped off by the Chaudary's horses. (13) That their crops could be saved only if the latter kept his horses under leash. (14) The Singhs, though feeling outraged at such a provocation, Remarked that they were desperately helpless to deal with him. They had large families to feed and support in the village, Otherwise they would have beaten him to death instantly. (15) So these aggrieved Singhs proceeded to a village Bhusa°, Which inhabited two Singhs named Baghel Singh and Amar Singh Dhillon. (16) From there Lakhmir Singh Sandhu® got the custody of those horses, And sold these to somebody in the forested region of (Malwa). He offered all the proceeds from the sale of the horses, To the free community kitchen run by Tara Singh at Wan. (17) Also reached the spot where the horses had been kept, As detectives held the two Dhillon Singhs responsible for the horses theft, The latter were at their wits ends to find a place to take refuge. (18) The (brave) Tara Singh who had shed all fears of death. And addressed Tara Singh (to heed his warning). (19) He threatened that either Tara Singh should handover the two cattle lifters, Or he would get them arrested by the authorities at Lahore. He warned Tara Singh to keep the thieves under his custody, Lest they should escape and put him into trouble. (20)

(21) Tara Singh declared that he had made a resolution, That he would sacrifice his life while fighting the Mughals. That he would never seek any refuge to save his life, And shed his mortal frame after killing so many others. (22) Thus, a little incident flared up into a conflagration, As it proved to be an inauspicious moment for the Singhs, The Jat chief went and complained to the authorities at Patti, That they were living safely in the safety of their houses. (23) He informed that since the Singhs were making collections forcibly, The people could pay their revenue to only one authority. The ruler of Patti felt so outraged at the insinuation, As if a sleeping lion was provoked out of its sleep. (24) When the Patti ruler asked Sahib Rai about the Singhs location, He informed that they were picketing at a village Wan! of Buttar Jats. There the (Tat Khalsa) Tara Singh had constructed his Mansion, And had spread his terror all around the place. (25) Then, the Patti ruler asked him for further information, As to how much force he had managed together there. The Chaudhary Jat informed him that Tara had no fort of his own, But a couple of two storeyed rooms for his shelter had he. (26) He kept a force of ten to twenty Singhs regularly, While Singhs, in small batches, kept visiting his place. Some of these Singhs were armed with swords and spears, With Sahib Rai leading this force from the front. This whole force, consisting of five horse riders and eighty foot soldiers, Launched on an expedition enthused with high spirits. (28) This force rushed post haste (from their headquarters), Lest the Singh should escape (before their arrival). They intended to surround the place before day break, And dispatch the Singhs to Lahore (after capturing them). (29)

Baghel Singh was the most dreadful among the Singhs, His capture would mean half the battle had been won. Then a battery of foot soldiers fell upon him, And wounded him fatally on the thighs with bullets. (38)

pages.searchText: The Singhs Choose Shahidi Over Escape An Episode that is Shocking An Episode that is Shocking After the first blows, the story pauses to weigh outcomes, reporting hui châlŵ phujdâr murd utrayô kambó ki jai while the Singhs measure what remains possible against what honour requires. Their answer is not strategic withdrawal but theological clarity: ham lar turak jitai nahi jahin is joined to singh sôû ju karai nit janga, defining the Singh through constant struggle rather than protected survival. The decisive note is martyrdom itself, because jin hônâ hai ihân shahida shows the companions affirming shahidi as the truthful end of the path they already chose.

(40) To Khan Bahadur!?, the then Nawab of Lahore. Hearing this development, the Singhs felt concerned, And approached Tara Singh to share their concern. (41) They remarked that since the Singhs had won the first bout, They should now go underground for the time being. Since the Singhs could never conguer the Mughals in a straight fight, Why should they die in vain (in an unegual fight. (42) Thereupon S. Tara Singh addressed these Singhs in such a vein, That he did not care to hold on to his mortal frame. He would rather prefer to follow the Guru's injunction, As the great Guru had ordained (in the time of an ordeal). (43) He alone was the Singh who engaged himself in daily fight, He alone was the Singh who feared not to die (for a cause). So he would fight to the finish at his own place, Nor would he desert his place to save his life. (44) The (Tat Khalsa) Singhs who were present at his place, He told all of them in clear cut terms: Only those who wished to sacrifice should stay along, While others should desert (before the fight started). (45) That was the only day for those who wished to desert, Next day, they might not find an opportunity to escape. Hearing this, some of his colleagues took to their heels, While some of them stayed put to sacrifice their lives. (46) Dohra: Those, not fully indoctrinated into Khalsa ideology, deserted, While those, fully committed to the Khalsa's cause, stayed. The latter were those who were fully motivated and committed, And to whom Guru's cause was too dear to forsake. (47)

pages.searchText: Tara Singh’s Companions Gather for Martyrdom An Episode that is Shocking An Episode that is Shocking After some companions failed to keep their promise of sacrifice, Tara Singh decided to inform the remaining Singhs and leave the choice to them. He remembered that they had all pledged themselves while eating from the same bowl. The page names the first group who answered: two Buttar brothers, Tara Singh’s own relatives and devoted warriors; Wasawa Singh and Koer Singh, Brahmins from a village read as Jhalli; and Samund Singh and Jhabar Singh, his Multani companions. More volunteers then arrive after receiving Tara Singh’s message, including Sura Singh the carpenter from Khalra if the reading is correct, Lakhmir Singh from Ghariala, Mali Singh and Gurbakhsh Singh, Bhim Singh and Badal Singh from Rattoke, and others whose names and places remain partly uncertain but still mark a gathering for martyrdom.

Once that heading appears, ab phir bat turkan val âî signals that state initiative has resumed and that the focus is shifting from local clash to a new expedition under Muslim command.

Then, skinning a tender lamb after slaughtering it, They prepared a war drum with its dried skin. (He said that as many Singhs rose from the ground once again As the number of drops of Singhs blood fell on the ground) After making a resolve, the Sikhs assembled (at Tara Singh's Bunga), Reposing their complete faith in God's (benevolent) Will. So that they might succeed in their cherished mission. (1) Now, let us look at the scenario in the Mughal's camp, Listen to their account, my dear Gursikh readers. As the custodian of Patti approached the authorities at Lahore, He narrated the account of his ignominous defeat. The more the Patti custodian read out (the defiant) Singhs names, The more infuriated and incensed became the Nawab. (3) He felt befuddled how these wily Singhs had mushroomed again. After he had hounded and eliminated every Singh, The more the Mughals had exhausted themselves in eliminating the Singhs, The more had the Singhs multiplied in their strength. (4) At this the Qazi taking the Nawab aside, remarked That the latter knew nothing about the mystery of Singhs resurrection.

Not a drop of blood be allowed to spill from their bodies, Then alone can the increase in their strength be checked. (6) Then at such a suggestion of the Qazi, a soldier interjected, That the revered Qazi was really speaking the truth. For this (holy) cause should the Qazi be made to lead the troops, So that he could help the troops in catching the Singhs alive. (7) He had never had an encounter with the mighty Singhs, He would never unite with his wife after an encounter with them. At this remark, the Qazi felt so much exasperated, That he could not speak a single word in his defence. (8) Then, the Nawab of Lahore made a pronouncement, That they must now proceed to crush the Singhs. (9) Was there anyone who could take revenge from the enemies of Islam, Who would not allow the Singhs to escape and take refuge? The Hindus must be eliminated even if one broke a thousand vows, Such had been the injunctions from the Prophet. (11) As the herald announced the launch of this expedition, The (assigned) troops put up a camp on the outskirts of Lahore. (12) These Singhs, somehow, passed the day in great stress, But proceeded to inform (Tara Singh) as the darkness descended. After arriving at Tara Singh's contingent and greeting them, He informed that the Mughal force was about to attack them. (13)

pages.searchText: Tara Singh Welcomes Martyrdom Tara Singh — The Mn Episode About Tara Singh — The Mn When warned about danger, Tara Singh refuses every language of escape, declaring main tau ab murd pavaun lahaura as though Lahore itself has already become the place where his death will bear witness. He strengthens that refusal by saying ham áp chahain turkan sir lâî, presenting initiative and courage rather than panic, and then insists that no hiding place can protect a man from the hour appointed for him. The closing meditation turns proverbial and absolute: jahin jahin jaîai tahîn tahin kala means death meets a person everywhere, so jau kahûn kal tç bhâj kai bachiyat exposes flight as illusion rather than wisdom.

pages.searchText: Episode 86 — Ghumanda Warns Tara Singh Invasion of Moman Khan Er Invasion of Moman Khan Er The Mughal advance is briefly diverted through Ghumanda, an Uppal Jat by caste, who outwardly guides Moman Khan’s men yet secretly sends word that Tara Singh should vacate his place with his companions before the force closes in. Tara Singh refuses the offer of safety because he has already resolved to make a sacrifice, treating withdrawal as a betrayal of the witness he intends to give. The page closes by showing the Singhs openly challenged the Mughals with the beat of a drum, a defiant signal that their stand has been chosen rather than forced upon them.

But since he (Tara Singh) had resolved to make a sacrifice, He would not run away anywhere from there. (7) And could easily return to his place as well. But since his fraternity would accuse him of being a coward, On the other hand, hearing about the arrival of troops, The residents of Dalla village came out to meet them. Assuring that they being the loyal subjects of the Mughal sovereign, Their entire village had no rebel Singh among them. (9) The Singhs then challenged the Mughals with the beat of a drum, Which the Mughal troops heard from a distance. pages.snippet: A friendly Pathan came running on horseback to warn the Singhs that escape was still possible, but Tara Singh answers that they have already accepted the path of witness and will not save themselves by concealment. The domestic scene that f
pages.searchText: The Pathan Warning and Tara Singh’s Refusal to Hide Invasion of Moman Khan Er Invasion of Moman Khan Er A friendly Pathan came running on horseback to warn the Singhs that escape was still possible, but Tara Singh answers that they have already accepted the path of witness and will not save themselves by concealment. The domestic scene that follows, with companions filling a big tub with water, only sharpens his rebuke: he says the body gets sanctified with the touch of a weapon when it is offered in righteous battle, not by comfort or delay. He therefore makes the issue plain for everyone present: anyone willing to escape should escape now, and whoever remains should come out armed into the field beside him.

As he had intimated them about the approaching troops, They should escape and take refuge in the wilds. (11) Tara Singh (acknowledging his service), told him, That he (Tara Singh) was indeed grateful to the brotherly Pathan. But since he had taken a vow to make a sacrifice, He would certainly sacrifice his life at his own place. (12) At that time S. Tara Singh was serving the other Singhs, By filling a big tub with water for bathing the Singhs. Then these Singhs beseeched Tara Singh while serving them, That he had already done a plenty of service to them. (13) Now it was their turn to do some service to him, So that they could also sanctify their bodies with his service. At this, S. Tara Singh addressed his companions, That one's body was sanctified only after being wounded in a war. (14) As the devout get their bodies sanctified, By getting themselves branded at Dwarka. Similarly, when a warrior gets wounded in war. His body gets sanctified with the touch of a weapon. (15) As S. Tara Singh went out to fetch water, Returning, he announced to the Singhs once again, That anyone willing to escape should escape now. (16) Otherwise, they should come out with their weapons, And stand in the battlefield leaving their shelters. Hearing this, the Singhs came out in the open, Leaving their shelter, they stood on the battlefield. (17) The Mughal troops launched an attack from the other side, With the beat of war drums and other trumpets. Launching their attack from all the four sides, They scattered like players in the rustic game of Sonchi?. (18) S. Bulakha Singh was the first to attack the invaders, Who wounded many Mughal soldiers with his sword. Then after being hit by an enemy arrow in the chest, He fell down and departed for his heavenly abode. (19)

pages.episodeTitle: Invasion of Moman Khan Er

pages.searchText: The Singhs Hold Their Ground Against Moman Khan Invasion of Moman Khan Er Invasion of Moman Khan Er When the charge begins, the Singhs stood in a circle with their backs towards each other so no side of the defense would collapse at once under cavalry pressure. The attackers intended to crush the Singhs with horses’ hooves, but the resistance was so fierce that the passage got blocked with the falling bodies and the fight turned into a chaotic knot of men, animals, and steel. Unable to break them cleanly, the Mughals fired and shot arrows from a distance until Tara Singh surged forward and caught hold of Takki Khan’s horse’s reins, drawing the clash toward single combat with the enemy leaders.

pages.searchText: Then the Singhs stood in a circle with their backs towards each other, Invasion of Moman Khan Er Invasion of Moman Khan Er Then the Singhs stood in a circle with their backs towards each other, As if they were going to participate in the game of Sonchi. As the Mughal troops attacked these circled Singhs, They kept on repulsing their attack from their side. (20) So much dust and din was raised from both the sides, As if a dust storm had broke in at night. The Mughal soldiers while riding on their horses, Intended to crush the Singhs with horse's hooves. (21) But as the Singh chopped off the horses heads, Their riders fell down feeling exhausted and defeated. And fell down, blocking the passage of their own troops. (22) As the soldiers from both the sides collided against each other, The passage got blocked with the falling bodies. As more and more soldiers came attacking, They too kept on falling on the heaped bodies. (23) While a few Mughal soldiers got wounded with their own weapons, Some others were hit by the weapons of advancing Singhs. There occurred such a blood bath from both sides, That soldiers from both sides got completely exhausted. (24) Thus, the attacks from both the sides slowed down, As it became difficult to wield small weapons in a close encounter. So the Mughal troops fired and shot arrows from a distance, And started killing Singhs while standing at a distance. (25) Although the Singh had not any muskets or small fire arms, Yet the Mughals bullets hit their own soldiers on the other side. Once again got an attack launched on the Singhs. (26) At that Takki Khan, while advancing on his horse's back, Hearing this, S. Tara Singh asked him to proceed a little further, And gave him option of attacking him (Tara Singh) first. (27) As Takki Khan shot an arrow while riding on a horse, Leaping up, Tara Singh caught hold of Takki Khan's horse's reigns, Even as Takki Khan's entire body was protected with a steely armour. (28)

pages.searchText: Bhima Singh and Lakhmir Singh Enter the Fight Invasion of Moman Khan Er Invasion of Moman Khan Er Even though Takki Khan was completely covered with a steel armour, Tara Singh pierced the tip of his sword into his face and showed that fearlessness could reach what armour could not protect. The taunt that followed mocked Tara Singh as though he were sitting there with the beetelnut packets, but the assault only drove the Singhs into a fiercer counterattack rather than shaking their nerve. The page then celebrates Bhima Singh in a mood of chivalrous ecstasy, catching the elephant by the ear and cutting down its support while Tara Singh turns and begins addressing Lakhmir Singh for the next decisive stroke.

Beckoning bleeding Taki Khan to come nearer to him, Chaupai: At this, Takki Khan told Moman Khan tauntingly, That Tara Singh was sitting there with the beetelnut packets. Asking the elephant driver to move his elephant, This warrior shot pairs of arrows in each and every attempt. (32) Reckoning the Singhs to be wounded and exhausted, He asked the elephant driver to move his elephant further. Thinking that he being perched higher on an elephant's back, Feeling emboldened at the sight of Singhs being in a minority. He assessed their strength by taking a round on the elephant's back. Being known as a great warrior among the Mughal troops, He shot pairs of arrows in each attempt at the Singhs. (34) Dohra: Then Bhima Singh (from Peshawar) in a mood of Chivalrous ecstasy, Pounced upon his enemy like a ferocious lion. Catching the elephant by the ear and pressing it hard, He made the elephant to sit down in an instant. While he killed the elephant's driver with a half-broken sword, He himself fainted from the blow of an elephant's prod. (36) Noticing Bhima Ssingh fainting, Tara Singh rushed to his aid, While addressing Lakhmir Singh in following words: When both of them (Tara Singh and Lakhmir Singh) used to graze buffaloes, Lakhmir Singh used to jump over a couple of buffaloes. (37)

pages.searchText: Lakhmir Singh Strikes and New Champions Appear Invasion of Moman Khan Er Invasion of Moman Khan Er When called forward, Lakhmir Singh said he was thinking the same, then pounced upon his enemy with the eagerness of a Singh who had been waiting for his opening. Though he was pierced in the shoulder, he still mounted the elephant by catching hold of a rope and fought at such close quarters that the mighty beast itself seemed reduced to a prop in the hands of the brave. The narrative then mocks imperial grandeur by calling a single elephant being of no use before shifting to the next Mughal response, where Mansa Ram and Daya Ram are summoned as fresh decorated challengers.

Remarking that a single elephant being of no use., The Singhs would allot such elephants to each one of their servants. (43) At this, Moman Khan summoned the (muscular) Purbia? soldiers, Who had been conferred with great wartime decorations. They had been ordered to accompany the Mughal troops, And they hailed from the village named Kundalpur. (45) Chaupai: Making a dash, as they pounced upon the Singhs, The Singh also came into combat from the other side. Mansa Ram and Daya Ram, (the renowned Purbia warriors), Were (also) slaughtered by the Singhs at the same place. (46)

pages.searchText: The Martyrdom of Tara Singh and His Companions Invasion of Moman Khan Er Invasion of Moman Khan Er After darkness had momentarily shielded the survivors, visibility increased with the break of dawn and the Mughal line resumed the attack without offering any honourable closeness to the fight. Instead they fired shots with their muskets from a distance and, once resistance ended, severed their heads from their bodies to display victory over men they could not subdue by courage alone. The page memorializes Tara Singh along with his twenty two companions, praises their devotion openly, and then turns the reader toward Episode 87 as the next chapter in the same martyred inheritance.

Following the great Guru's words in letter and spirit, He sacrificed his life rather than compromising his dignity. Till eternity, will their great deeds survive and last, In this otherwise fleeting world of change and flux. (51) Episode 87 (How the Randhawa Singhs were got slaughtered) (Dear readers) listen further to the episode of those Singhs, Who sacrificed and held the Mughals guilty of their execution. Reposing their faith in the (prophetic) words of the Guru, They sacrificed their lives in the true spirit of their faith. (1) After narrating their names, domicile, castes and sub-castes, I shall narrate their (deep) association with their faith. I shall narrate their deeds with as much faith as, I had heard about them from my veteran ancestors. (2) Among the cluster of twenty two villages of Randhawas near Chamunda, There was a village Kairon Nangal in the midst of this cluster.

pages.searchText: Episode 87 — The Randhawas Join the Khalsa how S. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie Episode About how S. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie Episode 87 begins by locating the Randhawa villages near Chamunda and Kairon Nangal, where a few among these Randhawas joined the Khalsa Panth and accepted the sharpened discipline that came with initiation. Armed and newly resolute, they are remembered as people who refused quiet submission and started waylaying (the Mughals) on the Lahore-Delhi highway, turning local roads into contested ground. That boldness drew an immediate response, because the Mughals launched an attack to eliminate them once the Randhawas became an open Khalsa challenge rather than a hidden sympathy.

Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie A few among these Randhawas joined the Khalsa Panth, After initiating themselves and ordaining the Khalsa armour. (3) As was ordained by Satguru (Guru Gobind Singh), They resolved to follow the Guru's ordained path. Joining the Khalsa Panth, they resorted to the path of fighting, And started waylaying (the Mughals) on the Lahore-Delhi highway. (4) Adopting the same tactics as followed by the Khalsa Singhs, They also raised the pitch of their fighting (against the Mughals). Hearing the news of their daily skirmishes and fights, The Mughals launched an attack to eliminate them. (5) These Singhs did not have any fortified fortress, So they would escape and hide themselves in the wilds, And in the swamps and ravines in their surroundings. (6) Whenever they heard about the impending invasion of the Mughals, They would desert their homes and hide in the wilds. Their families which were left behind in their village, Would somehow survive by mixing with the other people. (7) The Singhs would not stay at their homes during day time, But they would return home with the fall of night. So during the first Mughal raid the Singhs survived, And the Mughal force had to return empty-handed. (8) As they had to return empty handed from their expedition. Feeling crestfallen like a hunting tiger missing his prey, They stepped up their efforts to eliminate the Singhs. (9) As the Mughal troops were on the prowl to kill the Singhs, The Singhs, somehow, tried to mark their time. The Singhs fantasized that a time would come, When the Mughals too would have to run for their lives. (10) They (Singhs) too would have sovereignty over their land, And would collect revenue from their own territory. They were facing hardships in anticipation of that hour. (11)

pages.searchText: The Plot to Destroy the Randhawa Singhs how S. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie Episode About how S. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie The surviving Singhs did not disappear into anonymity; by taking refuge yet keeping their dress code and identity intact, they preserved both visible Sikh form and the possibility of renewed resistance. That persistence provoked local enemies into conspiracy, and the page says plainly that they wanted to get the Randhawa Singhs massacred before the line could gather strength again. Their greed matched their hostility, arguing that they should first get the Singhs land transferred to their names, and so they unfolded their (evil) plan before the Mughals as both political intrigue and property seizure.

Thus, they passed their time somehow and kept surviving, By taking refuge yet keeping their dress code and identity intact. (12) Chaupai: Now, dear readers, listen to the episode of those Singhs, Whom the enemies of (Sikh Panth) got massacred. There was a village Shahzada? of Sultani* residents, Who, though claiming to be Hindus, behaved like Muslims. (13) These Sultanis contrived with the Muslims Kalals, Who happened to be in service of the Mughals. Both of them conspired to agree on a resolution, That they should get the Randhawa Singhs massacred. (14) Since these Randhawa Singhs have fallen into their trap, They should first get the Singhs land transferred to their names. (After getting this landed property entitlement, transferred), They should get the Singhs progeny eliminated even to the extent of foeticide. (15) In this way, they would earn the pleasure of the Mughals, And they would receive robes of honour from the Mughals. Thus, contemplating the commission of both these crimes secretly, They unfolded their (evil) plan before the Mughals. (16) Dohra: So whatever proposals they made to the Mughals, The latter accepted their proposal ad verbatim. It not only included great honours and foeticide of Singh females, But transfer of ownership of (Singh) lands to their names as well. (17) Chaupai: The Mughals were already looking for such an opportunity, Whereby they could carryout a massacre of the Singhs. So as this Sultani-Kalal duo kept on spotting the Singhs, They wished to seek more concessions from the Mughals. (18) Dohra: The Singhs did not receive any information, That their own neighbours were informing against them. So they kept on hiding in the wilds during the day, And returning to their homes at night. (19) Chaupai: Whichever night or day was fixed for the Singhs assembly, The Singhs would assemble at a place on the fixed night. A wicked informer sent an information against the Singhs assembly, Who happened to be a Sultani from their own village. (20) * This Couplet is incomplete in handwritten Manuscripts.

pages.searchText: The Siege of the Randhawa Village how S. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie Episode About how S. Tara Singh Attained Mantra ie The betrayal becomes public when the informer reported about the Singhs assembly to the neighbouring Jats, turning private knowledge into the opening move of a coordinated assault. Soon the Mughal troops laid a siege to the village so tightly that not even a dog could escape through the siege, making survival depend less on strength than on the mercy of encircling enemies who had none. The massacre that follows is remembered through the arrest and killing of elders, especially by laying their hands on the fourteen Sikh elders, after which the page asks in grief whether anybody survived this ordeal out of their progeny.

(22) With death looming large over their heads, Where could the Singhs seek shelter on such a night? The wicked informer having reported the Singhs's assembly, The Mughal troops laid a siege to the village. (23) As the Mughal troops took positions all around the village, The wicked Hindu Jat peasants too reached there. That not even a dog could escape through the siege. So both the Sultanis and the Mughals massacred the Singhs, Laying their hands on the fourteen Sikh elders, They massacred all of them (on the spot). Whosoever else they came across from their families, They slaughtered those taking them to be Singh's progeny. (26) Whichever Singh or their progeny came into sight, They slaughtered him there and then with their swords. He might have survived out of their progeny. (27) In this way, the Majhail Singhs had endured all these ordeals, In the hope that their defiance would establish Khalsa Panth's sovereignty. They had hoped for a sovereignty at the cost of their lives, That is why they achieved sovereignty in due course of time. (28) Somebody might raise this question (about those Singhs), Did anybody survive this ordeal out of their progeny? I would try to give a hint about their survival. (29)

pages.searchText: Episode 88 — Nawab Kapoor Singh Enters the Narrative Nawab Kapoor Singh Enters the Narrative Episode of Randhawas (Singhs) of Chamunday and Kairon Natigiian This transition page moves out of the last Randhawa material and into the new leadership story, saying that after Sahib Singh’s survival the narrative now turns toward Nawab Kapoor Singh as a defining figure in the Panth’s next phase. The page functions as an overt episode handoff, using the older heading material to recall the strain after Banda Singh and to introduce Mughal reaction to renewed Sikh resilience. Its final movement introduces the reaction of the Mughal side to renewed Sikh resilience, making the page the hinge into Kapoor Singh’s contested rise.

They could congregate at the holy shrines of Dera Baba Nanak* and Khandoor Sahib, As well as at Taran Taran and other holy Sikh shrines. (6) Exhorting the Singhs to hold congregations fearlessly, At all those places which had been the abodes of the Gurus. The Mughals would not only exempt these congregations from taxation, But they themselves would provide security to these gatherings. (7) In this way they won the confidence of the Khalsa Panth, By holding out several kinds of promises and assurances. They invited the needy among the Sikhs to approach them. (8) Approaching the veterans Baba Binod Singh and Kahan Singh, They won their allegiance by presenting moneybags, Allowing them to keep a contingent of five hundred Singhs each, They won the support of many other Singhs with their help. (9) The Mughals managed to win over the Khalsa Singhs. But still they were as much scared of Banda Singh, As a (timid) quail feels scared of a (ferocious) hawk. (10) Even as the Mughals were marking time (for the right opportunity), The Khalsa Panth, too, was looking for the opportune moment, As the Mughals kept on offering financial doles, The Singhs kept on receiving these doles at Guru Chak daily. S. Darbara Singh? who had been the Diwan? of the Khalsa Panth, Had also been the treasurer of Khalsa Panth's finances. (12) Since he was highly venerated among the Khalsa Panth, He used to keep all the factions in good humour. Since no body considered him as his rival, He used to disburse uniforms to every one. (13)

The Khalsa Panth went on flourishing in this way, Even as they kept on indulging in factional fights as well. (14) [They (the Mughals) wished to eliminate the Singhs] No sooner did the Mughals manage to capture Banda Singh, Than they changed their stance (towards the Singhs). They, now, were too keen to eliminate the (Tat Khalsa) Singhs, Along with all others (Bandhayees) in one single stroke. (1) The (Tat Khalsa) Singhs, far from falling into their trap, Moved their camp farther from Guru Chak (into countryside). As the Singhs kept shifting their positions and locations, The Mughals also got obsessed with chasing the Singhs. (2) Where they could take cover and fight back. Neither did Singhs had possession of any mountains, From where they could fight the Mughals from a vantage-point. (3) At many places, Singhs had a straight fight with the Mughals, But sacrificed their lives when pressed too much. The Khalsa Panth landed itself in such a helpless situation, That they had to seek shelter in the wilds and ravines. (4) Banda Singh had let out a curse on the Khalsa Panth, When he had to confine himself in the fort (at Gurdas Nangal). The Khalsa Panth had to bear the consequences of their sinful act, Of not reaching out to the support of Banda Singh. (5) In the bands of small and big numbers. They started marking time somehow or the other, Either in each other's vicinity or at a distance. (6) In between this episode of Singh's (helpless ordeal), Let me narrate another episode as well. After that I would narrate the episode of Nawabship, As it came to be conferred on S. Kapoor Singh. (7)

pages.searchText: Episode 89 — Mulkhayyas, Bivaste, and Dinikhudai Mulkhayyas, Bivaste, and Dinikhudai Episode of Randhawas (Singhs) of Chamunday and Kairon Natigiian This hinge opens Episode 89, closing the Nawab Kapoor Singh material and introducing a new conflict. The episode begins with Mulkhayyas, Bivaste, and Dinikhudai, where clerical pressure and political mobilization gather into a fresh anti-Khalsa campaign. From there the page sets up Aslam Khan at Lahore and the wider agitation around him, serving as the bridge from Episode 88 into the next martial and ideological confrontation.

pages.searchText: Episode About Nawab Kapoor Singh, The Nihang Chief Nawab Kapoor Singh, The Nihang Chief Episode About Nawab Kapoor Singh, The Nihang Chief Episode 89 Episode About Nawab Kapoor Singh, The Nihang Chief (Dear readers) listen to the episode of volunteer Muslim recruits, Who kept themselves planted on the battlefield for the Islamic cause. Who sacrificed their lives for the cause of their Islamic faith, Together with Muslim general populace and the Islamic fundamentalists. (1) So listen to the episode of all those Islamic volunteers, And the plight through which these fundamentalists passed. Aslam Khan, being sick of fighting, retreated to Lahore, As the whole of Punjab region showed defiance to his rule. (2) The Mughals failed to collect any taxes from their region, As they alleged that the Khalsa had ransacked the whole area. His troops deserted him for want of money and wages, And who pays taxes/revenue without the fear of troops? (3) Even the emperor ceases to be a friendly supporter without money, And money comes only through revenue collections from the country. First Banda Singh had harassed and robbed this region, Then the Khalsa Panth Singhs ransacked the people. (4) As the emperor did not receive the revenue from (Lahore), He dispatched the Mughal force for collecting the revenues. This contingent consisted of one thousand horse - mounted troops, Which was commanded by a couple of Pathan Muslim warriors. (5) Attaullan Khan? and Mohabbat Khan? were these two Pathan warriors, Who were both very handsome and muscular in their looks. They were reputed to be great soldiers, And had their residences in the city of Faridabad. (6) From there (Faridabad )as these two warriors came to Lahore, Listen to the developments that took place there. The Muslim subjects (of the Punjab) came with a petition, With a faith that (these two warriors would listen to their woes. (7) Members of the Muslim clergy and several other mendicants, Pressed the Nawab of Lahore unitedly (for a firm action). Holding an audience at the Court of the Nawab, All the United Muslims made joint efforts (to retaliate). (8)
