(29) The agreed tax money could not be realized for payment, As offerings declined due to the arrival of Mughal troops. As the destined moment of truth had arrived near. (30) How could the Khalsa Singhs avoid picking up a fight, When they had developed a compulsive addiction for violence? It gave them immense pleasure to indulge in violence, Since they had became addict to fighting since their origin. (31) So Lakhpat Rai, arriving with troops at Amritsar, Confronted a few odd Singhs present there. Capturing these Singhs after a minor skirmish, He presented their captive Singhs before the Nawab. (32) Those who were prominent among the Khalsa Panth, He captured all of them along with Mani Singh, The whole situation took such a turn for the worst, That the opposite happened to what was intended. (33) As these Singhs were made to stand before the Nawab, The members of the Muslim clergy instigated the Nawab. When the Nawab demanded the payment of tax, The Singhs promised to sign a surety bond for making payment later. (34) As many financiers came forward to stand surety for the Singhs, Mani Singh prohibited all of them for standing any surety. The Singhs would neither pay any tax at present, Mani Singh felt that the long-awaited moment had arrived, When he would be able to fulfill the congregation's prophecy. He would wish to get his body dismembered bit by bit, Thus making his intention clear through a declaration. (36) Since the Khalsa Panth had no money to make a payment, He would instead offer his own life in place of money. The people of Lahore came in a body in support of Mani Singh, And stood with money in cash to pay the tax. (37)

pages.title: Clerical Verdict and the Order to Dismember Mani Singh
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi
pages.snippet: Once Mani Singh refuses conversion and rejects compromise, the Nawab turns to qazis and mullas to frame the punishment in legal and religious terms. The Sikh prisoners remain firm, insisting that they will not abandon their path even under
pages.searchText: Clerical Verdict and the Order to Dismember Mani Singh Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Once Mani Singh refuses conversion and rejects compromise, the Nawab turns to qazis and mullas to frame the punishment in legal and religious terms. The Sikh prisoners remain firm, insisting that they will not abandon their path even under the threat of exemplary violence. The verdict that emerges is designed to terrify. Mani Singh is sentenced to be dismembered limb by limb, a ruling that echoes the congregation’s earlier prophecy and transforms a court punishment into the literal fulfillment of words already spoken over him. At the place of execution, Mani Singh shows unshaken composure and even corrects the executioners when they begin too crudely. By insisting that the sentence be carried out joint by joint, he reveals both the horror of the order and the extraordinary steadiness with which he meets it.

pages.title: Realising the inevitability of the moment of making a sacrifice,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi
pages.snippet: Realising the inevitability of the moment of making a sacrifice, Mani Singh abandoned every possibility of a negotiation. He believed that Singh congregation's prophecy could never go in vain, Even if a million attempts were made to put it
pages.searchText: Realising the inevitability of the moment of making a sacrifice, Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Realising the inevitability of the moment of making a sacrifice, Mani Singh abandoned every possibility of a negotiation. He believed that Singh congregation's prophecy could never go in vain, Even if a million attempts were made to put it off. (38) Since the moment for the fulfillment of prophetic cause had approached. Summoning the members of the Muslim clergy and theologians, He sought their advice (for the execution of Mani Singh). (39) The Nawab asked the Singhs to get himself converted into Islam, If they wished their life to be spared by the Mughals. The Singhs remarked that they would never betray their faith, As they could forego many lives for the sake of their faith. (40) The Nawab asked the clergy to suggest ways of executing the Singhs, Exactly as it was prescribed in the Book of Koran. Then, as interpreted and directed by the theologians, The Islamic judge pronounced the manner of execution. (41) Mani Singh's whole body be dismembered limb by limb, So that it became a deterrent for the whole world. What was predestined was expressed through the cleric's words, Even as the Islamic judge became an instrument to unfold that curse. (42) That is why this manner of Mani Singh's execution, Came to be quoted from the books of the Islamic text. Since whosoever tried to subvert these would perish. (43) Then the Nawab of Lahore made a declaration, That Mani Singh's body be dismembered bit by bit. The official executioners, getting hold of Mani Singh instantly. Made him sit in the central place known as Nikhas* square. (44) At this Mani Singh reprimanded his executioners, Did they not know the meaning of cutting limb by limb? (45) As he would go on demarcating each organ of his body, They should go on chopping off his organs with their knives. Directing them to first chopp off the nodal parts of his fingers, Thereafter they should sever his fingers from their joints. (46)

pages.title: Mani Singh Endures Dismemberment Joint by Joint
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi
pages.snippet: The execution continues exactly as Bhai Mani Singh had demanded: joint by joint rather than in a single crude stroke. After the first cuts at the fingers and wrists, the butchers move on to elbows and shoulders while he remains absorbed in
pages.searchText: Mani Singh Endures Dismemberment Joint by Joint Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi The execution continues exactly as Bhai Mani Singh had demanded: joint by joint rather than in a single crude stroke. After the first cuts at the fingers and wrists, the butchers move on to elbows and shoulders while he remains absorbed in prayer and refuses to let the sentence be softened. The page dwells on the terrible precision of the punishment. Each limb is reduced piece by piece, yet Mani Singh keeps reciting Gurbani and accepts the ordeal as a conscious martyrdom rather than a defeat inflicted by the state. Witnesses who had come merely to watch are shaken by what they see. The executioners grow afraid as the martyr’s steadiness turns the spectacle of violence into a public testimony of Sikh resolve.

pages.title: Then, after getting his each finger cut from three places,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi
pages.snippet: Then, after getting his each finger cut from three places, He got his hands severed from the point of wrists. After that, whereas the butcher intended to dismember his shoulders, Bhai Mani Singh insisted on getting his arms cut from the elb
pages.searchText: Then, after getting his each finger cut from three places, Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Then, after getting his each finger cut from three places, He got his hands severed from the point of wrists. After that, whereas the butcher intended to dismember his shoulders, Bhai Mani Singh insisted on getting his arms cut from the elbows. (47) After the elbows, he got his shoulders chopped off, Getting the left shoulder-severed after his right shoulder. He got his second hand fingers cut in the same manner, Thus, getting his fingers and thumb severed inch by inch. (48) Just as both right and left arms were got severed, Similarly he got his feet severed inch by inch. Then, as the nodes of his two feet were got severed, Similarly he got his heel joints and knees dismembered. (49) The executioners witnessing this such a gory spectacle, They started gasping for breath with tension. They had heard about a mystic (Siddha) known as Dhandli, One of whose disciples was harassed by some people. This harassed disciple had let out a curse at one of the cities, Which sank a cluster of eighteen towns in an instant. (51) So, the executioner, taking out his sword from its sheath, Slashed out Mani Singh's head from his neck. Bhai Mani Singh, being engrossed in the recitation of Gurbani, His (mortal) human body did not register any pain. (52) Since his soul had got alienated from his body, His soul kept on reciting Gurbani even after (physical) death. Carrying on with the recitation of Sukhmani hymns, His soul crossed all boundaries of birth and death. (53) Although every human being is bound to shed his mortal frame, They alone die a meaningful and successful death, Who shed their mortal frame voluntarily in an instant, While keeping their communion with the Divine Lord intact. (54) I (Kabir) bask in the glory of its bliss, It is through the shedding of this mortal body, That one gets into perfect communion with the Divine.

pages.title: The Poem Exalts Mani Singh Above Earlier Martyrs
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi
pages.snippet: After describing the final cuts, the narrative turns from the scene of execution to praise. It compares Bhai Mani Singh with famous sufferers such as Mansur, yet insists that Mani Singh bore a still harsher trial because his body was severe
pages.searchText: The Poem Exalts Mani Singh Above Earlier Martyrs Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi After describing the final cuts, the narrative turns from the scene of execution to praise. It compares Bhai Mani Singh with famous sufferers such as Mansur, yet insists that Mani Singh bore a still harsher trial because his body was severed joint by joint before death. The page argues that he remained greater than Mansur because he kept Sikhi intact under torture and refused every inducement to break faith. His martyrdom is treated not as a private death but as the fulfillment of the congregation’s prophecy and the triumph of disciplined devotion. The poet closes by ranking him among the foremost Sikh martyrs and by fixing the event in remembered history. The tone becomes commemorative, preparing the transition from the execution itself to the wider aftermath of Mani Singh’s death.

pages.searchText: Dohra: (The Sufi saint) Mansur! had become very famous in the world, Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Dohra: (The Sufi saint) Mansur! had become very famous in the world, When both of his hands were chopped off in a single stroke. Bhai Mani Singh had undergone a far more grievous pain, By getting his body dismembered limb by limb. (55) A sage known as Suli Rishi preserved his human body, Despite being executed by the executioner's knife. Since Bhai Mani Singh did not preserve his body, He came to be known as a far greater martyr. (56) He kept his faith in Sikhism steadfast and intact. As the people of the world regretted and mourned his death, The Sikhs felt victorious and proud at his sacrifice. (57) As Bhai Mani Singh was able to keep and uphold his faith, The Sikh congregation's prophetic curse proved to be true. His sacrifice making him a chief among the Sikh martyrs, Ensured a seat with the Sahibzadas in the Divine court. (58) The supreme sacrifice which Bhai Mani Singh attained, Took place exactly in the year seventeen hundred and ninety-four, Rattan Singh (the author) has recorded this episode, As his father had given an eyewitness account of it. (59) (Bhai Mani Singh's sacrifice) in the words of a contemporary Bard: No one could excel Mani Singh (in sacrifice), Either from the rich or from the poor as well. Kabit: Being the greatest Sikh among the Sikhs, Being the greatest spiritual devotee among the devout, Bhai Mani Singh could be declared as unbeatable in faith, In the annals of Sikh faith throughout, Having earned a great applause in the world, Having sacrificed his life for the sake of religion, He got himself slaughtered for the sake of faith, Without displaying a trace of the slightest fear. Sikhs having been delighted with his sacrifice, The wicked having been contaminated with his act, With the sword of his spiritual enlightenment. He who claimed himself to be a Gursikh, No one could excel Mani Singh in sacrifice, Either from amongst the rich or the poor as well. (1)

pages.title: From Mani Singh’s Death to the Wider Persecution of the Khalsa
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi
pages.snippet: This page is a hinge between two narrative movements. It first recalls that Mani Singh accepted death after recognizing the weight of the Sikhs’ curse and that his body was carried to Nikhas Chowk Lahore, where the sentence was fulfilled as
pages.searchText: From Mani Singh’s Death to the Wider Persecution of the Khalsa Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi Episode About Nawab Kapor Singh Bhujangi This page is a hinge between two narrative movements. It first recalls that Mani Singh accepted death after recognizing the weight of the Sikhs’ curse and that his body was carried to Nikhas Chowk Lahore, where the sentence was fulfilled as a public warning. The text then notes that companions with Mani Singh were also seized and executed, widening the tragedy beyond one celebrated martyr. Their deaths show that the authorities intended to punish an entire community rather than a single defiant leader. From there the poem opens the next episode by broadening into a survey of state persecution under Khan Bahadur and Zakariya Khan. Different methods of execution, mutilation, and terror are introduced so that Mani Singh’s shahidi becomes the prelude to a longer campaign against the Khalsa.

pages.title: Divine Judgment and Nadir Shah’s Advance on Lahore
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom
pages.snippet: The poem argues that the mass persecution of the Khalsa created such an outcry that it reached the divine court itself. Heavenly judgment now turns against the Mughal order that had tormented the Sikhs and prepares the way for a devastating
pages.searchText: Divine Judgment and Nadir Shah’s Advance on Lahore Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom Episode About Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom The poem argues that the mass persecution of the Khalsa created such an outcry that it reached the divine court itself. Heavenly judgment now turns against the Mughal order that had tormented the Sikhs and prepares the way for a devastating invader from the northwest. In that frame, Nadir Shah reaches Lahore while Zakariya Khan is forced into humiliating submission and heavy payment. The invasion is presented as punishment for tyranny, not merely as another military episode in imperial politics. At the same time the turmoil opens roads and supply lines to Sikh action. The Singhs begin striking traffic along the Kabul-Delhi road, using the confusion of empire to challenge the very state that had tried to exterminate them.

pages.title: The Khalsa Reads the Invasion as a Divinely Timed Opening
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom
pages.snippet: This page explains how the Khalsa interpreted the Persian invasion. Since Mughal power was already devouring itself, the Singhs say that one thorn removes a thorn: one violent force can uproot another and expose the weakness of Delhi’s pers
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Reads the Invasion as a Divinely Timed Opening Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom Episode About Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom This page explains how the Khalsa interpreted the Persian invasion. Since Mughal power was already devouring itself, the Singhs say that one thorn removes a thorn: one violent force can uproot another and expose the weakness of Delhi’s persecuting regime. Prophetic language then frames the crisis as long foreseen. A hound from Kabul is said to have descended upon Hindustan, and the page links that prophecy to the chance for the Khalsa to regroup, shout Akal, and step forward without waiting for favor from any court. Kapoor Singh emerges as the leader who recognizes the moment clearly. He urges the Panth to treat the invasion not as chaos alone but as an opening in which the persecuted community can recover initiative and act with confidence.

pages.searchText: Nadir Shah Carries Off Delhi’s Treasures Nadir Shah Carries Off Delhi's Treasures Episode About Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom The poem now catalogs the plunder taken by Nadir Shah in language of astonishment and excess. At the center stands the Takht-e-Taus worth nine crores, alongside jewels, pearls, and courtly marvels that symbolize the prestige of the Mughal throne. Other prized objects are listed to deepen the sense of imperial humiliation: rare gems, storied heirlooms, and even celebrated curiosities associated with musicians and kings. The conqueror strips away both treasure and aura, turning Delhi’s claims to greatness into portable spoil. By ending on written transfers of territory and payment, the page shows that the loss was political as well as material. Lahore and its surrounding provinces appear less like secure Mughal possessions than prizes redistributed by a stronger hand.

pages.title: The Scale of Plunder and Slaughter in Delhi
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom
pages.snippet: This page sums up the devastation left by the invasion in stark, collective terms. The poet says that wealth beyond counting was carried off from the Mughal dominions and that the destruction of Delhi exposed the fragility of a court that h
pages.searchText: The Scale of Plunder and Slaughter in Delhi Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom Episode About Bhai Mani Singh's Martyrdom This page sums up the devastation left by the invasion in stark, collective terms. The poet says that wealth beyond counting was carried off from the Mughal dominions and that the destruction of Delhi exposed the fragility of a court that had imagined itself unassailable. Human loss is counted alongside treasure. The narrative highlights that seventy thousand killed in Delhi were largely defenseless people, making the catastrophe a moral indictment of imperial failure rather than a mere change of rulers. The conclusion is that the Mughals had effectively ruined themselves through their own corruption and violence. That judgment prepares the reader for the next episode, where the Khalsa’s suffering is again placed before the divine court and answered through history.

pages.title: Nadir Shah Hears Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Broken
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nadar Shah
pages.snippet: Nadir Shah asks Khan Bahadur who these Sikhs are after hearing repeated reports of their resistance. The answer begins with admiration: the Khalsa endure hunger and hardship, go without comfort in heat and cold, and still keep fighting with
pages.searchText: Nadir Shah Hears Why the Khalsa Cannot Be Broken Nadar Shah Episode About Nadar Shah Nadir Shah asks Khan Bahadur who these Sikhs are after hearing repeated reports of their resistance. The answer begins with admiration: the Khalsa endure hunger and hardship, go without comfort in heat and cold, and still keep fighting with the energy of people sustained by conviction rather than provisions. The page then sharpens that praise into martial proportion. The poem insists that each Singh fights a hundred, not because of numbers or equipment, but because death has lost its power to frighten those who see struggle for the faith as honorable. Khan Bahadur traces their origin back to Guru Nanak and admits that Mughal injustice against the Gurus has brought its own punishment. Nadir Shah therefore concludes that those under God’s protection cannot truly be conquered by worldly rulers.

pages.title: After Nadir Leaves, Zakariya Khan Turns Again on the Singhs
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nadar Shah
pages.snippet: The page first closes the Nadir Shah episode with a reflective note: some persecutors died in the turmoil, while others survived only long enough to continue unfinished violence. The poet presents this as received tradition, heard from elde
pages.searchText: After Nadir Leaves, Zakariya Khan Turns Again on the Singhs Nadar Shah Episode About Nadar Shah The page first closes the Nadir Shah episode with a reflective note: some persecutors died in the turmoil, while others survived only long enough to continue unfinished violence. The poet presents this as received tradition, heard from elders who remembered both judgment and survival. It then pivots decisively after Nadir left for Kabul. Humiliated rather than corrected, Khan Bahadur and Zakariya Khan return their rage toward the Sikhs and prepare a renewed campaign to scour the land of keshdhari Singhs. That transition matters because it marks a change from imperial collapse to local repression. Foreign invasion passes, but the machinery of anti-Sikh persecution remains in place and begins operating with even more bitterness than before.

pages.searchText: The Singhs Survive in Hiding, Hunger, and Motion Khalsa's Petition Being eae in the Divine Cups Episode About Khalsa's Petition Being eae in the Divine Cups The persecution drives the community into every kind of concealment. Some are hiding in ravines and forests, others in distant villages or among sympathetic households, while still others try to pass as ordinary cultivators living close to the soil. The page emphasizes repeated hunger as part of this wandering life. Many eat only every second or fourth day, count wild greens and bark as food, and treat even a little salt as a luxury when the state has made normal living impossible. Yet the Singhs do not simply disappear. Informers trail them, soldiers are summoned whenever they are spotted, and the Nawab’s written orders begin turning daily survival into a moving battle against a hostile countryside.

(14) While every informer against a Singh was entitled to a ten-rupee reward, Every successful killer of a Singh was entitled to rupees fifty. With such a big temptation thrown by the Mughal rulers, The result was the extermination of Singhs on a large scale. (15)

pages.searchText: Zakariya Khan’s Proclamation Turns Persecution into Policy Khalsa's Petition Being eae in the Divine Cups Episode About Khalsa's Petition Being eae in the Divine Cups This page shows repression taking formal legal shape. A written proclamation across Lahore orders that even Sikhs quietly farming or trading are not to be spared if they keep unshorn hair, turning visible Sikh identity into a mark for state violence. Bounties and permissions follow from that decree. Informers are rewarded, looters are indulged, and people are encouraged to hand over Singhs for questioning, imprisonment, or death, which lets private greed work together with official persecution. The poem then personalizes the suffering through stories of betrayal, family loss, and the seizure of elders linked with Bhai Taru Singh. By combining policy with memory, the page shows how anti-Sikh violence spread from courtly order into village society.

pages.searchText: Massa Ranghar’s Sacrilege Sets Up the Next Retaliation Khalsa's Petition Being eae in the Divine Cups Episode About Khalsa's Petition Being eae in the Divine Cups The late persecution episode is summarized through notorious names and local memory. Rama Randhawa’s territory becomes a proverb for danger, while stories circulate about villages where even travel feels more dangerous than surviving on wild food. The page then names the outrage that will define the next turn of the narrative: Massa Ranghar desecrated the Darbar Sahib and other informers helped deliver Sikhs, including Bhai Taru Singh, into Mughal hands. The violence is now not only political but openly sacrilegious. Finally the poem turns toward response. By introducing the episode of Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh, it signals that the long record of complaint and persecution is about to give way to remembered Sikh retaliation against Massa Ranghar.

(26) Another tyrant of Singhs was a Sandhu Jat Sahib Rai, Who happened to be an inhabitant of villege Naushehra. He killed a large number of Singhs after capturing them, And dispatched their severed heads to Lahore. (27) Becoming an informer against Bhai Taru Singh, He was responsible for Mughal troops raid on Taru Singh. These troops, after a raid, arrested Bhai Taru Singh, And took him to Lahore for executing him. (28) Episode 97 The Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh? (The Way they severed Massa Rangar's® head) (Dear readers) listen to the account of chivalrous feats of the Khalsa, How their miniscule minority conquered the Mughals in majority. Included among these chosen ones was the (Author's) grandfather, Who had taken a vow to sacrifice his life for his religion. (1) It was Nawab Khan Bahadur* (Zakariya Khan) of Lahore, Who had suppressed the Khasa Panth very much. Calling an assembly of all the representatives of the state, He had issued such a written proclamation at Lahore: (20 That whosoever provided a shelter to the Singhs, He would have to forego his own precious life. Whosoever did not inform about the Singh's approach, He would also have to be divested of his existence. (3) Whosoever established a relationship of blood with the Singhs, He would have to accept conversion to Islam. Whosoever handed over provisions to the Singhs, He would be converted to Islam for this offence. (4)

pages.title: Zakaria Khan’s Proclamation Deepens the Anti-Sikh Terror
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: Zakaria Khan’s proclamation turns the persecution of the Sikhs into a wider social campaign. Villagers are pressured to inform, those who shelter Singhs risk destruction, and whole districts become unsafe as fear and greed begin serving the
pages.searchText: Zakaria Khan’s Proclamation Deepens the Anti-Sikh Terror Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Zakaria Khan’s proclamation turns the persecution of the Sikhs into a wider social campaign. Villagers are pressured to inform, those who shelter Singhs risk destruction, and whole districts become unsafe as fear and greed begin serving the Nawab’s policy. The result is another scattering of the Khalsa. Some flee into forests, hills, and distant courts, while others survive by concealment and mobility because normal village life has been poisoned by surveillance and bounty seeking. Within that crisis the narrative points toward Mehtab Singh’s exile and grief. Even from Jaipur he continues hearing of Punjab’s misery, which prepares the moral ground for direct action against sacrilege and oppression.

pages.title: He created a scarce among the general populace.

Conferring robes of honour on some of the people, Chaupai: After this, people started supplying information about Singhs, Some of them even getting the Singhs arrested themselves. So miserable became the plight of Singhs (in Punjab). (5) Presenting Singhs bodies before the Mughals after killing them, They used to get rewarded with gold coins for their deeds. Since a confrontation developed between the people and the Singhs, The Singhs also started hitting back in retaliation. (7) Since the Singhs would take a refuge somewhere after hit and run, The wicked opponents would soon complain to the Mughals. Hearing the complaint, the Mughals would soon raid the place, Razing the whole village, sheltering the Singhs, to ashes. (8) If the Singhs took refuge in the wilds, leaving the sheltering villagers, The Mughal troops would start ruining the surrounding villages. At this, getting desperate at such a devastation, The Singhs abandoned the idea or taking refuge in their own country. (9) So, while some of the Singhs took refuge in the wilds in the South, Some others took refuge in the eastern mountains. Those who remained within the territory of their own state, Felt as scared as the quails in the presence of hawks. (10) Dohra: My grandfather, leaving the territory of his own state, He reached the city of Jaipur in the State of Rajasthan. After arranging a meeting with the state chief, He managed to get employment in the state service. (11) Chaupai: As more Singhs reached Jaipur after hearing of Mehtab Singh's employment, Mehtab Singh expressed his concern for his motherland. He enquired about the latest news from his homeland, And the areas which the Mughal troops had occupied. (12) The Singhs replied that it was difficult to describe, The atrocities that the Mughals had committed there. Neither could their tongue dare to utter those brutalities, Nor would his ears be able to listen to those. (13)

pages.title: News of Harmandir Sahib’s Desecration Provokes Mehtab Singh
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: The next outrage surpasses ordinary persecution. Reports spread of the desecration of Harmandir Sahib after Massa Ranghar takes possession of the sacred precincts and treats the shrine as a place for worldly revelry. Mehtab Singh’s anger be
pages.searchText: News of Harmandir Sahib’s Desecration Provokes Mehtab Singh Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The next outrage surpasses ordinary persecution. Reports spread of the desecration of Harmandir Sahib after Massa Ranghar takes possession of the sacred precincts and treats the shrine as a place for worldly revelry. Mehtab Singh’s anger becomes the center of the page. He cannot bear that Amritsar should suffer such humiliation while the Khalsa remains scattered, and he challenges the Singhs around him to answer dishonor with courage. The conversation is therefore not only about one enemy official but about Sikh responsibility itself. By turning grief into rebuke, the page prepares for a mission that will demand both stealth and martyr-like resolve.

pages.title: Neither could their lungs dare to describe those indignities,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: Neither could their lungs dare to describe those indignities, Nor could their hearts contain those in silence. Being caught between the devil and the deep sea, They could neither retaliate, nor bear with those indignities. (14) The Mughals
pages.searchText: Neither could their lungs dare to describe those indignities, Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Neither could their lungs dare to describe those indignities, Nor could their hearts contain those in silence. Being caught between the devil and the deep sea, They could neither retaliate, nor bear with those indignities. (14) The Mughals had committed the greatest sacrilege, In the sacred precincts of Darbar Sahib at Amritsar. The chief among the Mughals had kept a Courtesan, (For lewd dancing) in the sanctum sanctorum of Harmandir. (15) And Massa Ranghar was the name of this chief. Being a great sinner and a notorious evil doer, He had been desecrating the sanctity of Harmandir. (16) Hearing of this desecration, Mehtab Singh felt greatly incensed, As if he had been stung by a poisonous scorpion. He asked if there were no Singhs present there, Who could crush the head of such a defiler? (17) Had the Singhs abandoned their mission to defend the truth, Or Had they abandoned their mission of performing noble deeds? Counter-questioning him for his flamboyant bravado, Singhs asked, Why did he himself shirk from that daring challenge? (18) As he himself had fled away for saving his own life, How could he blame others for not facing the challenge? As he had saved his life by fleeing from the scene, So had others fled away following his footsteps. (19) Since all the Singhs had run away to save their lives, Hardly any Singh could be found there in Punjab. Since no body had heard of Singhs being there, People were poking fun at the so-called Singhs. (20) Since the Mughal Nawab had totally eliminated the Khalsa Panth, No Singh was supposed to be alive in the whole country. All those Singhs had perished who used to wage a war daily, As well as those Khalsa Singhs who used to meditate on God's name. (21) All those Singhs had become extinct who used to recite gurbani, As well as those who used to loot and slaughter the Mughals. There were no more such Singhs as observed the daily Sikh code of conduct,

pages.title: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh Accept the Mission
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: The taunts and lament now harden into decision. Sukha Singh joins Mehtab Singh and the two accept that the duty of striking Massa Ranghar cannot be postponed to some safer season. They therefore take leave of the Khalsa with full awareness
pages.searchText: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh Accept the Mission Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The taunts and lament now harden into decision. Sukha Singh joins Mehtab Singh and the two accept that the duty of striking Massa Ranghar cannot be postponed to some safer season. They therefore take leave of the Khalsa with full awareness that they may not return. The page treats their resolve as readiness for martyrdom, because success will require entering hostile ground where capture is almost certain if the plan fails. Preparation follows resolve. Disguise, secrecy, and a swift approach toward Amritsar are chosen so that devotion to the shrine can be expressed through bold but disciplined action.

pages.title: Nor were there any Singhs who sacrificed their lives with the shouts of Akal.
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: Nor were there any Singhs who sacrificed their lives with the shouts of Akal. Only the likes of him, the fugitive Singhs, had been left behind, Who had hastily escaped to save their skins. (22) Hearing this, S. Mehtab Singh felt so much mor
pages.searchText: Nor were there any Singhs who sacrificed their lives with the shouts of Akal. Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Nor were there any Singhs who sacrificed their lives with the shouts of Akal. Only the likes of him, the fugitive Singhs, had been left behind, Who had hastily escaped to save their skins. (22) Hearing this, S. Mehtab Singh felt so much mortified, As if he had been stung by a poisonous scorpion. So much mortified did he feel by these remarks, That he resolved to sacrifice his life without any fear. (23) There was one Sukha Singh of village Mari Kamboki, Who belonged to the community of carpenters. He volunteered to accompany Mehtab Singh, As he too was a devout Sikh of the Guru. (24) Both these Singhs bade farewell to the Singhs with Fateh, After seeking their permission for their mission with reverence. They declared their resolve to decimate the Mughals, And thereafter touch the sacred feet of Khalsa Panth. (25) If they sacrificed their lives for the Guru's cause, They would feel blessed both in life and death. Curse be on the mother and the father of a Singh, Who felt scared of fighting against the Mughals. (26) Why should a Singh be scared of death, A Singh was as fearless as the wife of a slain Rajput warrior, Who made an offering of Sindhur® as a vow to die with her husband. (27) Covering the distance in stages, the two Singhs reached their homeland, But they could not enter the periphery of Amritsar. Devising a strategy to accomplish their cherished mission, They decided to disguise themselves as revenue collecting officials. (28) The two Sikhs invoked the protection of the God Almighty, As they planned to hit their coveted target after reaching there. That there be no impediments to block their way. (29) The Divine Satguru, creating favourable circumstances for them, Made them to undertake their mission in the peak hours of the noon. They wrapped their faces with a loose garment, As one protected one's face during a dust storm. (30)

pages.title: Mehtab Singh Beheads Massa Ranghar at Amritsar
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh reach Amritsar at a carefully chosen moment. At the height of noon, when heat, rain, and routine have dulled the vigilance of the guards, they enter disguised as revenue officials carrying business for the local
pages.searchText: Mehtab Singh Beheads Massa Ranghar at Amritsar Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh reach Amritsar at a carefully chosen moment. At the height of noon, when heat, rain, and routine have dulled the vigilance of the guards, they enter disguised as revenue officials carrying business for the local authorities. Inside the desecrated complex they find Massa Ranghar absorbed in entertainment and unprepared for danger. Mehtab Singh strikes decisively and chops off his head before the garrison can understand what has happened. The deed is both revenge and restoration. By escaping immediately after the blow, the two Sikhs turn a sacrilegious scene into one of remembered Khalsa courage and righteous retaliation.

pages.snippet: It being the peak hour of the noon in the month of September, The Sun was at its hottest in this (humid) month. As it rained and stopped at intermittent intervals, It proved very convenient for accomplishing their mission. (31) As the scorc
pages.searchText: It being the peak hour of the noon in the month of September, Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan It being the peak hour of the noon in the month of September, The Sun was at its hottest in this (humid) month. As it rained and stopped at intermittent intervals, It proved very convenient for accomplishing their mission. (31) As the scorching heat made the guards recede into shade, The rest of the troops receded to their barracks to escape rain. Along with the melodies from the Rag Malhar. (32) With some of the guards dozing off or half-asleep, None of them could notice the entry of the Singhs. The two Singhs were able to reach the main entrance, Without any let or hindrance on their way. (33) Positioning their horses on each side of the main entrance, They concealed their spears behind the wall. They hid their swords beneath their loose robes, So that no security guard could object to their arms. (34) Who had come to deposit revenue proceeds. While some guards were distracted by the live music, Others were hypnotized by the courtesan's lewd dance. (35) As the Singhs thought this moment to be most opportune, As Divine Will wished to set everything right, It made their presence unnoticed by the watching eyes. (36) Both the Singhs finally reached the central spot, Where the musicians were playing on the music. Pulling out his sword from its sheath beneath his dress, Mehtab Singh lunged it courageously at Mass Ranghar's head. (37) As one plucks a pumpkin from a creeper. Whatever jewels Massa Ranghar was wearing around his neck, The other Singh took these off his neck guickly. (38) As there was raised a lot of hue and cry all around, The two Singhs mounted their horses and fled away. As the two Singhs, spurring their horses, disappeared into the wilds, Their brave act ended the (notorious) tale of Massa Ranghar. (39)

pages.title: Confusion Follows the Killing of Massa Ranghar
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: After the blow falls, the Mughal camp collapses into confusion. As the din and noise continued through the compound, the attackers had already ridden well beyond immediate pursuit, leaving the soldiers to shout, search, and discover too lat
pages.searchText: Confusion Follows the Killing of Massa Ranghar Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan After the blow falls, the Mughal camp collapses into confusion. As the din and noise continued through the compound, the attackers had already ridden well beyond immediate pursuit, leaving the soldiers to shout, search, and discover too late what had happened. The emotional balance then reverses across Punjab. The Sikh side celebrates the cleansing of the shrine, while the family of Massa Ranghar and his supporters enter mourning and alarm in Lahore. The Nawab experiences the killing as both insult and political danger. He becomes desperate to identify the culprits, because the beheading proves that even a protected tyrant can be reached by determined Singhs.

pages.snippet: As the din and noise continued for a long time, It could be heard for long at the peak of noon. As they had never apprehended any sudden attack, Although a large number of Mughal troops were stationed there, They remained careless and invol
pages.searchText: As the din and noise continued for a long time, Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan As the din and noise continued for a long time, It could be heard for long at the peak of noon. As they had never apprehended any sudden attack, Although a large number of Mughal troops were stationed there, They remained careless and involved in festivities. Feeling drowsy and sleepy in the summer noon's heat, They were overpowered by slumber at that moment. (41) Dohra: By the time, the Mughal soldiers mounted their horses, The Singhs had gone too far to be caught by them. Learning that their main custodian had been killed, They could do nothing but grieve over their loss. (42) Chaupai: As there was a joy and victory in the Singh's camp, There was a lot of sorrow and grief in the enemy camp. Then the grieving members of the family of Massa Ranghar, Proceeded to Lahore to appeal for a relief. (43) Demanding the arrest of the slaughterers of their chief, They pressed for cutting their bodies into pieces. Otherwise, they would approach the Nawab at Delhi, And complain that Lahore Nawab had lost his grip over the state. (44) So the Nawab came to know about this news, That the Singhs had killed Massa Ranghar. Swooping like a hawk from the skies on Massa Ranghar, The Singhs had disappeared unnoticed by anybody. (45) Hearing this news, the Nawab felt as desperate as, A fish felt when thrown out of water. (46) He ordered all those subjects to be summoned, Who had given written undertakings to be loyal subjects. He summoned all those on the pay rolls of the state, So that he could replace them from their appointed posts. (47) He ordered Niranjania Harbhagat to be summoned, Along with Karama Chhina!? from the village Chhina. Orders were issued to summon Rama Randhawa, As well as Dharam Dass from Jodh Nagar!?. (48)

pages.title: Informers Name Mehtab Singh and the Village Is Besieged
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: The Nawab now leans on collaborators, informers, and sectarian rivals to produce the names of the killers. Under threats and promises of favor, the search narrows until Harbhagat and others identify Mehtab Singh Bhangoo as the principal ave
pages.searchText: Informers Name Mehtab Singh and the Village Is Besieged Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The Nawab now leans on collaborators, informers, and sectarian rivals to produce the names of the killers. Under threats and promises of favor, the search narrows until Harbhagat and others identify Mehtab Singh Bhangoo as the principal avenger. Once his name is spoken, the pressure shifts to place and family. Mirankot becomes the focus of official suspicion, and Mughal officers move to seize relatives and local leaders who might reveal where Mehtab Singh has gone. The siege is therefore investigative as well as punitive. By surrounding the village and interrogating its people, the state tries to recover lost honor through coercion and exemplary terror.

pages.searchText: Who had been harassing the Singhs quite a lot. Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Who had been harassing the Singhs quite a lot. It is difficult to keep a count of all the informers, I (the author) have listed only his nearest neighbours. (49) Summoning all the Hindu Jat informers of the region, Nawab of Lahore ordered them to produce the killer Singhs. They must hand them over to the authorities at any cost, Those Singhs who had slaughtered Massa Ranghar. (50) Otherwise, the Nawab threatened to include them among the Singhs, And would eliminate them as well along with the Singhs. Since they had taken the responsibility for Singhs elimination, They had been boasting of having eliminated the Singhs completely. (51) So that he might raze the whole habitat to dust. Along with their names, hideouts and village names, Or whosoever would facilitate the capture of any Singh, He would be highly rewarded for his services. (53). Harbhagat, a follower of Niranjani sect, informed, That it was the handiwork of one Mehtab Singh Bhangoo. He had been reported to be a resident of Mirankot, A village situated at a distance of three miles from Amritsar. (54) Mir Kambar Ali had been given the custodianship of that village, By virtue of his being the spiritual guide of the emperor. So the Nawab, sending for the Sayyad Kambar Ali, Asked him to accompany the Mughal troops to his village. (55) The Nawab had not massacred the village population for Pir's sake, Although he had not desisted from harbouring the Singhs. (56) The Mughal troops laid a siege to the village after reaching there, Rendering Sayyad (Kambar Ali) helpless from protecting his village. Was taken into custody by the invading Mughal troops. (57)

pages.title: Natha Khehra Refuses to Surrender Mehtab Singh’s Son
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: When the Mughal commander closes in, he tries to force compliance through cruelty rather than negotiation. Noordin addressed Natha Khehra and demanded either the hidden Mehtab Singh or the child who represented his line, refusing any plea f
pages.searchText: Natha Khehra Refuses to Surrender Mehtab Singh’s Son Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan When the Mughal commander closes in, he tries to force compliance through cruelty rather than negotiation. Noordin addressed Natha Khehra and demanded either the hidden Mehtab Singh or the child who represented his line, refusing any plea for mercy. Natha Khehra understands that surrender would only invite more humiliation and death. He resolves instead to protect Mehtab Singh’s son even if the choice means abandoning safety and accepting battle on unequal terms. The page therefore turns from siege to rescue. Trust, kinship, and duty become stronger than fear, and escape begins under the shadow of almost certain pursuit.

pages.searchText: Noordin, who was a commander of the Mughal force, Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Noordin, who was a commander of the Mughal force, Addressed Natha Khehra, in the following words. He would have to wash his hands off his own life, Otherwise he must produce Mehtab Singh before him. (58) Mehtab Singh must be handed over to the authorities, Otherwise his harbourers would not be spared. That Mehtab Singh was not present in the village at that moment. (59) Offering himself for arrest to the chief of Mughal troops, He asked them to deal with him in any manner they liked. At this, Noorudin ordered him to produce Mehtab Singh's son, In case he wished his own life to be spared. (60) Provided they promised to spare the child's life. Noorudin retorted that he would not be spared. Because how could a murderer Singhs progeny be allowed to live? (61) Hearing this decision, Natha Khehra went to the child, And shook his head out of pity for the infant. He commiserated that incase he handed over the child, They would slaughter the child in an instant. (62) In case, he handed over the child to be Mughals, He would lose his face among the village elders. When Mehtab Singh demanded his son back left in his custody, He would feel stigmatized for breach of trust in heavens. (63) That he would die with the child rather than handing him over. If his own progeny survived after his death for the cause, They would earn the honour of being descendents of a benefactor. (64) So picking up the child of Mehtab Singh on his back, Naatha Khehra jumped over the wall in the back yard. Escorting the child under the protection of five men, The escorting party included his real son and his sister's son, As well as the family security guard and a menial. It being the peak of a hot summer's noon, They covered a lot of distance in the open fields. (66)

pages.title: Natha Khehra Escapes with Rai Singh Under Pursuit
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: Once the escape is discovered, the Mughal hunt begins in earnest. Natha Khehra escapes with Rai Singh and orders his companions to think first of the child’s survival rather than their own comfort or honor. He instructs his own kin to carry
pages.searchText: Natha Khehra Escapes with Rai Singh Under Pursuit Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Once the escape is discovered, the Mughal hunt begins in earnest. Natha Khehra escapes with Rai Singh and orders his companions to think first of the child’s survival rather than their own comfort or honor. He instructs his own kin to carry the boy onward while he and a few others stay near the rear to delay pursuit. The decision is strategic and sacrificial at the same time, because every moment gained may save the child but increase the danger to the rescuers. As gunfire and shouting close in, the page gathers momentum toward open combat. What began as concealment becomes a moving rear-guard action shaped by loyalty to Mehtab Singh’s house.

pages.title: Heard that Natha Khehra had escaped over the back walls.
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: Heard that Natha Khehra had escaped over the back walls. Informing the Mughal troops about the escape, He himself rushed to guide the Mughal troops. (67) So they must rush and kill the fugitives. Hearing this, the Mughal troops launched an
pages.searchText: Heard that Natha Khehra had escaped over the back walls. Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Heard that Natha Khehra had escaped over the back walls. Informing the Mughal troops about the escape, He himself rushed to guide the Mughal troops. (67) So they must rush and kill the fugitives. Hearing this, the Mughal troops launched an attack, After tracing the footsteps of the runaway fugitives. (68) At this juncture, Nantha Khehra, addressing his companions, Asked them to listen to his instructions carefully. He instructed them to run away with the child Rai Singh (Mehtab Singh's son), Addressing his own son, he asked him to runaway, While carrying the infant Rai Singh on his shoulders. If he abandoned the child at this critical hour, He would have to face social condemnation of the society. (70) In that case, people would accuse them of abandoning the child, For whom they had deserted their own home and hearth. They (Natha's son and child) should run and seek shelter in some village. (71) Once the child Rai Singh! was given a safe sanctuary, Since Rai Singh's father had left his son in his custody, He was prepared to face death for keeping his trust. (72) Upon this, Natha Khehra's son told his father, That it would not avail them to run away at that stage. Since death was hovering over their heads all around, It would no longer avail them to seek a shelter. (73) By this time, they were surrounded by the Mughal troops, Who opened a barrage of bullet fire on them. At this, Natha Khehra's party rushed back with a counter attack, And pushed the invading troops away from their proximity. (74) At this, the Mughal Commanders issued fresh instructions, That let the supporters of Massa Ranghar be summoned forth. Addressing the brothers of Massa Ranghar, Mughal Commander said, That they should now fight and take revenge from their enemies. (75)

pages.title: Natha Khehra’s Small Band Fights Off Massa Ranghar’s Supporters
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: The pursuers do not catch frightened fugitives but determined defenders. The poem says supporters of Massa Ranghar attack in force, expecting a quick victory over a small party that lacks the resources of a regular army. Instead Natha Khehr
pages.searchText: Natha Khehra’s Small Band Fights Off Massa Ranghar’s Supporters Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The pursuers do not catch frightened fugitives but determined defenders. The poem says supporters of Massa Ranghar attack in force, expecting a quick victory over a small party that lacks the resources of a regular army. Instead Natha Khehra’s band answers with fierce accuracy. Arrows, spears, and blades land so effectively that the attackers are shaken and begin calling for reinforcement rather than risking the fight alone. That escalation invites a broader encirclement. Harbhagat and Mughal officers coordinate the pressure from multiple sides, making it clear that the conflict has moved beyond private revenge into a state-backed manhunt.

pages.title: The Last Stand Narrows to the Child Rai Singh
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan
pages.snippet: The fighting grows still more desperate as losses mount around Natha Khehra. At the turning point Natha’s bow breaks, forcing him into close combat with the sword while mounted troops and muskets tighten the noose. One by one the defenders
pages.searchText: The Last Stand Narrows to the Child Rai Singh Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The fighting grows still more desperate as losses mount around Natha Khehra. At the turning point Natha’s bow breaks, forcing him into close combat with the sword while mounted troops and muskets tighten the noose. One by one the defenders fall until the scene contracts around the endangered child. Rai Singh survives the clash only by fleeing, stumbling, and hiding where the attackers assume no one could endure for long. The page keeps the reader close to that vulnerability. What had been a battle narrative now becomes a survival narrative in which the future of a lineage hangs on one wounded child slipping through chaos.

pages.searchText: A Market Woman Rescues the Wounded Child and Episode 98 Opens Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan Episode About Khanu Nawab, Nawab Zakaria Khan The attackers leave the child behind, convinced their blows have finished him. Yet he remains alive, and the story takes an unexpected turn when a passing woman carries him in a basket rather than abandoning him to the field. She brings him toward Rudiala, where his wounds are sewn and his survival is credited to divine protection. The rescue gives the narrative a moment of mercy after prolonged pursuit, slaughter, and attempted extinction. At the same time the page serves as a hinge into a new chapter of Sikh defiance. The survival of the child is followed by the opening of Episode 98, which introduces Bhai Bota Singh and the need for an even more public sign that the Khalsa still lives.

pages.title: Bota Singh Decides to Prove that the Khalsa Still Lives
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: The new episode begins in an atmosphere of false triumph for the persecutors. So many Sikhs have been hunted that many people now say the Khalsa is finished, and the mockery of Bota Singh as an impostor becomes the sharp expression of that
pages.searchText: Bota Singh Decides to Prove that the Khalsa Still Lives Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh The new episode begins in an atmosphere of false triumph for the persecutors. So many Sikhs have been hunted that many people now say the Khalsa is finished, and the mockery of Bota Singh as an impostor becomes the sharp expression of that public disbelief. Those insults do not drive him into hiding. Instead they persuade him that only a bold open gesture can prove the Khalsa still lives and still has the courage to act before the eyes of the state. Bota Singh therefore establishes a post near Nurddin’s Sarai with a companion identified by the tradition as socially marginalized and starts collecting a token toll from passersby. The gesture is deliberately provocative, meant to send unmistakable news to Lahore that the Khalsa has not vanished.

(10) He set up his post on a raised platform, At the intersection of road near Nurddin's Sarai. He named it as the fort of Bota Singh. (11) Along with his companion belonging to a schedule caste. pages.title: Bota Singh Writes a Defiant Toll Letter
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: Bota Singh wrote a letter that turns hiding into open defiance. He announces that he and his companion are openly stopping traffic, demanding an anna for a bullock cart and a penny for an ass in order to show that the Khalsa still refuses e
pages.searchText: Bota Singh Writes a Defiant Toll Letter Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Bota Singh wrote a letter that turns hiding into open defiance. He announces that he and his companion are openly stopping traffic, demanding an anna for a bullock cart and a penny for an ass in order to show that the Khalsa still refuses erasure. The letter is meant as a public insult to Mughal authority, so the Nawab dispatches troops at once. Yet the page frames the challenge less as robbery than as deliberate political theater staged by men who want the state to face them directly. When the soldiers arrive, the Singhs refuse compromise. They insist that the confrontation should happen face to face, making their small roadside stand into a declaration that Sikh courage can still command the road.

pages.searchText: The Two Singhs Rush Into Unequal Combat Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Negotiation is dismissed with contempt, because the Singhs say they have no business in court when the issue is already settled by tyranny and resistance. Instead they rush the Mughal force with staffs, stones, and spears, turning improvised weapons into marks of fearless resolve. The page delights in the disproportion of the contest. Against cavalry and trained troops, the Singhs move with the suddenness of a lion and refuse to give the enemy the psychological victory of seeing them hesitate. Every fresh attack only hardens their stance. The underlying point is that martyr courage had already stripped death of its terror, so numerical inferiority no longer controls the shape of the battle.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: Close fighting does not subdue the two Singhs. They wrench out arrows, strike at horses with their sticks, and force their opponents to abandon the easy confidence of mounted combat. Only after those efforts fail do the Mughals resort to mu
pages.searchText: Bullet Fire Fails to Break the Singhs Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Close fighting does not subdue the two Singhs. They wrench out arrows, strike at horses with their sticks, and force their opponents to abandon the easy confidence of mounted combat. Only after those efforts fail do the Mughals resort to muskets and opened a heavy shower of bullets. Even then the page emphasizes not the success of the volleys but the astonishing persistence of the wounded Singhs, who continue pressing forward after terrible injury. The narrative lingers on endurance as spectacle. A body broken by gunfire still refuses inward defeat, which is precisely why the episode magnifies martyrdom into public instruction.

pages.snippet: The page closes the encounter by honoring the two Singhs for fighting eye to eye until martyrdom. Their deaths are treated as the sealing proof of a public challenge that neither the Nawab nor his troops could morally answer except by overw
pages.searchText: Bota Singh's Martyrdom and the Opening of Sukha Singh's Story Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh, Sukha Singh The page closes the encounter by honoring the two Singhs for fighting eye to eye until martyrdom. Their deaths are treated as the sealing proof of a public challenge that neither the Nawab nor his troops could morally answer except by overwhelming force. The narrator then deliberately pivots away from mourning and into exemplarity. Now hear the story of Sukha Singh, whose life is introduced as the next demonstration of the same Khalsa daring in a new setting. This transition turns one martyr episode into the threshold of another. Heroic memory is not left behind; it becomes the atmosphere in which Sukha Singh's character first appears.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr
pages.snippet: Sukha Singh avoids his home because Mughal surveillance makes family space dangerous. His parents, however, try to reclaim him from the Panth by arguing that their household has no place in Sikh sovereignty and by treating his Khalsa commit
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Is Betrayed at Home and Jumps Into a Well S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Sukha Singh avoids his home because Mughal surveillance makes family space dangerous. His parents, however, try to reclaim him from the Panth by arguing that their household has no place in Sikh sovereignty and by treating his Khalsa commitment as a dishonor to caste expectations. Their deception culminates in intoxicating him and cutting his hair. When he awakens to that violation, his grief is so fierce that he refuses ordinary consolation and jumped into a deep well rather than continue under disgrace. The page therefore frames the crisis as spiritual betrayal rather than domestic conflict alone. What has been attacked is not merely Sukha Singh's appearance, but the covenantal identity by which he belongs to the Khalsa.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr
pages.snippet: An elder Singh intervenes to stop Sukha Singh from wasting his life in despair. He tells him to die fighting the Mughals if death is what he seeks, because martyrdom in service of the Panth is meaningful while self-destruction is not. Sukha
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Is Redirected Toward Purposeful Martyrdom S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr An elder Singh intervenes to stop Sukha Singh from wasting his life in despair. He tells him to die fighting the Mughals if death is what he seeks, because martyrdom in service of the Panth is meaningful while self-destruction is not. Sukha Singh accepts the rebuke and rejoins disciplined action. He enters the Khalsa ranks with renewed intention, resolving to strike the enemy cleverly and effectively rather than merely to advertise wounded pride. The page closes with movement toward Lahore. What began as shame is transformed into vocation, and the restless energy of the young Singh is redirected into service, daring, and calculated resistance.

(14) Better to die fighting the Mughals (than dying in vain), Better come out of the well and join the ranks of the Singhs. Be a martyr while fighting against the Mughals, This is the advice that I render unto you. (15) Sukha Singh, accepting the elderly Singh's advice, Came out of the well with this resolution in mind: That Singh's counsel being sound and correct, He must sacrifice his life fighting the Mughals. (16) Being more firm in his resolution to sacrifice, He decided never to die without a cause. Otherwise also he had not been drowned in the well, Although he was hell-bent on drowning himself. (17) Further, Sukha Singh, making a strategy in his mind, Decided not to throw an open challenge to the Mughals. After hitting the Mughals at random through stealth, There was a headmen of his own village, Who had in his possession a mare of very fine breed. Sukha Singh, on the pretext of taking the mare for water, Took away the mare in order to join the Khalsa ranks. (19) Sukha Singh, after joining the ranks of the Khalsa, Finally reached the camp office of (general) Sham Singh. Getting himself initiated from the (sacred) hands of Sham Singh, The latter developed a filial bond with his disciple. (20) Then, with a thought crossing Sukha Singh's mind, He decided to compensate his village headman for the mare. With this thought, he proceeded in the direction of Lahore, Disguising himself as a rustic peasant of the area. (21) With very little hair on his head (after the forced shave), He entered the centre of the sprawling city of Lahore. As he entered the market dealing in Gold and silver,

pages.title: Sukha Singh Funds the Khalsa Through Daring Lahore Raids
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr
pages.snippet: Inside Lahore, Sukha Singh proves both audacity and speed by seizing wealth in the city and escaping before the alarm can trap him. The exploit is narrated as tactical intelligence rather than random theft, because his true loyalty lies wit
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Funds the Khalsa Through Daring Lahore Raids S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Inside Lahore, Sukha Singh proves both audacity and speed by seizing wealth in the city and escaping before the alarm can trap him. The exploit is narrated as tactical intelligence rather than random theft, because his true loyalty lies with the Khalsa rather than with personal gain. Back among the Singhs, he settles what he owes for his horse and contributes the entire booty to the community kitchen. The gesture is central to the page, showing that courage without service would be incomplete and that the raid feeds the Panth before it elevates the raider. The closing lines sharpen his martial profile. Sukha Singh is remembered as a fighter skilled across many weapons, but that prowess is nested inside humility, discipline, and communal giving.

pages.searchText: Spotting out one such pouch on a trader's shoulder, S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Spotting out one such pouch on a trader's shoulder, Sukha Singh leapt up and snatched the hefty pouch Spurring his mare, he came out of the city gates, Without caring for the risk to his own life. (23) As the Sun's light was about to fade at dusk time, Sukha Singh fled as fast as the high velocity wind. As the traders and city guards kept on shouting, Sukha Singh headed towards his native place. (24) By the time the news spread all around, Sukha Singh had camouflaged himself in the wild. As the Mughal troops ran in hot pursuit of him, They crossed his hideout in another direction. (25) Sukha Singh, after returning to his contingent of Singhs, Sent money equal to the mare's price to its former owner. Thus paying a compensation of about three hundred rupees, He patched up his strained relations with the village headman. (26) He contributed the remaining amount to the community kitchen, Instead of sending it to his parents at home. In this way, Sukha Singh kept on going on expeditions, And bringing wealth through his acts of waylaying and robbing. (27) Being very bold and daunting in his religious zeal, Being quite skilled in wielding all kinds of arms, A mighty muscular warrior alone could dare to grapple with him. (28) Whatever he brought through acts of loot and plunder, He contributed the entire booty to the community kitchen. (29) Wherever the Mughal troops launched at attack, Like a mighty lion, he would jump into the fray. After wounding a few enemy soldiers with a dash, He would join the Khalsa ranks in a flash. (30) Not only could he shoot with small fire arms, But he could hit enemy horses with arrows as well. Such was his deft handling of spears, swords and daggers, As would put the enemy to death in an instant. (31)

pages.title: Sukha Singh's Reputation, Domestic Return, and Excommunication
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr
pages.snippet: The narrative balances Sukha Singh's reputation for bravery with quieter camp virtues. He performs ordinary service, recites bani, remains prepared for combat, and thereby shows that Sikh heroism includes devotion and labor as well as battl
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh's Reputation, Domestic Return, and Excommunication S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr The narrative balances Sukha Singh's reputation for bravery with quieter camp virtues. He performs ordinary service, recites bani, remains prepared for combat, and thereby shows that Sikh heroism includes devotion and labor as well as battlefield prowess. Family pressure nevertheless draws him back home long enough for marriage and domestic entanglement. After the death of an infant daughter, accusation and suspicion gather around him until he is excommunicated by the Khalsa Panth and left in painful separation from the fellowship that defined him. The page makes exclusion itself a form of torment. For a Singh formed by Panthic belonging, public disgrace wounds more deeply than bodily danger, setting up the need for a new proving ground.

pages.title: So widespread was Sukha Singh's fame as a warrior,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr
pages.snippet: So widespread was Sukha Singh's fame as a warrior, That he came to be reckoned among the bravest. He would stand with a hand fan in the midst of congregation, And bring wood for community kitchen's hearth fire. He would fetch water in a lea
pages.searchText: So widespread was Sukha Singh's fame as a warrior, S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr So widespread was Sukha Singh's fame as a warrior, That he came to be reckoned among the bravest. He would stand with a hand fan in the midst of congregation, And bring wood for community kitchen's hearth fire. He would fetch water in a leather bag for the thirsty, And bring food for the needy and the starving. (33) He would massage those who got fatigued and exhausted, And store water for the ablutions of his companions. He would squeeze the undergarments of elders after ablutions, And hold a water-bucket while they brushed their teeth. (34) And sing devotional songs to the accompaniment of music. And remain ever ready for a fight and confrontation. (35) Nor would he feel scared of fighting and rioting. When his parents would come to take him home, They would beg the Singhs to persuade him to go home. (36) Dohra: His parents came time and again ( to take him home), And begged the Singhs to prevail upon him to go home. And succeeded in solemnising his marriage. (37) Chaupai: Sukha Singh would visit his home at odd hours, But would soon return to his contingent for fear of Mughal's raid. After sometime, as his wife gave birth to a girl child, Who died soon either on her own or the mother having killed her. (38) As this news reached (Sukha Singh's) Khalsa contingent, Sukha Singh was ex-communicated by the Khalsa Panth. And being guilty of violating the Khalsa's glorious tradition. (39) They would keep him at bay branding him a killer of his daughter. Since the Khalsa Panth did not agree to condone his lapse, Sukha Singh felt extremely concerned about his isolation. (40)

pages.title: Abdali Marches to Delhi and a New Sikh Challenge Opens
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr
pages.snippet: The page closes the previous emotional thread quickly and opens a wider military horizon. Ahmed Shah after occupation of Lahore proceeded on an expedition towards Delhi, leaving part of his force behind and creating a fresh field of conflic
pages.searchText: Abdali Marches to Delhi and a New Sikh Challenge Opens S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr Episode About S. Bota Singh — Th Martyr The page closes the previous emotional thread quickly and opens a wider military horizon. Ahmed Shah after occupation of Lahore proceeded on an expedition towards Delhi, leaving part of his force behind and creating a fresh field of conflict around the remaining Afghan presence. Those troops move against a Sikh village and force a local band across the river, but the gesture only invites a sharper confrontation. Rather than ending Sikh resistance, imperial occupation multiplies occasions for challenge and reply. By the close of the page a taunting epistle has been sent to the Singhs. The narrative is therefore poised for formal exchange, with honor, insult, and public testing once again driving the next sequence.
