pages.snippet: As Sukha Singh's reputation had reached its zenith earlier, It now reached its nadir in the same proportion. Feeling worried and concerned in his own mind, He went into deep silence and remained incommunicado. (41) Episode 100 Another Episo
pages.searchText: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh As Sukha Singh's reputation had reached its zenith earlier, It now reached its nadir in the same proportion. Feeling worried and concerned in his own mind, He went into deep silence and remained incommunicado. (41) Episode 100 Another Episode About Sukha Singh (Satguru stood by the Khalsa) Ahmed Shah (Abdali)! after occupation of Lahore, Proceeded on an expedition towards Delhi. He left behind a sizeable section of his army, For the safety and security of the city of Lahore. (1) As his troops left Lahore (on their way to Delhi), They consisted of the most muscular giants of men, They boasted, where are those so-called brave Singhs, We would like to have a glimpse of them. (2) They were being led by the highest Pathan chiefs. With steel helmets on their heads, bodies wrapped in steel armour, They had steel coverings even around their legs. (3) With feet in steel shoes and hands in steel gloves, They had steel covers even on their horses. These Gilja sect Pathan soldiers launched an expedition, With the assistance of Pathan soldiers of Kasur. (4) In a village, that there was, known as Buddha Kot, Majority of its households belonged to the Singhs. Being informed about its location by the informers, The Mughal troops killed its inhabitants inside their homes. (5) The Singh contingent camping on this side of the river, Crossed to the other side at the approach of Gilja Pathans. Feeling very proud after making the Singhs retreat to the other bank, These Pathan troops sent an epistle to the Singhs. (6) Boasting of their bravado, they sent a despatch to the Singhs, That they constituted the elite force of Ahmad Shah Abdali. Since the Singhs proclaimed themselves as Lion-hearted-soldiers of the Guru, They (Pathans) had come to test their mettle with the Singhs. (7)

pages.title: The Durranis and the Singhs Exchange Formal Challenges
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: This page is built around taunt and answer. The Pathans try to define the Singhs as cowards who flee at mere arrival, while the Khalsa responds by stating its own terms for honorable combat rather than accepting the enemy's theatrical advan
pages.searchText: The Durranis and the Singhs Exchange Formal Challenges Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh This page is built around taunt and answer. The Pathans try to define the Singhs as cowards who flee at mere arrival, while the Khalsa responds by stating its own terms for honorable combat rather than accepting the enemy's theatrical advantage. The Sikh reply narrows the issue with striking confidence: they will fight only when they are armed with their small firearms, because the form of combat must match the discipline and practice that the Guru has sanctioned for them. Public negotiation thus becomes another way of asserting Panthic self-definition. The atmosphere tightens toward a single-combat trial. Beneath the boasting, both sides understand that the moral prestige of the encounter may matter as much as the immediate tactical result.

pages.title: They bragged that their mere arrival had made the Singhs run,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: They bragged that their mere arrival had made the Singhs run, And forced them to cross over to the river's other bank. Accusing the Singhs of being liars and fake Singh warriors, They branded the Singhs as cowards, slaves and serfs. (8) Cha
pages.searchText: They bragged that their mere arrival had made the Singhs run, Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh They bragged that their mere arrival had made the Singhs run, And forced them to cross over to the river's other bank. Accusing the Singhs of being liars and fake Singh warriors, They branded the Singhs as cowards, slaves and serfs. (8) Challenging the Singhs either to stand face to face before them, Or to return and have a straight fight with them. Inviting the Singhs boastfully to advance in batches of two, And let each pair test their muscles against a single Durrani soldier. (9) The Singhs, organizing a (special) religious congregation, Went through the despatch and deliberated upon its contents. Accepting their challenge, the Singhs sent back their resolution, That the Singhs would definitely have a fight with them. (10) The Singhs challenged the Durranis to advance in batches of ten soldiers, And let them be armed with the biggest fire arms they had. And the Singhs would be armed only with swords, shields and small muskets. (11) To this offer of the Singhs, they sent another alternate offer, That they would not use their fire arms in this fight. Their soldiers would be armed only with knives, daggers and swords, Instead of being armed with arrows and firearms. (12) They asked the Singhs also to come armed with swords and daggers, Instead of being armed with bows and firearms. To this offer, the Khalsa Singhs sent their own resolution, That they will fight only when they are armed with their small firearms. (13) They declared that it was ordained by their revered Guru, That Singhs must kill their wicked enemies with the small firearms. As these offers and counter offers regarding mode of confrontation continued, These contradictory proposals created a situation of uncertainty. (14) They thought of fighting with the Singhs under the cover of steel armours. But even being covered in steel armours, they were scared, So in the early hours of the morning, a Durrani soldier appeared, Who sent a messenger to the Singhs with a new message. He challenged that if there was anyone brave enough among the Singhs, He should come forward and fight single handedly with him. (16)

pages.title: Charat Singh Is Outraged by the Pathan's Insult
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: A lone Pathan escalates the confrontation by daring any Singh to meet him with limited arms and by implying that refusal would amount to written admission of defeat. The insult is calculated to wound honor before the clash of steel even beg
pages.searchText: Charat Singh Is Outraged by the Pathan's Insult Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh A lone Pathan escalates the confrontation by daring any Singh to meet him with limited arms and by implying that refusal would amount to written admission of defeat. The insult is calculated to wound honor before the clash of steel even begins. For a moment no one steps forward, and Charat Singh felt extremely outraged by that pause. His anger comes not from vanity alone but from the fear that hesitation may stain the reputation of the Khalsa before enemies already skilled in mockery. Sukha Singh then intervenes with harder judgment. He recognizes the Pathan's size, armor, and tactical danger, so the page becomes a study in how zeal, honor, and disciplined caution must be held together before battle.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: He challenged that let any Singh come armed with a sword, dagger and knife, And have it out with a single Durrani soldier. Otherwise Singhs would be branded as cowards, And their appellation Singh would be considered a fake. (17) Debunking
pages.searchText: He challenged that let any Singh come armed with a sword, dagger and knife, Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh He challenged that let any Singh come armed with a sword, dagger and knife, And have it out with a single Durrani soldier. Otherwise Singhs would be branded as cowards, And their appellation Singh would be considered a fake. (17) Debunking Singhs as cowards by naming Singhs individually, He chided the Singhs to admit their defeat in writing. Asking the Singhs to swear in the name of their Gurus, That not a single Singh could accept his challenge. (18) His parents would be applauded through out the world. Whosoever shirked from accepting his challenge, His parents would feel ashamed of begetting him. (19) 185 As had been the tradition with the Singhs to participate in the religious crusades, Why were they not forthcoming to uphold their glorious tradition now? Cursed be the Singhs and cursed be their Khalsa Panth, As no Singh came forward (to accept Gilja Pathan's challenge), S. Charat Singh? felt extremely outraged (at this humiliation). Carrying a double-edged sword only in his hand. (21) At this Sukha Singh felt extremely concerned about him, That a boy like Charat Singh could never defeat a Pathan. Since the entire body of a Pathan was covered by a steel armour, That boy would not be able to make a single hole in Pathan's armour. (22) The Singh youth just survived on green leafy vegetables. Spurring his horse, Sukha Singh rushed forward, Asking the youth: How could he overpower that Gilja Pathan? (23) How could his sword cut through Pathan's hefty constitution? As his horse too was protected by a steel armour. (24) He could carry a weight of thirty mounds on his body, As well as he never felt tired even after running for a hundred miles. Being so confident of his strength he was ready to fight with a sword, Why did not you (Charat Singh) take these factors into consideration? (25)

pages.title: Sukha Singh Prepares for Single Combat
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: After the Pathan's insult and Charat Singh's anger, Sukha Singh turns the insult into a vow to defend Khalsa honor. He says he cannot listen to abuse of the Panth while he still lives, and he treats the coming fight as obedience to the Guru
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Prepares for Single Combat Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh After the Pathan's insult and Charat Singh's anger, Sukha Singh turns the insult into a vow to defend Khalsa honor. He says he cannot listen to abuse of the Panth while he still lives, and he treats the coming fight as obedience to the Guru rather than a personal quarrel. The page then follows his deliberate preparation for the duel. Sukha Singh has his armor, gloves, and helmet brought to him, while Charat Singh helps equip both the Singh and his horse so that the encounter proceeds with discipline instead of reckless haste. Before riding out, Sukha Singh bows, gathers the Singhs into ardas, and places the outcome in divine keeping. Favorable omens appear as he mounts, so the movement toward the battlefield is framed as a righteous test already sanctified by prayer.

pages.title: Hearing these words as spoken by Sukha Singh,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: Hearing these words as spoken by Sukha Singh, Charat Singh acknowledged that that was true about the Pathan. But how could he (Charat Singh) bear to hear those words, From an arrogant Mughal soldier standing in front of him? (26) With that
pages.searchText: Hearing these words as spoken by Sukha Singh, Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh Hearing these words as spoken by Sukha Singh, Charat Singh acknowledged that that was true about the Pathan. But how could he (Charat Singh) bear to hear those words, From an arrogant Mughal soldier standing in front of him? (26) With that wicked Pathan hurling abuses from his mouth, I have decided to fight till the last breath of my life. (27) Since life and death are in the hands of Divine Satguru, Man is privileged to make earnest efforts. As One moment of meditation on the sacred name of God, Washes millions of human sins with its benediction, In the same way, I'll destroy this wicked Pathan, With the grace and protection of Divine Satguru. (24) Remarked Sukha Singh, Blessed are you, my dear boy, Now see how I deal with that audacious Pathan? With these words Sukha Singh sent for his steel armour, And covered his head and hands with steel helmet and gloves. (30) He saddled his horse covering it with a steel armour, Which he had once snatched from a Pathan soldier. Charat Singh helped him in wearing that armour, As well as decorated Sukha Singh's horse for an encounter. (31) Sukha Singh picked up his sharp sword after invocation, And slung his steel shield from his shoulders. He begged the five Singhs to pray for his victory to the Guru, So that the goddess Bhagwati's grace be on his side. (32) As he mounted his stead after a thanksgiving bow, A good Omen came to pass with a person's inadvertent right turn. Observing this good Omen Sukha Singh felt emboldened, As if he had already killed the Gilja Pathan. (33) As Sukha Singh started on his horse, After crossing one half of the flowing river, He stood on a plateau made of accumulated sand. (34)

pages.title: Sukha Singh Challenges the Pathan to Single Combat
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: Sukha Singh restrains Charat Singh and clears the field for a true single combat. Sukha Singh refuses to let the Pathan leave alive, because to spare him after such taunts would leave the slander of the Panth unanswered. The verbal exchange
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Challenges the Pathan to Single Combat Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh Sukha Singh restrains Charat Singh and clears the field for a true single combat. Sukha Singh refuses to let the Pathan leave alive, because to spare him after such taunts would leave the slander of the Panth unanswered. The verbal exchange becomes a formal declaration of intent. Sukha Singh openly predicts the Pathan's death, while both fighters advance with the kind of fierce composure that shows each man has accepted the duel's fatal terms. What matters on this page is the disciplined shape of courage. The Singh does not rush as part of a mob; he insists on meeting the challenger face to face so that the Khalsa's honor is defended in the clearest possible way.

pages.title: Persuading Charat Singh not to accompany him,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: Persuading Charat Singh not to accompany him, Sukha Singh instructed other Singhs as well to retreat. Then swearing an oath in the name of Satguru, Sukha Singh took a pledge to kill the (arrogant) Pathan. (35) Thereafter throwing a gauntlet
pages.searchText: Persuading Charat Singh not to accompany him, Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh Persuading Charat Singh not to accompany him, Sukha Singh instructed other Singhs as well to retreat. Then swearing an oath in the name of Satguru, Sukha Singh took a pledge to kill the (arrogant) Pathan. (35) Thereafter throwing a gauntlet to the defiant Pathan, Except that he would be burried in his grave there and then. (36) Khalsa Panth would eliminate him in such a manner, As truth wipes out every trace of falsehood at last. Had the Pathan become so arrogant when he started, That he considered the Singhs as timid as rabbits? (37) He would realize how a rabbit becomes as brave as lion, Since he had committed a grave error in challenging the Singhs. After uttering these words Sukha Singh stood firm at his place, While the Gilja Pathan also arrived to confront him. (38) As if they were exchanging pleasantries with each other. Holding on to their swords in their hands, Each one asked the other to attack first of all. (39) With both of them exchanging hot words with each other, Both of them started pushing and striking at each other. Sukha Singh warning the Pathan to be ready for the Singh's stroke, Suggested that the Pathan should have brought another supporter. (40) The Pathan retorted that he alone was sufficient to deal with the Singh, As he would pin the Singh down as easily as a lion pins down a goat. Thereafter, both of them after positioning their horses facing each other, Both of them took out their swords in their hands. (41) Each one of them asked the other to attack first of all, As if two real brothers were fondly playing together. Both of them, being skilled in wielding arms and weapons, Both of them knew how to duck and protect themselves. (42) Both of them attacked each other from the front, Both of them received each other's stroke on their shields. Both of them cast their (mighty) strokes on each other's shield, As if a black ironsmith's hammer struck hot iron on an iron block. (43)

pages.title: Sukha Singh Kills the Pathan and the Khalsa Charges
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: The duel turns savage as shield, sword, and horse all begin to fail under repeated blows. What began as formal combat collapses into a close struggle on the ground, showing how evenly matched and determined both fighters are. At the decisiv
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Kills the Pathan and the Khalsa Charges Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh The duel turns savage as shield, sword, and horse all begin to fail under repeated blows. What began as formal combat collapses into a close struggle on the ground, showing how evenly matched and determined both fighters are. At the decisive moment, Sukha Singh seizes a fallen knife and kills the Pathan. The victory preserves Khalsa honor precisely because it is won after endurance, improvisation, and refusal to yield when the contest becomes desperate. The single combat immediately widens into collective battle. The Khalsa charges once Sukha Singh prevails, and Charat Singh moves through the mêlée to recover his companion as the enemy line begins to break.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: Dohra: With such mighty strokes from both the sides, Shields of both of them fell down after splintering. With each blow of their unmistakable strokes. (44) Chaupai: As the supporting belts of both were cut with sword strokes, All the dangl
pages.searchText: Dohra: With such mighty strokes from both the sides, Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh Dohra: With such mighty strokes from both the sides, Shields of both of them fell down after splintering. With each blow of their unmistakable strokes. (44) Chaupai: As the supporting belts of both were cut with sword strokes, All the dangling daggers and knives from the belts fell down. As the tips and sharp edges of their swords broke down, Both of them started grappling with each other. (45) As all the blood had drained out of the wounds, Their horses also lost their energy to support them. As each one's horse struck against the other's horse, Their riders too came too close to each other. (46) Dohra: Thus hitting and grappling with each other, Both of them tumbled down staggering on the ground. Getting seriously wounded due to the gaping head injuries, Both of them fell down and fainted on the ground. (47) Chaupai: As Sukha Singh regained little consciousness after some time, He raised his neck to survey the scene. Picking up a small knife he thrust it into Pathan's belly, Which scraped through the lungs and heart of the Pathan. (48) As he pulled it out of the Pathan's belly with full force, It took out all the intestines and arteries with it. As the great Guru had stood by His Khalsa Singh, Who had been extremely arrogant and defiant. Thus has Rattan Singh narrated this episode, As he had heard it from his elderly Singhs. (50) Chaupai: Thus shouting slogans of victory Sukha Singh retreated, And ran post haste towards the Khalsa camp. As the Gilja Pathans launched an attack from the otherside, The Singhs confronted them from their own side. (51) Charat Singh, spurring his horse, leapt forward, And picked up running Sukha Singh on to his horse. As Sukha Singh was carried to the other side of the river, Gilja Pathan troops were pushed to the other bank. (52).

pages.title: Sukha Singh Honored by the Khalsa
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: After the encounter, Sukha Singh and Charat Singh are described as bound in deep kinship: although they were two bodies, they were of one heart. Chiefs from the Khalsa contingents came to the camp, offered Sukha Singh a horse each, and prai
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Honored by the Khalsa Bhai Sukha Singh’s bravery Episode About Bravery of Bhai Sukha Singh After the encounter, Sukha Singh and Charat Singh are described as bound in deep kinship: although they were two bodies, they were of one heart. Chiefs from the Khalsa contingents came to the camp, offered Sukha Singh a horse each, and praised his bravery. Sukha Singh folded his hands before the Panth and sought forgiveness for the grave wrongdoing the narrative associates with the death of his daughter; the Khalsa accepted him and performed a joyful ardas. He returned all the offered horses except the one connected with Sham Singh, his foster father, and Rattan Singh closes the Sukha Singh episode as received from elders. The page then opens the next Sukha Singh episode, with Singhs ambushing Mughal and Pathan forces and raiding places such as Noordin Sarai and Sangharkot.

pages.title: Another Episode About Sukha Singh
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About Sukha Singh
pages.snippet: There after developed such a spiritual bond of kinship, Between Sukha Singh and Charat Singh after this encounter, That despite appearing to be two separate entities, They were united at heart in a spiritual bondage. (53) The chiefs of all
pages.searchText: Another Episode About Sukha Singh Sukha Singh Another Episode About Sukha Singh There after developed such a spiritual bond of kinship, Between Sukha Singh and Charat Singh after this encounter, That despite appearing to be two separate entities, They were united at heart in a spiritual bondage. (53) The chiefs of all the Khalsa contingents arrived at the camp, And made an offering of one horse each to Sukha Singh, Sukha Singh wished to be exonerated of female infanticide. (54) With folded hands Sukha Singh prostrated in the Khalsa tradition, In front of the assembly of Sikh congregation. Thereupon, inviting Sukha Singh to be a part of Khalsa commonwealth, The congregation performed a prayer signifying joyous forgiveness. pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Accepts the Amritsar Challenge Sukha Singh Another Episode About Sukha Singh The Mughal challenge at Amritsar is designed to shame the Khalsa in public by implying that no Singh dares approach the sacred pool under guard. After the Panth hears the taunt in silence, Sukha Singh steps forward and declares that he would bathe in the broad daylight rather than creep in secretly at night. His answer matters because it turns the contest from military bravado into open religious defiance. He announces that, with the Guru's grace, he will enter the guarded place plainly and show that fear cannot regulate Sikh devotion. The page closes with practical preparation for the exploit. Sukha Singh adopts a disguise and rides toward Amritsar, combining daring, planning, and faith in a single deliberate act.

pages.searchText: Sukha Singh's Daylight Bath; Mehtab Kot Opens Sukha Singh Another Episode About Sukha Singh Sukha Singh carries out his vow by approaching the pool in disguise, letting his horse drink, and then dismounting for the sacred bath. The Mughals were dumbfounded to witness such a scene once his Sikh identity became clear in the very place they had tried to seal off. Instead of fleeing silently, he raises the Khalsa cry and openly challenges the guards before escaping their fire. The episode presents the bath not as private devotion alone but as a public act of spiritual and political resistance. By the end of the page, the story turns toward a harsher new campaign against the Singhs. The transition introduces the pressure that will define the Mehtab Kot sequence, where persecution spreads beyond Amritsar into the countryside.

The proclamation turns the whole countryside into hostile ground for the Khalsa. Because refuge disappears so widely, a small group of Singhs withdraws into the rough riverine country associated with Mehtab Kot. Their survival depends on obscurity, endurance, and whatever shelter the wild terrain can still provide. Spies and officials quickly notice their vulnerability and urge a rapid strike. The page therefore frames Mehtab Kot as both a refuge and a trap, created by persecution and exposed by informers.

Mughal troops ran in all four directions so that the assault would overwhelm the camp before it could properly form for battle. The first shock is deadly because the Singhs are caught in a vulnerable condition. Even so, the page emphasizes how quickly disorder gives way to resolve once they understand that escape is impossible and martyrdom may be near. The fight is recast as a test of steadfastness rather than numbers. The survivors stand where they are, while absent companions begin to hurry back toward the sound of gunfire.

The page closes by stressing renewal rather than mere survival. Morning finds the Khalsa strengthened in spirit, and the battle at Mehtab Kot becomes another proof that persecution cannot extinguish their resolve.

pages.searchText: Khalsa Conduct and the Lion Cave Episode Begins Mehtab Kot Episode About Mehtab Kot The page continues its portrait of persecuted Khalsa life by showing that the Singhs hide by day and move by night, refusing to surrender initiative even when heavily outnumbered. Their survival is presented not as passive concealment but as a disciplined rhythm of stealth, endurance, and sudden action against Mughal camps. From that wider description the narrative narrows into a specific ordeal, introducing the tale of Singhs who must take shelter in a lion's cave near Mirankot. Laddha Singh emerges as the central name in this setting, and the new sub-episode begins to translate collective Khalsa conduct into one intense local test. The transition matters because it shows how general persecution produced improvised refuges and legends of defiance. The Singhs remain under pressure on every side, yet the story insists that hardship only sharpened their courage and mutual loyalty.

pages.searchText: The Lion Cave Is Betrayed to the Mughals Mehtab Kot Episode About Mehtab Kot Inside the cave, the hidden Singhs preserve a strict communal ethic, sharing whatever food can be gathered and making room for any brother who reaches the refuge. Small night journeys for grain and vegetables keep them alive, but the arrangement remains precarious because concealment is their only shield. That shield fails when the cave is betrayed to the Mughals, who learn who is inside and close in around the refuge. Laddha Singh Bhangoo, Ram Singh, and Sulakhan Singh Gill are identified, and the attackers begin to treat the cave like a trap that can be reduced by patience and force. The besiegers choose musket smoke as their first main method, hoping to suffocate or drive the Singhs out without facing their resistance in open combat. The page thus turns the cave from sanctuary into a battlefield shaped by confinement, ingenuity, and endurance.

pages.snippet: The Mughal assault on the cave becomes methodical as the attackers pour smoke into the opening, force villagers to dig, and then look for new ways to make the hiding place unlivable. Pressure from outside is relentless, but the trapped Sing
pages.searchText: The Singhs Endure the Siege of the Lion Cave Mehtab Kot Episode About Mehtab Kot The Mughal assault on the cave becomes methodical as the attackers pour smoke into the opening, force villagers to dig, and then look for new ways to make the hiding place unlivable. Pressure from outside is relentless, but the trapped Singhs answer with the same stubborn improvisation that has marked the entire episode. Within that struggle, the Singhs block the opening against smoke and fire by sealing gaps, using cloth and damp material, and refusing to panic while the siege intensifies. Their defense is as much moral as physical, because each improvised barrier declares that they will not simply be flushed out like animals. Local villagers also slow the attackers by dragging out the labor demanded of them, and nightfall finally breaks the immediate momentum of the operation. The page therefore preserves the cave episode as a contest of patience in which Khalsa resolve repeatedly frustrates superior force.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Kot
pages.snippet: Chaupai: Putting the muzzles of all their muskets in the cave's opening, The Mughals let out a volley of bullets inside the cave. As the cave got filled with dense smoke and darkness, The Singhs felt choked with smoke and lack of air. (16)
pages.searchText: Chaupai: Putting the muzzles of all their muskets in the cave's opening, Mehtab Kot Episode About Mehtab Kot Chaupai: Putting the muzzles of all their muskets in the cave's opening, The Mughals let out a volley of bullets inside the cave. As the cave got filled with dense smoke and darkness, The Singhs felt choked with smoke and lack of air. (16) As the Singhs felt extremely tortured inside the cave, They made attempts to block the entry of smoke. Whatever articles of clothing they had with them, They corked the cave's opening with those clothes. (17) Then, the Mughals, thinking of another strategy, Thought of forcing the people to dig out the whole cave. Deciding on such a strategy and sending their troops, The Mughals brought the people with spades in their hands. (18) People, being quite clever, came with the troops, And they were also made to dig the caves with the spades. But they struck the spades so oddly that the spades got dismantled, For which lapse they were roughed up by the Mughal soldiers. (19) Dohra: As the soldiers went out to call the carpenters, For fixing the dismantled spades in to the handles, The darkness descended on the scene, And the troops returned to their barracks. (20) Set the Cave's opening on fire after filling it with wooden logs. As the raging fire burnt the corked clothings, The Singhs inside underwent a lot of torture. (21) And plugged the opening with a moistened clay batter. As they attempted to save their lives somehow, Darkness descended on the scene once again. (22) The people (in the meanwhile) frightened the Mughals, That other Singhs would definitely attack them at night. As the Mughals deserted the place being scared, The people gathered around the cave from all sides. (23) They brought the Singhs out after putting out the fire, Such being the ordeal through which the Singhs passed. I (the author) having heard from those who faced it, Have narrated it after a thorough contemplation. (24)

pages.title: Conclusion of the Lion Cave Episode and Opening of Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Kot
pages.snippet: The narrative closes the lion cave ordeal by stressing that even after grievous suffering the Singhs did not abandon their claim to honor, sovereignty, or Sikh discipline. The moral of the episode is therefore not escape alone, but proof th
pages.searchText: Conclusion of the Lion Cave Episode and Opening of Subeg Singh Jambar Mehtab Kot Episode About Mehtab Kot The narrative closes the lion cave ordeal by stressing that even after grievous suffering the Singhs did not abandon their claim to honor, sovereignty, or Sikh discipline. The moral of the episode is therefore not escape alone, but proof that persecution could not break the Khalsa's inner resolve. From that conclusion the book makes an explicit hinge into a new sakhi: Episode 105 opens with Subeg Singh Jambar, introduced as a firm Sikh whose standing is recognized widely enough to draw both confidence and scrutiny. The page marks the change clearly, using the end of one ordeal to prepare a different kind of martyrdom narrative. Once Subeg Singh enters the frame, the nawab's court begins pressing him with the familiar mixture of summons, offer, and coercive expectation. The transition keeps the campaign of oppression continuous while giving it a new central witness.

pages.title: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: They did not give up their claim to sovereignty. It is for these sacrifices that sovereignty was conferred, On their commonwealth of Kshtryas, Artisans, wine traders and Jats. (25) Episode 105 The Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar (The Great
pages.searchText: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct They did not give up their claim to sovereignty. It is for these sacrifices that sovereignty was conferred, On their commonwealth of Kshtryas, Artisans, wine traders and Jats. (25) Episode 105 The Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar (The Great Guru upheld the Devout Sikh's Dignity) There lived a (devout) Singh named Subeg Singh Jambhar, Who was a staunch follower of Sikh ideology and its tenets. Even he was a devout Sikh of the Sikh Gurus, Who had begot Subeg Singh Jambar. (1) Educating his son in the Persian language in childhood, His father got him employed in the Mughal court. He, being a supplier of provisions to the Mughals on contract, He had his residence in the (central) city of Lahore. (2) The Mughals would, often, send him as their emissary to the Khalsa, As the Khalsa Panth, too, had a good opinion about him. Whenever the Mughals had any pressing issue to be sorted out, They would make him their emissary with many solicitations. (3) As he had gone (on diplomatic missions) to the Singhs many a time, The Singhs, too, wished to remain on good terms with him. His services would the Mughals utilize through various tactics, He, being a great well-wisher of the Khalsa Panth. He could sacrifice all that he possessed for the Khalsa Panth, Even at the cost of severing his closest family ties. (5) Such a human being was Subeg Singh Jambar, A man of ascetic, meditative and resolute disposition. (Dear readers), the author beseeches you to listen with concentration, The way the (wicked) Mughals dealth with such a pious man. (6) Taking Subeg Singh into custody from his village Jambar, The Mughals captured his infant son along with him. Offering various temptations of money, employment and landed property, The Lahore Nawab asked him to get converted to Islam. (7)

pages.title: Subeg Singh Rejects Conversion and Mounts the Torture Wheel
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Brought before the nawab and threatened with death, Subeg Singh refuses to convert and treats apostasy as worse than bodily destruction. His answer frames martyrdom as fidelity to dharam, not as a tragic accident, and it denies the court th
pages.searchText: Subeg Singh Rejects Conversion and Mounts the Torture Wheel Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Brought before the nawab and threatened with death, Subeg Singh refuses to convert and treats apostasy as worse than bodily destruction. His answer frames martyrdom as fidelity to dharam, not as a tragic accident, and it denies the court the moral satisfaction of thinking fear can purchase assent. The authorities then bind him to the torture wheel, but even there he continues to invoke Akal and remember Guru Nanak rather than bargain for release. The page presents physical torment and spiritual steadiness side by side so that the violence of the regime only clarifies the firmness of the Sikh prisoner. By the end of the scene, the nawab has failed to shake Subeg Singh through threat alone and begins looking for new methods of pressure. That shift prepares the next escalation, in which cruelty is redirected toward the martyr's family.

pages.title: Otherwise Subeg Singh should get prepared to die,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Otherwise Subeg Singh should get prepared to die, With his body being crushed between the wheels with spokes. At this, lowing his head in acceptance, Subeg Singh remarked, Blessed be that instrument and the moment (when he dies for his fait
pages.searchText: Otherwise Subeg Singh should get prepared to die, Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Otherwise Subeg Singh should get prepared to die, With his body being crushed between the wheels with spokes. At this, lowing his head in acceptance, Subeg Singh remarked, Blessed be that instrument and the moment (when he dies for his faith). (8) He begged the Nawab to put him on the torture rack, And have done with him without any further loss of time. As he had been a devout Sikh of the great Gurus, He would feel blessed to shed his mortal frame for his faith. (9) Great was the Nawab, greater still was his faith in Islam, Great must be his sense of justice, he being a legal expert. Should he (Subeg Singh) convert to Islam for fear of death, Would he never die after his conversion to Islam? (10) If death is imminent even after getting converted, Why should he give up his own religion in this life? He would gladly convert to Islam to escape death, As Islam was very dear to the worthy Nawab, So was his (Subeg Singh's) own religion very dear to him. He pleaded to be immediately executed on the torture rack, And be done away with without any further loss of time. (12) Firmly refusing to be got converted to Islam, He reiterated his resolve to sacrifice his life for his faith. Thereafter, issuing the orders for his execution, Subeg Singh's body was fixed between the wheels with spokes. (13) As the two wheels, with his body in between, were put into motion, Subeg Singh did not forget to meditate on God's name. As he kept on repeating the name of the Divine Guru, He also shouted the Singh slogan of victory Akal! Akal. (14) Feeling more infuriated after hearing these Singh slogans, He ordered to move the wheels more speedily to silence the Singh's voice. The faster the wheels moved, the louder became the Singh's slogans, As he did not lose his faith in the sacred name of Guru Nanak. (15) Dohra: (Failing to subdue his spirits), the Nawab issued fresh orders, That Subeg Singh's body be unhinged from the torture rack. He ordered Subeg's son to be put on the same device, So that Subeg Singh might witness his infant son's torture. (16)

pages.title: The Nawab Torments Subeg Singh’s Son before His Father
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Unable to move Subeg Singh directly, the nawab has Subeg Singh's young son tortured and hung up before his father's eyes. The violence is calculated to turn paternal grief into religious surrender, making the child a lever in the attempt to
pages.searchText: The Nawab Torments Subeg Singh’s Son before His Father Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Unable to move Subeg Singh directly, the nawab has Subeg Singh's young son tortured and hung up before his father's eyes. The violence is calculated to turn paternal grief into religious surrender, making the child a lever in the attempt to break the elder Singh's resolve. Instead, Subeg Singh blesses the child's firmness and reads the boy's suffering as honorable rather than shameful. The page turns what should have been emotional blackmail into another witness to Sikh steadfastness, with father and son reinforcing one another under terror. The nawab then shifts from spectacle to temptation, offering life, estate, protection, and future status if either of them will accept Islam. Torture and reward become two faces of the same coercive project, but neither is yet enough to compel consent.

pages.title: The executioners, carrying on the orders of the Nawab,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: The executioners, carrying on the orders of the Nawab, Hung the infants body upside down with his legs tied. As they moved the spoked wheels with full force, Subeg Singh was made to see the torture with his own eyes. (17) Overwhelmed with e
pages.searchText: The executioners, carrying on the orders of the Nawab, Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct The executioners, carrying on the orders of the Nawab, Hung the infants body upside down with his legs tied. As they moved the spoked wheels with full force, Subeg Singh was made to see the torture with his own eyes. (17) Overwhelmed with emotion, Subeg Singh kept remarking, Blessed be his son and blessed be the day of sacrifice. Blessed be the person who died for his faith, Blessed be he who yearned for the lotus feet of the Guru. (18) Thereafter bringing the child down after so much torture, The Nawab tried to bring him round through these mortifications. Telling the child that he, being immature, lacked wisdom, Why should he lose his life by being obdurate? (19) Informing the child that while his father had enjoyed every joy of life, What good purpose would it serve to keep his faith, If he ended his life without enjoying the comforts of life? (20) Impressing upon the child to get converted to Islam, The Nawab offered to grant him a vast landed property. So long as the country remained under a sovereign rule, Nobody could deprive him of his possession of that property. (21) Addressing Subeg Singh once again, remarked the Nawab, That he should save his son's life from the executioner's sword. He should keep his family line alive by saving his son, By swearing on the Islam's Koranic religious verses. (22) The Nawab threatened to slaughter together with village populace, Otherwise he should instruct his son to convert to Islam. As his own life would also be spared after his son's conversion, Subeg Singh should show some concern for his son's life. (23) Survival of sons alone keeps a family line going, As families without sons are rendered issueless. Hearing this advice Subeg Singh said to the Nawab, That the latter was, indeed, speaking the truth. (24) Since he (Subeg Singh) had earned his livelihood from Nawab's service, It did not behove him to use unparliamentary words before his boss. He would tender only one advice to his son, That the great Guru alone was the preserver of a Sikh's life. (25)

pages.title: Subeg Singh Invokes the Gurus as the Torture Intensifies
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Subeg Singh answers the offers by arguing that mere survival has no value when purchased through betrayal of the Guru. The Gurus themselves surrendered their sons for the Panth, so he cannot preserve his own line by abandoning the very fait
pages.searchText: Subeg Singh Invokes the Gurus as the Torture Intensifies Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Subeg Singh answers the offers by arguing that mere survival has no value when purchased through betrayal of the Guru. The Gurus themselves surrendered their sons for the Panth, so he cannot preserve his own line by abandoning the very faith that gave his household meaning. That appeal to precedent transforms private suffering into continuity with Sikh history. What the court sees as stubbornness, the narrative presents as disciplined remembrance of how the Gurus placed truth above lineage, comfort, and worldly security. Frustrated by argument, the nawab abandons persuasion and orders the child's torture to be intensified again. The page thus hardens the confrontation into a direct contest between imperial cruelty and inherited Sikh resolve.

pages.title: Inevitability of death was an accepted universal norm.
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Inevitability of death was an accepted universal norm. How could man escape death as it is inevitable. The Sikh Gurus had served the cause of Khalsa Panth, Even as they sacrificed their lives together with their progeny. (27) All the four s
pages.searchText: Inevitability of death was an accepted universal norm. Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Inevitability of death was an accepted universal norm. How could man escape death as it is inevitable. The Sikh Gurus had served the cause of Khalsa Panth, Even as they sacrificed their lives together with their progeny. (27) All the four sons of the Guru had given up their life, Sacrificing their lives at the altar of goddess of war. As they had sacrificed their whole family for the sake of the Sikhs, What distinction would the Sikhs earn preserving their progeny? (28) As this dialogue continued for some time, The Nawab had different thoughts in his mind. As the kind of advice Subeg Singh was tendering his son, The child was getting more and more adamant in his conviction. (29) He thought he must separate the son from his father, And convert him to Islam through duress and threats. As the child's body would writhe in excruciating pain, He would forget everything about his Guru and guide. (30) The Nawab ordered to subject the child to extreme tortures, As well as grant land gifts if the child so desired. Thereafter, the executioners began to torture the child severely, With dragging him from his feet and giving blows on his face. (31) Revolving his whole body by dangling it from a single leg, Pricking his body with the their sharp teeth and nails, Inflicting pain by pulling at his nose and ears, They would threaten him with knocking down his teeth. Somebody remarked that the child was pretending to be unconscious, He must be skinned alive for his feigning unconsciousness. (33) My (author's) tongue fails to narrate the mortifications, Which were inflicted (on the tender body of this child). Instructing the executioners to fit him between the spoked wheels again,

pages.title: The Child Is Revived and Pressed toward Conversion
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: After extended torment, the child falls into a state that looks like the edge of death, and for a moment Subeg Singh reads the scene as proof that Sikh honor has been preserved. The executioners and court, however, are not prepared to let t
pages.searchText: The Child Is Revived and Pressed toward Conversion Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct After extended torment, the child falls into a state that looks like the edge of death, and for a moment Subeg Singh reads the scene as proof that Sikh honor has been preserved. The executioners and court, however, are not prepared to let the drama end there. Instead, the child is revived and pressed toward conversion, surrounded by those who try to rename his ordeal as rebirth into another faith. This maneuver aims to rewrite the meaning of suffering itself, turning near-death into an instrument of ideological capture. Subeg Singh is left astonished and heartsore as he watches the regime attempt to manufacture consent out of exhaustion and confusion. The page dwells on that shock in order to show how coercion seeks not only the body but also memory, identity, and speech.

pages.title: As the executioners got exhausted with their job,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: As the executioners got exhausted with their job, Exhausting all means of torturing a human body, The child also went into a spell of deep silence, As a fit of spasmodic convulsion hit his system. (35) At this, the executioner gave an indic
pages.searchText: As the executioners got exhausted with their job, Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct As the executioners got exhausted with their job, Exhausting all means of torturing a human body, The child also went into a spell of deep silence, As a fit of spasmodic convulsion hit his system. (35) At this, the executioner gave an indication, That the child was on the verge of death. Subeg Singh felt elated at this remark, As the revered Guru had upheld his self-respect. (36) Blessed be his son and blessed be the womb who begot him, As their faith had been vindicated through their noble deeds. Subeg Singh recalled another similar incident (of religious conviction), Where a father had voluntarily got his son sawn into two pieces. (37) Thereafter ordering a servant to fetch some water, The Nawab, after sprinkling a bit on the child's face, put it in his mouth. As the child regained a bit of consciousness, The Nawab patted him to bolster his self-confidence. (38) Telling the child that since he had been born again after regaining consciousness, He would not be accused of converting to Islam after a new life. Summoning all the Hindus who had converted to Islam, He made them stand by the side of the child. (39) Persuading the child through their glib talk, These converts prompted him to say he would convert to Islam. Drifting between spells of unconsciousness and awakening, He spoke a few words with a staggering tongue. (40) The Nawab heaved a sigh of great relief, As he made the child say, I would convert to Islam. The child has been misled to convert through threats of torture, Subeg Singh heard his own words reverberating into his ears. (41) Being bewildered (at this sudden turn of events), Subeg Singh felt extremely pained at heart. Summoning the child to where Subeg Singh stood, The Nawab remarked that the child was converting to Islam. To Subeg Singh's query: What made him think of converting to Islam? The child replied that he could no longer bear the torture. Hearing this, Subeg Singh was stunned into dumb-foundedness, As he felt extremely desperate at such a catastrophe. (43)

pages.title: Subeg Singh Reads the Boy’s Forehead and Challenges the Nawab
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Refusing to accept appearances, Subeg Singh asks to see the boy closely so he can understand what has happened under torture and pressure. The request gives the scene a sudden intimacy, shifting attention from the court's spectacle to the f
pages.searchText: Subeg Singh Reads the Boy’s Forehead and Challenges the Nawab Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Refusing to accept appearances, Subeg Singh asks to see the boy closely so he can understand what has happened under torture and pressure. The request gives the scene a sudden intimacy, shifting attention from the court's spectacle to the father's searching discernment. When he studies the child, Subeg Singh asks to see the boy closely in a spiritual as well as physical sense, interpreting the moment through destiny, inscription, and the Guru's Name. He symbolically wipes away the fate he reads on the boy's forehead while uttering Akal and Satnam, turning the body itself into a site of contest between imposed identity and recovered truth. The nawab, unsettled by that act, immediately tests whether the child will still repeat the kalma or return to Sikh speech. What follows becomes another trial of language, memory, and spiritual allegiance.

pages.title: Soon after it occurred into Subeg Singh's mind,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Soon after it occurred into Subeg Singh's mind, That he should have a look at his son's face. He must examine how he was going to recite the Koranic verse, And why was he willing to forget the Guru's Name. (44) Calling his son to him from w
pages.searchText: Soon after it occurred into Subeg Singh's mind, Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Soon after it occurred into Subeg Singh's mind, That he should have a look at his son's face. He must examine how he was going to recite the Koranic verse, And why was he willing to forget the Guru's Name. (44) Calling his son to him from where he stood with the Nawab, Subeg Singh attempted to persuade him gently. Had anyone threatened you with a sword? (45) As Subeg Singh looked at the child's forehead closely, He found that the child was destined to be converted. Shaking his head in desperation after deciphering the inscription, He expressed deep regret at his son's destined misfortune. (46) As Subeg Singh had deciphered from the child's forehead, His son was destined to be converted to Islam. Thereafter removing a shoe from one of his own feet, He touched the child's forehead with his bare foot. (47) The pious Khalsa (Subeg Singh) effaced the blasphemous inscription. With the chanting of the sacred name of the Divine creator, The predestined inscription was totally effaced. (48) It became an occurring well-known in the world, That the word Khalsa came to be inscribed on the child's forehead. As a saint, if he wills, could as much efface a person's destined lot, As he could alter altogether the predestined fortune. (49) As the Nawab looked at (Subeg Singh's strange gesture), He felt a bit disturbed in his own mind. Questioning Subeg Singh's touching child's head with his barefoot, The Nawab asked him to explain the implications of his act. (50) To Nawab's query, replied Subeg Singh in this vein, That the latter had effaced the child's predestined fortune. As the Nawab declared it to be a white lie, Subeg Singh asked the Nawab to confirm it from the child. (51) As the Nawab started questioning the child, The child turned a deaf ear to all his queries. Asking the child to get converted to Islam, He promisted to spare his life after his conversion. (52)

pages.title: The Child Reaffirms Waheguru and Father and Son Are Imprisoned
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: When questioned again, the child firmly rejects the nawab's kalma and answers instead with the Guru-given invocation of Satnam and Waheguru. The reversal undoes the court's attempt to stage a conversion and restores the scene to the moral u
pages.searchText: The Child Reaffirms Waheguru and Father and Son Are Imprisoned Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct When questioned again, the child firmly rejects the nawab's kalma and answers instead with the Guru-given invocation of Satnam and Waheguru. The reversal undoes the court's attempt to stage a conversion and restores the scene to the moral universe claimed by Subeg Singh. Clerics, Quranic recitations, and renewed pressure all fail to secure a stable submission. The page emphasizes that even institutional religion allied with state power cannot master a conscience reawakened in the Guru's memory. At last the nawab gives up on immediate success and has father and son imprisoned. The sakhi closes by preserving the episode as a remembered martyrdom sequence whose meaning lies in steadfast refusal rather than physical escape.

pages.snippet: At this child told the Nawab (in unmistakable terms), That his own faith's teachings were dear to him. As he (the child) had received God's true Name from his Guru, The Guru had blessed him with the Divine name Waheguru. (53) Getting infuri
pages.searchText: At this child told the Nawab (in unmistakable terms), Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct At this child told the Nawab (in unmistakable terms), That his own faith's teachings were dear to him. As he (the child) had received God's true Name from his Guru, The Guru had blessed him with the Divine name Waheguru. (53) Getting infuriated at the child's curt, bold reply, The Nawab ordered the child to be tortured severely. After this, even when the child was tortured far more severely, The child felt comforted at his chastisement. (54) As the saintly child Prehlad? had not experienced pain, Subeg Singh's son, too, derived comfort from his torture. The more the child was beaten and thrashed, The more the child rejoiced at his persecution. (55) The executioners got exhausted with mortifying the child, As they had exhausted all means of persecuting him. At this, it occurred to the Nawab's (disturbed) mind, That some kind of a magic spell had been cast on the child. (56) Summoning the Muslim clerics and Islamic theologians, He asked them to neutralize the alleged magic spell. Asking them to try their best through the Koranic incantations, They must get the child converted to Islam. (57) The clerics failed to get the child converted. All their efforts at conversion ended in vain. (58) As the Nawab got exhausted after practising every torture, He could not see through the Guru's mysterious support of His Sikhs. Thereafter summoning both Subeg Singh and his son to his court, The Nawab ordered the discontinuation of every torture. (59) The way both father and son were put behind the bars, Rattan Singh had narrated the account thoroughly. Since the Guru had upheld the dignity of Subeg Singh, His persecution has become a legend of supreme sacrifice. (60) It was in the year eighteen hundred two of Bikrami Samvat, (That the father son duo were persecuted by Lahore Nawab). This is how the legend of Subeg Singh's sacrifice occurred, Dear devout readers listen to its contents with faith and devotion. (61)

pages.title: Episode 105 Closes and Bhai Taru Singh Enters the Narrative
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Khalsa's Conduct
pages.snippet: Rattan Singh closes the previous sakhi by saying he has written it as he heard it from his father, then turns the reader toward a new narrative movement. The page is a hinge rather than a single scene, because it deliberately finishes the e
pages.searchText: Episode 105 Closes and Bhai Taru Singh Enters the Narrative Khalsa's Conduct Episode About Khalsa's Conduct Rattan Singh closes the previous sakhi by saying he has written it as he heard it from his father, then turns the reader toward a new narrative movement. The page is a hinge rather than a single scene, because it deliberately finishes the earlier account before announcing a fresh episode. Episode 106 opens with Bhai Taru Singh, presented as a fearless martyr from the Majha village of Poolha whose scalp could be taken from his head but whose faith could not be taken from his heart. He is introduced as a disciplined, truthful, and devout Singh whose steadfastness will condemn the oppressor rather than save his own life. The page also frames the political problem that drives the episode: the Lahore nawab cannot understand how the scattered Singhs continue to live when they hold no offices, pursue no ordinary trade, and are hunted on every road. That question leads directly into the search for the hidden networks that keep the Khalsa alive.

pages.title: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.snippet: The way I (the author) had heard this legend from my father, I (Rattan Singh) have narrated it in this episode. I have narrated the way in which I had heard it, Now (dear readers) listen to another new episode. (62) Episode 106 The Episode
pages.searchText: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar Subeg Singh Jambar Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar The way I (the author) had heard this legend from my father, I (Rattan Singh) have narrated it in this episode. I have narrated the way in which I had heard it, Now (dear readers) listen to another new episode. (62) Episode 106 The Episode About Taru Singh — A Fearless Martyr (Never would he flee from his impeding death) Dear devout readers listen with concentration and devotion, The episode about Bhai Taru Singh! (a fearless Singh Martyr). Who got Khan Bahadur damned in the Dinive Court, By getting his own scalp removed from his head. (1) He being an inhabitant of the Majha region of Punjab, He resided in village Poolha? in perfect peace and piety. Being a man of resolute, meditative, upright and abstemious disposition, He was known by the name of Taru Singh Nihang. (2) As the Lahore Nawab neared the end of his tether, It was in the year of 1802 of Bikrami Samvat, That Bhai Taru Singh performed an act of supreme sacrifice. Summoning his subjects, the Nawab made an enquiry, Where from did the Singhs manage to get their wherewithal? Nor were they known to carry out any business or employment. (4) Whatever they received by way of offerings in their shrines, Had also been banned through a royal decree. Whatever the Singhs, received in charity in the name of Sikh Gurus, That too had been prohibited through his royal orders. (5) Why did they not die of starvation and hunger, When all kinds of provisions had been made scarce. With Mughal troops blockading all the highways, The Singhs were being killed through search and shoot operations. (6) In whatever village was a Singh reported to be residing, He had ordered that village to be razed to the ground.

pages.title: How the Hidden Singhs Were Sustained
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.snippet: The nawab boasts that the villages linked to the Singhs have been ravaged, their kin dragged out of hiding, and Mughal parties sent everywhere to strike them down. On the surface, the regime appears to have cut every ordinary path of liveli
pages.searchText: How the Hidden Singhs Were Sustained Subeg Singh Jambar Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar The nawab boasts that the villages linked to the Singhs have been ravaged, their kin dragged out of hiding, and Mughal parties sent everywhere to strike them down. On the surface, the regime appears to have cut every ordinary path of livelihood and reduced the fugitives to hunger and disguise. Yet the hidden Singhs were still being fed, and that stubborn fact unsettles the court. The page turns on the contradiction between relentless persecution and the continued survival of men who should, by the nawab's reasoning, have already perished from want. A malicious informer then reveals the answer: local Sikhs and sympathizers feed themselves only after feeding the Khalsa, willingly accepting privation so that the hunted Singhs can keep moving. The regime's military pressure has therefore failed to break the moral economy that sustains the Panth.

(10) Chaupai: Harbhagat Niranjania* (a rival to the Guru's seat) remarked, That whatever the earlier informer had reported was indeed true. (11) They were prepared to face starvation and destitution themselves, But they could not bear a Singh suffering for want of food. They could keep themselves warm in winter by sitting around a fire, But they got expensive garments stitched for the fellow Singhs. (12) They sent their entire earnings to the Singhs (in the wilds). They also sent their proceeds to Singhs without fail. (13) Even those who were serving at distant places, They also offered all their wages to the Singhs. Even those among them who had gone abroad, Were sending their money to their dear, devout Singhs. (14) Dohra: Hearing this account, the Nawab shook his head in distress, Remarking that the Khalsa Panth was indeed very formidable. Since the Khalsa could hardly be eliminated by him, God alone had the power to decimate the Khalsa Panth. (15)

pages.title: Harbhagat Names Taru Singh of Poolha
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.snippet: The nawab now demands names, ordering his men to identify those who send provisions to the Singhs so they can be destroyed as examples. Harbhagat Niranjania answers by turning suspicion into accusation and directing state violence toward sp
pages.searchText: Harbhagat Names Taru Singh of Poolha Subeg Singh Jambar Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar The nawab now demands names, ordering his men to identify those who send provisions to the Singhs so they can be destroyed as examples. Harbhagat Niranjania answers by turning suspicion into accusation and directing state violence toward specific Sikh householders. He points to Taru Singh of village Poolha, describing a cultivator who pays what is due, keeps only a little for himself, and sends the remainder onward to the Khalsa. Taru Singh is thus portrayed not as a rebel sustained by wealth, but as a village Sikh who converts ordinary labor into support for a persecuted community. The page widens that portrait by bringing in Taru Singh's mother and sister, who live austerely, reject rival devotional claims, and move supplies discreetly toward the Singhs; it then introduces Mehtab Singh as another dangerous supporter living more openly in militant fashion. Together these details explain why the state begins to pursue Taru Singh's household with special determination.

Always having a band of fifty odd Singhs under his command, He waylaid the people and robbed them of their possessions. (24)

pages.title: Arrest of Bhai Taru Singh and the Bhardana Sikhs’ Rescue Plan
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.snippet: The narrative first recalls Mehtab Singh's rough methods of extracting resources, after which the nawab orders Harbhagat to seize him with a substantial force while sending a smaller detachment for Taru Singh. The contrast shows that the co
pages.searchText: Arrest of Bhai Taru Singh and the Bhardana Sikhs’ Rescue Plan Subeg Singh Jambar Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar The narrative first recalls Mehtab Singh's rough methods of extracting resources, after which the nawab orders Harbhagat to seize him with a substantial force while sending a smaller detachment for Taru Singh. The contrast shows that the court reads Mehtab as a field threat but Taru Singh as a household supporter who can be captured more easily. The detachment succeeds in taking Taru Singh and carries him toward Bhardana, where crowds gather for a glimpse despite official blows and intimidation. In that tense pause between arrest and transfer, the Bhardana Sikhs wanted to free him and began to discuss rescue as a sacred duty rather than a mere act of local loyalty. When the proposal reaches Taru Singh, however, he refuses to let the sangat risk themselves for his release. The page therefore ends not with escape but with the martyr's own insistence that the Panth must measure duty by a higher standard than immediate survival.

pages.title: Bhai Taru Singh on the Gurus’ Sacrifice for the Panth
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.snippet: Taru Singh answers the rescue proposal by declaring that he will not run from death when death has come through service to the Panth. For him, martyrdom is not an accident to avoid but a conscious offering that aligns his own fate with the
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh on the Gurus’ Sacrifice for the Panth Subeg Singh Jambar Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar Taru Singh answers the rescue proposal by declaring that he will not run from death when death has come through service to the Panth. For him, martyrdom is not an accident to avoid but a conscious offering that aligns his own fate with the path already shown by the Gurus. He argues that the Gurus had given their own heads for the Panth, and not only their own heads but also the lives of sons and descendants. The point is not rhetorical excess: it grounds his refusal in a remembered chain of sacrifice through which Sikh dignity and collective purpose were preserved. From that memory he draws a political lesson as well, namely that any hope of sovereignty or communal honor under Mughal oppression demands willingness to suffer rather than compromise. His answer turns personal arrest into a meditation on how the Panth grows through costly fidelity.

pages.title: Bhai Taru Singh Explains Why the Guru’s Vow Cannot Be Undone
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar
pages.snippet: Continuing his reply, Taru Singh says one sheath cannot hold two swords and that two sovereign claims cannot share one throne. The image compresses the page's argument: the Khalsa's path and imperial domination cannot both be preserved inta
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh Explains Why the Guru’s Vow Cannot Be Undone Subeg Singh Jambar Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar Continuing his reply, Taru Singh says one sheath cannot hold two swords and that two sovereign claims cannot share one throne. The image compresses the page's argument: the Khalsa's path and imperial domination cannot both be preserved intact, so sacrifice becomes the price of truth. When the gathered Sikhs ask why the Gurus accepted such suffering, Taru Singh says the Guru's utterance cannot be erased because it was written in the divine court. What has been spoken and sealed in that higher register must be fulfilled even when fulfillment demands bodily loss. He therefore insists that a Sikh cannot seek to save his own life after the Gurus have spent theirs for the community, while also pointing the sangat back toward the older history of Guru Nanak and Babur. The page becomes a threshold from Taru Singh's martyrdom into the larger retrospective explanation that follows.

pages.searchText: Episode 107: Sakhi of Babur Subeg Singh Jambar Episode About Subeg Singh Jambar Episode 107 opens with the Sakhi of Babur and explicitly announces a retrospective turn away from Taru Singh's immediate scene toward the older cause of Guru-suffering. The page frames this as the beginning of an explanatory history rather than a break in devotional seriousness. Using the comparison of an incautious boon, the poet says Guru Nanak's utterance toward Babur later required endurance and suffering for the sake of the Sikhs. Readers are asked to listen closely because the new episode explains how a spoken blessing can reverberate through later generations. From there the narration starts laying out the political stage around Talvandi Rai Bhoi, Daulat Khan Lodhi, and the conditions that will draw Babur into the story. The page therefore functions as both a fresh episode opening and a deliberate return to early historical causation.

pages.searchText: Daulat Khan’s Sons Rise, Then Fall under Bairam Khan Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi Episode About Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi The page continues the account of Daulat Khan's household by saying that Daulat Khan's wives received Guru Nanak's blessing and then bore the sons they had long desired. Those sons are named and positioned as the fruit of grace before the narrative shifts to their political advancement. As the four boys mature, they enter service and become nawabs or high officials at the Delhi court under the Lodhi order. Their rise links Guru Nanak's blessing with worldly prominence, but only briefly, because court politics remain unstable and dangerous. After Sikandar Lodhi's line passes on, Bairam Khan's arrogance ruins experienced governance, and Daulat Khan's sons are among those destroyed in the ensuing violence. The page therefore pairs fulfilled blessing with sudden reversal, preparing Daulat Khan's desperate appeal for justice.

pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Flees to Guru Nanak after the Slaying of His Sons Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi After the murder of Rai Bhoi and the spreading fear at court, confidence in Bairam Khan collapses and officials begin to scatter, hide, or think only of escape. The courtly world that had once rewarded Daulat Khan's house now feels exposed to arbitrary destruction. News reaches Daulat Khan that his sons have been killed, and Daulat Khan flees toward Eminabad in search of the one refuge still imagined as trustworthy. The movement is both geographic and spiritual, carrying him away from compromised political power and toward Guru Nanak's presence. By the end of the page he is no longer a grand court figure but a bereaved father hurrying to fall at the Guru's feet. That shift from office to supplication gives the next scene its emotional weight and moral urgency.

pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Urges Guru Nanak to End Pathan Rule and Take the Throne Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi Having laid out the facts of his ruin, Daulat Khan places himself in Guru Nanak's refuge and asks for protection against the Pathan order that has devoured its own supporters. The page presents him as a petitioner who now sees truth more clearly than he did while secure in office. In the boldest part of his plea, Daulat Khan urges Guru Nanak to take the throne of Hindustan so that tyrannical rule might be broken at its root. His request is not merely personal revenge; it is a proposal that spiritual authority should replace failed and violent kingship. Guru Nanak does not seize that invitation, instead remaining detached from worldly ambition and indicating that he has come to bestow sovereignty, not to hoard it for himself. The page thus closes the appeal by distinguishing divine mission from temporal possession while leaving the political problem fully exposed.

(23) May the Guru protect him or cause him to perish. Since Bairam Khan had slaughtered the Guru's devotees, Daulat Khan was pleading before the Guru for justice. (24) The Guru, for upholding the dignity of his devout followers, Since the Pathan ruler had turned cannibalistic, Pathans sovereignty over India must be done away with. (25) Either the great Guru himself should become a sovereign ruler, Or he should anoint his son as the new sovereign. The sovereignty over India being of great significance, The Guru must preserve it in his own household. (26) Hearing this, the great Guru told Daulat Khan, That he was in no need of any sovereignty. Of what consequence was the sovereignty of India, When he had renounced millions of such sovereignties. (27) It was for the task of bestowing sovereignty on others, That the Divine Lord had sent him (the Guru) in the age of Kaliyuga. Since the life of a sovereign was always a bed of thorns, The Guru experienced great happiness in meditation on the Divine. (28) Why should he (the Guru) take over such a sovereignty, That Daulat Khan was talking about time and again? Would the people not heap ridicule upon him, For having grabbed it after forsaking it earlier? Hearing this, all hopes of Daulat Khan about, Guru's acceptance of sovereignty were dashed to the ground. After this, Daulat Khan abandoned all efforts, To press the Guru again and again to become a sovereign. (29) In case the Guru refused to accept sovereignty himself.

pages.searchText: Guru Nanak Warns Daulat Khan and Sends Him to Kabul Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi Episode About Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi Daulat Khan presses Guru Nanak to strip sovereignty from the Pathans even if it must pass to another dynasty, but the Guru warns him that once bestowed on the Mughals it would never return to the Pathans. The prophecy does not merely promise a change of rulers; it tells Daulat that he is asking for a transfer he will never be able to undo. Guru Nanak then turns prediction into instruction. He tells Daulat Khan to go swiftly to Kabul and place the matter before Babur, making clear that the coming upheaval has already entered the field of destiny. Encouraged by that command, Daulat Khan leaves joyfully in disguise rather than as a grand courtier. The page presents his departure in a fakir's garb as both political secrecy and the first outward sign that the old Pathan order is already cracking.

Meanwhile Bairam Shah had blocked all routes to Kabul, Somehow managed to creep into the city of Kabul.

pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Reports Hindustan's Disorder to Babur Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi Episode About Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi After initial difficulty reaching the conqueror, Daulat Khan was given audience with Babur and finally able to speak about conditions in Hindustan. He lays before Babur the secrets of Delhi and the weakness of the Lodhi-Pathan establishment, turning private grievance into a full political briefing. His complaint is that misrule has become structural rather than accidental. Experienced officers and wazirs were slain or discarded, while immature and incapable men were elevated into posts that required judgment, discipline, and strategic sense. The page then sharpens that complaint with proverbial force. Rai Bhoi's warning that small men cannot accomplish great tasks becomes the moral of the courtly diagnosis, explaining why the kingdom has become vulnerable to an invader who knows how to seize opportunity.

He got into touch with Babur in a moment's time. (39) Babur, according a state honour to Daulat Khan, Heard the whole account about India from the latter. Disclosing all the state secrets of Delhi court to Babur, Daulat Khan revealed the complete strength of the Lodhi Pathans Army. (40) Disclosing Bairam Khan's slaughter of all the seasoned custodians, The new custodians, failing to govern their states efficiently, Had started accusing their predecessors for misgovernance. (41) He had slaughtered all the higher officials of the state, Together with the Provincial custodians and ministers. In their place, he had appointed immature rustic adolescents, Giving them higher positions of state and court officials. (42) The miniscule number that survived this ruler's tyranny, They, too, had lost every hope of their survival. All the feudal chiefs, too, became frustrated with the situation, Even as the Maratha custodians in the south were also replaced. (43) Rai Bhoi who, being the seniormost among the ministers, Was also the wisest and the most sensible among them. As he witnessed the elimination of all the senior functionaries, He realized that the state administration was going to the dogs. (44) Being the emperor's well-wisher he advised the king in good faith, That the dwarfs could never accomplish tasks worthy of giants. Neither should the great warriors deserved to be killed, Nor could the petty people accomplish the higher tasks of the state. (45) Episode from Satswayya How can a lowly minion of a state, Accomplish a task worthy of a giant? How can the surface of a huge war-drum, Be sewn with the skin of even one hundred rodents? (46) Hearing this, the emperor got Rai Bhoi slaughtered, Thus putting to death his own well-wishers.

pages.searchText: Rai Bhoi's Death and the Minister's Counsel to Babur Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi Episode About Bhai Taru Singh — A Fearless Manyi The page closes the Rai Bhoi thread by showing how badly wisdom is repaid under corrupt rule. Rai Bhoi was slain without offense, and there was great outcry because the ruler had destroyed his own well-wisher instead of listening to him. From that lament the narrative pivots into Babur's next decision. Though Babur was made ready to advance on Hindustan, his advisers insist that conquest cannot be undertaken blindly in a land guarded by saints and holy men. The minister's counsel focuses above all on Guru Nanak. Babur is told to seek Guru Nanak's permission before marching further, because temporal force alone will not be enough if the spiritual order of India stands against him.

So being revered by both the communities, Both Hindus and Muslims remained keen to receive his blessings. (3) So, perfect was he in his spiritual dispensation, As if he was eternally in communication with the Divine. He (the minister) himself had confirmed Guru Nanak's divinity, As everything that Nanak predicted came out to be true. pages.searchText: Babur Challenges Nanak's Authority and Marches to Meet Him Babur Babur reacts skeptically when Daulat Khan says Guru Nanak can bestow or withhold sovereignty. He asks who Nanak is to grant kingship and then resolves to go see him, treating the encounter as a test of spiritual claim rather than an act of devotion. His tone remains threatening as well as curious. Babur says that if the saint proves false he should be punished or converted, while if he is genuine Babur will judge the matter from direct experience rather than rumor. The army therefore advances toward the Guru with a mixture of challenge and expectation. As the page closes, the narrative prepares the meeting by placing Babur's political ambition alongside the Guru's unhurried spiritual authority.
