pages.searchText: Babur Reaches Punjab and Sends Daulat Khan to Guru Nanak Babur Episode About Babur ... The narrative now moves into the Punjab campaign and evokes the Guru's own testimony against invasion with the line about Khurasan and Hindustan. As Babur takes Saidpur and pushes onward, the violence of empire is set beside the moral witness that will judge it. Babur asks Daulat Khan to locate Guru Nanak near Eminabad and bring him into contact with the imperial camp. Even offers of land and favor are placed on the table, but the page makes clear that worldly inducements cannot measure the Guru's station. When Daulat finally approaches, courtly status falls away. Daulat Khan dismounted and bowed at the Guru's feet, coming on foot before a presence that does not need armies, titles, or gifts to command obedience.

The creator, not taking the blame (for decimating the Pathans) upon Himself, Willed the Mughals to launch an invasion on India. Babur kept on entrusting the enroute territory after getting a ransom. Thereafter, summoning Daulat Khan to his own camp, Babur issued orders to him to the following effect: (16) Nanak's seat had been reported to be near Emnabad. Was Nanak still at his own seat or had he made good his escape, Scared out of his wits by the approach of Mughal troops? (17) And ask Nanak to enter into negotiations with him (Babur). Assuring Daulat Khan of not ill-treating Nanak in anyway, That no scare of any kind could unnerve the great Guru. The Guru, being the creator and destroyer of the whole world, The whole universe prospered under the command of his Divine Will. (19) Dohra: The spot where Guru Nanak sat in deep meditation, Was situated upon a mound of hard rocks and pebbles. So immovable remained Guru's seat that it never shook, Even if the whole earth and mountains shook and guaked. (20) Spotting out the Guru's seat after arriving in its vicinity, He started walking on foot after dismounting from his steed. (21) Bowing his head and paying obeisance from a distance, Daulat placed his head at the lotus feet of Guru Nanak. Having remained prostrated at the Guru's feet for long, The great Guru asked Daulat Khan to rise from the ground. (22)

pages.title: Daulat Khan Brings Babur Toward Guru Nanak
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Daulat Khan reports the situation to Guru Nanak and explains that Babur wants an audience with him. The Guru does not rush toward imperial summons; instead he calmly directs the movement of the meeting on his own terms. To prepare that enco
pages.searchText: Daulat Khan Brings Babur Toward Guru Nanak Babur Episode About Babur ... Daulat Khan reports the situation to Guru Nanak and explains that Babur wants an audience with him. The Guru does not rush toward imperial summons; instead he calmly directs the movement of the meeting on his own terms. To prepare that encounter, Mardana is told to play the rabab so that music rather than force becomes the medium through which Babur and his people are drawn near. The page uses that moment to show that the Guru's court gathers itself through sound, serenity, and command rather than through royal ceremony. Babur also asks what sort of offering should be brought before such a pir, and Daulat reminds him that spiritual and temporal authority alike rest with the Guru. The meeting is therefore framed not as a king honoring a subject, but as a ruler trying to understand the court before which his own power may have to bow.

Thereupon, the Guru asked Mardana, his companion, That he should strike a melody on his stringed instrument. (25) Chaupai: As Mardana struck a melodious tune on his Rabab, The Mughal troops rushed to listen to this fascinating music. That Guru Nanak himself had arrived at his army camp. (26) As Daulat Khan brought information about Guru Nanak's arrival, Thereafter, calling for his royal mode of conveyance, Babur wished to pay a visit to Guru Nanak himself. (27) (Before proceeding) Babur enguired from Daulat Khan, What kind of offering should Babur place before Guru Nanak. Daulat Khan informed Babur the Guru needed no offerings, As all the people received their cherished boons from Nanak. (28) All temporal and spiritual powers were vested in Guru Nanak, As Babur himself would observe after his arrival there. Thereupon, Babur informed his companion Daulat Khan, that, It behoved not a royal personage to approach a saint empty-handed. (29) On a visit to a mendicant, a monarch, and one's teacher. One is bound to fail in getting their blessings, Without placing a (token) offering before them. (30) Chaupai: Upon this, advising Babur to make an offering of cannabis, Daulat Khan asked Babur to place it before the Guru. Thereafter, carrying a bag full of cannabis leaves, Babur placed it before the Guru after dismounting from a horse. (31)

pages.title: Guru Nanak Rebukes Babur's Demand for Miracles
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: When Babur finally speaks, he asks why the Guru appears displeased with him and invites scrutiny of his own worth. He wants to know whether he is raw or ripe, true or false, as though spiritual authority were something that could be tested
pages.searchText: Guru Nanak Rebukes Babur's Demand for Miracles Babur Episode About Babur ... When Babur finally speaks, he asks why the Guru appears displeased with him and invites scrutiny of his own worth. He wants to know whether he is raw or ripe, true or false, as though spiritual authority were something that could be tested like a courtly riddle. Guru Nanak refuses that frame. He explains that saints do not stage wonders for the vanity of kings and that no one should mistake spectacle for truth. Instead, he directs Babur back toward the source of all real power. What men call miracle is only mercy or wrath from God, and neither can be manufactured to entertain ambition or flatter conquest.

pages.searchText: Thereafter the Guru, after according due honour to the Mughal ruler, Babur Episode About Babur ... Thereafter the Guru, after according due honour to the Mughal ruler, Asked him the reasons for being cross with him (Nanak). The Guru told Babur that he never obstructed Babur's advance, As he (the Guru) had been all long sitting on that rocky seat. (32) The Guru asked Babur to mete out any punishment to the former, As he had been contemplating at the time of his departure. Babur was free to allay his apprehensions that he had, Whether Guru Nanak was a fake or a genuine prophet. (33) The Guru was willing to offer himself for a close scrutiny. Found genuine, Babur could acknowledge Guru Nanak as a spiritual prophet, Found fake, he was free to get the Guru slaughtered. (34) Truth resides and rests with the Divine Lord, Elsewhere it is never found and observed. The temporal monarchs and rulers of kingdoms, Have all been putting spiritual prophets to test. (35) As Babur wished the Guru to workout some miracles, The Guru would loath to display any such feats. Display of miraculous feats not only invited Divine wrath, These also alienated the spiritual saints from the Divine as well. (36) Why could such a prophet not become a monarch as well? Power of working out miracles vested in the Divine Lord, alone, For which people accepted Him as the Supreme God. (37) He is terribly harassed by the people of this world. Whosoever lives in intimate communication with God, He always shuns the temptation to work out miracles. (38) As Babur was too keen to see demonstration of miracles, It was not a morally justifiable act on his part. Either resulting in blessings or ending up in disasters. (39) While serving with devotion saints bring out their blessings, Blessings and curses both work out as miracles, While alienating a spiritual prophet from the Divine Lord. (40)

pages.title: Babur Submits and Seeks Guru Nanak's Favor
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Babur now realizes that Guru Nanak already knows the intention he has not fully spoken aloud. That recognition breaks his earlier arrogance and convinces him that the Guru stands near the divine in a way no imperial calculation can master.
pages.searchText: Babur Submits and Seeks Guru Nanak's Favor Babur Episode About Babur ... Babur now realizes that Guru Nanak already knows the intention he has not fully spoken aloud. That recognition breaks his earlier arrogance and convinces him that the Guru stands near the divine in a way no imperial calculation can master. Using the courtly idiom of the account, Babur addresses Guru Nanak as a great pir and asks whether the hopes that brought him here can truly be fulfilled. The political question returns, but in a changed tone. Babur no longer speaks as a challenger testing a saint; he speaks as a seeker who wants confirmation that the transfer of rule he has heard about lies within the Guru's knowledge and permission.

pages.searchText: Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs, Babur Episode About Babur ... Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs, Who seize others belonging with coercion and duress. If ever a saint indulges in working out miracles, He is sure to find himself alienated from the Divine. (41) Upon this, Babur realized Guru Nanak's omniscience, Since the Guru had laid bare all Babur's secret thoughts. He decided to share all his fears and aspirations, After he felt assured about Guru Nanak's omniscience. (42) Babur felt convinced after his interaction with Guru Nanak, That the latter had really an intimate relationship with God. Since there existed no distinction between God and Guru Nanak, He must seek his blessings for getting a sovereignty over India. (43) If, God willing, the Guru Nanak answered his prayers, All his dreams and aspirations will get materialized. If, God forbid, Guru Nanak declined his prayers, He would not lose anything substantial of his own. (44) Why should he poison his future through his insolence, After this, folding his hands in supplication, Babur put forth, His dire necessity in words couched in politeness. (45) Prostrating at the lotus feet of Divine Guru Nanak, Babur begged for his aspirations to be fulfilled, Acknowledging Guru Nanak as the great Hindu prophet, He had sought the Guru's blessings in his dire need. (46) Acknowledging Guru Nanak to be as great as he had heard, Babur declared the Guru as the greatest among spiritual prophets. Admitting that after having a glimpse of the Divine Guru, He felt assured of Guru Nanak's Divine attributes. (47) Finding the Guru as venerated as in narrations he had heard, Babur found the Guru spiritually Supreme after a through probe. Whatever divine attributes of the Guru had Daulat Khan narrated, Babur had observed and confirmed with his own eyes. (48) The way the (Lodhi) Pathans had got the Guru's followers assassinated, Daulat Khan had narrated the whole account to Babur. Babur also knew about Guru's displeasure with the Lodhi Pathans, As well as the Guru's will to dispense with their rule over India. (49)

pages.title: Babur Asks for Hindustan and Is Directed Toward the Prophet
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Having abandoned open defiance, Babur states his request plainly. He says he came because he was called and asks Guru Nanak to grant him the throne of Hindustan rather than leaving the matter hanging in hints and half-confessions. Guru Nana
pages.searchText: Babur Asks for Hindustan and Is Directed Toward the Prophet Babur Episode About Babur ... Having abandoned open defiance, Babur states his request plainly. He says he came because he was called and asks Guru Nanak to grant him the throne of Hindustan rather than leaving the matter hanging in hints and half-confessions. Guru Nanak refuses to flatter that ambition in worldly language. If Babur claims kingship under God and appeals to pirs and prophets, then he must carry the question beyond politics and seek its answer through the higher court he himself invokes. Babur accepts the rebuke and asks for a way to approach that reality. The page thus turns the scene away from conquest alone and toward an ascent in which imperial desire must pass through prophecy, submission, and spiritual testing.

pages.searchText: It was Guru's will to call the Mughals from Kabul, Babur Episode About Babur ... It was Guru's will to call the Mughals from Kabul, As the Guru, being omniscient and privy to the Divinee Will. Babur told the Guru that the former had arrived at Guru's bidding, Since Daulat Khan had invited him (Babur) in the Guru's name, The Guru must protect and stand by his humble servant. Babur begged the Guru to make him occupy India's throne, Dohra: Babur said he had approached Guru Nanak with a fond wish, That the great Guru be Babur's spiritual mentor. Babur begged for a sovereignty over the Indian throne, So that his writ might run over the twenty-two states. (52) Chaupai: Upon this Baba Nanak reminded the supplicating Babur, That the latter wished to be made a sovereign by Prophet Mohammad. Babur expressed his inability to seek Prophet's (Mohammad's) blessings. (53) Since his prophet was inhabitant of the Divine Court, It was located across the seven skies (in heavens). How could Babur (a human being) reach that Divine abode, About which he had heard but never seen it with his eyes? (54) The Guru reminded Babur that he had boasted of being an emperor, Whose writ ran over half of humanity on the earth. How could he not reach his Islamic Prophet Mohammad, As he boasted of having the powers of five spiritual prophets? (55) Promising Babur to enable him to reach his prophet, The Guru directed Babur to seek sovereignty from his own prophet. Babur should reach the Divine Court in his prophet's company, Where his prophet would get a written sanction for his sovereignty. (56) Dohra: Hearing this, Babur bent on his knees in thankfulness, Begging Guru Nanak to enable him to have a glimpse of his own prophet. Being extremely confident of his prophet's divine powers, Babur was sure of getting India's sovereignty sanctioned. (57) Chaupai: Thereafter, Satguru Guru Nanak directed the Mughal emperor, That Guru's staff would lead Babur to the Divine court. Thereafter handing over his staff to the emperor Babur, Guru Nanak instructed Babur to sit on the ground in front of the staff. (58)

pages.title: Babur Enters the Heavenly Court by Satnam
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Guru Nanak now equips Babur for a visionary ascent rather than a political bargain. He teaches him the repetition of satnam and marks him for the journey, turning the emperor's request into an initiation that depends on remembrance instead
pages.searchText: Babur Enters the Heavenly Court by Satnam Babur Episode About Babur ... Guru Nanak now equips Babur for a visionary ascent rather than a political bargain. He teaches him the repetition of satnam and marks him for the journey, turning the emperor's request into an initiation that depends on remembrance instead of force. Led upward toward the heavenly threshold, Babur discovers that rank alone gains him nothing. The gate opens when he invokes satnam, proving that even an emperor enters the higher court only by the Name rather than by sword, lineage, or command. Inside, Babur beholds Guru Nanak's banner, devotional music, scripture, and radiant assembly in divine presence. The scene makes the hierarchy unmistakable: temporal empire may shake Hindustan, but Guru Nanak's sovereignty is already manifest in a court beyond earthly kingship.

pages.title: With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff, After which it would take Babur wherever he wished to go. With the continuous recitation of God's holy Name Satnam, The Guru's staff would take Babur and his prophet
pages.searchText: With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff, Babur Episode About Babur ... With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff, After which it would take Babur wherever he wished to go. With the continuous recitation of God's holy Name Satnam, The Guru's staff would take Babur and his prophet to heaven, Where nobody would stop their entry into the Divine Court. The same Divine Court was it where prophet once had gone, But was made to return the same moment to his abode. (60) With Guru's staff with them, they could stay there for many hours, While his prophet could converse with God for long. Staying there in the Divine Court for a longer spell, He and his prophet could seek whatever they wished. (61) With a respectful bow did Babur depart from Guru Nanak, Wondering at heart at the promised great miracle. Babur departed after holding the Guru's staff. (62) The moment Babur performed the proffered incantations, The Guru's staff took him on a flight the same moment. Flying across the seven skies with the Guru's staff, Babur reached the exclusive territory of the Divine Court. (63) He found the Divine Court bolted and barred from inside, Which did not open even at the approach of prophet Mohammad. But the moment Babur recited the Guru's word Satnam, In an instant opened all the doors that were barred and locked. (64) Babur witnessed Guru Nanak's standard fluttering in heavens, And heard spiritual hymns being recited from the holy books. Spiritual melodies were being recited to the accompaniment of music, Filling the whole environment with a spiritual ambience. (65) Thus, Babur saw with his own eyes after reaching there, Guru Nanak's standard fluttering inside the Divine Court. Observing Nanak's standard fluttering at the entrance, Babur had a glimpse of God seated on the Divine seat. (66) Sparkling as the crystal waters of the scared Ganges, Its saffron cloth fluttered as majestically as, If a spark of lightening had flitted across its surface. (67)

pages.title: Babur is shown Guru Nanak's heavenly court
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Babur is shown Guru Nanak's heavenly dharamsal, a radiant spiritual court filled with saints, holy attendants, and every sign of divine abundance. The page lingers over its trees, fragrance, pillars, and jeweled architecture to show that Gu
pages.searchText: Babur is shown Guru Nanak's heavenly court Babur Episode About Babur ... Babur is shown Guru Nanak's heavenly dharamsal, a radiant spiritual court filled with saints, holy attendants, and every sign of divine abundance. The page lingers over its trees, fragrance, pillars, and jeweled architecture to show that Guru Nanak's authority exceeds any earthly throne. After this heavenly tour, Babur is taken onward to the enclosure associated with the Prophet, where he sees the mosque, the standard, and the gathered assembly at prayer. He is brought forward before the prophet so that he can present the desire weighing on his mind. Babur asks for the throne of India, hoping that his petition will be granted from that court. Instead, the encounter prepares the blunt refusal that follows on the next page, where he learns that this sovereignty is not in the prophet's gift.

pages.title: The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees, Bearing the names of Parjat, Kalap Birchh, Santaan, Harichandan and Mandhar. Besides, there were other trees laden with flowers and fruit, As well as the mythical cows of the K
pages.searchText: The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees, Babur Episode About Babur ... The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees, Bearing the names of Parjat, Kalap Birchh, Santaan, Harichandan and Mandhar. Besides, there were other trees laden with flowers and fruit, As well as the mythical cows of the Kamdhen breed. (69) With rare Chinta Mani? stones were the walls of Divine Court built, With fragrant golden paint were these rare walls painted. With Vaduraya? stones were pillars of Divine Court erected, With the fragrant Sandalwood was its majestic roof inlaid. (70) With corals were the doors of the Divine Court made, With designs on the philosopher's stone were these doors carved. After taking Babur on a round of the Divine Court, The Guru's staff brought him back to the Divine entrance. (71) Thereafter taking Babur to his (Islamic) prophet's enclosure, The Guru's staff showed him the Muslim cleric reciting an Islamic prayer. Babur was shown a glimpse of his Prophet's standard, Which had not been dyed in blue for a long time. (72) There was situated a mosque, place of Muslim worship, That was designed as per Prophet's own tradition. As Babur had a glimpse of his spiritual prophet Mohammad, He started prostrating and supplicating before him. (73) Prophet Mohammad himself was seen praying to God, Entreating the Divine Lord to accept his supplication. Followed by thousands of other Muslims spiritual saints. (74) Directing Babur to stand in the queue at the back, Summoning Babur from the back to his own proximity, Prophet Mohammad asked Babur about the purpose of his visit. (75) Babur pleaded to be blessed with a sovereignty over India, So that his writ might run over the twenty-two Indian provinces. That He had no divine sanction for granting a sovereignty over India. (76)

pages.title: In the Vision, the Prophet Directs Babur Back to Guru Nanak
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: In the narrative’s visionary scene, the Prophet answers Babur without ambiguity: sovereignty over India belongs to Guru Nanak, not to him, and Babur should seek that favor from the Guru instead. He can promise rule in Khorasan and for the T
pages.searchText: In the Vision, the Prophet Directs Babur Back to Guru Nanak Babur Episode About Babur ... In the narrative’s visionary scene, the Prophet answers Babur without ambiguity: sovereignty over India belongs to Guru Nanak, not to him, and Babur should seek that favor from the Guru instead. He can promise rule in Khorasan and for the Timurid line, but not dominion over Hindustan. The refusal leaves Babur shaken and ashamed, because he has returned from heaven without the prize he wanted most. His body trembles, his confidence collapses, and he can see no easy path either back to the prophet or onward into battle. Caught between dread and ambition, Babur sinks into anxious reflection over how he can cross this ordeal at all. The page ends with him in spiritual crisis, searching for a way to approach the one authority who can still help him.

pages.title: Sovereignty of India being the sole prerogative of Guru Nanak,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Sovereignty of India being the sole prerogative of Guru Nanak, Babur should have no expectations from his prophet about it. (77) The former had no jurisdiction over India's sovereignty. He advised Babur to get his cherished desire fulfilled
pages.searchText: Sovereignty of India being the sole prerogative of Guru Nanak, Babur Episode About Babur ... Sovereignty of India being the sole prerogative of Guru Nanak, Babur should have no expectations from his prophet about it. (77) The former had no jurisdiction over India's sovereignty. He advised Babur to get his cherished desire fulfilled from Guru Nanak, By whatever modes of supplication he deemed fit to appease Nanak. (78) Chaupai: The Guru's staff which brought him to the heavens, His blessings should Babur invoke to get sovereignty. Sovereignty over India not being in his jurisdiction, The prophet had powers to grant sovereignty over Khorasan alone. (79) He had already granted Khorasan's sovereignty to Taimurlang, Whose legal heirs were entitled to inherit his legacy. Those were declined forthwith by Prophet Mohammad. (80) Landing at his camp with the grace of the Guru's staff. So frustrated and listless had Babur felt, As if his mortal frame had broke in twain. (81) Babur fainted on his arrival at his army camp, So severely was he struck with a sense of remorse. He recalled the prophetic words of his own minister, Who had warned him about the presence of a great Hindu prophet. (82) Dohra: Being equally scared of returning to his Islamic prophet, As well as going ahead with an appeal to Guru Nanak, Was Babur really caught on the horns of a dilemma, As that of a snake which fails either to swallow or vomit out a poisonous lizard. (83) Chaupai: With Babur's whole frame being in convulsions with fear, Was he severely struck with a rising wave of doubts. His Islamic prophet having rejected his pleas, He had thrown Babur at the mercy of a Hindu prophet. (84) Whom should he look up to in his hour of dire need, Whom should he supplicate before for his dream fulfilment? Having been caught in the whirlwind of life, His own prophet had left him in the lurch. (85)

pages.title: Babur resolves to seek Guru Nanak's grace
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Babur's despair begins to clear when he remembers that even Muhammad acknowledged Guru Nanak as the true spiritual authority for India. That recognition convinces him that his only hope is to fall at Guru Nanak's feet and beg directly for m
pages.searchText: Babur resolves to seek Guru Nanak's grace Babur Episode About Babur ... Babur's despair begins to clear when he remembers that even Muhammad acknowledged Guru Nanak as the true spiritual authority for India. That recognition convinces him that his only hope is to fall at Guru Nanak's feet and beg directly for mercy. He therefore turns to Daulat Khan and asks him to help arrange an approach to the Guru. Babur abandons royal pride, returns in humility, and prepares himself to speak not as a conqueror but as a supplicant. The page closes in a mood of reverence, with Babur praising Guru Nanak's unmatched nearness to the Divine and presenting himself as the servant of the Guru's servants. What began as political ambition is now recast as an appeal for grace.

pages.title: How could his ship of life reach its shore without a mariner,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: How could his ship of life reach its shore without a mariner, Whom should he pray for a survival from this ordeal? Thereafter a thought came to Babur's mind, Which provided a great solace to him. He recalled how even his own spiritual proph
pages.searchText: How could his ship of life reach its shore without a mariner, Babur Episode About Babur ... How could his ship of life reach its shore without a mariner, Whom should he pray for a survival from this ordeal? Thereafter a thought came to Babur's mind, Which provided a great solace to him. He recalled how even his own spiritual prophet Mohammad, Had confirmed that Nanak alone was the only prophet in India. (87) That he should seek blessings of Guru Nanak. Nanak being the greatest among the spiritual prophets, Babur accused the latter of landing him in trouble. He, being caught badly in the life's whirlwinds, Daulat must plead before the Guru to be Babur's saviour. (89) Taking Babur along, did Daulat Khan approach the Guru, With folded hands, did they bow before the Guru. Professing to be the most humble slave of the Guru, Babur pleaded before the Guru for his dream to be fulfilled. (90) Narrating whatever he had observed at the Divine Court, Babur put forth his observations before Guru Nanak. Being omniscient about what happened here and there, The Guru gave a faint smile and kept his cool. (91) Thereafter (struck with wonder and awe), remarked Babur, Nobody could ever gauge the spiritual profundity of Guru Nanak. The Guru, being the (dearest) son of God Divine, He alone could match the Divine in attributes Divine. (92) Both God and Guru Nanak being inseparable, The Guru's will prevailed in every phenomenal occurring. Infinite was the limit of Guru Nanak's blessings, As his will was the cause behind every happening. (93) Being himself the Divine and merciful like Him, Guru Nanak was the creator and the compassionate. He, being both the prophet and the spiritual guide, Impossible was it to plumb the depth of the Guru's mystigue. (94)

pages.title: Guru Nanak grants Babur conditional sovereignty
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Babur pleads that he entrusted himself to Daulat Khan only because he had staked everything on Guru Nanak's name, and he now asks the Guru to preserve his honor. Guru Nanak responds with compassion, accepts the petition, and prepares a symb
pages.searchText: Guru Nanak grants Babur conditional sovereignty Babur Episode About Babur ... Babur pleads that he entrusted himself to Daulat Khan only because he had staked everything on Guru Nanak's name, and he now asks the Guru to preserve his honor. Guru Nanak responds with compassion, accepts the petition, and prepares a symbolic act to show how the boon will be measured out. He asks for Babur's bag of intoxicant and pours out seven handfuls of bhang, granting a line of rule that will run through seven generations. The gift is real, but it is given as a marked favor rather than as an unconditional right. Guru Nanak then warns that India has been bestowed for a trifling exchange and can also be taken back. Babur immediately protests that a boon once granted should not later be revoked, setting up the Guru's stern answer on the next page.

pages.title: Claiming to repose complete faith in Nanak's Divinity,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Claiming to repose complete faith in Nanak's Divinity, Had Babur surrendered to Daulat Khan's proposal. Imploring the Guru to protect his (Babur's) honour, Let the Guru deal with him (Babur) as he willed. (95) Taking pity on Babur after hea
pages.searchText: Claiming to repose complete faith in Nanak's Divinity, Babur Episode About Babur ... Claiming to repose complete faith in Nanak's Divinity, Had Babur surrendered to Daulat Khan's proposal. Imploring the Guru to protect his (Babur's) honour, Let the Guru deal with him (Babur) as he willed. (95) Taking pity on Babur after hearing his entreaties, The Guru asked him to bring forth his bag of cannabis. Hearing Guru's willingness to shower his blessings, Babur opened his bag full of of cannabis leaves postehate. (96) As the Guru put seven handfuls of cannabis leaves into Babaur's lap, The Guru turned the cannabis bag upside down. With the giving of seven handfuls of cannabis thus, The Guru blessed Babur with sovereignty upto his seven dynasties. (97) Looking at the Cannabis leaves lying on the ground, The Guru was at liberty to take back his blessings again. Even the sovereignty already granted to the seven dynasties of Babur, The Guru would take it back at an appropriate moment. (98) Thus, the Guru, in a moment of carefree abandon, Vested Babur with India's sovereignty for a pittance. Little realizing that this blessing would recoil upon his own house, Much as Lord Shiva's blessing to Demon Bhasmantar!? had recoiled. (99) When the Guru addressed these words to Babur that, He had conferred India's sovereignty on Babur for a pittance. The Guru had also made a commitment at that moment, That He would be entitled to revoke his blessings. (100) Thereafter, Satguru Guru Nanak made it absolutely clear, Drawing the attention of emperor Babur to his words. The Guru would snatch India's sovereignty perforce, When Babur would no longer be present on the scene. (101) Hearing this conditional grant of sovereignty by Guru Nanak, Babur addressed the Guru in the following vein: Taking back a boon after it had been granted, Amounted to going back on one's own words. It was as ignominious to withdraw a favour granted, It was dishonour to take back a granted boon, As it brought a great disgrace to the giver. (102)

pages.title: Guru Nanak warns Babur that a boon can be withdrawn
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Guru Nanak answers Babur by explaining that a boon can be withdrawn when the recipient proves unworthy of preserving it. Gifts received freely carry obligations, and divine favor does not remain with rulers who violate the moral terms under
pages.searchText: Guru Nanak warns Babur that a boon can be withdrawn Babur Episode About Babur ... Guru Nanak answers Babur by explaining that a boon can be withdrawn when the recipient proves unworthy of preserving it. Gifts received freely carry obligations, and divine favor does not remain with rulers who violate the moral terms under which it was granted. He then turns prophetic and tells Babur that Mughal sovereignty will be revoked if his descendants persecute the later Gurus. Babur folds his hands in protest, insisting that his house reveres the Guru and that such betrayal should not come from his line. The narrative immediately begins to test that claim by turning toward the later emperors. The page pivots from Babur's plea to the historical record of how Jahangir and his successors will be judged through their treatment of the Sikh Gurus.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: Dohra: Thereupon, Guru Nanak reminded (the arguing) Babur, That favours granted were withdrawn under certain conditions. Sometime the recipient, receiving a boon gratis, Proved unworthy of preserving such a boon. (103) Chhand: Such a boon D
pages.searchText: Dohra: Thereupon, Guru Nanak reminded (the arguing) Babur, Babur Episode About Babur ... Dohra: Thereupon, Guru Nanak reminded (the arguing) Babur, That favours granted were withdrawn under certain conditions. Sometime the recipient, receiving a boon gratis, Proved unworthy of preserving such a boon. (103) Chhand: Such a boon Divine in return for nothing, Had Mansoor!? (an Iragui Sufi Saint) acguired. Failing to contain its spiritual worth in himself, The boon cost (that unfortunate saint) his life. Being as evanescent as the highly volatile camphor, It is difficult to contain a boon received gratis. It disappears as instantly as camphor exposed to fire, Dohra: Thereupon, Guru Nanak told Babur in a prophetic vein, As his successors would persecute Guru's successors, The Guru's Will would revoke his blessed sovereignty bestowed on Mughals. (105) Chaupai: Thereupon, with folded hands pleaded Babur before Guru Nanak, How could his progeny persecute the Guru's successors? With Babur's House holding Guru Nanak in high esteem, How could his successors dare to harm the Guru's House? (106) Hindustan's sovereignty being the monopoly of the Hindu prophets, Guru Nanak was supreme among those Divine prophets. Mughals having been made sovereign rulers by Guru Nanak, How could Mughals afford to turn against Nanak's House. (107) Dohra: The moment Babur's successors tyrannized Guru Nanak's dynasty, The Guru should take back India's sovereignty from Babur. It was on the basis of that solemn commitment, That Mughal's rule should extend beyond his seven dynasties. (108) Chaupai: With this agreement, the Guru conferred sovereignty on Babur, His first three dynasties did honour this solemn commitment. Babur, being succeeded by his own son Himanyun to the throne, Never uttered a single word against the Guru's glory. As the fourth Mughal emperor Jahangir ascended to India's throne, He became a captive in the hands of bigoted Muslim clerics. (110)

pages.title: The Mughal line breaks Babur's covenant with Guru Nanak
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: The prophecy unfolds across the Mughal generations as court clerics and emperors turn against the Sikh Gurus. The page recalls the harm done under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, connecting imperial power to the suffering inflicted on Guru Arjan,
pages.searchText: The Mughal line breaks Babur's covenant with Guru Nanak Babur Episode About Babur ... The prophecy unfolds across the Mughal generations as court clerics and emperors turn against the Sikh Gurus. The page recalls the harm done under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, connecting imperial power to the suffering inflicted on Guru Arjan, Guru Harkrishan, Guru Tegh Bahadur, and the Guru's household. These persecutions prove that the Mughal rulers broke their covenant and failed to preserve the sovereignty that had been granted conditionally. What Babur received through supplication, his successors squandered through arrogance, violence, and religious hostility. By the close of the page, Guru Nanak's warning stands vindicated: the dynasty's seven-generation lease on power is exhausted by breach of trust. The moral is not merely political decline, but the collapse of rulers who claimed as their own what had been given only under divine terms.

pages.searchText: These clerics, having fell foul of (fifth Sikh Guru) Guru Arjun, Babur Episode About Babur ... These clerics, having fell foul of (fifth Sikh Guru) Guru Arjun, Laid the whole blame (for Guru Arjun's execution) on a Kashtriya!* courtier. Auranzeb, being the sixth in the Mughal dynasty, He entered into a big strife with the Sikh Gurus. Summoning the infant Sikh Guru Harkrishan (to Delhi), The Guru shed his mortal frame after blaming Aurangzeb. (112) Aurangzeb executed (the ninth Sikh Guru) Guru Tegh Bahadur, The blame squarely came to be laid on Aurangeb's head, For the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur's four grandsons. (113) Guru Gobind Singh, having contemplated over Guru Nanak's prophecy, Contemplating to sacrifice his life to get the Mughals damned, Guru Gobind resolved to adopt this course. (114) Thus fulfilling his vow with his own supreme sacrifice, The Mughal's seven generations dynastic rule came to an end. Suffering persecution for his own prophetic words of promise, The Sikh Gurus sacrificed themselves to uphold Guru Nanak's words. (115) Thus, did the Mughals having committed a breach of trust, Went back from their vows made to Guru Nanak. Throwing all their solemn pledges to the winds, They claimed having attained sovereignty on their own. (116) Claiming themselves to be powerful and autonomous, They claimed to have decimated India's Hindus. Claiming their spiritual prophet (Mohammad) to be closest to God, They rejected Hindu prophets (the Gurus) proximity to God. (117) Such was the extent of ignorance and willful disobedience, Into which had the Mughal emperors been engulfed. Being hynotised by the glib talk of the bigoted Muslim clerics, The Mughal rulers violated all their solemn commitments. (118)

pages.title: Episode 109 opens with Bhai Taru Singh's ordeal
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Babur ...
pages.snippet: This transition page closes the Babur sequence and clearly opens Episode 109 with the story of Bhai Taru Singh. The heading itself frames the ordeal as a test to keep the faith till his last breath, shifting from imperial prophecy to Sikh m
pages.searchText: Episode 109 opens with Bhai Taru Singh's ordeal Bhai Taru Singh's Ordeal Opens Episode About Babur ... This transition page closes the Babur sequence and clearly opens Episode 109 with the story of Bhai Taru Singh. The heading itself frames the ordeal as a test to keep the faith till his last breath, shifting from imperial prophecy to Sikh martyrdom and steadfastness. Bhai Taru Singh explains his position to the gathered Sikhs and is then taken away toward Lahore by Mughal officials. The congregation responds with prayer, asking that he remain victorious in spirit even as the state begins to impose its punishment. The page also sketches the severity of the prison scene, contrasting Mughal coercion with Taru Singh's calm acceptance of divine will. Its narrative function is to mark the handoff into Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom episode rather than to continue the Babur sequence.

pages.searchText: Episode About Satguru (Guru Nanak) Satguru (Guru Nanak) Episode About Satguru (Guru Nanak) Episode 109 Another Episode (May God help the Singh to keep his faith till his last breath) The way Bhai Taru Singh explained his point of view, To the congregated Sikhs (of his neighbouring village). The way he passed through the self-imposed ordeal, I (the author) would narrate the whole chain of events. (1) Thereafter, picking up Bhai Taru Singh from their camp, The Mughul officials left for Lahore in the early hours of morning. After paying a ransom in cash to the Mughal officials. (2) Thereafter, praying with folded hands in a congregational prayers, The people prayed for Bhai Taru Singh's success in his ordeal. The Sikh congregation prayed to God Almighty. May God help to keep his faith till his last breath. (3) After the officials reached Lahore with Bhai Taru Singh, They put him behind the bars in a prison. Bhai Taru Singh being kept imprisoned for many days, A large number of devout Sikhs came to pay obeisance. (4) The more the Mughal officials tortured Bhai Taru Singh, The more upbeat and in high spirits he remained. The more Bhai Taru Singh abjured any food and drink, The more contented and pious he felt within. (5) The more he abandoned all hope of keeping alive, The more fearless and immune he became from death. Who accepts and acquiesces in God's Will in good cheer. (6) One who abides by the will of God Divine, One who carries a torch in his hand,

pages.snippet: This page is another hinge, because it finishes the Bhai Taru Singh opening and then clearly launches Episode 110 with the praise-laden heading for Mehtab Singh. The narrator tells readers to listen now to the second tale of Mehtab Singh, s
pages.searchText: Episode 110 opens with the story of Mehtab Singh Mehtab Singh's Story Opens Episode About Satguru (Guru Nanak) This page is another hinge, because it finishes the Bhai Taru Singh opening and then clearly launches Episode 110 with the praise-laden heading for Mehtab Singh. The narrator tells readers to listen now to the second tale of Mehtab Singh, signaling a fresh martial episode rather than a continuation of the previous one. Harbhagat and Mughal forces move to seize Mehtab Singh, but his fame as a fearless Singh already terrifies his enemies. The Singhs keep to hidden terrain and remain prepared for battle, while the search for him spreads through the countryside. The page also ties this new episode back to the Lahore setting created by Taru Singh's imprisonment, so the transition feels deliberate rather than abrupt. It names both the narrative handoff and the new focus on Mehtab Singh's coming clash with Mughal authority.

pages.searchText: Another Episode About (Taru Singh) (Taru Singh) Another Episode About (Taru Singh) Episode 110 Another Episode About (Taru Singh) ((Praise Be to Mehtab Singh) (Dear devout readers) listen to another episode, About Mehtab Singh (a great Singh Martyr), Had proceeded to take into Mughal's custody. (1) Having been allotted a large contingent of Mughal troops, He proceeded to take Mehtab Singh into custody. Mehtab Singh being, always with a large contingent of Singhs, Mehtab Singh being a mighty warrior and a Singh perfect, His very name sent shivers down the enemy's spine. The Singhs, who put on their armour by swearing on Mehtab Singh's name, They would always remain prepared to do or die. (3) The possible hideouts of Mehtab Singh the Mughal spies indicated, Were those raided by the troops of Harbhagat Niranjania. The Singhs having camouflaged themselves in the wilds, Mughal troops did feel scared of getting into the wild growth. (4) Who would always fight to the finish, killing so many Mughals. As Harbhagat kept on looking for Mehtab Singh for many days, Mehtab Singh came to hear about this witch hunt from Singhs. (5) Mehtab Singh heard of Bhai Taru Singh's being taken a prisoner, The Mughal officials having taken him to the city of Lahore. With Bhai Taru Singh making a supreme sacrifice of his life, A turmoil was bound to erupt at the Divine Court. (6) Laying the blame for his sacrifice squarely on Lahore's Nawab, Keeping his faith with hair intact till the last breath, Bhai Taru Singh would lay the blame squarely on the Mughals. (7) Acquiescing and abiding with the will Divine, Would Taru Singh succeed in proving the Mughals guilty. Praise be to the Singh who wages a religious war, Praise be to him who sacrifices accusing the Mughals. (8)

pages.title: Mehtab Singh Resolves to Join Bhai Taru Singh
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About (Taru Singh)
pages.snippet: The page opens with a reflection on martyrdom: death is fruitful when one keeps faith and Sikhi even while facing the Turks or Mughals. It praises Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Dyal Singh, Subeg Singh, and Subeg Singh’s son as examples who held the
pages.searchText: Mehtab Singh Resolves to Join Bhai Taru Singh (Taru Singh) Another Episode About (Taru Singh) The page opens with a reflection on martyrdom: death is fruitful when one keeps faith and Sikhi even while facing the Turks or Mughals. It praises Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Dyal Singh, Subeg Singh, and Subeg Singh’s son as examples who held their faith under torture. Mehtab Singh then measures himself against that line of martyrs. He asks what merit there is in preserving his body while hidden, how he could sit near those martyrs in the Divine court, and why he should waste a human birth without seeking the status of martyrdom. Thinking of Bhai Taru Singh as his intimate companion, Mehtab Singh decides to go toward Lahore and join him through sacrifice. He tells the Singhs with him to join other groups, while he sets out with a staff in hand rather than preparing for ordinary armed combat.

pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About (Taru Singh)

pages.searchText: Most successful and glorious is the act of dying, (Taru Singh) Another Episode About (Taru Singh) Most successful and glorious is the act of dying, Among all the ways of shedding one's mortal frame. Provided he keeps his faith and his religious vows, Praise, more praise be to Bhai Mani Singh, Who got his body dismembered to keep his faith. Praise be to Bhai Dyal Singh of Shahesar, Praise be to Subeg Singh Jambar and his son, Praise be to all those Singhs who kept their faith, Who shed their mortal frame in the name of their Guru. (11) Hardly any noble deed was he (Mehtab Singh) doing, Spending whole of his life remaining incognito. How could he hope to sit in the line of great martyrs, In the Divine court of the Almighty after leaving this world? (12) How could he join the ranks of those great Singh martyrs, How could he join the company of the blessed ones? He had wasted most of his life in mundane affairs. (13) Why should he miss the opportunity of attaining a Martyr's status? Damned be a person taking human birth and then dying, Thus, contemplating his death on these (patriotic) lines, Mehtab Singh readied himself to join Bhai Taru Singh. Bhai Taru Singh being one of his intimate friends, He must join his company after shedding his mortal frame. (15) Addressing the fellow Singhs of his own contingent, He asked them to join some other contingent of the Singhs. He himself would proceed in the direction of Lahore, So that he could join his colleague Bhai Taru Singh. (16) With these words, Mehtab Singh proceeded towards Lahore, Carrying a single wooden staff after disarming himself. Arms being meant for fighting on the field of battle, He would present himself before the Nawab only with a stick. (17)

pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About (Taru Singh)
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Mehtab Singh's Martyrdom and Taru Singh's Summons

pages.searchText: Mehtab Singh meets martyrdom and Bhai Taru Singh is summoned Mehtab Singh's Martyrdom and Taru Singh's Summons Another Episode About (Taru Singh) This page closes the Mehtab Singh episode as Haribhagat Niranjania seizes him, carries him toward Lahore, and allows him a final sight of Bhai Taru Singh before martyrdom. The account dwells on Mehtab Singh's execution on the spoked wheel as an act of fearless witness rather than defeat. Even in custody, the Singh remains spiritually triumphant, and Taru Singh is said to rejoice at the martyr's steadfastness. The page therefore serves as both a memorial to Mehtab Singh and a preparation for the next trial awaiting the Panth. By the end of the page, the narrative turns toward Bhai Taru Singh's own appearance before authority. It works as a hinge that closes one martyrdom and opens the next confrontation with Mughal power.

(24) Episode 111 Episode About Mehtab Singh Chaupai: As the narrative, once again, returns to Bhai Taru Singh, Dear devout readers must listen to it with concentration. As Bhai Taru Singh wished to call on the Nawab, The court official arranged a meeting between the two. (1)

pages.title: Bhai Taru Singh rejects the Nawab's demand
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh
pages.snippet: Bhai Taru Singh enters the Nawab's court with Sikh greetings and immediately provokes anger by refusing to show fear. He questions why he is being harassed when he pays revenue, lives honestly, and shares his earnings in charity. The disput
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh rejects the Nawab's demand Mehtab Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh Bhai Taru Singh enters the Nawab's court with Sikh greetings and immediately provokes anger by refusing to show fear. He questions why he is being harassed when he pays revenue, lives honestly, and shares his earnings in charity. The dispute sharpens when the Nawab presses him to abandon Sikhi and accept Islam. Taru Singh insists that he would never convert, because fidelity to the Guru matters more to him than life itself. The page therefore frames his ordeal not as a political interrogation but as a public test of religious steadfastness. Taru Singh's calm defiance establishes the moral terms for everything that follows.

pages.title: Bhai Taru Singh entered the court with traditional Singh greetings,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh
pages.snippet: Bhai Taru Singh entered the court with traditional Singh greetings, So incensed felt the Nawab hearing these Sikh greetings, As if somebody had rubbed salt after slicing his fingers. (2) Bhai Taru Singh, facing the Nawab in his royal court,
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh entered the court with traditional Singh greetings, Mehtab Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh Bhai Taru Singh entered the court with traditional Singh greetings, So incensed felt the Nawab hearing these Sikh greetings, As if somebody had rubbed salt after slicing his fingers. (2) Bhai Taru Singh, facing the Nawab in his royal court, Asked the latter to pay attention to his (Taru Singh's) words. On what pretext was the Nawab torturing Bhai Taru Singh, When the latter had done no harm to the Nawab. (3) He had been paying the land revenue for it to the state. He had been paying the prescribed tax on it as well. (4) He had been sustaining his family on that income. He had been sharing those provisions with others in need. (5) What did the Nawab lose by the latter's austerity, That he (Nawab) was bent on persecuting the latter? Being incensed and outraged by Bhai Taru Singh's argument, The Nawab used unparliamentary words against the latter. (6) The Nawab asked Bhai Taru Singh to get converted to Islam, Otherwise the former would not spare the latter's life. Bhai Taru Singh retorted that he, being a stranger to fear, Could conversion to Islam save him from death, And must uphold his faith till his last breath. (8) Thereafter, the Nawab repeated his proposal once again, The latter must convert to Islam if he wished to live. In terms of financial package or landed property. (9) He could also ask for a Mughal Pathan bride, As well as live in comfort in a palatial mansion. Upon this, Bhai Taru Singh made these remarks: The Nawab must grant what was dearest to the latter's heart. (10)

pages.title: The Nawab orders Taru Singh's scalp to be scraped
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh
pages.snippet: The Nawab promises favor and survival if Taru Singh will only convert, but Taru Singh asks instead for the strength to keep his faith and kes intact until death. His refusal transforms the hearing into an act of state violence against a vis
pages.searchText: The Nawab orders Taru Singh's scalp to be scraped Mehtab Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh The Nawab promises favor and survival if Taru Singh will only convert, but Taru Singh asks instead for the strength to keep his faith and kes intact until death. His refusal transforms the hearing into an act of state violence against a visibly unyielding Sikh. Furious at that answer, the Nawab ordered the barbers to shave off his sacred hair and break the sign of his discipline by force. When the barbers fail, the regime escalates further and calls for his scalp itself to be scraped away. The page highlights both the cruelty of the punishment and Taru Singh's unwavering resolve under it. Mughal force grows harsher exactly because his faith cannot be shaken.

pages.title: If it pleased the Nawab to be compassionate towards him,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh
pages.snippet: If it pleased the Nawab to be compassionate towards him, He must not ask Taru Singh to convert to Islam. The Nawab must suggest such a way out to Taru Singh, As would enable the latter to keep his faith till his last breath. (11) Feeling hi
pages.searchText: If it pleased the Nawab to be compassionate towards him, Mehtab Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh If it pleased the Nawab to be compassionate towards him, He must not ask Taru Singh to convert to Islam. The Nawab must suggest such a way out to Taru Singh, As would enable the latter to keep his faith till his last breath. (11) Feeling highly enraged at these words of Bhai Taru Singh, The Nawab started using abusive language against the latter. Ordering his minions to give severe shoe beatings to the latter, He ordered the barbers to shave off his sacred hair. (12) Thereupon, Bhai Taru Singh said (in a prophetic vein) to the Nawab, That this ordered shoe-beatings would recoil upon his own head. The Sikhs who were perfect in their faith in their Gurus, They would sacrifice their lives with their sacred hair intact. (13) As the Nawab ordered the barbers to shave off his head, Their shaving blades failed to shave the Singh's (sacred) hair. As the barbers tried again and again to do their job, Their hands became numb and bereft of energy. (14) The more the Nawab threatened the shaving barbers, The more they felt their hands trembling with fear. So great was the impact of the devout Sikh's spiritual power, That the barbers felt the loss of their eyesight. (15) The Nawab felt either Bhai Taru Singh had cast a magic spell, Or had he offered the barbers some gratification. Asking for the summoning of a couple of cobblers, He ordered them to scrape Taru Singh's scalp along with the hair. (16) Upon this, Bhai Taru Singh rejoiced at such an order, As his scalp would go off with his sacred hair intact. As he was going to keep both his word and faith, He felt the great Guru had stood by his devout Sikh. (17) As Bhai Taru Singh burst out in joyous words Akal! Akal! The Nawab plugged his ears in disgust and despair. He ordered the cobblers to peel off the latter's scalp. (18) Ordering to remove the latter's scalp along with the hair, The Nawab ordered the cobblers to ply their tools. Following whatever they were ordered to carry on, The cobblers placed their sharpened scrapers on Taru Singh's head. (19)

pages.title: Onlookers foresee the fall of Mughal rule
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh
pages.snippet: As Taru Singh's scalp is scraped, he endures the pain without a cry, while the crowd recoils at the spectacle. The scene becomes a public indictment of the Nawab rather than a humiliation of the prisoner. Witnesses openly say that Mughal ru
pages.searchText: Onlookers foresee the fall of Mughal rule Mehtab Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh As Taru Singh's scalp is scraped, he endures the pain without a cry, while the crowd recoils at the spectacle. The scene becomes a public indictment of the Nawab rather than a humiliation of the prisoner. Witnesses openly say that Mughal rule would not last long after such an outrage against a holy Singh. The page also records the shock felt across religious lines, showing that even many observers recognized the act as a violation that invited judgment. The Nawab nevertheless keeps pressing Taru Singh, trying to mock his earlier claim that his hair could not be taken apart from his head. Instead of weakening him, the torture only deepens the sense that prophecy is about to answer imperial violence.

pages.searchText: Placing a sharpened scraper on Taru Singh's head, Mehtab Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh Placing a sharpened scraper on Taru Singh's head, They pressed its sharp edge from the forehead side. Then scraping from the forehead upto the ears, They scraped Taru Singh's scalp from the rear end. (20) Not a single cry did escape from brave Taru Singh's lips, Praise be to the noble deed done by a great Sikh. Dumfounded and breathless felt the onlookers, Pitifully cried those who heard about this evil deed. (21) The wiser among the populace cried in a prophetic vein, The (tyrannical) rule of the Mughals would not last long. It was in the year eighteen hundred and two in Bikrami Samvat!, That Bhai Taru Singh had made this supreme sacrifice. (22) It was in the year Seventeen hundred and ninety-one in Bikrami Samvat, That Hakikat Rai? had met a similar fate. The Nawab had rather become more vain and arrogant. (23) With the treatment that the (bigoted) Nawab meted out to Taru Singh, His fame spread far and wide (in the Islamic world). While the Singhs mourned (the torture of Bhai Taru Singh), The Muslims rejoiced at the prowess of their Nawab. (24) There existed a place where the Sikhs congregated, Where Bhai Taru Singh disfigured body was placed. The Nawab asked the devout followers of Taru Singh, That his body be consigned to the flames after his death. (25) Allowing not a single cry to escape from his lips, Bhai Taru Singh kept on meditating on God's Name. So thoroughly was his head splattered with blood, As if he had immersed himself in the sacred Ganges. (26) So had Mansoor got both his hands chopped off, Letting his arms awash with his own sacred blood. As Mansoor's prayers and sacrifice had reached the Divine Court, Highly exasperated had felt the executing Muslim clerics. (27) The Nawab of Lahore put forth a poser to Bhai Taru Singh. How could Taru Singh justify his much touted claim, That he would not part with his hair without his head? (28)

pages.title: Bhai Taru Singh prophesies the Nawab's affliction
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mehtab Singh
pages.snippet: Taru Singh answers the Nawab's taunt by insisting that his hair was never truly separated from his head, because his scalp went with it. He then turns from defense to prophecy and declares that the Nawab will not escape the consequences of
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh prophesies the Nawab's affliction Mehtab Singh Episode About Mehtab Singh Taru Singh answers the Nawab's taunt by insisting that his hair was never truly separated from his head, because his scalp went with it. He then turns from defense to prophecy and declares that the Nawab will not escape the consequences of persecuting a saint. The page explicitly opens the next episode by warning that the Nawab developed a blockage in his urinary tract as the divine answer to this cruelty. Taru Singh’s words recast punishment as a spiritual judgment already set in motion. This makes the page a transition from courtroom martyrdom to the Nawab's bodily torment. The narrative no longer asks whether the ruler will suffer, but only how quickly the curse will take hold.

pages.title: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Rejecting the Nawab's claim of removing his (Taru Singh's) hair as false, Bhai Taru Singh explained that his hair had gone along with his scalp. Since his body alone had been dispossessed of his hair, Nawab's claim on both these counts had
pages.searchText: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Rejecting the Nawab's claim of removing his (Taru Singh's) hair as false, Bhai Taru Singh explained that his hair had gone along with his scalp. Since his body alone had been dispossessed of his hair, Nawab's claim on both these counts had been proved false. (29) Explaining his remarks further to the (arrogant) Nawab, He told the Nawab that the latter had not understood his words. Since his (Taru Singh's)(sacred) hair remained intact on his scalp, Bhai Taru Singh had deliberately not shed his mortal frame, So that he could thrash the Nawab with shoe-beatings. Since nobody had ever taught the arrogant Nawab a lesson, The Nawab had gone scot free with Hakikat Rai's murder. (31) Now Bhai Taru Singh would thrash the Nawab with shoe beatings, And chase him to the seat of his Islamic spiritual prophet. Bhai Taru Singh would not spare the Nawab in any case, Otherwise the Nawab would claim himself as the mightiest. (32) He would let go off the Nawab only after presenting him before the prophet, Thereafter, he would present the Nawab in the Divine Court. If, in the Divine Court, the prophet still vouched for the (tyrant) Nawab, The prophet, himself would get chastised along with the Nawab. (33) The Nawab had, somehow, been acquitted of Hakikat Rai's murder, But this time, he would not be spared of Divine retribution, His spiritual prophet too would be damned into hell, If he ever made an attempt to vouch for the wicked Nawab. (34) Warning the Nawab to get ready to meet his nemesis atlast, He would kill him by getting his urinary and intestinal tract blocked. Warning him to be ready for being damned forever in hell, He would chase the Nawab with shoe beatings to the doors of hell. (35) Episode 112 Episode About Bhai Taru Singh (Synonymous Are the Guru And the Khalsa) The moment Bhai Taru Singh let out his prophetic warning, The Nawab developed a blockage in his urinary tract.

pages.title: The Nawab's urinary torment begins
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: The curse takes effect immediately as the Nawab writhes in unbearable urinary agony and finds relief nowhere. Neither posture, clerical recitation, nor established Muslim holy men can ease the torment that has seized him. His suffering grow
pages.searchText: The Nawab's urinary torment begins Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh The curse takes effect immediately as the Nawab writhes in unbearable urinary agony and finds relief nowhere. Neither posture, clerical recitation, nor established Muslim holy men can ease the torment that has seized him. His suffering grows more terrifying because he begins to imagine the spirits of martyred Singhs closing in around him with weapons drawn. What had looked like a worldly illness is now understood as a visitation tied directly to Bhai Taru Singh’s words. By the end of the page, the Nawab's confidence in his own religious world has failed. Desperation begins pushing him toward the very Khalsa he had tried to crush.

pages.title: Panting for breath like a fish thrown on a sandy desert,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Panting for breath like a fish thrown on a sandy desert, The Nawab felt tortured by his urinary ailment. (1) A minute on the floor, a minute on the bed would the Nawab stretch, Resting for a while, soon would he get up with a start. Claimin
pages.searchText: Panting for breath like a fish thrown on a sandy desert, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Panting for breath like a fish thrown on a sandy desert, The Nawab felt tortured by his urinary ailment. (1) A minute on the floor, a minute on the bed would the Nawab stretch, Resting for a while, soon would he get up with a start. Claiming that they would heal the Nawab of his ailment, Were the Muslim clerics summoned to the royal court. The more they cast their spells after chanting the Koranic verses, The more shrieks did the tortured Nawab let out. (3) Appearing in the guise of blue robes with heavy clubs in hands, Did the spirits of martyred Singhs thrash the Nawab with heavy clubs. The more the clerics invoked the Muslim spiritual prophets, The more did the spirits torture and punish the Nawab. (4) Directing the wicked Nawab to crawl ahead of them, Did the Singhs spirits chastise the Nawab in this way. Noticing the Singh spirits standing in front of him, Did the Nawab see them bradishing their daggers and quoits. (5) Observing these apparitions did the Nawab shake with fear, Meditating upon the spiritual prophets name all the while. The more he invoked the prophets through various incantations, The more the prophets spirits felt scared of the Singh spirits. (6) His spirit came rushing in aid of the Nawab. But with the touch of their sharp daggers and quoits, Did the Singh spirits chase and pursue those spirits. (7) Did the Nawab abandon his dependence on the Muslim clerics. Thus abandoning all hope of being relieved of pain, Did the Nawab seek protection of the Khalsa Panth. (8) Whenever a person gets afflicted with any affliction, He takes no delight in any activity of this world. It is for this reason that the afflicted people worship, The prophets and spiritual saints of other religions as well. (9)

pages.title: The Nawab seeks pardon through the Singhs
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: After failing to obtain relief from one set of holy men after another, the Nawab finally admits that ordinary remedies cannot undo what a saint has spoken. He comes to believe that Singhs alone could lift the curse pronounced by a Singh, because only the Panth can answer the wron
pages.searchText: The Nawab seeks pardon through the Singhs Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom After failing to obtain relief from one set of holy men after another, the Nawab finally admits that ordinary remedies cannot undo what a saint has spoken. He comes to believe that Singhs alone could lift the curse pronounced by a Singh, because only the Panth can answer the wrong done to Taru Singh. That realization drives him to summon Sikh intermediaries and plead for help. He is no longer bargaining from power, but begging for access to the mercy of the very community he persecuted. The page marks a sharp reversal in authority. Mughal office now looks helpless, while spiritual legitimacy sits with the Khalsa and with the martyr whose curse still governs events.

pages.title: As people fail to get relief from some of these prophets,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: As people fail to get relief from some of these prophets, They proceed to worship the prophets of other religions. Wavering in their own faith, they worship others prophets, Thus these fools lose faith in their own religious ideology. (10)
pages.searchText: As people fail to get relief from some of these prophets, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh As people fail to get relief from some of these prophets, They proceed to worship the prophets of other religions. Wavering in their own faith, they worship others prophets, Thus these fools lose faith in their own religious ideology. (10) Very few there are perfect in their faith and piety, Who repose their faith in their own spiritual saints in adversity. There are a few devout Sikhs in this world of ours, Who do not renege from their faith in the time of adversity. (11) Ordering the release of all the prisoners from the state prison, Did the Nawab prostrate in front of them in vain. Neither did the blockage in his urinary tract get cleared, Thereafter, did it occur in the (harassed) Nawab's mind, That Singhs alone could uplift the curse meted out by a Singh. They alone could save him from the impending doom, As the Nawab of Lahore summoned the Singhs of the city of Lahore, They arrived at the court feeling scared of Nawab's wrath. Prostrating before these urban Sikhs with folded hands, The Nawab begged them to seek a pardon for his sins. (14) Beseeching them to persuade Bhai Taru Singh to pardon him, He requested them to replace Bhai Taru Singh's scalp on his skull. As these Sikhs conveyed Nawab's petition in subdued tones, Bhai Taru Singh responded to Nawab's appeal as follows: (15) Of what avail was the Nawab's desperate appeal now, How could his (Taru Singh's) scalp be restored to its original place? Warning the Nawab to use all his powers to save himself, Bhai Taru Singh would not let him stay alive in this world. (16) Then did the Nawab realize in his heart of hearts, That no person on earth could save him from death. Whosoever dared to intercede on his behalf, He too would get damned along with the Nawab. (17) The more the Singh spirits thrashed him with their clubs, The more convulsions did the Nawab's body undergo. The more the Singh spirits threatened and scared him, The more short of breath did the Nawab's lungs feel. (18)

pages.title: Subeg Singh fears a saint's curse
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: The Nawab’s plea reaches Subeg Singh, who listens but does not rush to intercede. He warns that the Khalsa Panth alone could arbitrate the ruler’s fate, because no courtier can casually overturn a saint’s judgment. Subeg Singh also fears th
pages.searchText: Subeg Singh fears a saint's curse Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh The Nawab’s plea reaches Subeg Singh, who listens but does not rush to intercede. He warns that the Khalsa Panth alone could arbitrate the ruler’s fate, because no courtier can casually overturn a saint’s judgment. Subeg Singh also fears that merely carrying the Nawab's case might expose his own household to ruin if Bhai Taru Singh refuses. The Nawab therefore has to abase himself further, touching feet and pleading for someone willing to take the risk. This page slows the story into moral deliberation rather than instant rescue. Even sympathy for suffering cannot erase what the Nawab has done or the spiritual hierarchy now standing over him.

pages.title: Upon this, did it occur to the Nawab once again,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Upon this, did it occur to the Nawab once again, The Khalsa Panth alone could be the saviour of his soul. Getting S. Subeg Singh released from the state prison, The Nawab narrated the tale of his weal and woe to him. (19) Telling him that S
pages.searchText: Upon this, did it occur to the Nawab once again, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Upon this, did it occur to the Nawab once again, The Khalsa Panth alone could be the saviour of his soul. Getting S. Subeg Singh released from the state prison, The Nawab narrated the tale of his weal and woe to him. (19) Telling him that Singh spirits were out to wreak vengeance on him, The Nawab had exhausted all endeavours to invoke his prophets. The Singh spirits chased and decimated the prophets spirits. (20) His last hope of survival being vested with the Singhs, The Khalsa Panth alone could be the sole arbiter of his fate. Shaking his head as a gesture of disgust and denial Subeg Singh told that a Saint's curse could never be revoked. (21) Feeling highly scared in his own mind of Bhai Taru Singh's rebuff, Subeg Singh thought better not to meddle into mighty Singh's affairs. Lest Bhai Taru Singh should heap a curse on him as well, Which would then damn his family for generations to come. (22) Thereafter, did Subeg Singh maintain a stony silence, Upon this, prostrating himself in front of Subeg Singh, The Nawab touched his feet begging for mercy. (23) Thereupon a second thought did Subeg Singh feel, That he should convey Nawab's plea to Bhai Taru Singh. Entreating Subeg Singh to pay his respects to the great Singh, The Nawab begged him to be relieved of his affliction. (24) Beseaching Subeg Singh to touch Bhai Taru Singh's feet on his behalf, He authorized Subeg Singh to make any commitment from his side. Never again would the Nawab ever torture the Singhs in future, If his life could be spared now by Bhai Taru Singh. (25) In case Bhai Taru Singh did not pardon the Nawab, The latter would meet his end with an excruciating pain. Volunteering to die but begging to be relieved of urinary blockage, The Nawab begged Bhai Taru Singh to let him die without torture. (26) Whatever pleas had the Nawab made to Subeg Singh, The latter conveyed all those appeals to Bhai Taru Singh. Reacting sharply to the narration made by Subeg Singh, He accused the latter of vouching for a wicked tyrant. (27)

pages.title: Bhai Taru Singh refuses to plead for the Nawab
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Bhai Taru Singh responds by laying down a clear principle: he would sacrifice everything for a Sikh, but he will not advocate for a wicked oppressor who has earned a righteous curse. The page stresses that Khalsa Panth alone being empowered
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh refuses to plead for the Nawab Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Bhai Taru Singh responds by laying down a clear principle: he would sacrifice everything for a Sikh, but he will not advocate for a wicked oppressor who has earned a righteous curse. The page stresses that Khalsa Panth alone being empowered to annul that curse does not mean the Panth is obliged to excuse injustice lightly. Meanwhile the Nawab's treatment fails, and each attempted remedy only worsens his condition. His desperation keeps sending petitions back through intermediaries, but Taru Singh's moral clarity remains intact. The result is a page about disciplined mercy rather than simple vengeance. The Panth is shown as possessing power over the case, yet also insisting that power must answer to righteousness.

pages.title: Let a Sikh ask for a favour for a fraternal Sikh,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Let a Sikh ask for a favour for a fraternal Sikh, Bhai Taru Singh would readily make the greatest sacrifice for him. Let a Sikh walk a single step for favouring a fellow Sikh, Bhai Taru Singh would dust his feet with his own hair. (28) Now
pages.searchText: Let a Sikh ask for a favour for a fraternal Sikh, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Let a Sikh ask for a favour for a fraternal Sikh, Bhai Taru Singh would readily make the greatest sacrifice for him. Let a Sikh walk a single step for favouring a fellow Sikh, Bhai Taru Singh would dust his feet with his own hair. (28) Now that the inevitable curse had been heaped on the Nawab, Subeg Singh should desist from recommending a wicked man's case. Bhai Taru Singh would not harm Subeg Singh, being a Singh, Any other mediator would have met the Nawab's fate. (29) As Subeg Singh returned without any assurance, Much did the Nawab grieve, indeed, over his fate. The more the apothecaries administered their concoctions, The more did the Nawab's urinary affliction aggravate. (30) Unable to bear pain in his bladder in silence, Would the Nawab burst out in louder shrieks. Returning once again to Subeg Singh for help, The Nawab sought protection from the Khalsa Panth. (31) Being cursed by a Singh of the stature of Bhai Taru Singh, Nobody could dare to wipe out that curse. Khalsa Panth alone being empowered to annul that curse, No one else could save the Nawab from that curse. (32) The water that creates destroys those creations as well, The water that drowns buoys the drowned as well. The Khalsa Panth, who destroys the wicked (enemies), Could as well pardon them if it so desired. (32) Begging Subeg Singh to trace the location of Tat Khalsa, He should rush posthaste there on Nawab's behalf. Beseaching him to prostrate before the Khalsa on his behalf, The Nawab entreated Subeg Singh to plead his case. (34) As he had been guilty of committing a great sin, He owed an explanation and accountability for his misdeeds. Even the Sikh Gurus had inscribed in the holy Sikh scripture, That an oppressor of a saint had no where to belong. (35) Not only was the denunciator of a saint worst than a slaughterer, But damned and destroyed was he by the wrath of Divine God. The sinner could be redeemed as well if the saint so willed, Such was the inscription in the holy Sri Guru Granth Sahib. (36)

pages.title: The Nawab appeals to the Khalsa's mercy
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: The Nawab tries a new line of argument by invoking Sikh teaching about collective prayer and saintly compassion. He repeats that wherever five Singhs prayed together with folded hands, divine authority was present among them. He also cites
pages.searchText: The Nawab appeals to the Khalsa's mercy Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh The Nawab tries a new line of argument by invoking Sikh teaching about collective prayer and saintly compassion. He repeats that wherever five Singhs prayed together with folded hands, divine authority was present among them. He also cites scriptural language to argue that even one who has wronged a saint may still be forgiven if the saint so wills it. On that basis he begs the Khalsa to prove the truth of Gurbani through a public act of mercy. The page therefore turns his petition into a theological appeal rather than a merely political one. He asks not for restored honor, but simply for release from agony, even if death follows immediately after.
