pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Dohra: He (the Nawab) had also heard of another spiritual edict, Which some of the Khalsa Singhs had conveyed to him. Wherever the five Singhs prayed together with folded hands, The Divine Will manifested itself among those Singhs. (37) Cha
pages.searchText: Dohra: He (the Nawab) had also heard of another spiritual edict, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Dohra: He (the Nawab) had also heard of another spiritual edict, Which some of the Khalsa Singhs had conveyed to him. Wherever the five Singhs prayed together with folded hands, The Divine Will manifested itself among those Singhs. (37) Chaupai: Whatever had been inscribed in the sacred Guru Granth, The Sikhs believed it truly to be the word of God. That he, too, wished to test the veracity of that inscription, So said the Nawab of Lahore to Subeg Singh there. (38) He had also heard the Singhs reciting the sacred text, Which had been inscribed under the title Sukhmani?: Though Perpetrator of atrocities on the saint has nowhere to belong, But even a sinner is redeemed if a Saint pleaseth, sayeth Nanak. (39) Though slandering of a Saint is the worst kind of affliction, But even a slanderer attains salvation if a Saint wills, sayeth Nanak. Though none can provide protection to a slanderer of a saint, Even such a sinner can be absolved of sin if a saint wills, says Nanak. (40) Nobody can save the slanderer of a saint, If these words of the Satguru be true, Must he be demonstrated the truth of these words. (41) Dohra: None else was a sinner more steeped in sin than the Nawab, None else was greater in piety than the Khalsa Panth. Whatever truthful inscriptions had been recorded in Sukhmani, Let their truthfulness be put to test and verified. (42) Whatever spiritual power was vested in Gurbani, The same Divinity was vested in a congregation of five Singhs. Subeg Singh must, therefore, proceed to the chief among Singhs, Whosoever he might be occupying that glorious seat. (43) Even if the Singhs refused to condone his sins, They should at least concede to this much relief. That the Nawab be relieved of urinary affliction only once, Though his life be taken away by Taru Singh the same moment. (44) With such a mission, proceeded Subeg Singh Jambar, And arrived soon where the Khalsa Singhs camped. He greeted the Khalsa Singhs with the Khalsa greetings, While paying obeisance and respects to the venerated Khalsa. (45)

pages.title: The Khalsa debates how to answer Lahore
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Subeg Singh carries the plea into a Sikh gathering presided over by leaders of the Khalsa, where Bhai Taru Singh's martyrdom is first remembered with grief and anger. The sangat curses the Nawab's cruelty before anyone even considers the re
pages.searchText: The Khalsa debates how to answer Lahore Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Subeg Singh carries the plea into a Sikh gathering presided over by leaders of the Khalsa, where Bhai Taru Singh's martyrdom is first remembered with grief and anger. The sangat curses the Nawab's cruelty before anyone even considers the request for mercy. Soon the Singhs become desperate to launch an attack on Lahore, debating disguise, night assault, and martyrdom as better answers than negotiation. Their first impulse is not softness, but a warrior’s instinct to avenge sacrilege and defend the Panth’s honor. This page is therefore charged with communal energy and strategic debate. Mercy remains possible, but only after anger has been fully voiced and measured against Khalsa discipline.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Holding a religious congregation of the Singhs, They accorded a respectable welcome to Subeg Singh. S. Kapoor Singh occupied the Singh chief's seat. (46) He cursed the wicked Nawab while kicking the ground. Uttering words of lavish praise f
pages.searchText: Holding a religious congregation of the Singhs, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Holding a religious congregation of the Singhs, They accorded a respectable welcome to Subeg Singh. S. Kapoor Singh occupied the Singh chief's seat. (46) He cursed the wicked Nawab while kicking the ground. Uttering words of lavish praise for Bhai Taru Singh, He heaped curses on the Nawab of Lahore. (47) Who had upheld the Sikh ideology at the cost of his life. As he had offered his scalp to be removed from his head. (48) Thereafter, narrating in a manner the Nawab had instructed him, S. Subeg Singh conveyed the latter's appeal to the Singhs. Hearing this appeal the Singhs flared up so much, As if a spark of fire had touched a heap of explosives. (49) After listening to Subeg Singh's account of Nawab's misdeeds, The Singhs became desperate to launch an attack on Lahore. Either they must succeed in beheading the Nawab, Or they must make a supreme sacrifice of their own heads. (50) Someone opined that they being very small in number, How could they reach Lahore (to settle scores with the enemy)? Someone else opined that they must enter Lahore in a disguise, Still another suggested that they must sneak and attack at night. (51) Either they must kill the enemy or themselves perish in a fight, So that they become martyrs in the cause of their Sikh faith. They must proceed Bhai Taru Singh in martyrdom, And raise their voice for justice in the Divine court. (52) Some said that they must make their lives worthwhile, And proceed to seek martyrdom after a hasty prayer. With Bhai Taru Singh as their captain on a spiritual voyage, They must board his ship of martyrs to cross the ocean of life. (53) Thereupon listening to the sentiments of devout Singhs, The latter had also resolved to take the wicked Nawab along, After beating him severely with his own shoe-lashings. (54)

pages.title: The Khalsa weighs mercy, honor, and saintly power
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Once the first wave of anger settles, the assembly reflects on Bhai Taru Singh's spiritual authority and on the renown of the Panth. His words are treated as sharper than weapons, so any response must honor both justice and the Khalsa's pub
pages.searchText: The Khalsa weighs mercy, honor, and saintly power Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Once the first wave of anger settles, the assembly reflects on Bhai Taru Singh's spiritual authority and on the renown of the Panth. His words are treated as sharper than weapons, so any response must honor both justice and the Khalsa's public character. Subeg Singh argues that a generous answer would magnify Sikh glory, because the Divine Guru and the Khalsa were bound together in the life of the devout community. The saints’ power present in the Khalsa makes mercy meaningful precisely because it is not weakness. The page thus turns from battle-talk to theological self-understanding. The Panth considers how to preserve both the authority of Taru Singh's curse and the higher reputation of Sikh compassion.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh

pages.searchText: Praising Bhai Taru Singh for his great noble deed. Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Praising Bhai Taru Singh for his great noble deed. His curse could cut through the proverbial Sumer mountains. (55) Bhai Taru Singh had uprooted the Nawab's dynastic rule, His spirit would even tumble down the Islamic prophets. Would he tumble down like the shield of a wounded soldier. (56) Whosoever dared to save the life of cursed Nawab, Would he be dashed to the ground by the Singhs spirits. Whosoever dared to protect the Nawab from a saint's curse, Would he be blown into millions of pieces with a single stroke? (57) Thereafter, addressing a congregation of the devout Singhs, He asked his dear colleagues to pay attention to his words. He informed them that with the Nawab, being on the verge of death, Dohra: Thereafter Subeg Singh made another plea to the Singhs, That the Nawab had sought Khalsa's merciful protection. In case the Khalsa refused to be magnanimous in their pardon, The Khalsa's glorious image of pardoning the humble would get tarnished. (59) Chaupai: The Khalsa being a worthy embodiment of all the Divine virtues, Their virtuous utterings have unlimited far-reaching implications. Bhai Taru has illustrated the strength of Khalsa's spiritual powers, As he has made the Nawab realize the consequences of his misdeeds. (60) The Nawab himself had admitted before Bhai Taru Singh, That Divine Guru and Khalsa were synonymous with each other. After verifying the veracity of a Khalsa Singh's solemn pledge, Had the Nawab sent Subeg Singh for mediating on his behalf. (61) After realizing that the Khalsa being worthy of all accomplishments, Had the reckoned the Khalsa to be truly great. Believing that the Khalsa could accomplish every task, Had he realized the Divine Guru and Khalsa being integrated. (62) That the Divine Guru and the Khalsa were embodied in each other, Had the (Tenth) Guru prophesied at the time of his last departure. The Divine Saints and the devout Sikhs being inseparable, The devout Sikhs wielded all the Divine powers of saints. (63)

pages.title: Khalsa Authority and the Nawab's Conditions for Relief
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Subeg Singh explained that the Nawab had come for protection not merely to save his body, but to test whether the saintly attributes once associated with holy men were now alive within the Khalsa. Bhai Taru Singh, he said, would abide by th
pages.searchText: Khalsa Authority and the Nawab's Conditions for Relief Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Subeg Singh explained that the Nawab had come for protection not merely to save his body, but to test whether the saintly attributes once associated with holy men were now alive within the Khalsa. Bhai Taru Singh, he said, would abide by the Khalsa’s decision, so the Panth treated the appeal as a matter of collective authority rather than private favour. The Khalsa therefore framed terms before any relief would be granted. The Nawab must restore the twelve villages linked with Amritsar, return the old endowments that had been disturbed, and publicly rename the disputed settlement as Singhpura. In this way the Panth turned a dying ruler’s plea into a moment of political and spiritual vindication. Mercy would be considered, but only after the Nawab acknowledged the Khalsa’s standing and repaired at least part of the injustice done to Sikh institutions.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh

pages.searchText: That those saintly attributes had come to be vested in Khalsa, Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh That those saintly attributes had come to be vested in Khalsa, Was the Nawab keen to ascertain their vestige. (64) To the same Guru Khalsa had the Nawab come for protection, As well as for verifying the spiritual legacy of the Khalsa Panth. Must the Khalsa vindicate their being spiritual legatees of the Guru, By ridding him of his ailment of the urinary tract. (65) The way the wicked Nawab had asked him to narrate, Had Subeg Singh narrated the whole account to the Khalsa. Also had he sought the consent of Bhai Taru Singh for this petition, Who had paid his respects and obeisance to the Khalsa. (66) Refusing to succumb to anyone else's pressure to change his decision, The Khalsa Panth alone did he hold in the highest esteem. Never feeling offended by whatever the Khalsa Panth decided, Would Bhai Taru Singh abide by the Khalsa Panth's decision. (67) Whatever did the Khalsa Panth deem fit (in their collective wisdom), Would Bhai Taru Singh deem proper (being a humble Singh). That the Khalsa must not have any reservations regarding Taru Singh, Said Subeg Singh to that august gathering of the Singhs. (68) They felt Bhai Taru Singh would abide by their decision. After arriving at a unanimous resolution on the issue, The Khalsa Panth decided to adopt the following resolution: (69) The Nawab must restore the twelve villages to the Khalsa Panth, Which were allocated earlier to the sacred shrine at Amritsar. The Nawab must handover the territorial custody himself, Of all those tiny and bigger helmets to the Khalsa Panth. (70) Was an inhabitant of Farzullah Khan's household. The village which had been named after Farzulla Khan, Was indeed founded by the ancestors of Nawab Kapoor Singh. (71) The Nawab, after leasing out this village in writing to the Singhs, Must rename that ancient village as Singhpura. Nawab Kapoor Singh, feeling outraged at such a demand, Refused to accept anything that was given in charity. (72)

pages.title: The Khalsa Orders a Demonstration of Taru Singh's Authority
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Once the Khalsa had settled the conditions, the Nawab’s terror of death drove him to seek protection of Guru Granth Sahib and to ask how relief might come. The Singhs answered that his cure must itself demonstrate the spiritual authority he
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Orders a Demonstration of Taru Singh's Authority Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Once the Khalsa had settled the conditions, the Nawab’s terror of death drove him to seek protection of Guru Granth Sahib and to ask how relief might come. The Singhs answered that his cure must itself demonstrate the spiritual authority he had mocked and persecuted. Five devout Singhs were appointed to pray that he be touched by Bhai Taru Singh’s shoe, that his blockage be released, and that his life end before Taru Singh’s own final departure. Subeg Singh carried that hukam to Lahore and then to Bhai Taru Singh, who accepted the Panth’s command without hesitation. The page thus turns the Nawab’s suffering into an enacted lesson about Sikh authority. The cure would not come through court medicine or clerical prestige, but through the very martyr whose humiliation the state had tried to enforce.

pages.searchText: Once the Khalsa Panth had taken over the city of Lahore. Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Once the Khalsa Panth had taken over the city of Lahore. The (devilish) Nawab was now quoting the Guru's scripture in desperation, When his death was looming large over his cursed head. (73) Fear of death was the deadliest of the human afflictions, Thus spoke the venerated Nawab Kapoor Singh to the Singhs. Birth and death were two of the several human afflictions, Dohra: It was for seeking liberation from this kind of affliction, That the Nawab had sought protection of Guru Granth Sahib. It was for the manifestation of the spiritual prowess of the Guru, That the wicked Nawab must be given a live demonstration. (75) Chaupai: Though the wicked Nawab never deserved to be pardoned, Yet for his faith in Guru's words, he deserved to be saved. Thereupon, selecting five devout Singhs out of the congregation, Were they asked to offer a prayer to this effect: (76) May the Nawab get himself touched on his person, By Bhai Taru Singh with one of this own shoes. May the Nawab get relieved thereafter of his urinary blockage, Before shedding his mortal frame before Taru Singh. (77) Before touching the Nawab's person with a Singh's shoe. Must not the Nawab undertake any other activity, Before seeking permission from Bhai Taru Singh. (78) Must Bhai Taru Singh be informed about this development, That had the Khalsa decided to vindicate the truth of Guru's words. Thereafter, paying his obeisance with thanks to the Khalsa, Did Subeg depart with the decision of the Khalsa Panth. (79) Dohra: For conveying the unanimous decision of the Khalsa Panth, Did Subeg Singh arrive at the city of Lahore. Approaching Bhai Taru Singh first of all, Did he narrate the Khalsa Pnath's decision in detail. (80) Chaupai: After hearing the whole account from Subeg Singh, Did Bhai Taru Singh pay obeisance to Khalsa Panth. Declaring Khalsa Panth the sole arbiter of all things, Did Bhai Taru Singh declare to sacrifice his life for the Panth. (81)

pages.title: Bhai Taru Singh Accepts the Khalsa's Decision
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: Bhai Taru Singh replied that when the entire Khalsa Panth had permitted the act, he had no standing to oppose it. The prayer by the five devout Singhs, he said, would carry weight in the Divine Court, so the Nawab’s fate now rested on the a
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh Accepts the Khalsa's Decision Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh Bhai Taru Singh replied that when the entire Khalsa Panth had permitted the act, he had no standing to oppose it. The prayer by the five devout Singhs, he said, would carry weight in the Divine Court, so the Nawab’s fate now rested on the authority of the Panth rather than on imperial power. Subeg Singh took this assurance back to Lahore, where the terrified ruler dismissed his attendants and urgently asked for Bhai Taru Singh’s shoes to be brought. Once that symbolic submission was made, the urinary blockage cleared, and the Nawab’s agony immediately subsided. The narrative then broadens into a precedent from Kashmir, where tyranny and forced conversion had once ended in a ruler’s own humiliating affliction. That comparison makes the Nawab’s cure read not as a private miracle, but as part of a recurring moral pattern in the text.

(83) Khalsa having decimated the mighty Nawabs with cannabis husk, With the mere touch of their clubs on the ground, Thereafter, having proceeded to the Nawab of Lahore, Did Subeg Singh narrate the whole account to him. Communicating the Khalsa's unanimous prayer for Nawab's well-being, Subeg Singh communicated the whole process of prayer. (85) After listening to what the Khalsa had communicated, The Nawab ordered all his Muslim colleagues to leave. Being in great haste (to get relieved of his pain), He asked for Bhai Taru Singh's shoes to be brought immediately. (86) A new pair of shoes was put on Bhai Taru Singh's feet. The desperately needy Nawab got his forehead touched by it. (87) As the highly painful urinary blockage got cleared, The grateful Nawab burst out in words of thanks-giving. Bhai Taru Singh having obliged him with a favour, It was indeed a moment of great good luck for the Nawab. (88) A similar precedent had already taken place, Which the Khalsa Panth had repeated in his (Nawab's) case. It had taken place during the oppression committed in Kashmir, When the Muslim ruler had stripped countless Hindus of their sacred Janeau*. (89) Except for the thirteen Hindu families who survived somehow, All other Hindus were forcibly converted to Islam. Thereafter was the Muslim ruler afflicted with such a severe headache, As if he was going to breathe his last. (90)

pages.title: Nawab cured, celebrates the Khalsa, and summons Subeg Singh
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Bhai Taru Singh
pages.snippet: This page closes the Kashmir precedent by recalling that even a ruler who had despised Hindus was told to submit to the symbolic touch of a Hindu’s shoe strapped on to the Nawab’s head. The old story mirrors Lahore closely and prepares the
pages.searchText: Nawab cured, celebrates the Khalsa, and summons Subeg Singh Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About Bhai Taru Singh This page closes the Kashmir precedent by recalling that even a ruler who had despised Hindus was told to submit to the symbolic touch of a Hindu’s shoe strapped on to the Nawab’s head. The old story mirrors Lahore closely and prepares the reader to see the Nawab’s relief as proof that the Khalsa Panth had cured him through a power the state could not command. Back in Lahore, the restored Nawab began speaking openly of Sikh truth and of Guru Nanak's Karah Parshad, acknowledging that the Panth had answered him where his own camp had failed. The city illuminated at night in celebration, and the mood in court shifted from mockery to astonishment. With that public change of heart, Subeg Singh, summoned to the royal court, became the key intermediary between the Nawab and the Sikhs. The page serves as a hinge between miraculous relief and the administrative concessions that soon follow.

pages.searchText: Subeg Singh gains authority and the Nawab soon dies Subeg Singh Gains Authority; the Nawab Dies Episode About painful death of Nawab Khan Bahadur Another Episode About the Nawab Khan Bahadur When the Nawab asked him what reward he desired, Subeg Singh declined mere personal favour and instead asked for a state coin to be struck in his name along with effective political authority. He wanted gains that could actually protect the Panth rather than flatter one man. Armed with that leverage, Subeg Singh Jambar moved quickly against the machinery of persecution. The gallows dismantled, punishments were reversed, and the public signs of state terror against Sikhs began to disappear from Lahore. The Nawab died without further torment soon afterward, exactly as Bhai Taru Singh’s word had implied. Observers in the narrative read that death as proof that the Guru had upheld Sikhi’s honour; some Muslim observers are shown losing confidence in the old order.

pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh hears of the Nawab's death and prepares for departure painful death of Nawab Khan Bahadur Another Episode About the Nawab Khan Bahadur Episode About painful death of Nawab Khan Bahadur Another Episode About the Nawab Khan Bahadur The page first closes the Nawab sequence by declaring that Bhai Taru Singh preserved the Khalsa Panth's honour when the ruler who oppressed the Sikhs fell exactly as foretold. Bhai Taru Singh and Bhai Subeg Singh rendered great service by turning state violence into a public vindication of the Panth. News of the Nawab's death then reached Bhai Taru Singh himself, and he responded with serenity rather than surprise. He told his companions to ask for his funeral pyre to be prepared, as though the time of his own departure had already been plainly announced. Sacred observances were then arranged around him with joy and reverence. The page opens the martyr’s final scene not in panic, but in calm readiness for a death already accepted as part of divine order.

pages.snippet: After Bhai Taru Singh’s passing, the poem raises him above ordinary remembrance and names him greatest among the martyrs. The contrast is sharpened by the image of the Nawab suffering a hundred shoe beatings a day in the next world, while Taru Singh receives honour among the fear
pages.searchText: Bhai Taru Singh's Martyrdom Becomes Living Memory Bhai Taru Singh After Bhai Taru Singh’s passing, the poem raises him above ordinary remembrance and names him greatest among the martyrs. The contrast is sharpened by the image of the Nawab suffering a hundred shoe beatings a day in the next world, while Taru Singh receives honour among the fearless dead. The narrative then turns from martyrdom to living memory by describing the planting of a flag post in memory of Bhai Taru Singh at Lahore. His shrine-like presence becomes a source of blessing, healing, and courage for those who approach it with faith. Whosoever listened to the legend of Bhai Taru Singh, the text says, could hope for worldly aid, bodily recovery, and spiritual firmness. The enduring gift of the martyr is not only protection in crisis, but strength to keep his faith to his last breath.

pages.snippet: This transition page first completes the Bhai Taru Singh sequence by recalling the destruction that overtook the persecuting household of Khan Bahadur. It then turns sharply into a new political landscape following the death of Nawab Khan Bahadur Zakariya Khan. Lahore and Multan
pages.searchText: Lahore's Succession Crisis Sets Up Renewed Persecution Bhai Taru Singh This transition page first completes the Bhai Taru Singh sequence by recalling the destruction that overtook the persecuting household of Khan Bahadur. It then turns sharply into a new political landscape following the death of Nawab Khan Bahadur Zakariya Khan. Lahore and Multan became contested centers of succession, and Shah Nawaz seized power while rivals struggled for control. In that unstable court, the old hostility to the Sikhs quickly returned under new hands. The page therefore sets up the campaign of oppression on the Singhs led by Shah Nawaz and enforced through officials such as Lakhpat Rai and Jaspat Rai. What follows is not an isolated quarrel, but a new round of organized state violence against the Khalsa.

pages.searchText: The Khalsa Resolve to Raid Horses Instead of Scattering The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Under this renewed persecution, the Singhs survived by hiding in forests and among the reeds while Mughal forces blocking their way from all sides tried to flush them into the open. Even rivers and channels became killing grounds, with enemy fire following them into places that should have offered temporary shelter. At night the Khalsa gathered its dead and wounded and debated whether breaking apart would save them. Yet many argued that to scatter would harm their prestige and make sovereignty impossible if the Panth abandoned the field too readily. They therefore returned to the Guru’s prophecy of sovereignty and chose a harder course. Instead of dissolving, they resolved to steal horses from the sleeping Mughals and continue the struggle through cunning raids rather than formal battle.

(9) With the Mughal forces blocking their way from all sides, Would the Mughals fire shots to kill them. As the Singhs would dive into the water and swim, Would the Mughals shoot them as they surfaced. (10) Dohra: Ousted from their homes Singhs sought refuge in the wilds, Driven out of the wilds would they dive into water. Now with their failing to survive even in the water, Where else could they move to save their lives? Chaupai: With the fall of night would the Singhs get some relief, As the Mughal troops would return to their base camps. Then would the Singhs throw the dead among them into the river, And pick up those lying on earth wounded and maimed. (12) Someone suggested that they must scatter allover the region, Another opined that scattering would harm their prestige. (13) They must keep up their fight against the Mughals, As no other alternative would solve their problem. As continuous strife and fight alone would set things right. (14) In case they tried to shun fighting with the Mughals, How could they realize their cherished aim of being sovereigns. Thus, did the Khalsa Panth arrive at a unanimous resolution, That they must keep chasing the Mughal troops at all costs. (15) Must they steal horses from the sleeping Mughals at night, So that the Singh foot soldiers could also mount those horses. Hearing this resolution, many Singhs got ready for the venture, Being desperate to take on the sleeping Mughal troops. (16)

pages.searchText: Night Horse Raids Turn Pursuit into Highway War The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Acting on that resolve, the Singhs infiltrated the Mughal camp at night and seized the horses from the Mughals’ camp before the enemy fully understood what was happening. Those who resisted were cut down, and each successful raid weakened and depleted the Mughal force. When larger detachments pressed back, the Sikhs vanished into marsh, brush, and cane, learning to camouflage themselves among the thick reeds until pursuit lost coherence. They turned concealment into a weapon and reappeared only when striking conditions favoured them. From there the campaign broadened beyond survival into disruption of imperial movement itself. The Singhs began harrying the main highways to Delhi, Lahore, and Peshawar, showing that even when hounded from fixed ground they could still make the roads of empire unsafe.

pages.searchText: The Singhs Ravage Lahore and Turn Toward Imnabad The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About the Slaughter of Jassu (J du Rai) After striking at Mughal camps and slipping away with horses, the Singhs widened their raids until they laid waste around Lahore and made the highways unsafe for imperial traffic. They fought while vastly outnumbered, then vanished again into brush, marsh, and broken ground before the larger forces could trap them. The page stresses how poor the Khalsa still was at this stage: they had no stores, weapons, clothing, or money fit for a settled kingdom. Their only wealth was faith in the Guru's word, and that conviction kept them moving even when hunger, wounds, and exhaustion would have broken ordinary soldiers. From that hard experience the narrative draws a political lesson as well as a military one. The Singhs begin reasoning that without forts, war could not be sustained for long, so they look beyond mere raiding and turn their attention toward richer districts such as Imnabad, where supplies and durable strength might be seized.

pages.searchText: The Khalsa Demands Grain at Imnabad The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About the Slaughter of Jassu (J du Rai) At Imnabad the story introduces Jaspat Rai as a revenue officer whose exactions had made the countryside miserable. Hungry Jats left their homes and joined the Singhs because the local administration had bound, beaten, and impoverished the people instead of protecting them. The Khalsa nevertheless opens with negotiation rather than plunder. Their message is plain: we have no enmity with you, only with the Turks, and the Singhs have long hungered for food after weeks of fighting and flight. They ask for grain at a fair price and offer to move on without disturbing his district if he behaves reasonably. Jaspat rejects that opening, answers with threats and contempt, and turns what might have remained a bargain over provisions into a challenge that can only end in violence.

pages.searchText: Jaspat Rai Threatens the Khalsa and Is Slain The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About the Slaughter of Jassu (J du Rai) Jaspat Rai's reply is meant to humiliate as much as frighten. The memory of Bhai Mani Singh's dismemberment was revived when he boasted that the Singhs could be cut to pieces, mutilated, and dragged before the Nawab in the same degrading fashion. That threat hardens the Khalsa instead of cowing it. The Singhs first offer ardas and resolve on action, treating the confrontation as a test of honor rather than a mere dispute over provisions. Once battle begins, the encounter ends quickly and decisively. The Singhs charged and struck with the sword, Jaspat Khatri was slain and his wealth taken, and the stores seized at Imnabad briefly relieved the desperation that had haunted the previous pages.

Being reminded of (the merciless persecution of Bhai Mani Singh), Did the Singhs resolve to take revenge for the martyr's execution. Since his brother was instrumental in getting Bhai Mani Singh arrested, Must the Singhs settle scores with this (bragging) enemy. Thus, was he himself robbed of his own life, Who had launched a crusade to kill the Singhs. Climbing up the elephant (which Jaspat Rai was riding), Did Nibahoo Singh bring him down with a sword's blow. (49) Thus, Nibahoo Singh mounting upon the elephant, Took hold of all the jewellery after beheading the Dewan. Rest of the valuables did he throw down, Which the Singhs did pick up in a large quantity. (50) It was in the year eighteen hundred seventy-four!9, As per the Bikrami Samvat of the Indian Calendar, That had the Singhs taken possession of a lot of treasure, After beheading the Kshtriya Dewan (of Emnabad). (51)

pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai Swears to Destroy or Convert the Khalsa The killing of Jassu / Jadu Rai after Bhai Taru Singh’s martyrdom Episode About the Slaughter of Jassu (J du Rai) This page acts as a hinge between episodes. After Jaspat's death the Singhs were no longer destitute, because the plunder of Imnabad had given them money, grain, and breathing room, but the narrative immediately turns to a larger and darker retaliation. A new heading shifts the scene to Parol, Kathuha, and Basohli in the Jammu region, opening the Chhota Ghallughara sequence. Lakhpat Rai laid his turban at the Nawab's feet and turned private grief into a public vow of vengeance for his slain brother. He declared that he would not retie that turban until the Khalsa had been either annihilated or driven into apostasy. With the Nawab's blessing, funding, and armed backing, he vowed to destroy or convert the Khalsa and began organizing the campaign that would soon engulf the countryside.

Was there a massacre on a large scale, Which took place at all these three places. (1) Since the day Jaspat Rai was slaughtered by the Singhs, Not only was the city of Emnabad destroyed, It was thoroughly ransacked by the Khalsa as well. (2) A lot of treasure that was in possession of Jaspat Rai, Did the impoverished Singhs lay their hands upon. Did the Singhs not care a fig for other monarchs. (3) Hearing the news of Singhs slaughter of (his brother) Jaspat Rai, Did Lakhpat Rai place his turban at the Nawab's feet. His turban would he put on his head only after, He had decimated the Khalsa Panth of Singhs. (4) Making a solemn vow to liquidate the Singhs, Did he determine to invade and kill them instantly. Hearing this solemn resolution of Lakhpat Rai, Did the Nawab offer to fund his entire mission. (5) Branding the Khalsa Panth as a good-for-nothing sect, Was it the creation of one of the Kashtriyas (Guru Nanak). Vowing himself to be worthy of being called a Kshtriya, Only after he had converted the Khalsa Panth into Islam. (6) This Sham organization was created by a Kashtriya, Which came to be known as the Khalsa Panth in the world. He vowed to claim himself to be Kshtriya, Only after had he liquidated the Khalsa Panth. (7) Thus did he boast of his arrogant bravado, Of which the Nawab did approve and support. Making Lakhpat Rai the commander of Mughal troops, Did the Nawab place all the troops under his command. (8)

pages.snippet: Once the campaign is approved, persecution becomes policy. Lakhpat Rai and the Nawab proclaim that whoever bore the name Singh was to be killed, and they begin the purge by seizing Sikh servants, retainers, and other dependents who could be
pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai Orders the Killing of Every Singh The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Once the campaign is approved, persecution becomes policy. Lakhpat Rai and the Nawab proclaim that whoever bore the name Singh was to be killed, and they begin the purge by seizing Sikh servants, retainers, and other dependents who could be found within easy reach. The order is not confined to armed fighters alone. Officials are told to seize and kill the Sikh servants, while houses are searched and panic spreads among both Sikhs and their Hindu associates who know that an accusation or even a name may now be enough to bring death. Alarmed by the cruelty of the decree, Hindus gathered together in alarm and petitioned Lakhpat Rai. They pleaded that the captives were innocent dependents rather than rebels, but the regime has already chosen collective punishment over justice and refuses to soften its line.

Let anyone claim himself to be called a Singh, Would Lakhpat Rai destroy whole of his village. (9) In the first attempt did he arrest those Singhs, Who had been in service as officials of the state. Handing them over to the state executioners, He ordered them to behead those Sikh officials. (10) Was there a lot of hue and cry among the populace. Organizing themselves into a joint deputation, Beseeching him to desist from executing Sikh officials, As they had no hand whatsoever in any criminal activity. Claiming to approach him on behalf of those innocents, Did they plead for forgiveness to those innocent Sikh officials. (12) Having been approached by all the brothers from his Kshtriya fraternity, Dewan Lakhpat Rai must heed to their sane advice. The Kshtriya delegation including Kaura Mal? and Kunjahi Mal, Also had Kashmiri Mal as one of its members. (13) It also included Lachhi Ram, the chief among the Dewans, Who was held in high esteem by the whole kshtriya fraternity. Approaching Jaspat Rai, did they plead for mercy to the Sikh officials, Their appeal being backed by Dewan Surat Singh. (14) The delegation also included Dilay Ram and Hari Mal, As well as Behloo Mal who also joined. Hari Singh and Gulzar Singh too joined the delegation, Along with Bhai Des Raj (from the Lahore province). (15) Beside these, most of the Hindus joined the delegation, Along with the Sikh saints and their devout followers. All of them pleaded with one voice for mercy, That the Sikh officials be released for the sake of all the Hindus. (16) Including the saintly mendicants and those belonging to ascetic orders. Lakhpat Rai rejected the appeals of all these well meaning people, Of such an evil and obdurate disposition was he made of. (17)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara)

pages.snippet: The deputation's appeal fails completely. Lakhpat Rai is denounced for the killing of Bhai Mani Singh, yet he refuses even a short delay for Somvati Amavas and treats every request for mercy as proof that the Khalsa's enemies must press har
pages.searchText: Mercy Is Rejected and Anti-Sikh Proclamations Begin The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) The deputation's appeal fails completely. Lakhpat Rai is denounced for the killing of Bhai Mani Singh, yet he refuses even a short delay for Somvati Amavas and treats every request for mercy as proof that the Khalsa's enemies must press harder, not relent. His rage spreads beyond executions into symbolic persecution. The Guru's hymns and sacred texts were concealed, the public utterance of Waheguru was suppressed, and even the name of the Guru became something officials tried to erase from open life. Having rejected both mediation and religious restraint, the state now moves openly toward war. Lakhpat Rai uses proclamation and sacrilege together, preparing artillery, troops, and orders for a campaign that will hunt the Singhs far beyond the towns where the arrests began.

pages.searchText: Reiterating that would he never budge an inch from his stand, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Reiterating that would he never budge an inch from his stand, Truly were the Singhs justified in killing his brother. (18) Being instrumental in getting Bhai Mani Singh arrested and slaughtered, Truly had his brother received retribution for his evil deed. While majority of the Kshtriyas departed cursing him, Some of the elders did stay behind with Lakhpat Rai. (19) With folded hands did these Venerable elders plead, That Lakhpat should atleast grant them this little concession. That day being the auspicious day of Somvati Amavas?, He should do what he intended to do on the next day. (20) Refusing the elders to grant even this little concession, Did this obdurate ignorant autocrat execute the Sikh officials. Getting his royal proclamation announced in the city, Did he prohibit the worship of the Sikh Gurus. (21) Would he not spare the life of any such offender. Having prohibited the recitation of Sikh Guru's hymns, Did the Guru's followers proceed to conceal the sacred texts. (22) Reiterating to wipe out the Sikh epithet Waheguru for God, A grocer's usage Gurd* for jaggery being coterminus with Gur, Would he invade and raze his whole village to dust. (24) That he invaded the Khalsa forces (with a vengeance). Equipping his troops with cannons and small fire arms, He got those weapons fired at the Khalsa Panth troops. (25) Ordering his horse, elephant mounted and foot-soldiers to invade, He also made the general populace to follow the troops. Thereafter, the Mughal Nawab sent such written dispatches, That those who professed allegiance to him should support the Dewan. (26)

pages.searchText: Forces Are Summoned from Across the Province The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) The anti-Sikh campaign quickly becomes provincial rather than local. Troops are summoned from Multan and Bahawalpur, while additional calls go out to Kasur and Attock so that pressure can be applied from several directions at once. The hill chiefs are warned not to withhold their contingents, and fresh recruits swell the field army gathering under the Nawab's authority. With so many detachments converging, the Khalsa finds that places which once offered cover or negotiation are now being folded into a single hostile net. Lakhpat Rai himself mounted his elephant and advanced with the force, turning the mobilization into a public spectacle of power. The result is immediate panic and dispersal, because the Singhs can see that this is no passing raid but a determined expedition meant to exhaust them.

This included the troops deployed upto Kasur and Attock, As well as the troops stationed in the Doab triangle®. (27) Despatching the state messengers to all the hill chiefs, He told them not to keep any active soldier at home, As he would not spare his life who shirked his duty. (28) So stern being the orders of the Mughal Nawab, Who could dare to defy his royal proclamation? As nobody could dare to disobey his orders, All the people wished to run for the Singhs lives. (29) Whosoever paid a visit to Dewan Lakhpat Rai, By way of mourning the death of Jaspat Rai. Such a visitor would also join the ranks of deceased Jaspat, As he would never be allowed to return home alive. (30) Making fresh recruitment to his Mughal army, Everyone was recruited whosoever came to be enlisted. Boasting of overpowering Singhs in a couple of days, Would he rest only after his mission was completed. (31) As the Dewan Lakhpat Rai mounted his elephant, Even the sun seemed to be eclipsed with war's dust and din. Such indeed did the din and noise rise in the whole region, That no where could the Khalsa be allowed to take shelter. (32) Appearing to uproot the Khalsa root and branch, Did the incensed Nawab proceed to avenge his brother's death. As do the dry leaves fly before a raging storm, So did the Singhs run for shelter ahead of Mughal invasion. (33) Those who had joined the Singhs for instant favours, Those who had reposed their faith in their Guru, Did they stick to their mission, being firm in faith. (34) As this information about war spread among the populace, So did the Mughal forces went in hot pursuit of Singhs.

pages.snippet: As pressure mounts, fear begins to work inside Sikh society as well as outside it. Mothers asked them to have their hair shorn and disappear among the Jats, urging the young to save themselves by blending back into village life before the d
pages.searchText: Only the Steadfast Khalsa Remains The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) As pressure mounts, fear begins to work inside Sikh society as well as outside it. Mothers asked them to have their hair shorn and disappear among the Jats, urging the young to save themselves by blending back into village life before the dragnet tightened further. Not everyone accepts that counsel. The true Khalsa remained, even as wavering men fell away and families tried to pull sons and brothers back from what looked like certain destruction. Among those who stayed, the debate turned to strategy rather than surrender. The elders' advice favored mobility over grand display, urging the Singhs to survive by sudden strikes, dispersal, and return instead of offering themselves up in one doomed stand.

Beseeching their sons to return home for safety, Their (desperate) mothers asked them to have their hair shorn. (36) Steadfast remained those who by their faith did abide, Deserted all those who in their faith did waver. To the heavens did their souls go who had sacrificed, Sovereigns of the land did they become who survived. (37) Stood their ground those alone as were the true Khalsa Singhs, Though Singhs strength was as insignificant as a pinch of salt in a heap of flour, Yet they were as visible among Mughals as a spark of lightening among dark clouds. (38) Reckoning the strength of Mughal forces to be large in number, The Khalsa Singhs did assemble in a religious congregation. How should the Khalsa fight with the Mughal troops, As they had launched an invasion in their largest strength. (39) Those being hot-headed and brave among the Singhs, Did they vote for an instant spat with the Mughals. Those being seasoned and battle-hardened veterans, Did they advise to adopt a hit and run strategy. (40) Rightly had the elders narrated a war strategy, That hit and run indeed was the best kind of battle. Fight or perish were indeed half as good as hit and run. (41) Opportunate desertion being approved by the Guru as a good strategy, Hit and run strategy indeed was the best policy. Guru himself having deserted the field while battling, Was there indeed nothing sinful about hitting and running. (42) Many a time did Lord Krishna desert the field of battle, In the mid-ocean he had to sit for protection. Pandavas* to had to run away to save their lives, As advised by elderly veterans among the Khalsa Panth, The brave Singh warriors did obey their sane advice. Taking shelter among the wilds (as and when reguired). (44)

pages.title: Lakhpat Rai Tightens the Pursuit with Fire and Cannon
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara)
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha
pages.snippet: The Singhs initially strike the enemy's front ranks hard enough to show that courage has not left them. But after the first shock, Lakhpat Rai reorganizes the pursuit so that cannon in front and supporting fire from behind make repeated cha
pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai Tightens the Pursuit with Fire and Cannon The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) The Singhs initially strike the enemy's front ranks hard enough to show that courage has not left them. But after the first shock, Lakhpat Rai reorganizes the pursuit so that cannon in front and supporting fire from behind make repeated charges increasingly costly. He then attacks the terrain itself. Pathways are cut through cover, thickets were burned, and the Khalsa is denied the forests and broken ground that had previously let smaller bands escape larger forces. Under this pressure the Singhs are driven from refuge to refuge without rest. The running battle now becomes a campaign of attrition, with fire, artillery, and encirclement gradually pushing the exhausted fugitives toward the river routes ahead.

Thereupon feeling concerned at such a colossal loss of life, Did Dewan (Lakhpat Rai) attribute this loss to the lack of strategy. (45) Adopting an alternative strategy of troop deployment of his forces, He decided to deploy horse-mounted cannons in the front. Supporting this cavalry column by hand-operated guns from behind, Deploying the columns of foot-soldiers at the rear end of his army, Dewan Lakhpat, being scared of Singhs, himself remained in the rear. (47) As and when the running Singhs returned to hit the Mughals, They found themselves helpless in the face of canon fire. Being helpless, would the Singhs return to enter the wilds, Such being the ordeal confronting the Khalsa Panth. (48) Beyond the cannon's range, would the Singhs retreat into the wilds, But little could they do to escape the attack from the Mughal cavalry. Would the Singhs kill those who got separated from the main army, Thus did the Singhs survive the ordeal many a time. (49) Thereafter, summoning the forest guards (managing the forest), Setting on fire the thick bushes to make inroads, The guns were positioned to take aim at the Singhs. (50) The Singhs being harassed and hounded to the extreme, Could not find anything to feed on and survive. And emerged out of the wilds (being helpless). (51) Dohra: While some took refuge in the wilds on this side of the river, Others hid themselves in the wilds on the other side of the river. Did the Singhs carry on their march forward. (52) Chaupai: Reaching a point where the river Ravi could be swum across, Did the Singhs Swim through the river to reach the other bank. With the Singhs marching along the river's other bank, Were they chased and pursued by the Mughal forces. (53)

pages.snippet: By now the Khalsa is near collapse from constant flight. Food and water failed, horses are worn down, and day and night march has left the Singhs with little chance to camp, cook, or tend their wounded before the next movement becomes neces
pages.searchText: The Famished Khalsa Looks Toward Treacherous Hill Allies The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) By now the Khalsa is near collapse from constant flight. Food and water failed, horses are worn down, and day and night march has left the Singhs with little chance to camp, cook, or tend their wounded before the next movement becomes necessary. Their equipment is failing as badly as their bodies. Broken bows, blunted weapons, and famished mounts show that the campaign is being fought beyond the limits of ordinary endurance, with survival depending more on resolve than on any secure line of supply. In that condition some hope that the hill chiefs or nearby Hindu households might offer relief, but the narrative prepares the reader for betrayal rather than sanctuary. The same hill interests that had abandoned Banda Singh Bahadur are about to fail the Khalsa again, turning desperate trust into another snare.

pages.searchText: Failing to put up a camp at any vantage point of safety, The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Failing to put up a camp at any vantage point of safety, Did the Singhs continue their march day and night. Running short of every kind of provisions and equipment, Having no access to any kind of arms and ammunition, How could the Singhs pick up a fight with the Mughal troops. Their weapons having been blunted with continuous usage, The Singhs too had gone without sleep for days together. (55) The bows having been broken with a long use and wielding, Blades of their spears having remained struck in enemy's bodies, They could find no blacksmiths to sharpen their blades. (56) Their horses having become listless for want of proper feed, Not to talk of any provisions in the form of food grains, Travelling (on foot) proverbially Known as partial death, Starvation is taken to be synonymous with (complete) death. Both these calamities having struck the Singhs together, These proved to be most catastrophic for the Khalsa Panth. (58) Having been stretched to the extreme with these calamities, The Singhs thought of seeking assistance from the Hindu brotherhood. Sneaking into the wilds on the slopes of hilly terrain, They expected to find some favours from their Hindu brethren. (59) For protection of the Hindus and decimation of the Mughals, Truly was the Khalsa Panth created (by the Divine Guru). Knowing little that these (hilly) Hindus being allies of the Mughals, They would certainly play foul with the Singhs. (60) After having invited Banda Bahadur to lend them support, They had played a fraud with Banda Singh Bahadur. After Banda Bahadur had slaughtered the Mughals, They were instrumental in getting Banda Bahadur defeated. (61) The Singhs did not realize the hilly Hindu's treachery, That they had been traitors since the beginning. The Singhs had really forgotten (their past records), That they had handed over Banda Bahadur's followers to the Mughals. (62)

pages.snippet: Thereafter, toward Basohli the battered Singhs marched on without provisions, rest, or trustworthy allies. Seeing a large assembly of hill people, some of them hoped for relief and approached in good faith, only to find that the gathering h
pages.searchText: The Hills Betray the Fleeing Khalsa at Basohli The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Thereafter, toward Basohli the battered Singhs marched on without provisions, rest, or trustworthy allies. Seeing a large assembly of hill people, some of them hoped for relief and approached in good faith, only to find that the gathering had no intention of sheltering them. Instead, hill forces slaughtered many Singhs on the spot and handed others over to the Mughals, who cut them down immediately. The same pattern unfolded around Parol and Kathuha, where fleeing Singhs were trapped, seized, and destroyed rather than allowed to pass through in safety. Driven toward the hills as a last resort, the survivors discovered that forces already summoned by the Nawab of Lahore had occupied the heights above them. Pressed from the slopes and from the rear, they fought with blunted weapons, searched in vain for Lakhpat Rai, and finally turned towards the river in hope of finding some way out.

pages.searchText: The Khalsa Finds the Flooded River Impassable The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) The Singhs stood on the river bank after retreating and found the river flowing in full torrent and flood. Whirlpools churned across the current, uprooted trees came hurtling downstream, and even great stones and boulders were being dragged away by the force of the water. The Khalsa called for someone to test the passage so the rest might follow, and two brothers from Dalewal entered the current to sound a crossing. They never returned, and their loss convinced the camp that the river offered no real escape from the tightening Mughal pursuit. After that failed attempt, the Singhs concluded that an open death in battle was better than drowning helplessly in the torrent. Remembering the Guru's praise for one who dies fighting facing the enemy, they abandoned thoughts of a crossing and prepared to meet their attackers on land.

pages.searchText: The Singhs Climb Under Fire Along the Hillside The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) The Singhs camping on the hillside tried again to climb out of the trap, but hill troops guarded the ridges and blocked every pass. From above came stones, bricks and bullets, while Rajput positions added cannon fire that tore through anyone who tried to force a way upward. Even under that barrage, the Singhs briefly seized one enemy post before superior numbers pushed them back. Refusing to give up the ascent, they dug trenches and underground bunkers wherever they could, using knives, daggers, spears, and swords to carve footholds into the slope. That improvised fieldwork let them renew the climb with more order and protection. By sheer persistence they won another hold on the hillside and began cutting some earth with swords for making steps so that men and horses could continue moving above the river.

pages.searchText: The Mountain Retreat Becomes a Choked Killing Ground The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Some survived while others stumbled on the steps as the Singhs tried to push along the narrow mountain route; the river drowned those who tumbled from the slopes below. The passage became so choked with desperate fighters that neither the men behind could reach the front nor those ahead could turn back in any orderly way. Everywhere the retreat turned into a siege, because there was no room to march forward and no path to reverse the movement. Men slipped, collided, and were swept away, while the crush of bodies on the hill made every small mistake fatal. Hunger and thirst then deepened the ordeal until it seemed impossible even to drink a drop of water. As the pressure mounted, the Mughal side hardened the pursuit further by placing a reward of five rupees for each Sikh’s head, turning the retreat into a hunted massacre.

Once that order was given, the Mughals renewed their assault with cannon, cavalry, and close pressure on the trapped Khalsa. The Singhs answered with a fierce counterattack that briefly drove back mounted assailants and revived their spirits in the middle of disaster. In that moment Sukha Singh resolved that the struggle had to be carried directly against the man directing the slaughter. Before striking, however, he learned that Lakhpat Rai stood behind a heavy security cordon around him, protected by infantry, horsemen, camel swivels, and artillery. Sukha Singh still tried to reach him, but a small cannon shot smashed one of his legs and broke the attack before it could be completed.

pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Holds the Retreat Despite His Wound The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Sukha Singh retreated from the place where he was hit, but he repeatedly turned back toward the fight instead of yielding to his wound. He refused to disarm himself despite a grievous injury and kept placing himself wherever the endangered Singhs needed steadiness most. The battle raged partly on the mountains and partly on the foothills, while the Khalsa measured their shrinking strength against a far larger enemy that was still closing from every side. Outnumbered, hungry, and trying to move horses through broken terrain, they recognized that stubbornness alone would not win the day. A fresh resolution followed: they would scatter, preserve as many lives as possible, and return later with better preparation. The page frames that decision not as cowardice, but as a tactical withdrawal that kept the campaign alive for another round of struggle.

pages.searchText: Khalsa scatters and Sukha Singh directs the retreat The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) The Khalsa then declared that they must scatter themselves in all the directions and later reassemble in the Majha region to renew the struggle. The decision acknowledged that the present battlefield could no longer be held, but it also turned dispersal into an organized plan for survival and future resistance. Sukha Singh counseled the Singhs on how to carry out the retreat, telling those on foot to keep climbing while mounted men guarded them from below. He tried to preserve some order in the breakup so the weakest parties would not be abandoned immediately under Mughal pressure. Even with that guidance, the separation was painful and chaotic, as comrades and families were torn apart in the confusion. The movement away from the hills thus became both a military dispersal and an emotional sundering for a community already battered by hunger, pursuit, and loss.

pages.searchText: Sukha Singh leads a breakout through Mughal lines The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Sukha Singh rejected the hope that the Singhs could ever survive through stealth alone while the enemy kept closing in. He called on them to follow after him and strike straight at the strongest Mughal defences rather than wait to be hunted down piecemeal. That charge shattered several forward posts, and the Singhs seized weapons from those who resisted before pushing ahead again. Their brief success opened a way toward cover, letting a large part of the battered force move off instead of dying where it stood. Seeing a way out, Sukha Singh led them toward a wild growth that promised concealment, but the danger did not end with that movement. Mughal forces still pressed from both flanks, and cannon fire from both the Mughal flanks punished anyone who lagged behind the main breakout.

pages.searchText: Night refuge in the jungle and the Mughal use of civilians The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) As darkness fell, the Singhs finally gained a little shelter in the jungle while the Mughal camp drew back for the night. That pause gave the fugitives a few hours to breathe, but it did not restore the strength of men already fatigued, famished and naked from continuous fighting and flight. At midnight they moved again, only to find the hunt renewed as Mughal detachments closed in on the forest routes. The Singhs realized that desertion and escape alone would not avail, so they fought in bursts while trying to reach a bigger patch of jungle where pursuit might be blunted. The Mughals answered by widening the chase beyond their own regular troops. They called the public with a beat of drum, armed villagers and camp followers, and drove these auxiliaries into the brush so the Sikhs could be flushed from cover even when the main army could not see them directly.

As the Mughals were continuously hunting for the Singhs, Fatigued, famished and naked were Singhs rendered, They were again surrounded by the Mughal troops, Whichever Mughal soldier dared to enter the wild, The Singhs did pounce upon him and killed him. Whichever Singh ventured to get out of the wild, The Mughals too did attack and despatch him to death. (138) That desertion and escape alone would not avail. Till they could reach a bigger patch of jungle for shelter. (139) Dohra: As the Singhs attempted to enter a smaller patch, Would the Mughal troops harass the Singhs a lot, But as the Singhs got into a bigger patch, Would the Singh kill the Mughals in large numbers. (140) That they must summon a large gathering of people. They must push this crowd into the jungle, Thereafter, as the Dewan called the public with a beat of drum, The public gathered there in response to this proclamation. As the Mughals pushed these subjects into the wild, They were armed with muskets and sharp spears. (142) Dohra: Thus did these subjects confront the Singhs, Adopting several kinds of tactics and maneavours. This intrusion did create a piquant situation, As the Singhs were at their wit's ends to deal with public. (143)

pages.searchText: Sukha Singh turns on the intruders and the Singhs cross the river The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) Sukha Singh then warned that the Singhs would have to kill the people for their own survival if they wished to remain alive in the jungle. Once the Khalsa rushed at the armed intruders, the Jat intruders started fleeing, leaving horses, garments, and weapons behind as they scattered. That reprieve gave the survivors a moment to regroup and head for the Majha region rather than remain trapped in the same killing ground. They forced a rapid march through hostile country and then faced yet another river barrier on the road to safety. To cross it, the Singhs had to makeshift boats of reeds and grass and trust the current once more. After landing, they endured stretches of burning sand so fierce that many tore off their garments to make footpads, turning even their clothing into part of the struggle to survive.

They could stay in the wild in peace and safety, Only after they had done away with these intruders. (144) Would these civilian intruders eliminate the Singhs, In case the Singhs failed to get rid of these subjects. Thus did besieged Singhs survive with the daring of a burglar alone, As the Divine Satguru had ordained the Khalsa's survival. (145) As the Singhs rushed upon to pounce on the intruders, The Jat intruders started fleeing before them. As the Singhs robbed those whom they caught, They let many of those escape who chose to flee. (146) The Singhs snatched the horses of many an intruder, While many others left their robes and weapons behind. Though the prominent warriors had all exhausted. (147) As the Singhs got a temporary relief from fighting, Did they decide to head for the Majha region. As the next immediate region belonged to wicked Rama Randhawa, Did the Singhs resolve to cross this region in a single night. (148) As the Singhs confabulated how to cross the river, Did they endeavour to wade through this river. Camping upon the river's bank under the searing heat at noon, Did the Singhs make make-shift boats of reeds and grass. (149) As the Singhs waded through the river to the other bank, Did they take rest there for a few hours to relax. Thereafter, saddling the horses by tying their buckles, Did the Singhs launch on their march on an onward mission. ((150) Whatever equipage had the Singhs carried with them, It got drowned in water during their passage through the river. They got their feet scorched in the hot sands, As they had to walk through the sandy terrain barefooted. (151) So intensely hot and sandy was the river plateau, As if somebody had laid out a hot plate. The Singhs had to tear off their dresses to make footpads, So that they could protect their feet from being scorched. (152)

pages.searchText: Transition from Sukha Singh’s Escape to the Parol–Kathua Survivors The Chhota Ghallughara at Parol and Kathuha Episode About Massacre at Parol and Kathuha (Chhota Cha oh ara) This page finishes the escape after the slaughter by describing the Singhs crossing into Majha after forcing their way through the river country. They move through the hot Jaito tract, gather again in the jungle, and tend Sukha Singh’s shattered leg while the survivors pause to recover after months of strain. The account notes that Sukha Singh remained laid up for many months while the rest of the band slowly reorganized itself. The scene is less about triumph than endurance, showing how a broken remnant kept itself alive after the massacre. The page then turns into a hinge and opens the next episode by returning to the survivors left at Parol and Kathua. Some men tried horses, others tried the hills, but every line of retreat was narrowing under pursuit from Lakhpat Rai’s side and from hostile country around them.

pages.searchText: Episode 117: Starvation, Betrayal, and the Turn Against the Hills Counting the Singhs after the massacre Another Episode Another Episode-Head Count af Singhs Malye The trapped survivors discover that the hills are no refuge. Men who descend are hunted, those who remain above are encircled, and hunger becomes as deadly as the enemy because food cannot be secured anywhere in safety. The strongest emotional note on the page is betrayal by the hill chiefs. The Singhs reflect that they had fought Mughal power in ways that also benefited the hill rulers, yet the same chiefs now help tighten the noose instead of offering shelter. Out of that anger and desperation the survivors harden themselves again. Rather than die passively, they turn back toward the mountains, striking where they can and trying to force a path through a region that has already decided against them.

The Singhs who had reckoned the steep hills to provide protection, Had to return to the base failing to find a foothold. (5) Such was the catastrophe from all sides that fell upon Singhs, That no initiative on the part of Singhs could be of any avail. For want of any food did the Singhs keep dying of starvation. (6) As the Singhs kept on being killed in whatever direction they proceeded, Did the Singhs keep standing still in extreme desperation. Thereupon did the Singhs arrive at this conclusion, That they had never done any harm to the hilly people. (7) The Khalsa Panth had rather killed the enemies of hill chiefs, As well as done deeds of good to the hilly people. The Singhs had all along been fighting with the Mughals, So that the latter could not overpower the hilly regions. (8) As the Singhs had exterminated and killed the Mughals, The hill chiefs had been relieved of paying revenue to the Mughals. Had these hill chiefs been traitors from the beginning, As they had even played foul with the (tenth) Sikh Guru. (9) After this observation, did the Singhs climb up the mountains, Proceeding with a rush to ransack that region. Thus thousands of Singhs crossed through the mountains, As they could no longer afford to stay put among the hills. (10) With Mughal troops being in hot pursuit of the Singhs, They kept on being beheaded as had fallen on the way. Even as the Mughals got fed up with massacring the Singhs, Some of the Singhs still did survive this massacre. (11) Dohra: At places would the Singhs get into a fight with the Mughals, At places would the famished Singhs rob others for food. At places where they could not buy provisions even for a price, Would the Singhs survive on pulling and eating vegetation. (12)

pages.searchText: From Disguised Escape to the Kiratpur Muster Roll Counting the Singhs after the massacre This page records the cruel aftermath of the mountain flight: provisions are scarce, even money cannot reliably buy grain, and many Singhs die from hunger before they can find a secure route away from the cordon. The survivors endure not only military pursuit but a landscape in which ordinary sustenance has been cut off. Those who manage to live do so by concealment and improvisation. Some bind up their hair, alter their appearance, and move quietly through Mandi and Kullu until they finally reach Kiratpur in disguise instead of marching openly as warriors. The page closes the episode with a reckoning in the sixth month, distinguishing the dead from those who straggled through alive. It serves as a muster roll of loss before the narrative turns from escape and survival toward those marked for death in the slaughter.

(13) Would the Singhs be denied provisions even for a price, Such being the ordeal faced by the Khalsa Panth. Branding them as the companions of Banda Bahadur, Were the Singhs accused of having harassed the populace. (14) Would the Singhs desert being out numbered by the enemy, Neither did any sovereign lend a moral support to the Singhs, Thereafter, did the Singhs get into a disguise, Tying their long hair in knots and flowing locks. Thus did they succeed in reaching Mandi? and Kullu*, Disguising themselves as menials and daily wagers. (16) Thus did they spend a few days in peace in a place, Being known as the region belonging to a gueen with a clipped nose. Returning thereafter to Kiratpur (a holy Sikh shrine). (17) Whosoever survived from the jaws of death, Had he to pass through the hills with great effort. Did they manage to reach Kiratpur, the holy shrine. (18) Thereafter, was the head count of Khalsa forces made in the sixth month, After sending written dispatches to the scattered Singh contingents. Only after this head count were all the Singhs identified, As to who had survived and who had perished then. (19) Episode 118 Another Episode — The Head count of Singhs Martyred in Chhota Ghallughara I Chaupai: (Their heads were piled up in dome-shaped heaps) (Dear readers) now listen to the narrative of all those Singhs, Who had passed through this dark night of death and destruction. Of those who had survived by sneaking into the wilds, As well as of those who had taken refuge in Majha region after return. (1)

pages.searchText: Episode 118 Close: Basoli Captives, Uncertain Death Toll, and the Turn to Shah Nawaz the Destined Death of Lakhu and Shah Narat Episode About the Destined Death of Lakhu and Shah Narat This fragment gathers the fate of those who did not escape. Captives from Parol and the men who collapsed in the hills are carried into Basoli jail and severed heads are displayed as trophies, reducing the massacre to an inventory of humiliation as well as death. The page emphasizes how little of the Khalsa remnant remained. Only a small number survive, very few horses are left, and even the poet admits that the total slaughter could not be counted exactly because the dead lay scattered across many routes of flight and capture. The closing lines date the great disaster and pivot to the next moral sequence. After recounting the uncertain death toll, the narrative turns toward the destined downfall of Lakhpat Rai and Shah Nawaz, whose pride and cruelty invite their own destruction.

Whatever account had my father narrated to me, So have I (Rattan Singh) got it recorded to (David Murray). That a massacre on such a massive scale occurred, Which the Mughals had perpetrated on the Singhs. (8) Episode 119 Episode About Ram Rauni After the massacre that he perpetrated on the Singhs.

pages.title: Condemnation of Shah Nawaz and Lakhpat Rai
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ram Rauni
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position
pages.snippet: After the massacre, Shah Nawaz is presented as drunk on power and dreaming of a still higher station, while Lakhpat Rai shares in the same swollen arrogance. The page frames both men as rulers whose apparent success has already made them fi
pages.searchText: Condemnation of Shah Nawaz and Lakhpat Rai Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Episode About Ram Rauni After the massacre, Shah Nawaz is presented as drunk on power and dreaming of a still higher station, while Lakhpat Rai shares in the same swollen arrogance. The page frames both men as rulers whose apparent success has already made them fit objects of divine judgment. It then lingers on their anti-Sikh persecution in deliberate detail, stressing that the word Guru was forbidden, the name of Nanak was twisted into insult, and listeners to the Guru’s bani were pressured toward Islam by men who treated reverence itself as a crime. The page also remembers desecration of scripture as part of the same campaign of contempt. By gathering these offenses together, the narrative prepares the complaint that heaven itself will answer in the pages that follow.

pages.snippet: Laying his claim to the sovereignty over India, Did he dream of occupying the Mughal throne at Delhi. (1) Doomed to be burdened with doing evil deeds. Such indeed being the will of the Satguru Divine, Destined were these two to be damned in
pages.searchText: Laying his claim to the sovereignty over India, Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Episode About Ram Rauni Laying his claim to the sovereignty over India, Did he dream of occupying the Mughal throne at Delhi. (1) Doomed to be burdened with doing evil deeds. Such indeed being the will of the Satguru Divine, Destined were these two to be damned indeed. (2) Such indeed is the working of the fate inexorable, That it makes sinners commit more and more sins. Do they sink and perish under the burden of their own sins. (3) What to talk of their bigger atrocities and excesses, They even prohibited the uttering of the word Guru. The word Gurd (jaggery) being co-terminus with word Guru, They ordered its nomenclature to be changed to sweets. (4) That the word Nanak be mispronounced as Nanu. That whosoever was found listening to hymns of Nanak, Let he be immediately converted to Islam under duress. (5) That wherever he happened to lay his hands upon the Sikh sacred text, He ordered it to be thrown instantly into the river. That after he had wiped out the name of Nanak's Khalsa Panth, Would he claim himself to be a true Kshtriya indeed. (6) As such atrocities and excesses occurred in this world, The information about these reached the Divine Court. Summoning the divine messengers visiting the earth, The Divine Lord enquired how did all these excesses happen? (7) Narrating the whole account the Divine messengers did say, That (Guru) Nanak's name was being maligned in the world. As the Divine Lord did not punish the evil-doers, There spread darkness of evil throughout the world. (8) As darkness disappears with the lighting of a lamp at home, As the whole sky gets illuminated with the rise of the sun, So illuminating were the hymns of (Guru) Nanak indeed, That the whole mankind got enlightenment from his hymns. (9)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ram Rauni
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position
pages.snippet: The response to the complaint is immediate and theological: divine punishment was decreed against the slanderers who had mocked the Guru and oppressed the Sikhs. The page makes clear that worldly upheaval is not random but the chosen instru
pages.searchText: Divine Retribution and Abdali’s Advance Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Episode About Ram Rauni The response to the complaint is immediate and theological: divine punishment was decreed against the slanderers who had mocked the Guru and oppressed the Sikhs. The page makes clear that worldly upheaval is not random but the chosen instrument of that judgment. From that point the narrative turns to history in motion as the Kabul ruler is driven toward Lahore and Ahmad Shah Abdali advances into Punjab. Lakhpat Rai and Shah Nawaz attempt to work within the Afghan invasion, but the movement of armies now serves a justice they do not control. The page leads directly toward the fighting around Sirhind. What begins as a decree in the divine court becomes a campaign on the ground, with imperial ambition and retribution converging in the same war.

pages.title: Thereupon, the Lord Divine did make His will declare,

pages.snippet: Thereupon, the Lord Divine did make His will declare, That the contemnors be meted out an exemplary punishment. Let those be punished who deserved to be punished, Let they be instantly presented with their evil deeds. (10) As soon as the Di
pages.searchText: Thereupon, the Lord Divine did make His will declare, Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Episode About Ram Rauni Thereupon, the Lord Divine did make His will declare, That the contemnors be meted out an exemplary punishment. Let those be punished who deserved to be punished, Let they be instantly presented with their evil deeds. (10) As soon as the Divine Lord did express His Will Divine, Fate, the Divine instrument, did decide to fulfil His Will. Prompting the (Afghan) ruler ruling at Kabul, Destiny made him move on the road to Lahore. (11) As a sharp thorn takes out another thorn embedded in the flesh, It was in the year eighteen hundred and four? of (B.S.), That there rose a storm of (vengeance and aggression). It was after the death of Nadir Shah*, the Afghan ruler, That Ahmad Shah Abdali? intruded into India. (13) Taimur Shah* being the son of Ahmad Shah Abdali, Both father and son had had a glimpse of Delhi's grandeur. Thus, with Delhi having been the object of their desires, They captured Lahore after their advent in India. (14) As Dewan Lakhpat Rai became an ally of the Afghan ruler, Nawab Shah Nawaz too became a camp follower of the Afghans. Such being the destined design of the Divine Will, Lakhpat Rai too adopted the strategy of aligning with the Afghans. (15) (Opposing this alliance) were forces led by Kamar Din, Who were joined by forces of a Rajput warrior Madho Singh. With more forces under the command of Prince Shahzada, Finding the (rich) city of Sirhind being unguarded by any force, Ahmed Shah Abdali arrived with in sixty miles of Sirhind. Thus entering the Sirhind province from another riverine passage, He put up his camp in the vicinity of Sirhind. (17) Making a dash did Abdali ransack the city of Sirhind, As well as the royal treasury of the Delhi Mughals. It was here in the Sirhind province of the Mughal empire, That there raged a fierce battle continuously for twenty-two days. (18)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ram Rauni
