pages.snippet: The battle narrative turns when cannon fire kills Kamar Din, yet Mir Mannu hid his father's death so the Mughal line would not break in panic. By keeping the loss secret and pressing the fight, he helps reverse the field at the very moment
pages.searchText: Mir Mannu’s Victory and the Seizure of Lakhpat Rai Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Episode About Ram Rauni The battle narrative turns when cannon fire kills Kamar Din, yet Mir Mannu hid his father's death so the Mughal line would not break in panic. By keeping the loss secret and pressing the fight, he helps reverse the field at the very moment when collapse seemed possible. The page then notes the Afghan setback and the recovery of Mughal authority, with Abdali forced back toward Kabul and away from Lahore. Victory in battle is immediately joined to a second reckoning in politics, because the man who survives the field now decides whom to punish at home. That political reckoning falls on Lakhpat Rai. Mir Mannu seizes him, fines him, and hears Kaura Mal rehearse the crimes committed against the Sikhs, turning the page from warfare into an indictment of anti-Sikh brutality.

pages.snippet: The cannon which had been lying abandoned at Sirhind, A cannon ball having been fired from this reassembled cannon, Did it hit Kamardin killing him on the spot. (19) Did keep his father's death a secret (from his troops). He waged a fresh b
pages.searchText: The cannon which had been lying abandoned at Sirhind, Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Episode About Ram Rauni The cannon which had been lying abandoned at Sirhind, A cannon ball having been fired from this reassembled cannon, Did it hit Kamardin killing him on the spot. (19) Did keep his father's death a secret (from his troops). He waged a fresh battle soon after his father's death, By placing his father's (dead) body atop an elephant. (20) He placed a special attendant in such a way (along the dead body), That he kept on responding to the salutes of his soldiers. So much motivated felt the Mughal troops by this gesture, That they made the Afghan troops run for their lives. (21) As the forces of Indian Mughal emperor became victorious, Ahmad Shah Abdali ran back to Kabul with his forces. As Mir Mannu's forces carried on in hot pursuit, Ahmad Shah Abdali had to vacate the city of Lahore. (22) Than he took Dewan Lakhpat Rai into his custody. Imposing a penalty of thirty lakh rupees for his treachery, Dewan Kaura Mal, having been a devout follower of the Sikh Gurus, Did pay a ransom of ten lakh rupees (for taking a custody of Lakhpat Rai), Narrating all the atrocities perpetrated by Lakhpat Rai on the Sikhs, Reminding Lakhpat Rai of having arrested the innocent Sikhs, He had killed those innocents on the auspicious day of Somavati Amavas!2. (25) Accusing him of not postponing the executions on that (auspicious) day, Narrating him the whole account of his misdeeds, Dewan Kaura Mal laid bare all his atrocities on the Singhs. (26) Holding him sguarely responsible for the massacre of the Sikhs, The Dewan accused him of killing poor Sikhs in their homes. Blaming him for prohibiting the worship of Sikh Gurus, The Dewan held him responsible for destroying the sacred Sikh texts. (27)

pages.searchText: Lakhpat Rai’s Humiliation and the Opening of Ram Rauni Ram Rauni and the Sikh defensive position Episode About Ram Rauni Kaura Mal’s revenge is public and degrading rather than merely administrative. Lakhpat Rai is chained, disgraced before others, and finally thrown into a sewage pit so that punishment mirrors the moral filth the text attributes to his conduct. The page uses that humiliation to close one episode cleanly. The poet marks the sequence as completed, ending the account of retribution against a persecutor whose power once seemed unassailable after the massacre. At once the narrative opens Ram Rauni and shifts back to the Khalsa. Hardship has taught the Singhs that they cannot live forever in scattered wandering, so they begin debating whether a defended position should be raised near Amritsar.

Asking the Sikhs to defecate on the head of this tyrant, The Dewan asked the people to urinate on his head. (28) Giving him retribution commensurate with his sins. Such a fitting harvest of humiliation did he reap, For the evil deeds that he had committed. (29) Exactly as the author (Rattan Singh) had heard, Same had he got recorded (with his patron). It was in the year eighteen hundred and five, In the Indian calendar of Bikrami Samvat. (30) Episode 120 Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. (For the digging of a water channel around its periphery, Did it come to be known by the name Ram Rauni) That it was impossible to confront the Mughals from the wilds. Thus, did they come to an agreement after confabulations, That must they wage battles from behind a walled cover. (1) Thereafter, did the Singhs wish to raise a walled cover, So that they could confront, fight and kill the enemy. Suggested someone that must they occupy an existing fort, Suggested another that wild growth was better than a fort. (2) Then did the veterans opine after a thorough deliberation, That even a lion did not feel safe without a shelter. Then after arriving at resolution at a religious congregation, The Khalsa Panth felt that even a lion felt protected in a wild. (3) Thereafter, did the devout Singhs put forth a proposal, How could they wage a war from a fort outside Amritsar? Why should they leave their Guru's sacred shrine at Amritsar, As even Kauravas and Pandavas had selected a secret place for war? (4) The Sikh shrines around Amritsar were as sacred to the Sikhs, As was Kurukshetra sacred to the Kaurvas and Pandvas.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal ..
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance
pages.snippet: This page records the inner debate over where the Khalsa should make its stand. The argument that wins is spiritual as much as military: it is better to die near the Guru's shrines than to seek a safer but less meaningful refuge elsewhere.
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Resolve to Defend Amritsar from the Sacred Shrines Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. This page records the inner debate over where the Khalsa should make its stand. The argument that wins is spiritual as much as military: it is better to die near the Guru's shrines than to seek a safer but less meaningful refuge elsewhere. The discussion turns repeatedly to the sanctity of Amritsar and the memory attached to its sacred places. Instead of abandoning the center of Sikh devotion, the Singhs weigh the five holy sites and imagine defense growing out of the geography blessed by the Gurus themselves. By the end of the page, the decision is moving toward action. The sacred shrines of Amritsar are no longer only places of pilgrimage; they are becoming the ground from which a new fortification will be raised.

pages.searchText: It was better to die in war near a sacred Sikh shrine, Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. It was better to die in war near a sacred Sikh shrine, At it would redeem a Sikh for thousands of next births. (5) Chaupai: Therefore, should the Singhs search for a suitable site, Thus did say one of the veterans among the Singhs. The five Sikh shrines (at Amritsar) that the Guru had constructed, Were these indeed more sacred than even Kurukshetra. (6) Must they never depart from this place of sacred shrines, As no other place was more sacred than Amritsar. Must they make supreme sacrifices in the proximity of Gurudwaras, As no other option was better for shedding one's mortal frame. (7) Dohra: They must wage a war against the Mughals, After raising a walled fort at their sacred place. While death at that place would take their souls to heavens, Survival in war would make them claimants for sovereignity. (8) Chaupai: Thereupon, a Sikh narrated an incident (about Amritsar), Whereby he had seen a great miracle that happened there. There had he seen a (pregnant) goat separated from the heard, Which did deliver a couple of offsprings at that place. (9) As a couple of wolves had spotted out the goat's offsprings, They tried their best to snatch those newly born offsprings. Never did the (brave) goat let the wolves snatch the lambs, As I myself kept on watching this miraculous event. (10) That they would rather not listen to such a narration, Preferring to repose their faith in their own Divine Guru, They would prefer to sacrifice their lives at their Guru's lotus feet. (11) That all good omens had coincided at that place. They must agree to adopt one of the shrines for a fort, Out of the five sacred shrines that the Guru had raised. (12) Dohra: These five Sikh shrines founded at Amritsar, Consisted of Harmandar, Bibek Sar? and Kaulsar.° Added to these were shrines of Santokhsar* and Ramsar, Which were established by Guru Ramdas himself. (13)

pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance

pages.searchText: The Singhs Build Ram Rauni with Their Own Hands Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. Once the site is chosen, the page becomes practical and communal. A foundation is laid near the sacred complex, and the fort begins not as a royal project but as a labor shared directly by the Khalsa itself. The text stresses that Singhs themselves served as masons, diggers, and builders. Walls rise quickly, gates are prepared, and the work of defense is performed by the same hands that will soon be required to fight. A surrounding watercourse helps give Ram Rauni its shape and name, while the enclosure gathers several hundred defenders into one protected camp. The page therefore turns a religious resolution into visible architecture and collective discipline.

pages.searchText: At one of these five Sikh sacred shrines (founded by the Guru), Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. At one of these five Sikh sacred shrines (founded by the Guru), Must the Khalsa Panth construct a fort (for their defence). Let the Mughal forces invade and get themselves killed, Must they raise a fort as formidable as the Ranthambore*. (14) At a spot where had the Guru got dug a small well, Did the Khalsa Panth lay the foundation for a fort. With Singhs themselves working as Masons and labourers, Were these Singhs so fearless and brave at heart. (15) The more one worked and served in the community kitchen, The more venerated and higher in status was he reckoned. The greater the amount of hardwork one did put in, The greater the veneration and the applause he earned. (16) Nor did anyone share his individual woe with another. With as much speed and haste did they raise the walls, As had Hanuman's simian force raised a bridge over the sea. (17) Did the Singhs keep raising all the four walls at a time, As they never got tired day in and dayout. The more the elders implored them to go slow, The more the Singhs ran faster to complete the job. (18) Truly were they committed to make it a sacrificial monument. As also did they bring whatever they could lay their hands on. (19) For the digging out of a water channel around its periphery, Did it come to be known by the name of (Ram) Rauni. Digging trenches around the (inner) bank of this water-channel, Themselves did these devout Singhs alternate as masons and menials. And succeed they did in making a shelter for themselves. (21) Five hundred in total strength were these Singhs there, Truly had they taken a vow to make the supreme sacrifice.

pages.title: The Mughal Assault on Ram Rauni Begins
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal ..
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance
pages.snippet: The building of Ram Rauni is answered almost immediately by siege. When news reaches the Mughal side, Mir Mannu dispatches Dina Beg with Kaura Mal, Sadiq Beg, Aziz Khan, artillery, and allied hill forces to crush the Sikh concentration befo
pages.searchText: The Mughal Assault on Ram Rauni Begins Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. The building of Ram Rauni is answered almost immediately by siege. When news reaches the Mughal side, Mir Mannu dispatches Dina Beg with Kaura Mal, Sadiq Beg, Aziz Khan, artillery, and allied hill forces to crush the Sikh concentration before it can settle into strength. Inside the fort, the Khalsa understands that the enemy is numerically heavier and better supplied. The defenders still choose open resistance, sending out small bands ready for martyrdom rather than accepting confinement as a slow surrender. The page also begins the technical struggle of siege warfare. As the attackers push forward and prepare covered approaches, the Singhs answer by using the channel and defensive works around Ram Rauni to blunt the first Mughal pressure.

pages.searchText: Than they invaded this hiding place all of a sudden. Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. Than they invaded this hiding place all of a sudden. At the head of a Mughal force to launch an attack. (23) This expedition also had Aziz Khan, another custodian. Many hill chiefs were also made to launch an attack, Who had joined the expedition with enormous artillery guns. (24) Thereupon, organizing a contingent of deadly striking force, The Mughal commanders pushed it to towards (Ram) Rauni's enterance. The Khalsa Panth, at that moment of truth, did realize, That had they (the Singhs) been outnumbered by the Mughals. (25) Must then (the Singhs) make such a sacrifice while killing the Mughals, That it should be known very well through out the world. This being a religious war to defend one's faith and ideology, Thereafter, a battery of ten (brave) Singh having come out, Did cut through the ranks of the raiding striking force. With an odd survivor returning to join the Singhs inside the fort. (27) Like a lion would the Singhs pounce upon the Mughals, Like a lightening through the clouds would the Singhs strike. In the pitch darkness of the night would the Singhs attack, Thus would the Mughuls get killed instead of Singhs in darkness. A single Singh being dominant over a hundred Mughals, Singhs in a fewer number even would harass the Mughals. (29) Were there some odd number of Singhs in hiding, Who might have taken shelter in caves and wilds? Thus would they make a supreme sacrifice in this fight. (30) Then, as the Mughal troops dug a tunnel (to enter the fort), The Singhs deepened the surface of the water channel. As many Singhs kept sitting inside the water-channel, They kept on blocking the Mughal's digging of the tunnel. (31)

pages.title: The Besieged Singhs Choose Assault over Dishonor
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal ..
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance
pages.snippet: With provisions thinning and pressure mounting, the Khalsa refuses the idea of saving itself through flight or humiliation. The page states the choice in martial terms: better to die fighting than flee in disgrace when the Panth’s honor is
pages.searchText: The Besieged Singhs Choose Assault over Dishonor Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. With provisions thinning and pressure mounting, the Khalsa refuses the idea of saving itself through flight or humiliation. The page states the choice in martial terms: better to die fighting than flee in disgrace when the Panth’s honor is already on trial before the world. That resolve becomes action in coordinated assaults against Mughal posts. The defenders strike from one side, seize positions where they can, and try to turn a siege into a series of sudden local reversals that keep the enemy off balance. Even when losses mount, the example draws in more fighters rather than breaking morale. Ram Rauni thus appears not merely as a fort under pressure but as a school of disciplined self-sacrifice in which one wave of Singhs replaces another.

pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance
pages.snippet: Though least scared of death while fighting a battle, The Singhs did feel concern at the scarcity of provisions. As the concentration of Mughal troops kept on increasing, The Singhs felt they were destined to die inside the fort. (32) There
pages.searchText: Though least scared of death while fighting a battle, Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. Though least scared of death while fighting a battle, The Singhs did feel concern at the scarcity of provisions. As the concentration of Mughal troops kept on increasing, The Singhs felt they were destined to die inside the fort. (32) Thereafter, the Khalsa Panth, after a thorough confabulation, felt, That deserting the field, at that stage, would be undignified. It would be far better to perish while fighting on field, As their fight would become a subject for legends. (33) So must they launch an attack from one of the flanks, Making a supreme sacrifice at the hands of Mughals. Must they perish after killing double the number of Mughals, Such a rare fight must they wage against the Mughals. (34) Thus, making a dash did the Singhs make a fierce attack, Truly did they succeed in capturing a Mughal position. Truly did the Singhs harass and disperse that contingent. (35) Truly were the Majhail Singhs great warriors supreme, As indeed they had been initiated with a double-edged dagger. (36) Thus for days without end did the fight carry on, As the Khalsa Panth continued to wage a war. In no way, could the Mughals eliminate the Khalsa Panth, As two Singhs kept on substituting the one who died. (37) Thus could the Singhs never be eliminated completely, As water never dries up from a waterlogged earth. Would those Singhs as had gone underground nearby, Sneak somehow into fight against the Mughals. (38) As the news of the Singhs dying in battle kept pouring, More and still more Singhs kept on entering the field. If, perchance, a Singh failed to sneak into the fort, Would he keep encircling the fort in great anger. (39) Vow indeed he would take to perish with his companions, So determined would he be to settle scores with the Mughals. Otherwise what face would he show to his Guru after death, If he failed to display his daring in the field of battle. (40)

pages.title: The Besieged Khalsa Hears Jassa Singh Seek Reunion
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal ..
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance
pages.snippet: The siege tightens as the attackers reduce the remaining openings around Ram Rauni and try to shut every avenue of relief. The defenders understand that the Mughals blocked every entrance, yet their answer is not surrender but a renewed res
pages.searchText: The Besieged Khalsa Hears Jassa Singh Seek Reunion Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. The siege tightens as the attackers reduce the remaining openings around Ram Rauni and try to shut every avenue of relief. The defenders understand that the Mughals blocked every entrance, yet their answer is not surrender but a renewed resolve to die fighting if no other path remains. At that moment the page introduces an important reconciliation. News arrives that Jassa Singh and the men once estranged from the Khalsa now want reunion with the Panth and wish to share the same danger instead of remaining apart from the besieged Singhs. The request matters because Ram Rauni is becoming a place where old divisions are burned away by common peril. The fort gathers not only fighters under attack but also scattered Sikh loyalties that are being pulled back into one body.

As the Singhs kept on duplicating in place of each dead, Did the Mughals realize the real strength of the Singhs. Leaving no passage whatsoever for the Singhs entrance or exist. (41) It was through these open spaces that the Singhs entered the fort, As well as managed to bring some sort of ammunition. Now when every kind of entrance was barred and blocked, Did the Singhs realize that was their death imminent then. (42) Let the Singhs slaughter those whosoever dared to attack them, Was this indeed a unanimous resolution of the Singhs. Let the Singhs slaughter, kill and make a supreme sacrifice, No sooner did the Khalsa Panth arrive at the above resolution, Than there did arrive a Singh from outside to join their ranks. In the following words did he address the Khalsa Singhs: That the approaching contingent of soldiers consisted of enlisted Singhs. (44) There used to be one Jassa Singh from the family of carpenters, Whom the Khalsa Panth had turned out for committing female foeticide. (Being an outcast) had he joined the army of Dina Beg, Along with hundreds of his camp followers as well. (45) Thereupon, the messenger Singh conveyed the sentiments of approaching Singhs, That they (Jassa Singh's followers) too would sacrifice along with the Singhs. They too were prepared to join to ranks of the Khalsa, Provided the Khalsa Panth took them back into their fold. (46) Khalsa Singhs retorted that it was indeed a moment of truth, Truly was it an opportune moment for coming into the Khalsa fold. Certainly would the Guru reward them for their noble deed, Truly would the Khalsa's prayer be vindicated in their favour. (47) That must he fend for himself without their support. As for them, they would certainly enter the (Rauni) fort, As indeed would they sacrifice with the Khalsa Panth. (48) Jassa Singh, too, told his companions in the same vein, That he himself never wanted to be separated from the Panth. He, too, would be too glad to enter the Khalsa fold, As the Khalsa had always been forgiving to its errant Singhs. (49)

pages.title: Jassa Singh Rejoins the Khalsa and Ram Rauni Becomes Ramgarh
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal ..
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance
pages.snippet: This page completes the reconciliation by describing a petition sent by arrow into the fort, allowing Jassa Singh to seek acceptance without breaking the lines. Once the message is received, the estrangement is set aside and he is welcomed
pages.searchText: Jassa Singh Rejoins the Khalsa and Ram Rauni Becomes Ramgarh Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. This page completes the reconciliation by describing a petition sent by arrow into the fort, allowing Jassa Singh to seek acceptance without breaking the lines. Once the message is received, the estrangement is set aside and he is welcomed back into the Khalsa with the men who came in the same spirit. The page then widens from personal reunion to political change. Mir Mannu recalls his forces toward the crisis elsewhere, while Kaura Mal secures Sikh help by negotiation, gifts, and recognition that the Khalsa must be treated as a real power rather than a hunted remnant. In that changed setting Ram Rauni acquires new stature and begins to be remembered as Ramgarh. What began as a desperate enclosure around Amritsar is recast as a fortified Sikh center linked to alliance, revenue, and restored unity.

pages.snippet: Thereafter, writing down his petition for his merger, Jassa Singh shot it with an arrow to the Khalsa Panth. He was ready to surrender to the Khalsa Panth, Provided the Khalsa was willing to take him into their fold. (50) Accepting his peti

Thereafter, writing down his petition for his merger, Jassa Singh shot it with an arrow to the Khalsa Panth. He was ready to surrender to the Khalsa Panth, Provided the Khalsa was willing to take him into their fold. (50) Accepting his petition, did the Singhs give their consent for merger, Deeming it an opportune moment for a reunion of the separated. Soon after, did Jassa Singh tell his commander Dina Beg, That the latter must relieve him (Jassa Singh) of his services. (51) Thereafter, winding up his affairs with the Mughal commander, Did Jassa Singh enter the Khalsa Panth's forces inside the fort. No sooner did Jassa Singh enter the Khalsa fold, There prevailed such a providence as the Divine Satguru willed, That it wished to fulfil Khalsa Panth's mission. Thus was the city of Multan invaded (at the same time), By Shah Nawaz!*, the son of late Nawab Khan Bahadur. (53) The Mughals getting panicky about their own security, Did Mir Mannu!* order the recall of his forces. The proposal was discussed and debated with Mir Mannu. After getting Mir Mannu's approval for seeking Singhs allegiance, Dewan Kaura Mal got the Singhs aligned with his own force. (55) Aligning these Singhs from the Patti region of Majha, Dewan got half the revenue of this region sanctioned in favour of the Singhs. The twelve villages which once belonged to Guru Chakk, These, too, were attached with Ram Rauni through a written deed. (56) Since that day did Ram Rauni come to be known as Ramgarh, More and more famous did it become since then. Ramgarhias of Jassa Singh's family were made custodians of Ramgarh, For having entered into the Khalsa Panth in the time of dire need. (57) Rattan Singh (the author) had narrated as he had heard, The whole narration from the elders of his generation. Now would he narrate, (dear readers) the further account, How did Khan Bahadur's son Shah Nawaz happened to be decimated. (58)

pages.title: From Ram Rauni’s Battle to the Valour of Kaura Mal
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal ..
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance
pages.snippet: The page first closes the Ram Rauni struggle by looking back on the battle and on the fate awaiting Shah Nawaz after his earlier arrogance. It acts as a retrospective seal on the siege narrative before the story shifts to the next political
pages.searchText: From Ram Rauni’s Battle to the Valour of Kaura Mal Kaura Mal and the Sikh alliance Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal .. The page first closes the Ram Rauni struggle by looking back on the battle and on the fate awaiting Shah Nawaz after his earlier arrogance. It acts as a retrospective seal on the siege narrative before the story shifts to the next political and military movement. The new emphasis falls on Episode 121 and on Kaura Mal, a devout Sikh ally whose sympathies lie with the Panth rather than with persecutors. The text presents him as a supporter of prayer, congregation, and practical assistance rather than empty courtly display. This creates a marked tonal change from siege endurance to alliance and initiative. The Khalsa is no longer merely surviving a cordon; it is preparing to move with support from a figure whose piety and courage are central to the next episode.

The way Shah Nawaz happened to meet his end, (My dear readers) listen to the account further. (59) Episode 121 Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal (Title of Bahadur Conferred on Kaura Mal) Dohra: A number of Khalsa Singhs joined Kaura Mal, As they considered him a devout Sikh of the Guru. Being assured of the Khalsa Singh's support. (1) Chaupai: Wherever the Khalsa Panth organized a congregation, Regularly would he listen to the morning and evening prayers, Daily would he make an offering of provisions to the Khalsa Panth. (2) Daily would he sit among the Singhs after a due permission, Daily would he offer provisions to the community kitchen, Making an offering of five rupees to each Nihang chief. (3) Gladly would he pay a penalty of five rupees, For getting permission for smoking a pipe. Surely would he be able to arrest Shah Nawaz, Claiming to be having blessings of the Divine Guru. (4) Instantly, did the Khalsa contradict his claim, As the Khalsa would fain to eliminate him altogether. As he had got innumerable number of Singhs slaughtered, How could they spare his life once he came in their sight. (5) Shah Nawaz's real brother, too, was sent with him. Was this force despatched towards Shah Nawaz's camp. (6) Chaupai: While Shah Nawaz was the custodian of Lahore, Had he looted, oppressed and slaughtered so many people. It was for these atrocities that Mir Mannu? sent this force, To join the forces under the command of Dewan Kaura Mal. (7)

pages.title: Kaura Mal’s Battle with Shah Nawaz
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal
pages.snippet: This fragment concentrates the clash between Kaura Mal and Shah Nawaz into a sharp battlefield encounter. As both sides commit themselves, the Singhs around Kaura Mal encourage steadfastness and turn the struggle from anxiety into direct of
pages.searchText: Kaura Mal’s Battle with Shah Nawaz the Valour of Kaura Mal Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal This fragment concentrates the clash between Kaura Mal and Shah Nawaz into a sharp battlefield encounter. As both sides commit themselves, the Singhs around Kaura Mal encourage steadfastness and turn the struggle from anxiety into direct offensive action. The decisive stroke is delivered against Shah Nawaz himself. In the fierce close of the encounter, the Singhs beheaded Shah Nawaz and turned his fall into the clearest sign that his power had finally been broken. The page ends by converting battlefield success into public honor. Kaura Mal receives recognition for the feat, and the episode closes with the sense that courage aligned with the Panth has defeated both cruelty and arrogance.

pages.searchText: As the battle raged between both the forces, the Valour of Kaura Mal Episode About the Valour of Kaura Mal As the battle raged between both the forces, Both the armies were expecting to win the battle. Stood facing each other in the field of battle. (8) The Mughal troops from both sides having become allies, Upon this, reposing complete faith in the Divine Guru, Kaura Mal positioned the Singh soldiers around him. (9) As Shah Nawaz mounted a forceful attack, He moved his horse to stand in front of Kaura Mal. Kaura Mal beckoned the Khalsa to avail of that opportunity, As Shah Nawaz was going to attack the former. (10) Asking Dewan Kaura Mal not to lose heart at all, Must he forewarn the Singhs as the enemy approached, Assuring him of their being in complete readiness, Instantly would they slaughter the enemy as he arrived. (11) That the latter had been an ungrateful untrue to his salt. He must, therefore, either get ready for a fight, Or else bow down and salute a Mughal ruler. (12) At this Kaura Mal did inform his Singh supporters, That such abusive words indeed was Shah Nawaz uttering. At this, as the (incensed) Singhs fired their muskets, Did a bullet hit right into Shah Nawaz's heart. (13) With a bound did he fall from his horse, As he could not stand up after being hit by a bullet. Thereafter, a Singh after getting down from his horse, Picked up his head after beheading Shah Nawaz. (14) As his severed head was presented before Mir Mannu, Delighted did he feel at the sight of his beheaded enemy. Picking up a pen and a paper did Mir Mannu confer, The title of Bahadur on Kaura Mal in writing. (15) The noble service that Kaura Mal had rendered unto the Khalsa, Was indeed rewarded immediately (by the Divine Guru). Listen further to the episodes (dear readers), As were these narrated by the author's ancestors. (16)

As they did take a dip in the sacred pool at Amritsar. (4) Listen to the sanctity of having a dip in the sacred pool, Holy would the place become where a Sikh planted his foot after pilgrimage, Whosoever got robbed and plundered by the devout Singhs, Whosoever got robbed and dispossessed by another, Surely would the guilty get penalized by the Khalsa, As the innocent would be cleared of all accusations. pages.title: Episode 123: Ahmad Shah Abdali Invited into India
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure
pages.snippet: The narrative opens a larger imperial crisis by describing confusion in Delhi after Muhammad Shah and the rivalry of grandees who cannot hold the center together. Court disorder, factional ambition, and regional distrust create the conditio
pages.searchText: Episode 123: Ahmad Shah Abdali Invited into India Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh The narrative opens a larger imperial crisis by describing confusion in Delhi after Muhammad Shah and the rivalry of grandees who cannot hold the center together. Court disorder, factional ambition, and regional distrust create the conditions in which outside invasion becomes possible rather than surprising. Into that weakness steps the Afghan power, and the page emphasizes that Najib Khan Ruhela invites Abdali into the struggle as an ally who can tip the balance. Ahmad Shah Abdali is therefore not only an invader from afar but a force summoned through Indian political fracture itself. By the end of the page, the disorder of the empire has become the prelude to a much wider war. Delhi’s internal rivalry prepares the ground on which Sikh, Mughal, Afghan, and Maratha ambitions will soon collide.

pages.searchText: Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh Episode 123 Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh (He fell a martyr while fighting and killing those Afghan troops) It was in the year eighteen hundred and ten! (B.S.), That Ahmad Shah Abdali? did come to invade India. He had come at the invitation of Najib Khan Ruhela, After the demise of Mohammad Shah, the emperor of Delhi. (1) There being four ministers of the four provinces of Delhi, Each one of them occupied one of the provinces each. These four ministers being rivals to each others prowess, They indulged in an internecine war to kill each other. (2) He introduced his minted coins known as Mansuri coins. He had strengthened his occupation of the Deccan province. (3) All these four ministers proving untrue to their salt, They had betrayed the emperor of Delhi, their master. He had aligned himself with Ahmed Shah of Gilja race. Another Muslim minister Gazdi* inviting the Marathas from the South, As Najib Khan Ruhela had constructed the Najibgarh fort, There grew a great hostility between the Mughals and Pathans. (5) As soon as Mohammad Shah did shed his mortal frame, Extreme chaos did come to prevail in Delhi. There remained mainly two contenders for power, As he intended to get the Mughals eliminated by the Pathans. Such being the will ordained by the Divine Satguru, He ordained that the Mughals be eliminated by the Mughals. (7) Having got a good opportunity during this internecine Muslim strife, The Singhs made a dash to kill the Muslims on both sides. As both the Muslim factions attempted to kill the Singhs, The Singhs, too, endeavoured to decimate both of them. (8)

pages.title: Dewan Kaura Mal Appeals to the Singhs
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure
pages.snippet: As Abdali’s advance unsettles Lahore and Sirhind, local calculations change quickly. The page shows how men who once maneuvered within Mughal politics begin seeking stronger partners, because the Afghan threat makes older arrangements look
pages.searchText: Dewan Kaura Mal Appeals to the Singhs Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh As Abdali’s advance unsettles Lahore and Sirhind, local calculations change quickly. The page shows how men who once maneuvered within Mughal politics begin seeking stronger partners, because the Afghan threat makes older arrangements look fragile and incomplete. The key development is that Dewan Kaura Mal invites the Singhs into alliance instead of treating them as expendable auxiliaries. He offers assurance, support, and recognition in exchange for help against Abdali, giving the Khalsa a role defined by negotiation rather than mere persecution. This marks a major shift in the story’s political logic. The Singhs are acknowledged as a power whose friendship matters, and Kaura Mal emerges as the courtly figure most willing to bind his fortunes to theirs.

pages.searchText: As after summoning the Marahatta reinforcements to his support, Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh As after summoning the Marahatta reinforcements to his support, The latter, seeking the support of Ahmad Shah Abdali from Kabul, He called for the Pathan reinforcements to his support. (9) Thereafter, as he had called for Ahmad Shah's support, But he also got Delhi vacated from Marhatta occupation. (10) He laid a siege around Najibu Khan Ruhela's forces for the second time. Who came rushing from Kabul (to crush the Marhattas). (11) Mir Mannu, having become lax after this development, As he received no support from Delhi (against Abdali). Dewan Kaura Mal fortified his defences at Lahore (to combat the invaders). (12) Thereafter, the Dewan sent a very warm invitation to the Singhs, That the Hindus and the Singhs were fraternal followers of the same Guru. Asking for the Singhs support on the basis of ideological affinity, He pleaded before the Singhs to push back Abdali's troops. (13) Offering not only to provide the Singhs with arms and ammunition, He was even prepared to offer a financial ransom to the Singhs. Procuring a written assurance from Mir Mannu in favour of the Khalsa, He sent that written despatch to the Khalsa Panth. (14) (Mir Mannu) assured the Khalsa to start a dialogue with them, Soon after they had (jointly) repulsed the (Afghan) invader. He would allow the Singhs to occupy that (Punjab) region, Which had always remained defiant to the Mughal rule. (15) (He narrated) that ever since Banda Bahadur's occupation of the hilly region, The Mughal empire had received no revenues from there. As these hill chiefs had harassed the Khalsa Panth in the recent past, The Khalsa Panth should occupy the entire hill territory. (16) They must settle scores with the hill chiefs in the whole Doon valley. They must collect as much revenue from the hills, As they collected from the Punjab region of their own. (17)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure
pages.snippet: The page begins with disorder inside the Sikh world itself, where factional violence follows the killing of Kushal Singh and prompts retaliation against the Bhangis. Instead of a single united front, the narrative pauses to show how interna
pages.searchText: Internal Strife, Lahore Unrest, and Sukha Singh’s Crossing Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh The page begins with disorder inside the Sikh world itself, where factional violence follows the killing of Kushal Singh and prompts retaliation against the Bhangis. Instead of a single united front, the narrative pauses to show how internal wounds can interrupt broader strategy. It then returns to Lahore, where tensions flare into clashes with butchers and townspeople near the city gates. Urban hostility and factional confusion together create a turbulent setting in which bold action feels both risky and necessary. Against that background Sukha Singh crosses the Ravi with a small chosen band and moves toward Abdali’s camp. His crossing is framed as the beginning of an audacious strike that will exchange safety for honor and direct confrontation.

pages.searchText: Thereafter, the Singhs having held an assembly, Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh Thereafter, the Singhs having held an assembly, Thereafter, putting up a camp at village Ghaniya Ke, Soon after, the Singhs themselves entered into a factional fight, Themselves they invited harassment from their own kin. Hari Singh! from the Bhangi contingent did betray the Khalsa, As he shot dead Kushal Singh Ramgharia (brother of Jassa Singh Ramgarhia). (19) As all the Singhs considered it to be an act of evil, They decided to ransack the seat of the Bhangis. As the Bhangis came to know about this raid, They fled away to a distant place to avoid violence. (20) As this contingent of ten thousand Bhangi Singhs fled, Were they attacked by a force of twenty thousand Singhs. In this way, the total strength of these Singhs taken together, Came to thirty thousands who constituted this fighting force. (21) Therefore, these Khalsa Singhs put up a camp at Lahore, Ata place in the vicinity of Shalimar gardens. As the Singhs took a round around the Lahori gate, They noticed the city butchers taking a cow for a slaughter. (22) As the Singh slaughtered those cow-slaughterers, The shopkeepers of Lahore shut their shops in protest. As the people of the city of Lahore attacked the Singhs, Here also the Singhs had to face a lot of harassment. (23) In the afternoon, after taking a dose of cannabis, (Warrior) Sukha Singh (carpenter) did go on a round. Though being a foster son of (warrior) Sham Singh!?, He was a native of village Mari-Kambo-ki!?. (24) Thereafter, without consulting any of his companions, Did he cross to the other side of the river Ravi. He was followed by a few other (Nihang) Singhs, Without keeping a proper count of those who followed. (25) As they approached the camp of Abdali's troops, As the Singhs refreshed themselves with waters of Ravi, There was a lot of commotion among the Abdali troops. (26)

pages.title: Sukha Singh Chooses Martyrdom Against Abdali
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure
pages.snippet: As news spreads that Singhs are approaching, Ahmad Shah’s camp is jolted into alert preparation and watches the horizon for the attack. The page makes the numerical imbalance unmistakable, because Sukha Singh and his companions are moving a
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh Chooses Martyrdom Against Abdali Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh As news spreads that Singhs are approaching, Ahmad Shah’s camp is jolted into alert preparation and watches the horizon for the attack. The page makes the numerical imbalance unmistakable, because Sukha Singh and his companions are moving against a force far larger than their own. What matters most is Sukha Singh’s moral choice under those odds. He openly chooses martyrdom over retreat, telling his companions that honor is worth more than survival purchased by withdrawal in the face of Abdali. The companions answer in the same spirit and refuse to desert him. Their decision turns a daring raid into a consciously shared act of sacrifice rather than a reckless impulse by one leader alone.

pages.snippet: As the Abdali troops noticed the Singhs advancing towards them, As Ahmad Shah Abdali sensed a threat to his security, He seemed to lose heart on that occasion. (27) Instantly did he deploy his contingents in front. Declaring that Hindustani
pages.searchText: As the Abdali troops noticed the Singhs advancing towards them, Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh As the Abdali troops noticed the Singhs advancing towards them, As Ahmad Shah Abdali sensed a threat to his security, He seemed to lose heart on that occasion. (27) Instantly did he deploy his contingents in front. Declaring that Hindustani troops had launched an invasion, He would never allow his troops to retreat to Kabul. (28) Asking his troops to pick up their swords for a fight, He deployed his troops right in front of the Singhs. (29) (But) only a few Singhs had actually crossed Ravi, Majority of them having put up in their base camp. While some had returned, a few had gone with Sukha Singh, (But) those reckoned to be the best warriors had remained behind. (30) As Sukha Singh noticed the approach of Abdali's forces, He reckoned his own companions to be small in strength. Thereafter, contemplating the whole situation from all angles, If he picked up a fight with the Abdali's troops, He and his companions would be greatly out numbered. As Singhs strength was as little as a pinch of salt in a flour heap, No sensible person would approve of their fighting with the Afghans. (32) If he chose to desert and run away from the battlefield, He would have to bear the humiliation of having been a coward. As he found himself caught between the devil and the deep sea, He considered it better to fight and make a sacrifice. (33) Thus did Sukha Singh convey his resolve to the Singhs. At that very spot, would they make a supreme sacrifice, For their religion and ideology would they certainly fight. (34) Still did Sukha Singh give an option to the accompanying Singhs, That those who craved for life could go back across the river. To which the Singhs retorted: How could they dare to desert him, As they had broken bread with him from the same bowl. (35)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure
pages.snippet: The companions who follow Sukha Singh enter the battle determined to be counted among the martyrs rather than to preserve themselves at any cost. Their charge briefly shakes the Afghan line and gives the page its fierce momentum, because th
pages.searchText: Sukha Singh’s Charge and Martyrdom Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh The companions who follow Sukha Singh enter the battle determined to be counted among the martyrs rather than to preserve themselves at any cost. Their charge briefly shakes the Afghan line and gives the page its fierce momentum, because the assault is driven by chosen sacrifice rather than by hope of easy victory. In the confusion of combat, Sukha Singh presses toward Ahmad Shah Abdali himself and tries to strike at the center of enemy power. The effort ends in martyrdom, but the attack leaves a lasting memory precisely because it carries the Khalsa spirit into the heart of the danger. After the clash, the survivors must disengage and begin a retreat towards Lahore under pressure. The page therefore combines heroic advance and painful withdrawal, preserving both the audacity of the attempt and the cost it exacted.

As the author's father (being infant) was instructed to return, He too, begged S. Sham Singh (to seek his approval to fight). In the meantime, as Abdali's forces arrived too close, The Singh spurred their horses to confront the enemy. (37) As the Singhs fired muskets, shots arrows and wielded their swords, Truly were the approaching Afghan troops pushed back. As the Singhs kept standing there instead of beating a retreat, Really had they made a mistake in their fighting strategy. (38) Hardly had the Singhs repulsed the attack of one of enemy's contingents, Surely was the Singhs strength reduced to as small a number, As is a pinch of salt found in a heap of wheat flour. (39) Thereupon did Sukha Singh think in his own mind, Gladly would he prefer to grapple with the Afghan chief, As Sukha Singh pushed forwarded in the midst of raging battle, As no body could communicate with him in his native tongue, Darkness did descend on the scene in the midst of din and dust. (41) As Sukha Singh did fail in his attempt to hit his target, He started killing rest of the Afghan troops of Abdali. As he fell a martyr while fighting and killing those Afghan troops, His stubbornness had had cost him his own life. (42) As Sukha had died fighting there with the Afghan troops, Rest of the Singhs did beat a retreat towards Lahore. As the retreating Singhs approached the city of Lahore, The inhabitants of Lahore opened a fierce fire on them. (43) As the Singhs suffered loss on both the fronts, Thereafter, the Singhs put up a camp on the outskirts, Where they passed the night while guarding their defences. (44)

pages.title: From Sukha Singh’s Martyrdom to Abdali’s Advance
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh
pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure
pages.snippet: Night falls after the action near Lahore, and the scattered Singhs choose to move towards Majha rather than remain exposed around the battlefield. The withdrawal is sober and practical, shaped by the loss of Sukha Singh and the recognition
pages.searchText: From Sukha Singh’s Martyrdom to Abdali’s Advance Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh Night falls after the action near Lahore, and the scattered Singhs choose to move towards Majha rather than remain exposed around the battlefield. The withdrawal is sober and practical, shaped by the loss of Sukha Singh and the recognition that survival now requires regrouping elsewhere. The page then turns from immediate aftermath to a larger historical accounting. It dates Sukha Singh’s martyrdom and asks how Abdali advanced so far, drawing the answer through the deaths of allies such as Dewan Kaura Mal and the submission of Mir Mannu under Afghan pressure. This makes the page a hinge between personal sacrifice and imperial consequence. A local martyrdom is set inside the wider reshaping of Punjab as Abdali rises through Lahore toward still greater dominance.

pages.searchText: As the night descended on the scene near Lahore, Ahmad Shah, Sukha Singh, and the Afghan pressure Episode About Ahmad Shah and Sukha Singh As the night descended on the scene near Lahore, Did the Singhs resolve to make a move towards Majha. As both the Mughals and the Afghans were equally wicked Muslims, Must the Singhs loot, plunder and ransack both of them. (45) Thus had passed eighteen hundred years in the Bikrami Samvat, As well as ten more years in the same Indian Calendar. When Sukha had made a supreme sacrifice of his life, Never can the Singhs and Muslim remain together, Well it does not augur such a combination indeed. The moment this deadly combination comes into being, Episode 123 (Contd.) Rest of the Episode Continues (It was during this skirmish that Dewan Kaura Mal died) God forbid, a reader may put forth a question: How did Ahmad Shah Abdali! proceed with his mission? Could he break the siege to enter the city of Lahore? The author must provide answer to these questions. (1) It was during this skirmish (between Abdali and Mughal forces), That (the venerable) Dewan Kaura Mal did shed his mortal frame. With him perished Sangat Singh (another Singh chief), As well as the chief of Jaswan principality of Jajowal. (2) As these skirmishes continued for several months, As Najib Khan Ruhela? created a fear psychosis from the otherside, Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the forces of Mir Mannu*. (3) With folded hands and a scarf round his neck did Mir Mannu submit, Prefering not to desert, did he become an ally of Abdali. Accepting to pay a ransom of fifty lakh rupees, Did Abdali nominate him as Lahore's governor on his behalf. (4) After Lahore's occupation, Abdali conquered Delhi as well, Appointing Najib Khan Rohela as ruler of Delhi on his behalf. As Abdali appointed the latter a minister to rule Delhi, The Mughal empire's writ ceased to run at Delhi at last. (5)

pages.episodeDisplayTitle: Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh
pages.snippet: This page opens Episode 124 and moves from Sukha Singh’s campaign into Delhi’s unsettled politics, where rival claimants and unstable alliances make every office insecure. Within that churn, Ghazi-ud-Din becomes a crucial name in the story,
pages.searchText: Episode 124 Opens: Adina Beg amid Delhi’s Disorder Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh This page opens Episode 124 and moves from Sukha Singh’s campaign into Delhi’s unsettled politics, where rival claimants and unstable alliances make every office insecure. Within that churn, Ghazi-ud-Din becomes a crucial name in the story, acting alongside Maratha interests while Najib Khan’s fortunes change. The page uses these power shifts to set up the weakened position of Adina Beg, whose future now depends on shrewd alliance rather than secure authority. This opening matters because it makes the next episode one of political recombination rather than straightforward battle. The field is being reset for new bargains, new resentments, and a fresh configuration of Sikh and regional power.

pages.searchText: Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode 124 Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh (Could anyone dare to save Jalandhar that day) Dohra: Many atime had many a ruler made attempts, To occupy Delhi, (so irrestible being the charm of this city). Thus had rulers both from the South and the West, A person who was holding the fourth position in the ministerial line, In the Mughal empire (under the reign of Mohammad Shah Rangila). Truly did he desert Delhi to join the Marathas, As the Mughal rule came to an end at Delhi. (2) He who was known by the name of Gazdi or Ghazi-ud-din!, He had earned the title Bridegroom from the Mughal emperor. Having entered into an alliance with the Malhar Marathas?, He had taken refuge with the Marhatta rulers. (3) Having stayed with the Marathas for many a year, He had made an attempt to take over Delhi. Promising to pay a ransom of one lakh rupees to Marathas, Who ran away from Delhi to a great distance. As Najib Khan Ruhela took refuge in the fort at Najibgarh*, The Marathas put up a camp at Delhi after its occupation. (5) The third Maratha chief being Tukoji Holkar with them. These Maratha chiefs stayed at Delhi for many days, As they dared not proceed further (towards north). (6) Chaupai: Being scared of the powerful forces of Gilja (Abdali) Pathans, As a period of one year passed in this way, Listen, dear readers, to the account of Dina Beg. (7) Truly had his stock run very low among the hilly people, As he had exhausted all his treasure and provisions. As he did not wield any power to recover his lost territory. (8)

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh

pages.snippet: Adina Beg is shown as politically strained and unable to recover his position through ordinary means alone. His advisers therefore push him toward alliance with Wadbhag Singh, recognizing that strength now lies in coalitions forged from sha
pages.searchText: Adina Beg Seeks Alliance with Wadbhag Singh Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Adina Beg is shown as politically strained and unable to recover his position through ordinary means alone. His advisers therefore push him toward alliance with Wadbhag Singh, recognizing that strength now lies in coalitions forged from shared grievance as much as from state office. The page also explains why such a partnership is plausible from the other side. Wadbhag Singh carries his own memory of violence and desecration at Kartarpur, so revenge and justice can converge with Adina Beg’s practical need for support. Negotiation follows from that overlap of motives, and the account keeps alliance with Wadbhag Singh at the center of the page. The episode thus opens by showing politics rebuilt through injury, ambition, and careful approach rather than through inherited stability.

pages.searchText: As he failed to recover his territory without any definite strategy. Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh As he failed to recover his territory without any definite strategy. Though many a stratagem did he make in his mind, Though many a strategy and plans had he devised, None of these could be of any avail to him. There did live a Sikh in the company of Dina Beg, If Dina Beg could forge an alliance with Wadbhag Singh, The latter could summon one lakh Singhs for his support instantly. As the Nawab Dina Beg heard about this (wonderful) proposal, He felt himself in dire necessity of the Singh's support. (11) As the focus once again shifted towards the role of Singhs, Listen dear devout readers to the account of their role. Wadbhag Singh too had taken a refuge among the hills, When the Pathans had massacred Kartarpur's (innocent) populace. (12) He too had been grinding his teeth angrily in vain, As he had failed to take revenge for this carnage. He too had taken a solemn vow never to sit in peace, Till he had avenged upon the Pathan rulers of Jalandhar. (13) As the Pathans had set the sacred shrine at Kartarpur on fire, Wadbhag Singh's heart had cried desperately at this desecration. There and then had he put off his turban from his head, Truly would he put it on only after he had avenged this disgrace. (14) Both being bruised at heart (by the audacious Pathans), The opportune moment having arrived, it knocked at their doors, As coincidently as Sugreev* had joined Lord Rama at a similar moment. (15) Dina Beg having put up his camp at Rajpura, There did he run a community kitchen amidst this chaos. Both Dina Beg and Wadbagh Singh being bruised at heart, Both waited with bated breath for the tide to turn in their favour. (16) Loss of custodianship of Jalandhar rankled as much in Dina Beg's mind, As did the arson at the sacred Sikh shrine in the mind of Wadbhag Singh. As the representatives of Dina Beg proceeded for holding negotiations, Wadbhag Singh also did not lose any moment to meet them. (17)

pages.searchText: Dina Beg Meets Wadbhag Singh at the Midway Camp Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Dina Beg and Wadbhag Singh agree to a midway meeting, where the Nawab arrives after the Sikh leader and receives him with deliberate warmth. They sit together, exchange assurances of respect, and speak openly about Dina Beg's failure to recover his province without Khalsa support. Dina Beg then asks for help recovering Jalandhar and says he will become Wadbhag Singh's disciple if the latter acts as his guide in the crisis. Wadbhag Singh answers that he first wants a written assurance allowing him to avenge the Pathans of Jalandhar and Kartarpur, including the destruction associated with Nasir Ali and the seizure of Muslim households. Only after that demand is accepted does the Nawab swear an oath on the Koran and promise to keep his word. With that written assurance secured, Wadbhag Singh prepares to summon the Khalsa so the campaign can proceed as both a political alliance and a religiously charged act of vengeance.

pages.searchText: Both agreed to fix the summit venue at the midway point. Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Both agreed to fix the summit venue at the midway point. As Wadbagh Singh reached the venue a moment earlier, Nawab Dina Beg too arrived at the place instantly. (18) As both dismounted from their horses at the same place, Both did shake hands with great warmth and expectation. As Dina Beg professed his faith in Wadbagh Singh's spiritual lineage, Wadbagh Singh reciprocated with good wishes for the former's faith. (19) Both having been seated at the negotiating table, Both of them bared their heart before each other. Pleading for Wadbagh Singh's support for taking back his territory, Dina Beg begged the former to make him his disciple. (20) Dohra: (Wadbagh Singh replied): Whatever carnage happened at Kartarpur, Had it been committed by the Pathan rulers of Jalandhar. That Wadbhag Singh would be free to commit massacre at Jalandhar, Dina Beg must give a written assurance to that effect. (21) As the latter had set the Thum Sahib shrine at Kartarpur on fire. As the Pathans had slaughtered the holy cows at Kartarpur, So would Wadbhag Singh burn the pigs at Jalandhar. (22) Definitely would he slaughter the Muslims at Jalandhar, For sure would he hand over Pathan females to the city's scavengers. (23) Dina Beg must accept these conditions in writing on oath, First would he get Doaba vacated from the Pathans, Afterwards should the Nawab fulfil his part of the deal. (24) Dohra: Whatever conditionalities were laid out by Wadbagh Singh, Thereafter, did he take an oath on the holy Koran, That never would he deviate from his solemn vow. (25) Chaupai: Thereafter, Wadbagh Singh sent a despatch to the Khalsa Panth, That both of them were the devout Sikhs of the Sikh Gurus. Let both of them join together for the welfare of the Panth, Let both of them join in an armed struggle (against the Pathans). (26)

pages.searchText: Khalsa Mobilization Toward Jalandhar Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Once the pact is sealed, Dina Beg prepared his contingent and moved his own camp toward the coming theater of war. Messages go out to the Sikh chiefs, gifts and pay are arranged, and the allied force begins to gather in strength for the push toward Jalandhar. As the Khalsa assembles, the opposing Pathans drew up opposite and their presence unsettles the Nawab's men. Dina Beg's camp senses the seriousness of the clash, and the Nawab leans on Wadbhag Singh to steady nerves and bring the Sikh force fully into the field. Wadbhag Singh reassures him that the Guru's Panth does not withdraw once it has given its word. The page closes with the alliance hardened, the message to the Singhs fulfilled, and both sides poised for the opening engagement toward Jalandhar.

He assured the Singhs as well through a written message, That they would find his forces stationed around Jalandhar. (27) He would deploy his troops ahead of the Singhs position, As he would take positions in the foothills of hilly slopes. As the Pathan troops put up a camp near village Panchat!?, Nawab Dina Beg felt threatened by this Pathan concentration. His Mughal troops having lost their wits under this threat, They found it even difficult to stay where they had positioned themselves. (29) Dohra: Hearing these developments of troop movements on both sides, Looting, plundering and ransacking through the region, Chaupai: Those, being mighty warriors among the Singhs proposed, But the veterans among them being in favour of Nawab's participation, They wished the Nawab's troops to start the fight first with the Pathans. (31) Let the Nawab's soldiers test their mettle first of all, Later on would the Singhs lead the attack on the Pathans. As the Nawab received the (good) news of Khalsa force's arrival, He felt as if a devout Muslim's wish had been fulfilled. (32) Dohra: Only then did the Nawab's forces get down from the hilly slopes, When they had spotted the Singhs with their own eyes. But very soon did he feel threatened at heart, Lest the Singhs themselves should seize power from him. (33) That the Nawab need not feel scared of the Singhs. After the Nawab felt convinced with Wadbagh Singh's assurances, Dohra: Thereafter, (Wadbagh Singh having made arrangements for a meeting), He arranged a summit between Shiam Singh!, Jassa Singh and Dina Beg. There (the Singh chiefs) not only received a ransom from the Nawab, They also imposed some amount of penalty on this Mughal chief. (35)

pages.snippet: Before the battle opens, Dina Beg proposes a joint morning attack so his troops and the Khalsa can strike the Pathans together. The Singhs bluntly warn him that once the fighting begins they will cut down whoever stands before them and will
pages.searchText: The Joint Attack and the Green Leaves Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Before the battle opens, Dina Beg proposes a joint morning attack so his troops and the Khalsa can strike the Pathans together. The Singhs bluntly warn him that once the fighting begins they will cut down whoever stands before them and will not pause to distinguish friend from foe. To prevent confusion, Dina Beg orders his own soldiers to wear green leaves on their headgear as a visible sign for the Sikh warriors. With that precaution settled, the hostile line is surveyed and the enemy is described in formal deployment, with artillery in the front and musketeers on both flanks. Even so, the Nawab remains anxious when the Khalsa does not appear at the exact moment he expects. The page therefore joins tactical planning to battlefield tension, showing how the alliance depends on Sikh timing, Sikh confidence, and clear signals amid the chaos.

pages.searchText: Thereafter, the Nawab did address the Khalsa Panth Singhs, Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Thereafter, the Nawab did address the Khalsa Panth Singhs, That he had reposed his complete faith in the Guru's forces. Thereupon he proposed a joint attack on the Pathans in the morning. Thereupon, did the Khalsa Panth told him in a lighter vein, That never would they fight along with the Nawab's troops. They remarked that when the Khalsa Panth picked up a sword, They killed all the Muslims irrespective of their allegiance. (37) Thereupon, the Nawab decided upon a distinction for his troops, That they would cover their headgears with green leaves. Thereupon, this distinction did the Khalsa Panth accept, As they would spare those Muslims who wore this distinction. (38) So did Mughal troops do the first thing in the early morning, As they covered their heads with the green stalks of wheat. Thereafter, leaving their camps where they were stationed, They launched an attack on the (Jalandhar) Pathans (39) The Pathan forces having decided their own strategy, They also fortified their defences facing the enemy side. Positioning their artillery canons heavily in the front, They positioned musketeers on both the flanks. (40) After deploying their horse-mounted troops in the centre, The Pathans devised a perfect strategy for a fight. As Nawab Dina Beg launched an attack with his troops, The (Gilja) Pathans repulsed the attack of Dina Beg's troops. (41) As the Nawab sent a messenger to the Khalsa Panth for help, A few Singhs turned up to his side to pick up a fight. Thus was Nawab's forces removed from the battle field, As the canon and musket firing had killed most of them. (42) As the Nawab's troops lost most of their sheen and morale, The nawab felt extremely worried in his own heart. Thereafter, the Nawab sent a message through horse-mounted messengers, That he was under severe attack without Khalsa Panth's support. (43) Thereafter, did the Khalsa Panth send a message, That Khalsa Panth's timing of attack was slightly different. Their routine included partaking of a dose of cannabis, Followed by a stroll and ablutions in the afternoon. (44)

pages.searchText: Karam Singh Leads the Khalsa Charge Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh The Khalsa now enters the field in its own manner, tying their turbans, fastening their arms, and reciting Gurbani before advancing. Their martial devotion is presented as the real preparation for combat, and they move forward only when spiritually and physically ready. When the Singhs reach the fiercest section of the line, the clash tightens and the Gilja front resists hard. At that moment Karam Singh of Paijgarh pushes toward the highest concentration of Gilja Pathans, making himself the spearhead of the Sikh assault. His charge turns the page from anxious waiting into heroic action. Karam Singh rides straight into the thickest danger, and the Singhs behind him begin to convert disciplined preparation into an unmistakable battlefield breakthrough.

(45) In the meantime, did the Singhs get ready for a fight, As they picked up their arms after partaking a heavy dose of cannabis. The frontline positions did these charged Singhs take up, As they had vowed to participate in that ideological war. (46) As the Khalsa Panth Singhs advanced further, They were repulsed by the Gilja Panth troops. At this, Nawab Dina Beg felt highly concerned, That the Singhs had not given good account of themselves. (47) There emerged a Singh warrior from the S. Sham Singh's contingent, S. Karam Singh was his name from the village of Paijgarh. There did he arm himself with armour and battle dress, After he had finished with his ablutions and daily routine. (48) Thereafter, did Karam Singh mount his horse, As he resolved to fight for his faith and ideology. He was determined to settle scores with the desecrators, As he never wished to return without accomplishing this task. (49) After wearing his coat of arms did he wear a steel helmet, As after slinging a sword did he wield a shield in his hand. After this, spurring their horse, did he make a move, As he took along those who were dear and loyal to him. (50) The spot where there was the highest concentration of Gilja Pathans, There did these Singhs arrive to launch an attack. As the Pathans were protected by a striking force in the front, The Singhs attacked those who were in the vanguard. (51) As this contingent in the vanguard spotted the advancing Singhs, They attacked the Singhs with a lightening speed. As the sword of one of them touched Karam Singh's head, His turban along with the steel helmet came down. (52) Karam Singh, being bare-headed without his turban, Did ply his sword on his Mughal rival's head, With a bound did the Pathan fall flat on the ground, As Karam Singh's sword had cut through his neck. (53)

pages.snippet: Karam Singh's reckless bravery becomes the emblem of the Khalsa attack, and even after losing his turban he keeps pressing forward bare-headed into the fight. The Pathans shelter behind the cannons and try to stabilize their line, but the S
pages.searchText: Karam Singh’s Breakthrough and the Durrani Retreat Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Karam Singh's reckless bravery becomes the emblem of the Khalsa attack, and even after losing his turban he keeps pressing forward bare-headed into the fight. The Pathans shelter behind the cannons and try to stabilize their line, but the Sikh advance refuses to break. As the pressure mounts, the Durrani formation begins to collapse and signs of surrender and confusion appear, including white flags raised amid the disorder. Dina Beg sends word praising the Singhs for the victory and asking them to hold their ground rather than scatter into uncontrolled pursuit. The key instruction is do not pursue the fleeing enemy, because the Nawab wants the field secured before the rout becomes a looting chase. Even so, the page ends with the Khalsa conscious that it has broken the enemy's confidence and forced a major retreat.

pages.searchText: As does the a falcon pounce without its crown. Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh As does the a falcon pounce without its crown. As Karam Singh kept him pinned down on the earth. (54) Chaupai: Thereafter, the Khalsa Panth Singhs launching an attack, Did put the Pathan forces upon the run in front of them. Upon this, the fleeing Pathans took shelter behind the canons, Which were firing double balls of fire-bombs. (55) As these artillery guns kept firing a volley of cluster bombs, The Singh warriors kept falling dead after being hit. Thereupon, taking up positions on the ground, The Singhs did fire a volley of bullets on the enemy. (56) As many of the Durrani Pathans were killed by these bullets, They rushed back to seek shelter for themselves. As the camels retreated with the camel-mounted guns, The Durrani Pathan troops too retreated to their camps. (57) Dohra: As Nawab Dina Beg surveyed the whole scene, He realized that the Khalsa Panth had won a victory. As he spotted out the fleeing Durrani Pathan troops, He raised white flags (symbolizing an end to fight). (58) Chaupai: The Nawab did send messengers to the Singhs posthaste, Congratulating them for the victory that they had won. He did advise them not to proceed any further, Advising them to put up a camp where they were. (59) Planting a flag for a proposed site of their camp, The Nawab advised them not to pursue the fleeing enemy. It was never advisable to go in hot pursuit of a deserting army, As there was always a risk of getting harmed from a hidden enemy. (60) Dohra: It happens many a time during the theatre of war, That even a fleeing army causes a fatal harm to the winner. Sometimes even a great warrior gets killed by a deserting army, Whose loss of life can never be repaired by any means. (61) Chaupai: As the Nawab's sole reguirement was victory over the Pathans, The Guru's Khalsa Singhs had delivered that victory unto him. As the Singhs put up their camp at the Nawab's suggested site, The Durrani Pathans did flee to reach their base camp. (62)

pages.snippet: Despite the earlier warning, sections of the Khalsa continue after the broken enemy and turn the retreat into a running night pursuit. They fall upon the fleeing Durrani troops at midnight, seize horses, weapons, and baggage, and keep the p
pages.searchText: Night Pursuit to Jalandhar Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Despite the earlier warning, sections of the Khalsa continue after the broken enemy and turn the retreat into a running night pursuit. They fall upon the fleeing Durrani troops at midnight, seize horses, weapons, and baggage, and keep the pressure on until the whole countryside feels the panic of defeat. By dawn the chase has reached the approaches to Jalandhar, where plundered columns and scattered survivors spread alarm through the city. The Khalsa strips the roads and outer quarters so aggressively that Jalandhar appealed to Dina Beg for protection through payment before the city should be fully sacked. The page therefore turns battlefield victory into political leverage. What began as a pursuit becomes a coercive demonstration that neither the Durrani fugitives nor the people of Jalandhar can ignore the power of the victorious Khalsa.

pages.snippet: By that time, the darkness of the night had descended on the scene, Such being the situation that prevailed over there. As all the Durrani troops fled to enter their base camp, Everyone ran for his life despite their commader's orders. (63)
pages.searchText: By that time, the darkness of the night had descended on the scene, Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh By that time, the darkness of the night had descended on the scene, Such being the situation that prevailed over there. As all the Durrani troops fled to enter their base camp, Everyone ran for his life despite their commader's orders. (63) Dohra: Those being more smart and impatient among the Singhs, Did they go in hot pursuit of the fleeing Pathan troops. As they observed the Pathan troops running for their lives, They plundered and robbed them of their horses. (64) The (pursuing) Singhs sent a messenger to the camping Singhs. Announcing a call for plunder with the beat of a drum, The Singhs started plundering whatever they could lay their hands on. (65) As everyone kept with himself whatever he plundered, Everyone got rid of his poverty and want of things. The Singhs also warned the Nawab through a messenger, That no one from his own camp should go on a looting spree. (66) The Singhs would plunder the Nawab's men as well if they went out, Besides crushing their heads if they dared to join this looting spree. Thus, the Singhs took possession of all equipment of the fleeing Pathans, Including the artillery guns which they deignited after capturing these. (67) Dohra: As the Pathan Chief Sir Balandkhan!? deserted his base camp, It was the time of midnight (as he made his departure). As all his equipage along with carriages was left behind, He could hardly reach Jalandhar by the break of dawn. (68) Chaupai: Hardly could he stay at Jalandhar for a few minutes, When the Singh forces arrived in hot pursuit of him. Many of his loaded carriages got stuck in the rivulets, As his troops ran on foot abandoning their horses as well. (69) All hell broke among the fleeing people of Jalandhar, As a band of plunderers and arsonists entered the city. Thereupon, the Singhs being at complete liberty to plunder, They robbed and plundered the fleeing people thoroughly. (70) As the entire Khalsa Panth contingents reached Jalandhar, They plundered all the localities in the city's suburbs. Upon this, the Muslim populace petitioned Nawab Dina Beg, That he must save Jalandhar even at the cost of a huge ransom. (71)

pages.snippet: Alarmed by the scale of the Sikh advance, Dina Beg looks for a way to save Jalandhar without openly breaking faith with Wadbhag Singh. He sends a secret petition to Jassa Singh, hoping the leading Sikh chief can restrain the sack in return
pages.searchText: Dina Beg’s Secret Petition to Jassa Singh Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Alarmed by the scale of the Sikh advance, Dina Beg looks for a way to save Jalandhar without openly breaking faith with Wadbhag Singh. He sends a secret petition to Jassa Singh, hoping the leading Sikh chief can restrain the sack in return for money and preserve the city under a negotiated settlement. The appeal reaches the Khalsa assembly, but Wadbhag Singh answers from a position of strength and insists that the old Pathan offenses must first be avenged. His challenge stiffens the whole gathering, and Dina Beg learns that payment alone will not override the moral claims already made in the name of the Panth. Only by humbling himself further can he keep the situation from spinning beyond his control. The page captures the moment when back-channel diplomacy, public Khalsa resolve, and personal authority all collide around the fate of Jalandhar.

pages.searchText: Jalandhar being most affluent, was there no dearth of money, Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Jalandhar being most affluent, was there no dearth of money, The people promised to pay in cash provided he stopped plunder. Thereafter, Nawab Dina Beg making a contact with Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, Did send a petition in complete secrecy from the Khalsa Panth. (72) Dina Beg could not send this petition publically, As he had signed a deal on oath with Wadbhag Singh. So he petitioned Jassa Singh Ahluwalia to save Jalandhar, Even at the cost of a cash ransom of his own choice. (73) Thereafter, as Jassa Singh Ahluwalia announced it with the beat of a drum, Wadbhag Singh heard this announcement being made. Thereafter, calling a meeting of all the Khalsa Panth contingents, Jassa Singh Ahluwalia held a religious congregation at one place. (74) An open challenge did Wadbhag Singh throw at this congregation, Brandishing a sword in the air did he throw a challenge, Thereupon, the whole Khalsa Panth raised their hands in approval, As no body could dare to go back from Wadbhag Singh's deal. Thereafter, a unanimous proclamation was made with a drum beat, That even Dina Beg would not be spared if he defended Jalandhar. (76) As Dina Beg heard this Khalsa proclamation with trepidation, He felt scared of being robbed even before the plunder of Jalandhar. Sending his instant response through the beat of a drum, He promised to present himself immediately before the Khalsa Panth. (77) Thereafter, presenting himself before Wadbhag Singh, Dina Beg begged to be sent on any front against the Pathans. Offering to make a payment of the amount settled in the past, He offered much more money as a token of thanks giving. (78) Thereupon, did Wadbhag Singh tell Dina Beg there, That Singhs would settle financial matters after massacring the Pathans, Only after burning the body of (dead) Nasir Ali, the Pathan chief, Would the Singhs undertake to settle the past issues. (79) Were there any Sikh converts from Islam present among them? They must take a Muslim female each as their wife, That being his mandate to those Sikh convert Singhs. (80)
