pages.snippet: Wadbhag Singh now dictates the terms in practice, warning Dina Beg to keep his own troops inside camp while the Khalsa enters Jalandhar. The city is subjected to selective vengeance and humiliation against its enemies, and the Nawab is left
pages.searchText: Jalandhar Settlement and Karah Parshad Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Wadbhag Singh now dictates the terms in practice, warning Dina Beg to keep his own troops inside camp while the Khalsa enters Jalandhar. The city is subjected to selective vengeance and humiliation against its enemies, and the Nawab is left to prove submission rather than command events. Once the pressure has done its work, Dina Beg returns with one lakh rupees and karah parshad as a visible acknowledgment of Sikh ascendancy. The money is handed over before the Khalsa, and the sacred offering is distributed in a setting that blends triumph, thanksgiving, and political settlement. The Nawab even praises the karah parshad as he tastes it, underscoring how far he has moved from bargaining partner to dependent ally. The page closes with cash, ritual, and public deference combining to ratify the Sikh victory at Jalandhar.

pages.searchText: Doaba Settlement and the Maratha Transition Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh Episode About Adina Beg And Sodhi Vad Bhag Singh The Dina Beg-Wadbhag Singh episode closes with further payment, praise for the sacred offering, and a final reckoning of the region's revenues. An additional sum is settled, the Doaba assessment is fixed at one and a quarter lakh, and the Khalsa agrees to stop the ransacking of Doaba once these terms are secured. The page then deliberately pivots into Episode 125, signaling that a new political landscape is opening beyond the immediate Jalandhar settlement. Mughal weakness around Delhi, Ahmad Shah Abdali's Kandahari power, and the rising role of the Marathas and the Khalsa are introduced as connected forces reshaping North India. Dina Beg again recognizes that major conflict cannot be managed without Sikh participation, so the transition leads directly into new negotiations and campaigns. This hinge page therefore both settles on one and a quarter lakh as the agreement and opens the wider story of Marathas and the Khalsa.

pages.searchText: Sadiq Beg Attacks the Khalsa Muster near Srainwal Sadiq Beg's Betrayal in Friendship The new episode opens with a large Sikh muster, as twenty thousand Singhs assemble under leading chiefs for the seasonal movement toward Anandpur and Hola Mohalla. Tara Singh led the contingent, and the gathering is presented as both martial and devotional before politics again interrupts the journey. Sadiq Beg has failed to honor earlier obligations, so resentment follows him even before open fighting resumes. When his revenue interests appear exposed, Sikh action against them helps turn suspicion into war and convinces him to answer with force rather than payment. He therefore launches a sudden attack near Srainwal, trying to hit the Khalsa while it is not yet fully concentrated. The page frames his conduct as betrayal precisely because it comes after negotiation, delayed payment, and the outward signs of friendship.

As this contingent endeavoured to turn back towards Sirhind, They could think of no other alternative at that moment of time. (5) As the Singhs observed the Mughal official party turning back, They attacked the revenue collecting party all of a sudden. After looting and plundering that party, did the Singhs proceed further, The moment Sadiq Beg heard about Singhs ransacking of his men, Instantly did he prepare his troops for a counter attack. Suddenly did they attack where the Singhs were camping, At a wayside inn in the vicinity of the village Srainwal. (7) As there was a sudden burst of fire from guns and muskets, The Singhs were at their wits ends to combat this sudden attack. As majority of best warriors had gone to celebrate Hola Mohalla, Others had gone into the countryside to purchase provisions. (8) As many among them had gone to fetch fodder and fuel wood, The whole Khalsa Panth force had scattered over the area. As no body could take the command to combat this attack, Everyone took to his heels bareheaded and barefoot. (9) As a few of these Singhs happened to be chiefs of their contingents, They did put up a brave front while taking cover in the villages. Among these chiefs were chiefs of Singhpura and Ahluwalia Misls, Who along with Dallewalia chief resolved to combat the Mughals. (10)

pages.snippet: The surprise attack throws parts of the Khalsa camp into confusion, but the Sikh chiefs rapidly begin to regroup around their banners and armed circles. Sangat Singh / Shyam Singh / Karora Singh and other leaders emerge in the narrative as rallying figures who help transform shoc
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Regroups after Sadiq Beg's Surprise Attack Sadiq Beg's Betrayal in Friendship The surprise attack throws parts of the Khalsa camp into confusion, but the Sikh chiefs rapidly begin to regroup around their banners and armed circles. Sangat Singh / Shyam Singh / Karora Singh and other leaders emerge in the narrative as rallying figures who help transform shock into organized resistance. The Singhs form a fortified circular camp, absorb heavy cannon fire and close-range punishment, and refuse to let the Mughals finish the battle in a single rush. Even when some of the line gives way, the chiefs steady the force and restore its willingness to fight at close quarters. Once the panic passes, the Khalsa rallies and charges back against men, horses, and gun positions alike. The page emphasizes recovery of nerve: what looked like a successful betrayal becomes another proof that Sikh cohesion can re-form under extreme pressure.

pages.searchText: Wounded Chiefs, Negotiation, and the Gazdi Transition Sadiq Beg's Betrayal in Friendship Episode About Sadiq Beg's Betrayal in Friendship By the close of the fighting, many chiefs were wounded, and the cost of the battle is measured through the battered bodies of leading sardars. Jassa Singh received two grievous wounds, making his suffering emblematic of the price paid by the Khalsa in a fight triggered by treachery. Sadiq Beg now falls back on negotiation and tries to repair the breach through envoys, compensation, and renewed promises of settlement. The Singhs hear the offer, but their answer is stern: delay in ransom would bring renewed plunder, because bad faith has already been proved in the field. This settlement talk also becomes a transition into the next political sequence. The page closes the betrayal episode while opening the wider Gazdi narrative, where arrogance, court intrigue, and new alignments will again shape the struggle.

pages.title: Gazdi's Pride Leads to Gang Bhat's Death
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Gazdi (The Minister)
pages.snippet: As Delhi's sovereign became slack in supervision, Gazdi grows swollen with pride and begins treating his ministerial authority as a stage for self-glorification. To fix that vanity in words, Gazdi asked Gang Bhat for praise and expected the bard to turn political power into poeti
pages.searchText: Gazdi's Pride Leads to Gang Bhat's Death Gazdi (The Minister) As Delhi's sovereign became slack in supervision, Gazdi grows swollen with pride and begins treating his ministerial authority as a stage for self-glorification. To fix that vanity in words, Gazdi asked Gang Bhat for praise and expected the bard to turn political power into poetic immortality. Gang Bhat refuses to flatter what he does not believe, insisting that he would not eulogize what was not true. His refusal costs him his life, and the killing becomes a moral indictment of Gazdi's arrogance rather than a display of legitimate strength. The page then broadens the accusation by suggesting that the same pride would damage Gazdi's larger alliances as well. What begins as a courtly demand for praise becomes an omen that Gazdi ruined the Marathas as well through the same blindness and overreach.

Not the slightest harm could he cause to the Jat ruler, Although he had plundered the entire region of Delhi. (7) Having been stung by the plain speaking by Gangbhat, The dying statement that this poet had made, Became a well-known maxim the world over: (8) Never can an impotent (coward) wage a war, Nor can the beat of his war-drum frighten anyone. I bid the whole gathering (court) a final adieu, As I (Gang Bhat) take my leave from the world. (9) With the same (prophetic) damnation did gazdi got struck, As the damned gazdi ruined the Marhattas as well. pages.searchText: Whole of India and the Gilja Pathans Gazdi (The Minister) Episode About Gazdi (The Minister) The narrative now widens from individual intrigue to a subcontinental struggle, explicitly signaling Episode 128 and the shift to Whole of India and the Gilja Pathans. The concern is no longer only Gazdi's character, but the effort to recover authority across Hindustan after repeated upheaval. In that larger frame, Mughal and Pathan forces united in response to Maratha advance and political fragmentation. Lahore is re-entered with strength, and the story presents the coalition as an attempt to restore order by consolidating Muslim power under renewed leadership. The proposed arrangement imagines three ministers and a Kandhari sovereign overseeing the realm, a formula meant to stabilize what war had broken apart. This page therefore serves as a transition from Gazdi's failings to the broad imperial contest that will dominate the next episode.

pages.snippet: The page first closes the preceding campaign against the Khalsa by showing how Jahan Khan kept chasing the Khalsa Singhs while scattered bands answered with sudden counterattacks. Even under pursuit, the Singhs looted from the vanguard and rearguard, avoided being pinned down, an
pages.searchText: Hattoo Singh Majhail Is Captured and Defies Abdali's Elephant Hattoo Singh Majhail The page first closes the preceding campaign against the Khalsa by showing how Jahan Khan kept chasing the Khalsa Singhs while scattered bands answered with sudden counterattacks. Even under pursuit, the Singhs looted from the vanguard and rearguard, avoided being pinned down, and many Singhs withdrew into Malwa, forests, and other hiding places until they could regroup. It then opens Episode About Hattoo Singh Majhail by introducing Hattoo Singh as a brave Majhail Sikh from the Kanna Kachha side whose night raid went wrong when his horse slipped beneath him. Captured alive and brought before Ahmad Shah Abdali, he is presented as a steadfast Singh who will not yield even when royal punishment is prepared. Abdali therefore ordered that he be crushed by a ferocious elephant, expecting the spectacle to terrify the Khalsa. Instead the elephant would not kill him, and even when Hattoo Singh was fastened for trampling the execution failed, turning the page into the opening of a martyrdom narrative rather than a routine execution.

pages.searchText: Hattoo Singh's Martyrdom Gives Way to the Bikaner Campaign Bikaner Hattoo Singh's ordeal ends here when the second elephant did not crush Hattoo Singh either, further enraging Ahmad Shah. The ruler finally had him tied between two elephants and torn apart, presenting his death as a public martyrdom rather than a defeat in battle. The page then turns to Episode About Bikaner, with Abdali still entrenched at Lahore while the Khalsa in Malwa struggled through want and accepted an invitation to aid Bikaner in its conflict with Jaisalmer. The Singhs fought effectively, but the Bikaner side broke faith and the Singhs were not paid the promised wages after the campaign was done. Because the Khalsa could not sustain his position under those conditions, the narrative explains why they began planning fresh raids for subsistence instead of remaining dependent on unreliable allies. The closing movement prepares the transition into the Bangar expedition by showing economic pressure, not greed, pushing the Singhs back into the field.

pages.searchText: The Khalsa Campaigns Through Bangar and Spares Jaipur the Bangar Region This page continues the Bangar expedition by showing the Khalsa consulting chiefs such as Alo Singh, Budho Singh, and Gurbakhsh Singh before moving through the region. Their negotiations determined which settlements would be protected, and eight villages saved from plunder after local intermediaries secured terms with the Singhs. Once those understandings were made, the Khalsa rode more aggressively across the surrounding tract, and Hansi, Narnaul, and Hissar were raided along with other vulnerable places. The page presents these movements as organized campaigning rather than random disorder, with the Singhs distinguishing between hostile targets and those placed under safeguard. Jaipur sent envoys to the Singhs to ask that their state be spared, invoking shared reverence for the Gurus and the practical value of peace. The appeal worked, the Singhs turned away from Jaipur, camped near the Yamuna, and the page then begins introducing Mit Singh Shahid for the next martyrdom episode.

pages.searchText: Bangar Expedition and Mit Singh’s Proposal Mit Singh — The Martyr Episode About Mit Singh — The Martyr The page closes the Bangar expedition: Malwa chiefs such as Bhai Alo Singh, Bhai Budho Singh, and Bhai Gurbakhsh Singh helped lead the Khalsa force, arranged settlements, and protected those under their care. Alo Singh saved eight Kaithal villages, while chiefs at Jind and Safidon sent ransom through the Malwa Singhs. The Khalsa then raided Hansi, Narnaul, Hissar, and the hill fort of Kama, after which Jaipur sent envoys asking to be spared as fellow followers of the Guru. The Singhs accepted the plea, turned back, and camped near the Yamuna. Episode 133 begins by introducing Tara Singh Gaiba of the Dalewalia Misl and Mit Singh, who would become a martyr fighting Jahan Khan’s forces. Mit Singh proposed that ten thousand independent-minded Singhs should cross the Yamuna at dawn, but Tara Singh warned that Mit Singh was acting on his own.

pages.title: Mit Singh Crosses the Yamuna into a Fatal Last Stand
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mit Singh — The Martyr

pages.searchText: Mit Singh Crosses the Yamuna into a Fatal Last Stand Mit Singh — The Martyr Tara Singh had warned Mit Singh against crossing Yamuna with a smaller force, arguing that a lightly supported raid would invite disaster once word reached larger enemy centers. Mit Singh pressed on anyway, leading a mobile Sikh band across the river into Rohilla territory and spending several days gathering plunder around Meerut. The warning proved true when Rohilla resistance hardened and troops from Lahore and Sirhind arrived to reinforce the pursuit. Their combined force attacked at sunrise with such force that the booty-laden Singhs were thrown into confusion, and many were cut down before they could form a proper defense. Even in that reversal, Mit Singh kept fighting as a martyr rather than retreating in panic. The turning point came when his horse fell after being hit by a bullet, leaving one of his feet caught and making it clear that the brave raid had turned into a sacrificial last stand.

pages.searchText: Shahid Ganj and the Opening of Mir Mannu Mit Singh — The Martyr Episode About Mit Singh — The Martyr The battle's cost is counted bluntly here, with the poem stating that five to six thousand Singhs perished in the defeat around Mit Singh's final stand. Enemy victors severed heads for display and loaded as many as eighteen cartloads of severed heads to carry off as trophies for their patrons. That grim procession did not reach its destination unchanged, because alarm spread near a Ghaggar-side sarai that Sikh forces were approaching. The carts were abandoned there, and Bhag Singh and Bhanga Singh gathered the heads, gave them cremation rites, and preserved the memory of the dead at the place that came to be known as Shahid Ganj. After closing Mit Singh's martyrdom, the page deliberately shifts tone and opens Episode About Mir Mannu. The new episode introduces the Lahore minister as a persecutor determined to hunt the Khalsa relentlessly, making this page a hinge between memorialization and a fresh cycle of repression.

pages.title: Mir Mannu's Officers Search Pandori for Hidden Sikh Families
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mir Mannu
pages.snippet: Mir Mannu responds to repeated Sikh raids near Lahore's outskirts by deciding that ordinary policing is no longer enough and that the Khalsa must be rooted out completely. Orders go out across the province to seize or kill Singhs wherever they can be found, turning his administra
pages.searchText: Mir Mannu's Officers Search Pandori for Hidden Sikh Families Mir Mannu Mir Mannu responds to repeated Sikh raids near Lahore's outskirts by deciding that ordinary policing is no longer enough and that the Khalsa must be rooted out completely. Orders go out across the province to seize or kill Singhs wherever they can be found, turning his administration into an instrument of systematic persecution. The pressure becomes so severe that whole Sikh families lose safe refuge in Majha and depend on scattered sympathizers for survival. One important hiding place is Pandori in the Majha area, where the household associated with saint Dadu Ram shelters vulnerable women connected to the Sikh community. When informers expose the arrangement, Mir Mannu's men descend on the site, arrest the grandson of saint Dadu Ram, and search the monastery for fugitives. The women escape immediate discovery only by taking on the red robes of that sect, a detail that underscores both the danger and the ingenuity of those being hunted.

pages.searchText: A Young Protector Defies Mir Mannu's Elephant Mir Mannu To shield the hidden women, the young religious leader publicly claims one woman as his sister and another as his daughter, while declaring the others members of his own following. By accepting that burden himself, he tries to stop Mir Mannu’s officers from exposing the Sikhs through further interrogation or assault. Mir Mannu orders the youth to be crushed by an elephant, but the beast instead touched his feet with his trunk and refused to carry out the execution. Even a second attempt fails, turning the scene into another testimony of moral courage and failed royal violence. Mir Mannu’s wife then persuades him to spare several captured Singhs, but the reprieve is short-lived. New intelligence soon leads the searchers to a large field overgrown with sugarcane, where yet another group of Singhs, including women, children, and elders, is surrounded.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Mir Mannu
pages.snippet: The Mir Mannu episode reaches its climax as the trapped Sikh households lament that mothers and sisters had no one to share their grief while the minister's terror campaign seemed unstoppable. In the middle of that chaos, Mir Mannu's horse
pages.searchText: Mir Mannu's Death and the Opening of Mathura And Koel Mir Mannu Episode About Mir Mannu The Mir Mannu episode reaches its climax as the trapped Sikh households lament that mothers and sisters had no one to share their grief while the minister's terror campaign seemed unstoppable. In the middle of that chaos, Mir Mannu's horse suddenly reared, threw him down, and his feet got entangled in the stirrup so that he was dragged to a painful death. His fall is treated as divine reversal: the persecutor who meant to crush the Khalsa dies helplessly, and the machinery of the hunt breaks apart almost at once. Captives are released, the immediate panic lifts, and the narrative closes his episode by tying political justice to the downfall of a tyrant. The same page then opens Episode About Mathura And Koel, widening the frame back to imperial politics after Panipat. Ahmad Shah Abdali now dominates the north, tribute flows from subordinate nawabs, and attention shifts toward Mathura and other Hindu centers that will define the next campaign.

pages.searchText: Bharatpur, Deeg, and Koel Stall Abdali's Advance Mathura And Koel Those who fled to Bharatpur survived the attack, and the Muslim troops pursuing them were driven back by heavy Jat artillery. After being repulsed from Bharatpur, the Pathan force camped at Mathura, where cannon fire left the Mughal-Pathan troops unable to press their attack. Large numbers of Jats entered Deeg, the Marathas held Ghumer, and another strong fort became the Jats’ main hope. Its water channel, massive walls, and heavy guns made it impossible to storm, tunnel under, or break with cannon. That fort was Koel, called Ramgarh by Hindus and Aligarh by Muslims, and it held provisions for twelve years. The Jats mocked passing Mughal troops, and Najib Khan worried that Abdali would be trapped before Koel, so he tried to explain the Jats’ war-drum as a sound from a religious seat.

pages.searchText: Abdali Maps Koel for a Systematic Siege Mathura And Koel The siege narrative sharpens here when Abdali refuses to ignore the taunts coming from the Jat stronghold at Koel and insists that he will not proceed farther until the fort is mastered. To him the drumming and bravado from inside are proof that the Jats were poking fun at him, so the campaign becomes a test of prestige as much as a military necessity. As his officers review the problem, the fort stocked with plenty of provisions is described as difficult to reduce by ordinary means. Its defenders are well supplied, the position is strong, and the discussion makes clear that a prolonged effort may be required before the road to Agra can be secured. Abdali therefore turns to studied siegecraft rather than impulse, consulting a book that dealt with the art of breaking forts and asking for the stronghold to be mapped precisely. He got a complete sketch design of the targeted fort traced so that the next move would be systematic and overwhelming.

Abdali rejects that advice, convinced that Agra itself cannot be controlled unless the surrounding Jat resistance is first broken. He then spreads his army around the fort from multiple directions while the defenders remain steady under Rai Mal's leadership. Fire from outside proves less decisive than hoped, water and fortifications frustrate mining, and the garrison's confidence makes the siege feel heavier with each passing day. By this stage, seven days having been wasted, impatience and embarrassment are growing among the attackers. The page captures the sense of a campaign that is expensive, frustrating, and in need of some dramatic escalation if Abdali is to recover the initiative.

pages.searchText: Abdali Raises a Night Rampart Over Koel Mathura And Koel Abdali next changes tactics by riding out with little ceremony so he can study the ground without revealing too much of his intention. He reconnoitres the approaches, measures heights and distances, and keeps the defenders guessing by shifting men forward and back instead of committing to an obvious assault. Once darkness falls, he summons his commanders and reveals the engineering answer he has chosen. A wall forty feet high is ordered at the commanding point near the fort, and the work is pressed so quickly that the defenders cannot interfere before dawn. By morning the Jats are astonished to find a new elevation towering over their position as if a mountain had risen overnight. Heavy weapons are mounted there, and the page turns the siege from stalemate into a carefully prepared bombardment that will soon break the balance.

pages.searchText: Koel Falls under Bombardment and Rai Mal Enters the River Mathura And Koel From the newly raised position, Abdali begins a crushing bombardment with several thousand musketeers on the top backed by artillery, arrows, and incendiaries. Smoke, fire, and noise overwhelm the fort so completely that day itself seems darkened, and the defenders are battered from above in a way they had not anticipated. As the pressure intensifies, Abdali allows one direction of escape to remain open, calculating that panic will do what direct slaughter cannot. Men begin fleeing toward the Yamuna, the fort's will collapses, and the siege ends less by negotiated surrender than by terror and exhaustion. Rai Mal's final humiliation seals the page: unable to bear the dishonor of defeat, he throws himself into the river after the stronghold is lost. The fall of Koel therefore becomes both a tactical victory for Abdali and a moral catastrophe for the Jat defenders.

With Agra and surrounding positions subdued, the narrative briefly surveys his larger settlement of north Indian affairs through appointments and renewed control in places such as Delhi, Sirhind, Lahore, and Amritsar. That wider frame is important because it shows the Afghan ruler turning from one set of enemies to another while the subcontinent still trembles from recent war. The mention of three lakh horse-mounted soldiers from the South and the redistribution of authority under Najib Khan underline the scale of imperial reordering now underway. The page then pivots directly toward Sikh history with the explicit signal, Now as came the turn of the Sikhs. In doing so it opens Episode 136 and prepares the reader for the Ghallughara near Malerkotla, where Abdali's reorganized power will collide with the Khalsa in a far more tragic campaign.

They mocked the refugees' hardship, forgot how often the Singhs had taken shelter in the Malwa region, and treated Sikh vulnerability as a chance for domination. Their threats soon became openly political as some Brars boasted that they had threatened the Singhs with elimination by inviting Mughal and Pathan authorities. (12) Branding themselves as great warriors in the whole world, The Brars claimed themselves to be the bravest of the brave indeed. Boasting of subduing the Majhail Singhs in a matter of minutes, So foolhardy did the Brars appear in their vainglorious boasts. (13) Dohra: Full five times had the Singhs fled from their own region, As and when the Gilja Pathans invaded them from the north. For periods from one year to two years during those invasions, Had the Singhs perforce taken shelter in the Malwa region. (14) Chaupai: Full five times had the Singhs to flee with their families, Seeking shelters with strangers during those desertions. The more the Singhs kept on putting off confrontation, The more the stupid Brars kept on getting proud and arrogant. (15) As the Singhs used to sneak into Malwa's forested region, The Mughal troops could not enter these jungles after the Singhs. After the Singhs arrived, the Brars too turned defiant against the Mughals, Otherwise earlier they used to pay revenue to the Mughals. (16) But after the great massacre (at Kupp), even the Brars turned hostile, As they also started killing the Singhs like the Mughals. Branding themselves as the greatest warriors and brave fighters, The Brars reckoned that the Singhs were no match for them. (17) Reminding the Singhs of passing their days in peace in Brar territory, The Brars taunted them of hiding themselves as fugitives. Approaching the Singhs after organizing themselves in a body, The Brars threatened the Singhs to eliminate them by inviting the Mughals. (18) Dohra: Was there one Sikh known as Ganda Singh, Of Dhand Kasel? village was he an inhabitant. His spouse had the Brars themselves kidnapped, But accused the Majhail Singhs of this abduction. (19) Resolving not to put up with Brar's excesses any more. The Brars had turned so faithless and mean indeed, That they had the audacity to challenge Khalsa Pahth's strength. (20)

pages.searchText: The Singh Families Are Removed and Binjhu Declares War the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars Episode About the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars Once the harassment becomes intolerable, the Singhs start pulling their families out of Brar households and placing them in safer settlements such as village Guru-ke-Kothay. The move makes clear that the conflict is no longer a matter of insults alone; both communities are preparing for sustained hostility. From there the dispute escalates into open organization for war, and the Brars of Binjhu declared war rather than stepping back from the provocation. Armed bands gather, attacks become regular, and the countryside begins to take on the feel of a local campaign rather than a village quarrel. The page closes by setting up an armed encounter between the Singhs and the Brars, with the Brars leaning on spear warfare while the Singhs answer with tighter discipline and firearms. The relocation of families and the call to arms together mark the true opening of the Brar conflict.

Thereafter, the brar residents of village of Binjhu declared war on the Singhs, After they had organized themselves into a fighting contingent. (22) Thereafter, did these Brars keep harassing the Singhs day and night, Robbing and killing the Singhs wherever they came across the latter. Thus did develop a confrontation between the Singhs and the Brars, As the latter started confronting the Singhs day in and day out. (23) The Singhs being smaller in strength in that makesift settlements, They somehow used to keep a few horses there during the night. As more Singhs would join them at the break of dawn, They would assemble there in a respectable strength. (24) Dohra: Despite this assemblage of Singhs, the Brars did not budge, Attacking the Singhs assembly in the afternoon hours of the day. As the Singhs were already in high morale after a dose of cannabis, There occurred an armed encounter between the Singhs and the Brars. (25) Chaupai: While a few Singhs were reciting verses from Chandi-di-Var, A few others were performing ablutions after answering nature's call. As all the Singhs rushed to fight after hearing the drum beat, The Brars started poking fun at the rushing Singhs. (26) Feeling that Singhs would never dare to come too close to the Brars, As they would keep the Singhs at bay with their sharp spears. Assuming themselves to be fortunate if the Singhs attacked them, As they would snatch the Singhs horses with their lances (27) Singhs, on the other hand, considered the Brars an easy game, As they would kill the spear-armed Brars by firing at them. Thus did start an encounter between the Singhs and the Brars. (28) As the Brars thought of wielding their spears against the Singhs, The Singhs prepared to shoot the spear-wielding Brars. As the Brars lances hurled at Singhs failed to hit, The Singhs would snatch a Brar's horse after shooting him. (29)

pages.searchText: The Brars Are Routed and Binjhu Is Emptied the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars Episode About the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars After enduring repeated nuisance and attack, the Singhs resolve to end the trouble decisively and meet the Brars in open fighting. Dust, smoke, and confusion fill the field, but the balance steadily tilts toward the Sikh side as mounted Brars are shot down or driven away. The scale of the reversal is marked by the capture of fifteen hundred horses, a detail that shows how thoroughly the Brar strength collapses once the battle turns. What began as harassment now ends in rout, with the Singhs seizing animals, prisoners, and the initiative. A follow-up strike leaves the village Binjhu of the Brars largely emptied as survivors flee toward places like Kotkapoora and Faridkot. The page presents this not as random plunder but as the clearing of a hostile base that had chosen war with the Khalsa.

For ending this daily nuisance being created by the Brars, The Singhs resolved to put an end to it once for all. (30) As a lot of dust, din and smoke cast a pall of darkness, Impossible it became to differentiate between colleagues and enemies. Some of the Brars had already been killed by Singhs shots, Some others were thrown down by their scared horses. (31) Hardly could the Brars wield their lances and spears, As they were on the run in front of the chasing Singhs. Only those among the Brars could save their lives, Who were swift-footed enough to escape on foot. (32) With the beat of a war-drums had the Brars come to kill the Singhs, With a whimper did they hid behind bushes to escape death. Such was the humiliation that the Brars had to face, That a few among them survived, in the darkness of the night. Not only did the Singhs catch hold of the fifteen hundred horses, They also took into their custody many of the Jat Brars. (33) After plundering some Brars while sparing a few others, Did the Singhs pack the rest of them to their respective homes. Warning to plunder and kill them again the next morning, Did the Singhs declare after the fleeing Brars. (34) The scared Brars took to their heels before the day break, As the Singhs attacked them once again at the break of dawn. The Singhs found the Brar households vacant and deserted, As all the males had fled away to seek shelter elsewhere. (35) Such was the plight that struck the village Binjhu of the Brars. So much were the provisions that lay stored in the Brar houses. (36) The vacant Brar houses did the Singhs occupy at Binjhu, For a few days did the Singhs stay there in those houses. The Brars did run to seek shelter at several other places, Which were located in territories of Kotkapoora and Faridkot. (37) Besides this, where there were bigger settlements of Brars, Their inhabitants settled at one place leaving their homes.

pages.searchText: The Brars Return by Night and Plot a Pathan Disguise the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars Episode About the Rift between Khalsa Panth And the Brars With the Singhs dominant in the area by day, displaced Brars can only come back at night to look at their abandoned homes and judge what has been lost. The memory is preserved as an ordered account rather than rumor, giving the episode the feel of a remembered local history. The page then shifts into a new plan of revenge: Resolving to disguise themselves in the guise of Gilja Pathans, the Brars decide that deception will accomplish what open fighting could not. Red robes, borrowed appearance, and calculated fear become tools for another round of conflict. This transition also serves as the hinge into the next Brar episode, where disguise and surprise replace the previous battle line. The story moves from the aftermath of defeat into a fresh attempt to unsettle and rob the Singhs through impersonation.

Resolving to disguise themselves in the guise of Gilja Pathans, They must launch an attack on the Khalsa Panth Singhs. (1) Seeing Gilja Pathans, would the Singhs take to their heels, Then would the Brars grab the Singhs total belongings. The same disguise then did the Brars put on, After resolving to cover their soldiers with red robes. Covering their own bodies with red coloured cotton wrappings, They hoisted red shawls on their lances as Pathan emblems. (3) Raising and unfurling these red coloured emblems atop their lances, The Singhs started beating drums as if these were drum-beats of war. The intelligence front-runners among the Singhs being always on the alert, Running fast immediately as they alerted the Singhs, They took to their heels without caring for their belongings. As the Khalsa contingent retreated for so many miles, Then did the contingent chiefs chalked out a strategy. (5) That they must stop to take stock of the whole situation. As they had already reached the end of the Malwa region, How could the Kabul-based Pathans invade them at that end? (6) If they (the Singhs) continued retreating and running further, Definitely would they die of thirst for want of water.

pages.title: The Pathan Disguise Is Exposed Among the Brars
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About the Brars
pages.snippet: The Brars try to recover the initiative by returning in Pathan disguise, but the ruse falters once the Singhs see they cannot safely keep retreating into waterless ground. The Khalsa halts where it stands, yields the outcome to the Guru's w
pages.searchText: The Pathan Disguise Is Exposed Among the Brars the Brars Another Episode About the Brars The Brars try to recover the initiative by returning in Pathan disguise, but the ruse falters once the Singhs see they cannot safely keep retreating into waterless ground. The Khalsa halts where it stands, yields the outcome to the Guru's will, and turns back under raised drums, standards, and shouted orders. From the rear guard, Charat Singh recognizes the Brars beneath their Pathan disguise and calls the alarm. His warning sends the Singhs charging back so quickly that some Brars are seized on the spot while others break and run. The page closes by widening the quarrel into a longer campaign of pressure on Brar villages. Mothers of captured sons come pleading after the Khalsa, livestock and tribute are taken from hostile households, and the Brars are gradually forced from open defiance into subordination.

As he did see through the Brars in Pathan disguise, Hearing this, the Singhs returned and attacked the Brars, Which the latter failed to repulse with all their might. So did the Brars desert with the Singhs in hot pursuit, Thus did the Singhs capture a few while the rest fled away. Pleading their cases for mercy before the Singhs, These mothers got their sons released from the Singhs. (11) As hostility developed between the Singhs and the Brars, The Singhs did not spare the Brars at any cost. As the Brars started constructing concrete buildings, The Singhs started digging bunkers around their settlements. (12) As the water-table receded and dried up in the dug-up wells, The Brars would desert that spot for want of water. The Singhs would allow a safe passage to the Brars, But they would seize their buffaloes and horses of quality breed. (13) Thus did the Brars get defeated by the Khalsa Singhs, For their own misdeeds did the Brars face harassment. From someone would the Singhs charge a ransom, From another would they demand his daughter in wedding. (14) Thus beating the Brars into submission as their subjects, The Singhs would stay put perforce in their homes. Then did the Brars become humble followers of the Singhs,

pages.searchText: The Brars Submit and the Kapoora Brar Episode Opens the Brars Another Episode About the Brars This page first closes the Brar quarrel on a note of submission. After returning to the same country, the Singhs are received by humbled Brars who invite them into their homes, and those who took pahul and joined the Panth are remembered as especially blessed. Rattan Singh then marks the account as one preserved from his father's testimony, giving the episode a deliberate narrative close before the next story begins. The hinge matters, because the page does not remain in the same mood for long. It turns directly into the Kapoora Brar episode, where Kapoora refuses to shelter the Guru out of fear that Mughal power will punish him with death by hanging. The Guru's prophetic response becomes the moral center of the new episode.

Rattan Singh (the author) as he heard from his father, He had narrated it as such the whole account. (17) Episode 139 Episode About Kapoora Brar If somebody puts up a poser to the narrator, Has he narrated the whole account about the Brars? As Satguru (Guru Gobind Singh) had predicted Kapoora's death by hanging, Had he described how did Kapoora meet his final end? (1) Let me (the author) now narrate the manner of Kapoora's death, I shall narrate the account as Guru's prophecy came to be fulfilled. When the Guru had reached Ktkapoora (after leaving Anandpur Sahib), Its (selfish) Nawab Kapoora Brar had behaved rudely with the Guru. (2) Considering him a devout follower, had the Guru entreated Kapoora, That he grant him (the Guru) shelter in his (well-fortified) fort. As the Mughal forces were coming in hot pursuit of the Guru, At no cost would they desist from a fight with the Guru. (3) Impossible would it be to fight the Mughals without a fort's protection, As even the mighty lion needs a jungle during his hunting spree. Should Kapoora provide shelter to the Guru in his fort, Definitely would the Mughals get defeated by the Guru's force. (4) As the Guru would bestow Kapoora with a sovereignty over a large region. Then the (rude) answer that Kapoora tendered unto the Guru, That insolent remark became the cause for his damned end. (5) As Kapoora's fate was sealed due to his insolent remarks, It made him renege from his faith in the Guru's words. Being motivated by his narrow selfish considerations of his own, He apprehended his own ouster by the Guru from his own fort. (6)

pages.title: Kapoora Refuses the Guru and Meets the Foretold Hanging
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Kapoora Brar

pages.searchText: Kapoora Refuses the Guru and Meets the Foretold Hanging Kapoora Brar Episode About Kapoora Brar Kapoora explains his refusal in blunt political terms: we are servants of the Turks, and if he shelters the Guru in his fort the imperial authorities will destroy him. His speech shows a chief trying to preserve his worldly position by abandoning the higher obligation of hospitality and loyalty. The Guru answers that such caution will not save him, because faithlessness itself has already chosen his ruin. The page frames the warning as a prophecy whose force is both temporal and spiritual, insisting that the Guru's word does not go in vain. The narrative then moves toward fulfillment as Isa Khan Manjh enters the story and Kapoora's intrigues rebound against him. What he feared outwardly finally happens in fact, and Kapoora is hanged just as the Guru had foretold.

pages.searchText: The Slaughter at Morinda Begins Kapoora Brar Episode About Kapoora Brar This page opens the Morinda episode, set in the year of the great massacre after the Khalsa has disciplined the Brars and begun moving toward fresh enemies. Ala Singh joined the Khalsa with his Phulkian following, and the combined force starts to measure where vengeance should next fall. The narrative broadens from one local feud into a coordinated misl action shaped by memory of earlier wrongs. That inquiry leads the Singhs toward Morinda, where officials associated with the town are singled out in the narrative as especially guilty in the chain of events around the younger Sahibzadas. The page therefore serves as both a fresh episode opening and a moral briefing for the assault to come.

After ransacking the Brars (of the Malwa region), That the United Khalsa Panth force made a move. (1) Thereafter did Ala Singh approach the Khalsa Singhs, With him did he bring his Phulkian fraternity. With him did he bring Singhs from Bhai dynasty, Who were led by Bhai Buddha Singh and Gurbakhsh Singh. (2) For attacking the Malerkotla rulers did he suggest, As there existed an enmity between Pathans and Malwais. So after looting, plundering and taking over their territory, The Khalsa Panth force marched ahead of Malerkotla. (3) As the Khalsa Panth force moved towards Sirhind, They returned as they saw the orchards around the city. The Mughal force which was stationed inside the city, It failed to come out being scared of the Khalsa force. (4) As the Khalsa found the Mughals morale quite low, The Khalsa felt emboldened at their own military strength. Reckoning the Mughals as timid as a frightened rabbit, They could capture and kill the Sirhind Mughals later on. (5) The Khalsa called an assembly of local inhabitants of the area, Who resided in and around the city of Sirhind. They must shortlist ten enemies of the Khalsa Panth, Who must be eliminated with the guidance of the locals. (6) There were Singhs in the Khalsa force from villages Gharuan! and Salodi*, Who had been with the Khalsa Panth since the beginning. Both these Khalsa Singhs pointed out with one voice, That the Muslims of Morinda were the worst enemies of the Singhs. (7) Their Muslim rulers were instrumental in the arrest of Sahibzadas, Thereafter had Wazir Khan slaughtered the Guru's sons. Both these Singhs suggested to the Khalsa Panth force, Must the Khalsa not spare those enemies at any cost. (8)

pages.searchText: Thirsty Singhs Are Provoked at Morinda the Slaughter At Maida; i Episode About the Slaughter At Maida; i The page begins with hesitation at the top: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia wished to put it off because Abdali's forces might still be close, yet the poem insists that what is fated has to happen. The march therefore continues under a sense that providence is driving the encounter forward whether the chiefs want it or not. That inevitability turns concrete when thirsty Singhs went to Morinda for water instead of pressing on in silence. From the town, armed Ranghars stand on the rooftops, watch the Sikhs below, and begin a campaign of provocation rather than letting the travelers pass. What might have remained a delayed quarrel is thus made immediate by insult, posture, and the refusal of Morinda's men to keep peace. The page sets up the clash as a confrontation invited by the town itself.

(11) Silently did the Khalsa force march in the same direction, As they had no mind to get into any skirmish (at Morinda). Though the Singhs from Gharuan reminded them again, Nobody paid any heed to these Singhs entreaties. As the Divine Will had ordained it to happen here, How could the Divinely ordained occurance be put of? (13) Whenever the Divine Will wishes an incident to happen, It takes an instant for such an occurance to materialize. A few Singhs of this contingent being thirsty for water, They went to the village (Morinda) to quench their thirst. pages.searchText: Ranghar Taunts Turn the Morinda March into Battle the Slaughter At Maida; i Episode About the Slaughter At Maida; i The rooftop abuse now sharpens into sacrilege and challenge. The Ranghars mock the Sikhs with references to the Sahibzadas, boast about earlier cruelty, and openly dare the Khalsa to stop and fight instead of marching on. When the Sikh side answers back, the Ranghars opened a volley of fire and the quarrel crosses the line into bloodshed. A shot hit one of Tara Singh's Singhs, making it impossible to treat the exchange as mere abuse. News of the firing races through the marching force and turns outrage into mobilization. By the end of the page the war drum is beaten and Morinda is no longer a place to bypass, but a target that must be punished.

pages.searchText: The Drum Call Summons the Misls Back to Morinda the Slaughter At Maida; i Episode About the Slaughter At Maida; i Once the insult and shooting are reported, senior leaders are briefed and the attack on Morinda is launched in earnest. The narrative stresses that this is not a private retaliation by a few offended men, but a deliberate response taken up by the Khalsa leadership. Many misls turned back at the drum beat, and contingent after contingent rejoins the action. The page takes care to present the return of these bodies as a collective rally, giving the coming assault the force of the wider Panth rather than a single jatha. With that strength gathered, the Khalsa attacks Morinda from all sides. Yet the defenders still manage to withdraw into a formidable fort, so the page ends with the assault underway but not yet complete.

pages.searchText: Charat Singh Covers Sirhind While the Fort Is Stormed the Slaughter At Maida; i Episode About the Slaughter At Maida; i At the critical pause before the breach, Charat Singh made a bold declaration that he would hold the Sirhind side himself. By taking responsibility for that flank, he frees the rest of the Khalsa to concentrate on opening the fort and carrying the assault inward. His movement unsettles the Pathan side and helps spread panic beyond the walls, while the main Sikh force prepares to storm the enclosure at close quarters. The page presents coordinated action rather than chaotic fury: one side contains reinforcement, the other presses the breach. Once the attack gathers full force, the Singhs climb without ladders and force their way into the stronghold with improvised means and relentless momentum. The fall of the position turns the Morinda action from siege into interior retribution.

pages.searchText: Jaani Khan and Maani Khan's Progeny Is Uprooted at Morinda the Slaughter At Maida; i Episode About the Slaughter At Maida; i Inside Morinda, the fighting becomes intensely personal and punitive. The Singhs strike down the Ranghar leadership at close range, crushing many heads with hammers as they identify those held responsible for earlier crimes. Among the names singled out above all others are Jaani Khan and Maani Khan, remembered here as the men who had handed over the Sahibzadas. The attack on their houses and heirs is narrated not as incidental battlefield killing, but as targeted vengeance against a known line of guilt. The narrative presents that destruction as fulfillment rather than accident, treating Morinda’s punishment as falling on the line of Jaani Khan and Maani Khan. The Singhs are shown carrying out a sentence that the story had long prepared.

pages.searchText: Morinda Closes and the Lakhmi Narayan Episode Opens the Slaughter At Maida; i Episode About the Slaughter At Maida; i This transition page first records the last shadows of Morinda's punishment. Those who had taken refuge in Hindu households are turned out under cover of night, while Jaani Khan and Maani Khan remain fixed in memory as the brothers tied to the arrest of the younger Sahibzadas. The narrator then closes the Morinda account with the Guru's judgment and an explicit statement that Rattan Singh has narrated what he heard. That closure gives the massacre an ending in testimony as well as in action. Before the page is done, however, a new episode opens around Lakhmi Narayan Kshtriya, a revenue officer whose movements and wealth draw Khalsa attention in the Doaba. The page therefore works as a hinge, ending one vengeance narrative and launching the next campaign of expropriation.

pages.searchText: Khalsa Sovereignty and the Kasur Episode Opening the Robbing of Luxmi Narayan Kshiriyg yes This transition page first closes the Lakhmi Narayan episode by stressing how deeply Khalsa collection had cut into Sirhind revenue. In the exchange with Abdali and Ala Singh, the Khalsa insists that sovereignty had already been granted to the Khalsa by their Guru, so it is not a favor to be requested from any emperor. That closing argument turns the page from revenue and diplomacy toward a fresh martial narrative. The poem explicitly asks the reader to listen to the episode about the city of Kasur, where a new grievance will test whether the Panth will act on its claims of protection and rule. By the end of the page, the Dal Khalsa forces set up camp near the Amritsar shrine and the focus settles on Hari Singh Bhangi and the congregational life around Amritsar. The page is therefore a hinge between one political episode and the opening scene of the first Kasur invasion.

The new Kasur episode begins with ordinary Khalsa discipline at Amritsar before a crisis interrupts it. There arrived a Brahmin from the city of Kasur, and he appears not as a court envoy but as a distressed petitioner demanding public justice from the Panth. His complaint is direct and urgent: his spouse had been abducted by Kasur Pathans, and he frames the outrage as a test of Khalsa responsibility toward vulnerable Hindus. The appeal presses on the old claim that the Khalsa having been created for the protection of the Hindus cannot ignore such tyranny without dishonor. The page closes with the matter moving from lament into formal hearing. Hari Singh instructs the Brahmin to present the grievance before the assembled congregation after the evening prayer so the case can be taken up in the proper collective setting.

pages.searchText: Hari Singh Weighs the Odds but Refuses to Abandon Kasur First Invasion on Kasur The Brahmin's insistence now forces the congregation into strategic debate. Veteran Singhs admit that the Singhs are outnumbered by the Pathans, and the strength of Kasur's garrison cannot be dismissed as a minor local problem. Even so, the moral weight of the petition keeps the question alive. Hari Singh treats the Brahmin's threatened self-destruction before the sangat as a disgrace the Panth cannot allow, and discussion shifts from whether the problem exists to how the Khalsa should answer it. By the end of the page, resolve has hardened. The encounter must now take place, and the leaders begin considering outside support, deliberate planning, and the degree of sacrifice that will be required if Kasur is to be attacked in earnest.

As arguments continue over delay and reinforcement, the congregation accepts that the matter should be placed before the Guru rather than settled by calculation alone. The proposal carries the whole body with it, and the whole congregation moved to take hukam from Guru Granth Sahib. In this telling, the campaign is not only a retaliation for one Brahmin household, but a mission requiring collective ardas and explicit spiritual sanction. The page closes with the hukam process underway and the sangat ready to hear whether Kasur should be struck. Debate, prayer, and common consent are fused into a single turning point before the march begins.

As the Khalsa nears Kasur, the imbalance in numbers sharpens argument inside the camp. The timid imagine disaster while the resolute insist that the Panth must either prevail or die honorably rather than retreat from a righteous cause. Into this debate comes timely intelligence: A Sikh traveler from Kasur happened to pass by them, and the chiefs immediately draw him into council. He becomes the means by which rumor is replaced with actionable knowledge about Kasur's gates, habits, and weak points. The page therefore holds together two kinds of preparation at once. Moral courage is tested in open discussion while reconnaissance quietly prepares the method by which the city can actually be entered.

Once the traveler’s report is heard, the Singhs take it as confirmation that the earlier hukam is unfolding in real conditions. The tactical principle becomes clear: the Khalsa Singhs should enter Kasur at midday. The plan depends on discipline rather than spectacle. Without unfurling their standards or beating the war drums, the Singhs are to pass inward quietly, as if they were traders rather than an attacking force. This page thus marks the conversion of spiritual assurance into practical stealth. The Khalsa chooses silence, timing, and deception in order to open the way for sudden violence once the city has been penetrated.

Once the infiltration turns to open combat, the Khalsa moves rapidly through Kasur with firearms, blades, and close-range strikes. Pathan resistance is broken piecemeal as the Singhs shift from one point of fighting to another before defenders can regroup. With organized opposition collapsing, the tone of the page changes from assault to sanctioned seizure. The Khalsa then ordered the looting and plundering of Kasur, turning victory into a broad confiscation of streets, mansions, markets, stables, and movable wealth. The page therefore preserves both the fury of the battle and the scale of its aftermath. Kasur is not merely attacked; it is opened up for punitive expropriation by the triumphant Khalsa.

After three days of ransacking Kasur, the narrative returns to the grievance that first set the expedition in motion. The Brahmin appears again before the chiefs, Reminding the Khalsa about his wife's captivity under the Pathans and forcing them to prove that the campaign will answer the original wrong rather than vanish into general loot. Hari Singh directs the matter into a formal and then practical resolution. Guided by the Brahmin to the responsible house, the Khalsa kills the abductors and restores the woman, completing the justice claim that had justified the march on Kasur in the first place. Before the page ends, however, the poem pivots to a fresh concern and opens the Dileramian episode. The Kasur campaign closes on fulfilled petition, and a new political-financial narrative begins immediately after it.

They had the audacity to capture Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, and the narrative treats that act as bringing judgment on their line. Having closed that moral reckoning, the poem opens a wider Lahore-centered story around Dileram. He is introduced as a man of rank, enormous stored wealth, and political importance in a period unsettled by Abdali, Maratha movement, and pressure on the Lahore nawab. The page therefore works as another hinge. One episode ends in judgment on past insult, while the next begins by following where wealth is hidden, transferred, and protected when larger powers destabilize the region.

Dileram's household tries to save itself by scattering valuables before the Khalsa closes in. His sons in Lahore transferred all their assets to Kasur, sending ornaments, cash, and dependents away for protection, but the move itself exposes how fear and hurried transport are already unraveling the family estate. The poem then turns back to Dileram's haveli, where the first wave of plunder strips away what lies openly at hand and rough opportunists are pushed aside by stronger claimants. What seemed like an ordinary sack quickly becomes a more methodical search for hidden or buried treasure inside the mansion. By the end of the page the conflict is no longer only about punishing a political enemy. The chiefs and returning soldiers realize that Dileram's wealth may be immense, and the hunt for concealed stores begins to govern the entire episode.

Once the allied misls settle around the estate, the Ramgharias and Ghanaiyas divide the plunder in equal parts and begin acting together against Dileram's surviving family. Their partnership gives the search both military discipline and a sense that every new discovery will immediately become a contested prize. Dileram's eldest son is seized, pressured, and forced to reveal where wealth has been hidden and who still controls portions of it. Under torture and fear of death, he yields locations, names, and caches that the attackers would not have found so quickly on their own. The page therefore turns the story from open looting to coerced extraction. Betrayal, confession, and the narrowing search for treasure now matter more than the original attack on Dileram's house.

Maali Singh asks not for scattered goods but for the single object that holds the finest value, pressing Dileram to name the choicest possession in the house. The answer points to a guarded steel chest taken from beneath the stairs and hidden in a protected room rather than among ordinary loot. Dileram identifies it as the repository of Begum Noor Jahan's jewels, a cache whose prestige matters as much as its price. The page lingers over the distinction between common plunder and courtly treasure, making clear why this particular discovery inflames ambition beyond the earlier division of spoils. From this point onward, the struggle is no longer only about who conquered Dileram. It is about who will secretly control the most illustrious part of his wealth before allies can insist on their lawful share.

pages.snippet: The jewel inventory continues through rings, ornaments, gold vessels, and other luxury pieces that suggest the chest contains an entire courtly treasury. Dileram can barely finish naming the contents before desire outruns description and th
pages.searchText: Greed Overtakes Maali Singh Dileramian contd Episode About Dileramian contd. The jewel inventory continues through rings, ornaments, gold vessels, and other luxury pieces that suggest the chest contains an entire courtly treasury. Dileram can barely finish naming the contents before desire outruns description and the value of the hoard begins to distort every judgment around it. Hearing what lies inside, Maali Singh grew still greedier, until greed itself reads like the true subject of the page. What had begun as shared conquest now tempts him toward secrecy, private advantage, and a deliberate breach with the Ghanaiyas. Unable to contain himself, he hurries to Jassa Singh with a proposal that the best treasure should be concealed rather than divided. The page closes on that conspiratorial turn, preparing the moral collapse that follows.

pages.searchText: Many of these were to be worn on hands and feet, Dileramian contd Episode About Dileramian contd. Many of these were to be worn on hands and feet, Several of these were studded with diamonds and rubies. Many of these were rings studded with diamonds, Several of these were bracelets and crowns for the head. (33) Decanters and goblets of gold were among these jewels, Pitchers made of gold studded with diamonds were there as well. How could he narrate the names of those innumerable jewels, The more Diley Ram talked about that hidden treasure, The more greedy did Maali Singh keep on becoming. The more avaricious a human being became, The less scared he felt of committing sins. (35) The moment Maali Singh Ramgharia heard about that box, And the contents that that box contained in it. Dazzled and out of his wits did he turn, And weakened in his moral scruples did he become. (36) The moment Malli Singh heard about that treasure, Inflamed with avarice he felt as if stung by a snake. As that poison (of avarice) poured into his system through his ears, How could it be cleansed without the services of a great psychoanalyst. (37) The more he thought about that valuable treasure, The more avaricious he became to acquire that wealth. All the moral scruples did he throw to the winds after hearing, Moving to and fro then did he stand gripped with tension. Shaking and trembling with the unbearable tension, Finally did he proceed to S. Jassa Singh Ramgharia for a bargain. (39) Soon did Jassa Singh observe his younger brother Maali Singh, Rushing in great haste towards his own camp. Either was he coming with the foreboding of some mishap, Or had he found a bigger treasure in the old mansion. (40) Maali Singh narrated the whole account he heard from (Diley Ram), About the huge treasure that he had found there. Never would he (Maali Singh) share that booty with the Ghnnaiyas, So must Jassa Singh suggest a strategy to conceal that treasure. (41)

pages.title: Jassa Singh Wavers Over the Hidden Treasure
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Dileramian contd.
pages.snippet: Jassa Singh initially answers Maali Singh in the language of honour, reminding him that the Ramgharias and Ghanaiyas had pledged to share what they captured together. He warns that wealth gained by breaking one's vow cannot remain clean pro
pages.searchText: Jassa Singh Wavers Over the Hidden Treasure Dileramian contd Episode About Dileramian contd. Jassa Singh initially answers Maali Singh in the language of honour, reminding him that the Ramgharias and Ghanaiyas had pledged to share what they captured together. He warns that wealth gained by breaking one's vow cannot remain clean profit, because the stain of dishonour will cling to it longer than the gold itself. Maali Singh refuses to yield, arguing from possession, kinship, and martial pride instead of from principle. He makes the dispute intensely personal, pressing his brother to choose blood loyalty over the public obligation created by alliance. That pressure changes the moral register of the story. Jassa Singh's hesitation shows that the treasure is already corrupting judgment, and the page ends on the brink of his surrender to a plan he knows is unworthy.

pages.searchText: Though Maali Singh dared not look at him in the eye, Dileramian contd Episode About Dileramian contd. Though Maali Singh dared not look at him in the eye, Jassa Singh forbade his brother from using such words. As Ramgharias and Ghannaiyas had taken vows to share things, How could the Ramgharias live after breaking those vows. (42) The wealth that one earns by backing out of one's vows, Ignominy does it bring besides the loss of such wealth. But never would Maali Singh budge from his new resolve, As his whole attention remained focused on that wealth. (43) Never could he live after sharing it with the Ghanaiyas, Surely would he stake his life for possessing that wealth. Ramgharias had occupied that ancient Mansion first, Though Jassa Singh had brought the Ghanaiyas there later on. (44) Dohra: Then did Jassa Singh tell his younger brother, That he stood by his solemn pledge for the present. In the old Mansion that belonged to Diley Ram. (45) Chaupai: Much did Jassa Singh try to persuade his brother, That transient and transitory was wealth indeed. A large fighting force did the ghanaiyas command, That united would all the Jat Sikhs stand against Ramgharias. (46) Hundred times larger in strength were the Jat Sikh troops. Immensely would these Jat Sikhs harass the Ramgharias, As earlier had they killed a Ramgharia Khushal Singh. (47) That moment had passed with their brother's death: said Maali Sigh, Now nobody would sleep in peace after harming the Ramgharias. Begging his elder brother to let him keep that treasure, Maali Singh assured him of giving good fight to the whole Sikh Panth. (48) Dohra: Then alone would Maali Singh keep his life, If Jassa Singh kept that wealth with themselves. Definitely would Maali Singh die fighting there, If his elder brother shared it with the Ghanaiyas. (49) Chaupai: On the horns of dilemma was Jassa Singh indeed, He could either keep his faith or save his brother. Jassa Singh too got carried away by lust for wealth, As he saved his brother but breached his faith. (50)

pages.title: A Secret Plan Forms Around Dileram's Chest
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Dileramian contd.
pages.snippet: After resisting for a time, Jassa Singh chalked out a strategy that would let the Ramgharias keep the finest treasure out of Ghanaiya hands. The first step is secrecy: those who know the chest's value must be controlled before the wider Kha
pages.searchText: A Secret Plan Forms Around Dileram's Chest Dileramian contd Episode About Dileramian contd. After resisting for a time, Jassa Singh chalked out a strategy that would let the Ramgharias keep the finest treasure out of Ghanaiya hands. The first step is secrecy: those who know the chest's value must be controlled before the wider Khalsa can demand an open accounting. Maali Singh accordingly removes the prized box from Dileram's old house and transfers it into his own camp, but concealment proves harder than seizure. Rumour spreads, tempers flare, and the allied camp fills with accusation as both sides suspect that the richest find has been withheld. When Charat Singh insists that Dileram himself be questioned, the conspirators recognize the danger of truthful testimony. The page thus shifts from hidden theft to the darker question of how witnesses will be silenced.

Then did Jassa Singh chalk out a strategy, That Maali Singh must take over that wealth in secrecy. Diley Ram's son must be taken into confidence about it, That he must not disclose it to the Ghanaiyas. (51) Surely would the Ghanaiyas snatch it after a fight. Thus did Maali Singh depart with this permission, Extremely delighted did he feel in his heart. (52) Keeping awake through out the night (in excitement), Did he enter the old mansion with a force next morning. Distributing the other items after opening the dark cell, Maali Singh did take up the possession of the prized box. (53) Dohra: Declaring that the (prized) box had fallen into his share, Through deceit and force did he justify his claim. Lifting it amidst the noise of claims and counter claims, Despatched he the box of valuables to his own camp. (54) Chaupai: Thereupon arose a hue and cry from both the sides, As the Ghanaiyas arrived with a force to fight. Ramgharias being already prepared for a fight, Things reached a pitch for a violent encounter. (55) While the Ghanaiyas alleged the box contained a huge treasure, The Ramgharias declared nothing worthwhile had come out of it. (56) Thereafter, S. Charat Ssingh entering the fray to decide, He insisted on hearing Diley Ram's version about it. Thereupon, Maali Singh, entertaining a wicked thought, He thought of getting Diley Ram eliminated before hand. (57) Thus did happen as the revered Guru had surmised, Cherishing this evil thought in his heart of hearts, The Ramgharias started thinking of committing this sin. (58) Dohra: Thereafter Maali Singh did think in his mind, Both their honour and wealth being at stake of getting lost, They must take steps to preserve their honour and dignity. (59)

pages.title: Hirday Ram Is Murdered to Bury the Evidence
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Dileramian contd.
pages.snippet: The Ramgharia party now treats murder as the price of preserving stolen wealth. A hired killer is rewarded, and Hirday Ram is lured into a routine scene of grooming and ease rather than into anything that looks openly violent. While attenda
pages.searchText: Hirday Ram Is Murdered to Bury the Evidence Dileramian contd Episode About Dileramian contd. The Ramgharia party now treats murder as the price of preserving stolen wealth. A hired killer is rewarded, and Hirday Ram is lured into a routine scene of grooming and ease rather than into anything that looks openly violent. While attendants are smearing his head with curd and preparing him as if for a bath, he is made vulnerable and then suddenly beheaded. The method matters: the page presents the killing as treachery carried out under false intimacy, not as death in fair combat. The narrator closes with judgment rather than triumph. By choosing murder to protect plunder, the offenders lose both moral standing and any lasting claim on the wealth they tried to hide.

(60) This wicked (Ramgharia) thought of committing such a sin, That sends shivers down one's spine who hears of it. Calling a malcontent, Maali Singh gave him a brief, That he would get rewarded for killing Diley Ram. (61) As his survival would upturn his whole game plan. Briefing how to make preparations for committing this murder, He asked him to behead him after smearing his head with curd. (62) Asking Diley Ram's grandson to pay him a visit, Maali Singh entreated him with a glib talk. Telling him about his having not washed himself for days, He made him wash his body in his own presence. (63) Making him bow down for cleaning his hair with curd, He got his head chopped of with a sword. Making the executioner run away from the scene, He declared the killer had escaped after that murder. (64) That his stone-hearted heart did not feel scared. For this evil deed did the Ramgharia lose everything, Lose indeed they did their faith as well as wealth. (65) For which the Ramgharias had betrayed the Ghanaiyas. Dear devout Sikh readers, listen to the whole account, As Rattan Singh had heard it and narrated it as such. (66) Plenty of wealth fell into Khalsa Panth's hands, Which wiped out all their want and indigence. The way Rattan Singh had heard of Kasur's ransacking, The same way had he recorded for his readers. (67)

pages.title: Bishambhar Dass Challenges the Khalsa in Doaba
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Dileramian contd.
pages.snippet: This hinge page leaves the Dileram affair behind and opens a fresh Doaba confrontation around Bishambhar Dass, the powerful agent of Dina Beg's widow. He appears with troops, artillery, and allied hill support, so the new episode begins not
pages.searchText: Bishambhar Dass Challenges the Khalsa in Doaba Dileramian contd Episode About Dileramian contd. This hinge page leaves the Dileram affair behind and opens a fresh Doaba confrontation around Bishambhar Dass, the powerful agent of Dina Beg's widow. He appears with troops, artillery, and allied hill support, so the new episode begins not with covert theft but with a public challenge over territory and authority. Bishambhar's message is blunt: the Buddha Dal must vacate the Doaba region if it wants peace. Instead of yielding, the Singhs receive the demand in congregation, take offense at the tone of the order, and answer by insisting that he should pay rather than command them. The page therefore functions as a clean narrative reset. One cycle of betrayal closes, and another opens in which control of land, military prestige, and ransom will determine the next clash.

pages.snippet: Bishambhar Dass answers the Sikh demand with defiance, saying ransom will be paid only if the entire Khalsa speaks with one voice and only after the Buddha Dal withdraws. The Singhs reject that posture by recalling that Dina Beg had an agre
pages.searchText: The Buddha Dal Refuses to Quit Doaba the Occupation of Doaba Episode About the Occupation of Doaba Bishambhar Dass answers the Sikh demand with defiance, saying ransom will be paid only if the entire Khalsa speaks with one voice and only after the Buddha Dal withdraws. The Singhs reject that posture by recalling that Dina Beg had an agreement with the Singhs, so Bishambhar has no right to pose as if he alone can rewrite the terms of the region. With negotiation hardening into challenge, both sides are pushed toward a test of nerve. The page stresses that neither camp is willing to budge, and that questions of alliance, honour, and coercion have become inseparable from the coming battle. Emboldened by numbers and support from hill chiefs, Bishambhar moves against a Sikh force that is scattered and comparatively thin on the ground. Even so, the Singhs prepare themselves for the fight instead of retreating from the claim they have made in Doaba.

(10) The Singhs asked Bishambhar Dass to ger ready for a fight, Lest he should blame them for not informing him in advance, (Late) Dina Beg had an agreement with the Singhs, That never would he ever fight with the Singhs. (13) It was a moment for the Kshtriya to suffer ignominy, It was a moment for the Khalsa to gain in strength. Bisambhar Dass wished to face the Singhs in direct encounter. (14) After Dina Beg (the Jalandhar custodian) had expired, Bishambhar Dass had doubled his army in strength. Vainglorious had he become after this increased number, As well as at the support of the forces of the hill chiefs. (15) He found the Singhs scattered on looting errands. Hoping to take over the Singhs camp in their absence, He launched an attack with such aspirations. (16) Like a swarm of locusts did he dispatch his troops, The Singhs, on their side, were already prepared for a fight, Though small in number were they there in their base camp. (17)

pages.title: Bishambhar Falls as Sikh Reinforcements Arrive
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Occupation of Doaba
pages.snippet: The battle first appears to go against the Singhs, whose smaller force is pressed by cavalry and driven back under the weight of the assault. That early advantage collapses when thousands of Singhs arrived after hearing the exchange of fire
pages.searchText: Bishambhar Falls as Sikh Reinforcements Arrive the Occupation of Doaba Episode About the Occupation of Doaba The battle first appears to go against the Singhs, whose smaller force is pressed by cavalry and driven back under the weight of the assault. That early advantage collapses when thousands of Singhs arrived after hearing the exchange of fire, turning what looked like a local setback into a massed Sikh counterattack. Bishambhar realizes too late that the field is slipping from him. He dismounts and stands his ground, but the Singhs close around him, kill him in the fighting, and break the coherence of his army at the moment its confidence should have mattered most. What follows is not a restrained victory but a sweeping seizure of camp wealth, animals, arms, and supplies. The page marks the military defeat of Bishambhar and the immediate conversion of that triumph into material advantage for the Khalsa.

Many a weapon did some of the Singhs pick up, Thus did they get rid of their endemic destitution. (24) The heavy artillery cannons they did not carry, Setting these on fire there and then in the field. It was in the year eighteen hundred and eighteen, That the Singhs killed Bishambhar and looted his treasure. (25)

pages.title: The Khalsa Consolidates Its Hold on Doaba
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Occupation of Doaba
pages.snippet: With Bishambhar defeated, the poem shifts from battlefield action to the political work of settlement. After collective resolve and prayer, the Singhs spread out to occupied villages in the Doaba region, turning a single victory into a broa
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Consolidates Its Hold on Doaba the Occupation of Doaba Episode About the Occupation of Doaba With Bishambhar defeated, the poem shifts from battlefield action to the political work of settlement. After collective resolve and prayer, the Singhs spread out to occupied villages in the Doaba region, turning a single victory into a broader pattern of local control. Possession is shown taking several forms at once: some settlements invite Sikh protection, some are retained through old relationships, and others are held because no one can dislodge the first claimant. Where rival claims arise, misl authority begins to matter more than raw momentum, because disputes must now be judged rather than merely fought. The page therefore explains how plunder matures into governance. Revenue, recognized possession, and expanding contingents show the Buddha Dal becoming not just a raiding force but a power able to stabilize and enlarge its own territorial order.

pages.snippet: Episode 147 opens by turning to the Taruna Dal, which had grown wealthy after the sack of Kasur and then heard that Bishambhar Das had been killed and the Doaba occupied by the Buddha Dal. Since the Buddha Dal had taken Doaba alone, the Taruna Dal wondered whether to fight them a
pages.searchText: Taruna Dal Misls Move toward Lahore, Nakka, and Multan Further Occupation of More Territory Episode 147 opens by turning to the Taruna Dal, which had grown wealthy after the sack of Kasur and then heard that Bishambhar Das had been killed and the Doaba occupied by the Buddha Dal. Since the Buddha Dal had taken Doaba alone, the Taruna Dal wondered whether to fight them as a united group or seek another opportunity elsewhere. Both factions envied the other’s gains, yet the narrative says each received what destiny gave. The Taruna Dal saw the region around Lahore lying open, sent three misls ahead and two toward Majha and the hills, and the Singhs of Majha began establishing control in their own villages. The Nakai contingent moved toward Nakka and the Bhangis toward Multan, while S. Charat Singh focused on Lahore’s outskirts. He occupied scattered pockets, placed a post at Gujranwala, and remained in long conflict with the Bhangi chiefs who held territory on both sides of the river.
