pages.title: Taruna Dal Pressure Leaves Lahore Exposed
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About the Taruna Dal . T
pages.snippet: This page closes the Taruna Dal episode by explaining how Sikh expansion after the Lahore-side raids kept widening the zone of Mughal weakness. So much land and revenue passed beyond effective control that the Lahore administration could no
pages.searchText: Taruna Dal Pressure Leaves Lahore Exposed the Taruna Dal . T Episode About the Taruna Dal . T This page closes the Taruna Dal episode by explaining how Sikh expansion after the Lahore-side raids kept widening the zone of Mughal weakness. So much land and revenue passed beyond effective control that the Lahore administration could no longer collect revenue with confidence outside the city itself. The political consequence is immediate. What had looked like scattered Sikh mobility now appears as a structural threat to Lahore's ability to govern, punish, and tax the countryside that sustained it. The page therefore serves as a bridge into the next confrontation. Ahmad Shah's side responds by sending stronger commanders into Punjab, preparing the entry of Sar Buland Khan and a more formal contest with the Khalsa.

pages.searchText: The Nawab Besieges Gujranwala Both Budha Dal and Tapuna Dal Episode About Both Budha Dal and Tapuna Dal . Episode 148 opens by showing how Sikh territorial gains in Doaba and around Gujranwala unsettle Lahore's governor. In anger and alarm, he besieged Gujranwala with artillery, hoping to break Charat Singh's growing position before it could attract wider Khalsa support. Yet the siege is not as secure as it appears from the outside. Sikh sympathizers and paid troops within the Nawab's own camp begin to think in terms of defection, coordination, and the advantages of aiding the besieged rather than the besieger. The result is a tense reversal of perspective. What looks like a Mughal enclosure is already becoming a trap for the force that laid it.

pages.searchText: The Nawab Flees and Charat Singh Grows in Strength Both Budha Dal and Tapuna Dal Episode About Both Budha Dal and Tapuna Dal . The siege unravels when reports spread that a larger Sikh host is approaching the field. Faced with warnings of an approaching Khalsa force, the Nawab loses nerve, and the cohesion of his camp begins to dissolve before the feared reinforcement even fully arrives. Night flight, confusion, and opportunistic looting follow. The same encirclement meant to crush Charat Singh instead enriches him, raises his standing, and helps extend Sikh influence across a wider northern belt. By the end of the page, the episode has shifted from siege survival to strategic expansion. Charat Singh emerges not merely as a defender of Gujranwala but as a chief whose success now draws wealth, fame, and new territory.

This transition page moves into the Sar Buland Khan episode by following Charat Singh toward the Rohtas position. Charat Singh crossed the Jhelum, assessed the fort and its defenders, and then used feigned withdrawal and altered movement to make the Pathans misread his intent. That deception matters more than brute force. By returning through another approach and closing in before the garrison can reset itself, he turns the confidence of the fort into vulnerability and panic. The page therefore introduces the capture sequence through cunning rather than frontal assault. Control of timing, routes, and perception becomes the Sikh advantage before the fort is fully overrun.

pages.searchText: Sar Buland Khan Submits Under Pressure The Capture of Sir Buland Khan Episode About The Capture of Sir Buland Khan Once the position is lost, Sar Buland Khan abandons the hope of recovering it by force and turns to negotiation. Charat Singh's advance and seizure of the surrounding advantage make clear that resistance now risks humiliation without any realistic path to victory. Envoys pass between the camps while the Sikhs tighten their hold, confiscate wealth, and treat the captive commander as a figure whose status itself can be monetized. In that atmosphere, a huge ransom was demanded, turning the khan's surrender into a public measure of Sikh leverage. The page thus joins military success to political theatre. Captivity, tribute, and the visible reduction of a major Mughal figure all deepen Charat Singh's authority.

pages.searchText: Sar Buland Khan Is Released and Sirhind Comes Into View The Capture of Sir Buland Khan Episode About The Capture of Sir Buland Khan This hinge page first lets Sar Buland Khan plead for subordinate status and mercy rather than continued imprisonment. Charat Singh answers from a position of sovereign confidence, stressing that even Ahmad Shah's uncle had been taken and that Sikh power now speaks in its own right rather than as a client of older courts. After that display of superiority, clemency follows. Provisions are given for the journey, safe onward movement is allowed, and the released noble becomes a witness to Charat Singh's prestige rather than a martyr to it. The page then pivots decisively toward Sirhind. A new military problem emerges, and the poem begins gathering the forces, routes, and intentions that will culminate in the next major Sikh strike.

pages.searchText: The Khalsa Moves Against an Exposed Sirhind Occupation of Sirhind And Slaughter of AN Khan Episode About Occupation of Sirhind And Slaughter of AN Khan The Sirhind episode opens with timely intelligence rather than immediate combat. News spreads that Sirhind was exposed because its officer was away on revenue collection, and that temporary weakness invites a rapid Khalsa move before the city can be properly secured again. The Singhs respond through consultation and collective resolve, treating the moment as one that must be seized rather than merely observed. Their decision turns scattered information into operational momentum. On the other side, warning reaches Zain Khan and forces him into anxious movement. The episode begins, therefore, with a race between Sikh initiative and Mughal recovery.

pages.searchText: Zain Khan Moves Quietly While the Singhs Close In Occupation of Sirhind And Slaughter of AN Khan Episode About Occupation of Sirhind And Slaughter of AN Khan Trying to avoid entrapment, Zain Khan advances carefully and suppresses the noise that would normally announce a commander on the move. Keeping all his war drums in the rear guard, he hopes to slip toward Sirhind before the Sikhs can concentrate fully against him. That caution does not save him, because intelligence passes quickly among the Singh contingents. Majhail and Buddha Dal forces converge, musket fire opens, and the conversation among the Sikhs hardens into a common resolve that Zain Khan must be stopped outside the city. The page is therefore about pursuit under pressure. One side relies on stealth and evasion; the other turns speed and memory of past wrongs into a tightening net.

The location where wounded Zain Khan had fallen becomes identifiable through the cries of his own men, allowing the Singhs to press in and complete the collapse of organized resistance around him. Even in victory, the narrative distinguishes between enemies who keep fighting and those who submit. Pathans who lay down arms are spared, while abandoned stores, animals, treasure, and artillery pass into Sikh hands. This page closes the pursuit and opens the next act. With Zain Khan dead near Sirhind, the destruction of the city itself becomes the looming subject.

pages.title: Sirhind Is Marked for Destruction
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About Sirhind
pages.snippet: The opening of the new Sirhind sequence explains why the city has become a moral target as well as a military one. The Singhs remember that the Guru’s young sons had been killed here, and that the city’s name remains bound to their martyrdo
pages.searchText: Sirhind Is Marked for Destruction Sirhind Another Episode About Sirhind The opening of the new Sirhind sequence explains why the city has become a moral target as well as a military one. The Singhs remember that the Guru’s young sons had been killed here, and that the city’s name remains bound to their martyrdom and the oppression associated with their killers. That memory transforms vengeance into collective policy. Sirhind is not merely to be raided but to be humbled, broken, and symbolically undone so that its punishment answers a long-carried grievance. The page therefore frames the coming destruction as deliberate historical reckoning. What follows will be narrated not as random looting, but as the execution of justice remembered across generations.

pages.searchText: The Khalsa Marks the Sahibzadas' Martyrdom Site Sirhind Another Episode About Sirhind This transition page carries the narrative from the destruction of Sirhind into a work of remembrance. After identifying the places tied to the younger Sahibzadas, the Khalsa agrees that a single memorial shrine should be established so the memory of their martyrdom will remain embodied in a public sacred site. Local elders are called to indicate the exact place and to recount what happened there in earlier days. The page therefore replaces the heat of battle with communal recollection, testimony, and the desire to anchor grief in durable form. It also opens the next episode by showing that post-victory authority includes the power to consecrate memory. The Khalsa does not only punish Sirhind; it begins shaping how that punishment and martyrdom will be remembered.

pages.searchText: A Memorial Is Proposed at the Precise Martyrdom Site Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind Episode About Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind Episode 152 continues by describing how the aftermath of the Sahibzadas’ killing lingers in local memory and conscience. Ordinary consolations fail, and the narrative pushes toward a remedy that acknowledges the sanctity of the place where the crime was committed. The solution offered is explicit: a memorial be built at the precise place where the Guru's sons were put to death. The page imagines the site not as abandoned ground but as a kept, illuminated, and attended place of reverence. In this way the memorial becomes both historical witness and devotional practice. The city that carried the stain of the killing is asked to preserve the very location it once tried to erase.

pages.searchText: The Panth Furnishes the Sirhind Memorial Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind Episode About Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind Once the plan is accepted, the Khalsa moves from proposal to institution. The Panth gathered there in ceremony, turning the site into a formal space of assembly rather than a merely remembered ruin. The page describes the furnishing of that space with a platform, canopy, lit lamps, recitation, and appointed service. Weapons and devotional music alike help frame the memorial as a living extension of Guru-centered presence within the Panth. What emerges is not a simple monument but a functioning shrine. Ritual, attendance, and endowed support together make remembrance part of daily discipline rather than a one-time gesture.

pages.searchText: The Memorial Account Closes and Sirhind's Hidden Wealth Reappears Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind Episode About Construction of A Memorial at Sirhind This page closes the memorial episode by stressing the purpose of written preservation. The account is said to have been set down so the Khalsa could hear, read and pray at the shrine, giving the memorial both literary and devotional continuity. From there the poem pivots into a new Sirhind-centered episode focused on remaining forts, buried treasure, and unfinished seizure. The city has already been judged and damaged, yet the search for what lies hidden beneath its structures shows that conquest is not materially complete. The result is another hinge in the broader sequence. A site of memory remains behind, while the narrative moves back toward possession, excavation, and the struggle over what Sirhind still contains.

The Khalsa chiefs first decide that the stronghold must be secured before its wealth is fully apportioned. In that setting Bhai Buddha Singh emerges as the key actor, negotiating for possession while others weigh whether purchase, seizure, and political necessity can be separated at all. The page underscores the scale of his payment and ambition: He had paid eighty thousand rupees in public view, with further maneuvering needed to clinch control. Yet the acquisition is darkened by cruelty toward the women of the fort, so possession arrives with both status and curse. This makes the page morally unstable in an important way. Success is real, but it is narrated through actions that also seed future decline and disrepute.

With Sirhind broken, the Khalsa must decide what its next march should be. The debate reveals diverging strategic instincts, the clearest of them being that Buddha Dal Singhs opined that the Khalsa must march towards Delhi in order to exploit momentum against major centers of power. Other factions imagine different horizons, including renewed pressure toward Lahore and other regional objectives. The page thus turns from a single victorious action into a debate about how a victorious confederacy should spend its energy. It also begins the movement into Episode 154, where territorial assignment and onward campaigning matter more than Sirhind alone. Victory produces not unity of destination, but a widening field of opportunity and disagreement.

After further raiding and occupation to the south and west, the force returned toward Jind and Karnal, showing that movement through the region is now tied to revenue, settlement, and political ordering rather than only to battle. The page then turns to apportionment: towns, tracts, and spheres of influence are distributed among recognized houses and lineages, including those connected to Baba Phool and Bhai Bhagtu. Settlement of Brar claims and acceptance of Sikh discipline become part of the same reorganization. By the end, the narrative presents Khalsa power as administrative as well as military. Forts are demolished, tribute is extracted, and old local structures are re-sorted under new authority.

pages.searchText: Malerkotla Is Spared Within a Shared Khalsa Order Occupation And Handing Over of Towns to the Descendents of Bhai Bhagtu And Baba Phool Episode About Occupation And Handing Over of Towns to the Descendents of Bhai Bhagtu And Baba Phool This page opens with scriptural praise for the transforming company of the saintly, then applies that moral frame to policy. Muslim residents and chiefs remain within territories now shaped by Sikh power, but the Pathans of Malerkotla are explicitly spared in keeping with the Guru’s remembered word and the distinctive moral status attached to that house. From there the poem moves into negotiated governance: tribute, shared tracts, and coordinated misl control replace indiscriminate devastation. Even where conquest has widened, not every place is treated as a target for the same punishment. The result is a more nuanced picture of Khalsa sovereignty. Mercy, obligation, common territorial arrangements, and alliance all sit alongside the force that made such arrangements possible.

pages.searchText: Khalsa Occupation on Both Sides of Lahore Occupation And Handing Over of Towns to the Descendents of Bhai Bhagtu And Baba Phool Episode About Occupation And Handing Over of Towns to the Descendents of Bhai Bhagtu And Baba Phool The page closes the previous account by saying that Bhai Bhagtu’s descendants, the people of Mehraj, Ranghars, and Pathans kept some land common so Khalsa forces could rest on the road to Delhi. If one Misl tried to seize that shared land, two others would oppose it, and local Muslim chiefs learned how gifts or ransom could divide the Khalsa Misls. The narrator adds that he is reporting what he heard from his father, who had been close to the Khalsa Panth. Episode 155 then begins: five Khalsa Misls stayed on one side, five crossed beyond Lahore, and Majha remained common because it surrounded the sacred shrine at Amritsar. The Taruna Dal then turned back toward Lahore and encircled the city, throwing Lahore into panic. After the Khalsa had taken Zain Khan’s Sirhind territory, the Gilja Pathans feared that the whole Khalsa would attack and concluded that they could survive only by fleeing.

Without deserting will they not be able to survive, Such were the thoughts which crossed their minds. (4)

This page opens the episode of Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Shahid, introducing him through verse headings and the first lines of his sakhi. The narrative presents Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh at Amritsar as a blue-clad warrior of disciplined conduct, daily practice, and readiness for martyrdom. The page establishes the episode boundary and identifies Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh’s role at Amritsar, with source page 687 remaining linked for provenance.

At the sacred shrine at Amritsar. (1) Strapping young and a greater warrior was he, Dressed in blue robes, of immaculate conduct was he. A dose of cannabis would he partake every morning, Early in the morning would he take a bath, Armaments of steel would he pay obeisance to, Those armaments would he carry after worshipping these. (3) A rosary made of steel beads and steel would he wear, With bracelets of steel would he adorn his wrists. Protection of these steel armaments would he seek. (4) Undergarments made out of one and quarter yard of cloth he would wear. With a steel armour would he cover his whole body, A daily religious congregation would this Nihang hold. (5) He alone deserves to be called a Nihang?, Who remains indifferent to joys and sorrows. He alone is worthy of being called highly detached, Whose constitution remains unaffected by pain or comfort. (6) He who is firm in conviction, character and meditation, He who is generous in charity and perfect in bravery. He who remains engrossed in his own regimen, Whenever an opportunity for waging a war arises, Never does he shirk from making a supreme sacrifice. Readily does he offer himself to combat that threat. (8)

pages.title: Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh as Warrior and Disciple
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: This page sketches Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh as a saint-soldier whose devotion and courage were already famous in the Panth. Wherever there is a war being waged, he is described as the Singh who moves first beneath the Khalsa standard and answ
pages.searchText: Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh as Warrior and Disciple Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh This page sketches Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh as a saint-soldier whose devotion and courage were already famous in the Panth. Wherever there is a war being waged, he is described as the Singh who moves first beneath the Khalsa standard and answers the beat of the war drum without hesitation. The narrative then grounds him in lineage and place. From his revered hands had he received Khandey-ki-Pahul from Bhai Mani Singh, he came from one village named Leel near Khemkaran, and within the Akal Takht premises did he keep his seat while facing the Guru's court in disciplined service. By ending with these details, the page prepares the reader for the coming ordeal. Gurbakhsh Singh is not introduced as a reckless fighter, but as a deeply formed Sikh whose spiritual discipline, battlefield readiness, and public honor explain why he will soon stand at the center of the Panth's response to Abdali's violence.

pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Wherever there is a war being waged, Wherever a beat of the war drum is heard, First among the front runners would he be to reach. (9) There had been one renowned Sikh martyr Bhai Mani Singh, From his revered hands had be received Khandey-k
pages.searchText: Wherever there is a war being waged, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Wherever there is a war being waged, Wherever a beat of the war drum is heard, First among the front runners would he be to reach. (9) There had been one renowned Sikh martyr Bhai Mani Singh, From his revered hands had be received Khandey-ki-Pahul. There was one village named Leel near Khemkaran, From that village in the Majha region did he hail. (10) Dohra: He would always be the first to move his camp, After him did the other Singhs make a move. Wherever he stood with his regimental banner, There did the others stand behind his banner. (11) That faced the sacred shrine Sri Darbar Sahib in Amritsar. Ever ready for waging a war did his contingent remain, Akal! Akal! They kept on reciting in meditation. (12) Listen to the heroic efforts which he did make, And the way he was instrumental in decimating the Pathans. The way the Gilja Pathan forces arrived from the other side, Suraj Mal* who had been the ruler of Bharatpur, City of Agra had he ransacked and occupied. All the Mughal treasures also had he unearthed. (14) Even then the Mughal treasury could not be exhausted. With Najiba Ruhela? had he come into conflict, Somehow had he himself perished in war. (15) Dohra: For the aim of settling scores with his father's killers, A massive force had his son managed to keep. Chaupai: Jawahar Mal, the Jat ruler, laid a siege to Delhi, Najiba Ruhela was thus confined inside the city. As the Ruhela chief felt the noose tightening around him, A petition for reinforcements did he send to Kabul. (17)

pages.title: Panic in the Panth and the Gathering at Akal Bunga
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: The crisis worsens after Abdali is summoned with promises of money and support for the enemies of the Sikhs. As the rumors spread, families of the Sikhs started deserting in panic, and suffering follows every path: some flee toward the hill
pages.searchText: Panic in the Panth and the Gathering at Akal Bunga Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The crisis worsens after Abdali is summoned with promises of money and support for the enemies of the Sikhs. As the rumors spread, families of the Sikhs started deserting in panic, and suffering follows every path: some flee toward the hills, some hide in forests, and others remain exposed to plunder and loss. Against that fear, the Khalsa gathers itself in prayer and counsel. Rehras verses were recited in Khalsa congregation held at Akal Bunga near the Akal Takht, and the Singhs first see their families to safety before turning to the question of how the Panth should answer this danger. Out of that assembly Gurbakhsh Singh raises the demand for true sacrifice. He asks whether there is any one such Singh among the Khalsa Panth who can offer his life in a way that will bring divine favor upon the community and steady the hearts of those who remain.

pages.title: Having committed to pay three lakh rupees as ransom,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Having committed to pay three lakh rupees as ransom, Ahmed Shah Abdali's forces arrived for his support. As rumours of Ahmed Shah Abdali's arrival spread, Families of the Sikhs started deserting in panick. (18) Those who rushed towards the
pages.searchText: Having committed to pay three lakh rupees as ransom, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Having committed to pay three lakh rupees as ransom, Ahmed Shah Abdali's forces arrived for his support. As rumours of Ahmed Shah Abdali's arrival spread, Families of the Sikhs started deserting in panick. (18) Those who rushed towards the hills for shelter, By the hill people were they looted and plundered. Those who tried to hide among the wilds and rivers bed, By the wild animals and decoits were they devoured. (19) Those who dared to stay in their own houses, By their adversaries were they got arrested. Wherever the Singhs arrived after deserting their homes, To many hardships and tribulations were they subjected. (20) Those who escaped into the forests and wilds, (Truly) did they become homeless at the mercy of others. As Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh heard these heart-rending tales, (Seriously) did he contemplate on the entire situation. (21) Rehras verses (Evening prayer) were recited in Khalsa congregation, It was held at Akal Bunga near the Akal Takht. The caravan of Sikh families was made to depart after a resolution, Khalsa force, without the families, remained stationed there. (22) Thereupon Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh made a declaration; Was there any one such Singh among the Khalsa Panth, Who, with his supreme sacrifice, could invoke Divine intervention, Whose invocation could get answered by the Divine Lord. (23) Must he be firm of conviction, character and meditation, A true follower of the Sikh code of conduct he must be. For community's welfare must he be ready to sacrifice, Like (Martyr) Taru Singh must he annihilate the Mughals. (24) Hearing this declaration, the congregated Singhs replied, None else could exceed him in character and piety. Who else but he had the power to move heavens, His prayer alone could reach the Divine Court. (25) Hearing this, Gurbax Singh accepted the congregation's will, Before the Khalsa Panth's verdict, did he bow down, Presenting himself with folded hands before the Khalsa Panth, Readily did he agree to wed the beauteous death. (26)

pages.title: Volunteers for the Fatal Wedding of Martyrdom
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: The congregation answers Gurbakhsh Singh's challenge by recognizing both his resolve and the gravity of the moment. He asks who would accompany him on this fatal wedding expedition, and the image of martyrdom as a wedding with death turns t
pages.searchText: Volunteers for the Fatal Wedding of Martyrdom Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The congregation answers Gurbakhsh Singh's challenge by recognizing both his resolve and the gravity of the moment. He asks who would accompany him on this fatal wedding expedition, and the image of martyrdom as a wedding with death turns the coming battle into a consciously embraced offering rather than a desperate last stand. The Singhs respond immediately. Many a Singh volunteered, bowing at his feet and declaring that they too were ready to give their heads, for by sacrificing their lives would they be wedding death in the Guru's cause and making good on the ideals taught in the Panth. The page also frames their zeal within scriptural and historical memory. Such a description has been given in Chandi Astotar, and as news spreads that the Singhs had assembled at Amritsar, the contrast sharpens between those inspired to heroic sacrifice and those whose weaker hearts begin to flee from Abdali's advance.

pages.title: Was there any other Singh steeped in Gurmat ideology,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Was there any other Singh steeped in Gurmat ideology, Who would accompany him on this fatal wedding expedition, Who would act as the Bestman to the bridegroom. (27) Hearing this, many a Singh volunteered to pick up the gauntlet, With many a
pages.searchText: Was there any other Singh steeped in Gurmat ideology, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Was there any other Singh steeped in Gurmat ideology, Who would accompany him on this fatal wedding expedition, Who would act as the Bestman to the bridegroom. (27) Hearing this, many a Singh volunteered to pick up the gauntlet, With many a supplication did they stand before him. A solemn declaration did those volunteers make, That they were too keen to follow his instructions. (28) Many more volunteers lined up with the earlier volunteers, They were ready to join as wedding guests on this fatal expedition. To those fellow volunteers thus did he remark, For their noble gesture would they be rewarded in the next life. (29) By sacrificing their lives would they be wedding death, With many a kingdom would they be endowed. The volunteers who would accompany him on this wedding expedition, One who confronts and faces death in war bravely, Such a description has been given in Chandi Astotar, By the sacred lips of Sri Guru Gobind Singh himself. (31) Whosoever offers his head on a platter to the Divine power, As a great sovereign is he born in his next life. Rightly so would it happen as he had stated, Exactly the same words of the Guru did Gurbakhsh Singh repeat. (32) As he wished to proceed to Delhi from there. Hearing that the Singhs had assembled at Amitsar, Then he wished to attack them (before proceeding to Delhi). (33) Hearing this, many a coward took to their heels, Them Gurbakhsh Singh asked to make a departure. The younger Singhs were devoted to the Guru's cause, Some of these did surely stay to make sacrifices. (34) Some of them had dressed themselves in blue robes, Some others had donned themselves in white or saffron robes. After a dose of cannabis they stood ready for a fight, At guard they stood in front of Akal Takht and Darbar Sahib. (35)

pages.title: The Martyr Procession Is Prepared Like a Wedding
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Once the volunteers are chosen, the Singhs begin to prepare as if for both battle and ceremony. Ever ready were they to make a sacrifice, so they arm themselves carefully, cleanse their minds through prayer, and transform their readiness fo
pages.searchText: The Martyr Procession Is Prepared Like a Wedding Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Once the volunteers are chosen, the Singhs begin to prepare as if for both battle and ceremony. Ever ready were they to make a sacrifice, so they arm themselves carefully, cleanse their minds through prayer, and transform their readiness for death into a disciplined liturgy of the Panth. The rites are explicitly devotional. Gurbani did they recite from Sri Guru Granth Sahib, they complete five verses of Anand Sahib, and sacred food is distributed in a mood that resembles both a congregation and a wedding feast arranged for a blessed occasion. Gurbakhsh Singh is then dressed and honored as the bridegroom of martyrdom. From the holy Darbar Sahib was he presented a garland, while perfume, weapons, and song combine to send him forth with joy rather than despair.

pages.title: Those addicted to opium took their daily dose of dope,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Those addicted to opium took their daily dose of dope, Intoxicated they made haste for a show down. Ever ready were they to make a sacrifice for the noble cause, In full battle gear and readiness did they stand. (36) Attired in Khalsa robes
pages.searchText: Those addicted to opium took their daily dose of dope, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Those addicted to opium took their daily dose of dope, Intoxicated they made haste for a show down. Ever ready were they to make a sacrifice for the noble cause, In full battle gear and readiness did they stand. (36) Attired in Khalsa robes and fully armed with arms, In complete readiness did they stand at guard. Gurbani did they recite from Sri Guru Granth Sahib, With devotion at the lotus feet of Sri Guru Nanak. (37) Like a wedding feast arranged on a happy occasion, With perfumes did these sacrificial Singhs embalm their bodies, As women folk scrub bridegroom-to-be's body with a perfumed dough. To the accompaniment of music did they sing sacred verses, As women folk sang paens in praise of the bride-to-be. (39) Then did S. Gurbakhsh Singh have a dip in the sacred pool, Thereafter did he sit on a platform at the Akal Takht. In fascinating brand new robes was he dressed, Tightly did he don a turban on his head, A small dagger did he don in between the Ouoits, There it stood atop his turban like a bridegroom's plume. (41) From the holy Darbar Sahib was he presented a garland, Highly bedecked it was with fragrant flowers. With a prayer on lips did he place it on his head, Steel bracelets around wrists and a garland around the neck, His sword did he carry on his (mighty) shoulder. From the ramparts of the Akal Takht did he come down, As he moved towards the holy Harmandir Sahib, With folded hands did he bow down to the Guru. His companions kept reciting the Gurbani verses, As felicitations were being sung on a felicitous occasion. (44)

pages.title: Prayer at Harmandir Sahib and the March to Battle
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: The ceremonial movement now becomes a public procession. Carrying the Khalsa standard a Singh moved in front, the war drums sounded, and gifts were distributed like alms from a wedding household as the jatha advanced through the sacred prec
pages.searchText: Prayer at Harmandir Sahib and the March to Battle Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The ceremonial movement now becomes a public procession. Carrying the Khalsa standard a Singh moved in front, the war drums sounded, and gifts were distributed like alms from a wedding household as the jatha advanced through the sacred precincts. The heart of the page is the prayer. Standing before the Guru in Harmandir Sahib, Gurbakhsh Singh bows, circles the shrine, and asks that his faith in Guru's ideology be vindicated so that his death may truly serve the Panth rather than merely display personal bravery. At the same time the enemy prepares in its own way. Gilja Pathans had covered themselves with steel helmets and armours, yet among the Singhs each one promised to sacrifice ahead of the other, turning the contrast between heavily protected soldiers and lightly equipped martyrs into a test of conviction.

pages.title: Carrying the Khalsa standard a Singh moved in front,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Carrying the Khalsa standard a Singh moved in front, War drums were beaten as the procession moved. Whatever money he had he gave in charity there, As bridegroom's parents dole out money to the menials. (45) Much in the manner of a tree wor
pages.searchText: Carrying the Khalsa standard a Singh moved in front, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Carrying the Khalsa standard a Singh moved in front, War drums were beaten as the procession moved. Whatever money he had he gave in charity there, As bridegroom's parents dole out money to the menials. (45) Much in the manner of a tree worship Singhs worshipped the Khalsa flag, A little bit of money was given in charity thereafter as well. As the procession of Singhs reached the main entrance, With bowed heads did they pay their obeisance. (46) Moving ahead as he entered the sanctum-sanctorum, A shower of floral petals was then made on him, By his companions who stood all around there. (47) Dohra: Standing before the Guru in Harmandir Sahib, Thus did Gurbakhsh pray before the Guru. Might his faith in Guru's ideology be vindicated, Might he be able to sacrifice as a devout Sikh. (48) Chaupai: On the other side had Gilja Pathans made elaborate preparations, As they had heard about concentration of Singhs in large numbers. Gilja Pathans had covered themselves with steel helmets and armours, But Singhs had hardly any armours to protect themselves. (49) Every eguipment had Gilja Pathans carried to kill the Singhs, Every preparation had the Singhs made to make a sacrifice. Long range deadly armours had the Pathans carried, With arrows, muskets and sophisticated carbines were they armed. (50) Ordinary weapons had the Singh carried in their hands, Many a Singh just carried club grinders, On the front line did they stand to make a supreme sacrifice. (51) Many a Singh were mounted on their horses, Each one vied with the other to be ahead of each other. Each one promised to sacrifice ahead of the other. (52) Did he sit at the Akal Takht. At the prospect of wedding a beautiful bride. (53)

pages.title: The Wedding Songs Give Way to Battle at Dawn
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Even on the threshold of combat the Singhs continue to surround Gurbakhsh Singh with devotional music. Gurbani verses were sung to the accompaniment of music, and the wedding imagery remains deliberate: the page insists that martyrdom shoul
pages.searchText: The Wedding Songs Give Way to Battle at Dawn Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Even on the threshold of combat the Singhs continue to surround Gurbakhsh Singh with devotional music. Gurbani verses were sung to the accompaniment of music, and the wedding imagery remains deliberate: the page insists that martyrdom should be entered with the same solemn joy that accompanies a sacred union. That mood shifts with the first light. With the break of dawn did the Pathans arrive, and Gurbakhsh Singh answers not with fear but with exhortation, reminding the Panth that retreat would stain their honor when the Guru's cause has already summoned them forward. His challenge is phrased as a rule for conduct in battle: A step taken ahead upholds a Singh's dignity. Hearing these words, the Singhs jumped all around, rushing toward the enemy with the eagerness of hunters closing upon deer and with death already accepted as their companion.

pages.title: Gurbani verses were sung to the accompaniment of music.
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Gurbani verses were sung to the accompaniment of music. Ghorian verses from Guru Granth were recited, More Gurbani verses were recited on demand. (54) With the break of dawn did the Pathans arrive, For them were the Singhs standing in wait.
pages.searchText: Gurbani verses were sung to the accompaniment of music. Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Gurbani verses were sung to the accompaniment of music. Ghorian verses from Guru Granth were recited, More Gurbani verses were recited on demand. (54) With the break of dawn did the Pathans arrive, For them were the Singhs standing in wait. Many a horse-mounted Singhs did fight in front, Many a Singh did fight as they stood on earth. (55) How could a few Singhs fight the Mughal hordes? Those martyred got wedded to fairies in heaven, Those still alive rushed to wage a war. (56) From all sides did the Pathans encircle the Singhs, Must the Singhs step forward to make sacrifices? (57) Dohra: A step taken ahead upholds a Singh's dignity, A step withdrawn compromises his honour. When an enemy places a sword on a Singh's head, Chaupai: Hearing these words, the Singhs jumped all around, Like a lion they rushed after herds of deer-like Pathans. For sacrificing themselves were the Singhs prepared, For remaining alive had the Singhs never wished. (59) Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh asked Singhs to rush forward, Sacrifice they must to cross the ocean of life. To the heavens whosoever wished to depart, With death disguised as fairy must he elope. (60) Whosoever wished to serve the cause of Khalsa Panth, With death disguised as fairy must he elope. In a Khalsa household would he be reborn, A sovereign would he become to kill the Mughals. (61) Thereupon, the Singhs remonstrated with the Nihang, They were the wedding guests and he the bridegroom. To the heavens would they surely follow his footsteps, His sovereignty would they share in the next life. (62)

pages.title: Gurbakhsh Singh Rejects Heaven and Charges the Enemy
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Here the page gathers the inner meaning of the vow into a concise declaration. Company of the Khalsa is what they craved for, not the rewards of paradise, so martyrdom is presented as fidelity to the Panth rather than as a private search fo
pages.searchText: Gurbakhsh Singh Rejects Heaven and Charges the Enemy Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Here the page gathers the inner meaning of the vow into a concise declaration. Company of the Khalsa is what they craved for, not the rewards of paradise, so martyrdom is presented as fidelity to the Panth rather than as a private search for heavenly compensation. That conviction immediately translates into conduct under fire. Not a single Singh turned his back from the fight, even as many a shot did they fire on Singhs from their muskets and the pressure of the Gilja attack grew heavier around Gurbakhsh Singh's small band. Gurbakhsh Singh responds by moving from exhortation to direct action. Gurbakhsh Singh threw away his own shield so that he could strike more freely, showing that he seeks a face-to-face death in combat and not merely survival beneath defensive cover.

pages.title: For the heavens, they had no attraction,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: For the heavens, they had no attraction, Company of the Khalsa is what they craved for. Of the fighting and getting killed were they not scared, Fight with the Mughals was what they yearned for. (63) Thereupon, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh made a
pages.searchText: For the heavens, they had no attraction, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh For the heavens, they had no attraction, Company of the Khalsa is what they craved for. Of the fighting and getting killed were they not scared, Fight with the Mughals was what they yearned for. (63) Thereupon, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh made a statement, The same solemn vow had he taken as well. Thereafter his death, would he be reborn in a Khalsa household, Then Gurbakhsh Singh did again tell his companions, In the meantime, as more Gilja Pathans came attacking, The Singhs dug their heels and kept on fighting and killing. Not a single Singh turned his back from the fight, Ahead and ahead did the Singhs keep advancing. (66) Then did Gurbakhsh Singh exhorted his fellow Singhs, Let not the Mughals escape from his brave companions, A war for defending their faith and ideology must they wage, Their swords must they wield after dismounting from their horses. (67) The Gilja Pathans failed to comprehend the Singh's words, Many a shot did they fire on Singhs from their muskets. Many a Singh were hit by those bullets fired, Many of them were those who were nearest to Gurbakhsh Singh. (68) Then Gurbakhsh Singh picked up his own sword, He rushed forward and hit a Gilja Pathan. It pierced the Pathan's heart after cutting his armour, As the Singhs advanced further making a dash, With the shields did the Pathans cover their faces. Gurbakhsh Singh threw away his own shield from his hands, Why should a Singh take shelter behind his shield. As the Gilja Pathans attacked with their swords brandished high, The Singh would stand straight to take their blows. (71)

pages.title: Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh’s Martyrdom
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Gurbakhsh Singh and the Singhs did not blink, bow their heads, or look behind; they kept moving forward until the Pathans fled, unable to withstand the Singhs’ sword blows. From a distance the Pathans fired guns and arrows, wounding him so
pages.searchText: Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh’s Martyrdom Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Gurbakhsh Singh and the Singhs did not blink, bow their heads, or look behind; they kept moving forward until the Pathans fled, unable to withstand the Singhs’ sword blows. From a distance the Pathans fired guns and arrows, wounding him so badly that the wounds could not be counted. Shots cut through his flesh and bones, yet he did not accept defeat or show pain. Blood poured from his body like oil from a press and water from a pierced pouch, but Gurbakhsh Singh kept moving forward rather than turn back. As his strength failed, he prayed that the Guru preserve his honor and accept his martyrdom. More Gilja Pathans arrived, lifted Singh bodies on spears, and Gurbakhsh Singh struck again, cutting through lances while refusing to chase fugitives or let anyone say he had retreated.

pages.title: Instantly did the Pathans take to their heels,
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: Instantly did the Pathans take to their heels, As no body had the guts to bear the Singhs blows. (72) Standing from a distance did the Pathans fire shots, A volley of arrows did they shoot at the Singhs. So intensely did those shots pierce
pages.searchText: Instantly did the Pathans take to their heels, Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Instantly did the Pathans take to their heels, As no body had the guts to bear the Singhs blows. (72) Standing from a distance did the Pathans fire shots, A volley of arrows did they shoot at the Singhs. So intensely did those shots pierce through his body, That it was difficult to keep a count of the wounds. (73) Many of those shots cut through his flesh and bones, But never did the Singh accept defeat or felt the pain. Such a stream of blood burst forth from his body, As if oil was draining out from an oil crushers chamber. (74) Such fountains of blood burst forth from his body, As water with pressure leaked from the leather pouch. The more Gurbakhsh Singh marched ahead and ahead, The more the fountains of blood burst forth from his body. (75) Desperate did the Singh get after the draining of blood, Incapacitated he became for moving and fighting. Lest he be guilty of retracing his steps from the field. (76) May God Almighty's grace be upon His devout Sikh, May he not have to feel ashamed in the Divine Court. May his sacrifice be perfect and worthy of Divine acceptance, Time and again the devout Singh begged for Divine grace. (77) Then more and more Gilja Pathans there arrived, A large force did they bring along with them. The Singhs copses did the Gilja Pathans pick up, On the tips of their long-handled lances and spears. (78) Thereupon, Gurbakhsh Singh made a fresh attempt, At this not a single Pathan dared to confront him, Nor did Gurbax Singh chase the running Pathans. (79) Never did the Singhs turn their faces back, Lest not anybody accuse the Singhs later on, That the Singhs had retraced their steps in fight. (80)

pages.title: Gurbakhsh Singh Offers His Head in Combat
pages.episodeTitle: Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh
pages.snippet: The battle now narrows to Gurbakhsh Singh’s body itself. Spears pressed the Singh’s body down, yet even when weight and numbers forced him toward his knees, he did not lose his grip on his sword. The narration emphasizes that he fears only
pages.searchText: Gurbakhsh Singh Offers His Head in Combat Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The battle now narrows to Gurbakhsh Singh’s body itself. Spears pressed the Singh’s body down, yet even when weight and numbers forced him toward his knees, he did not lose his grip on his sword. The narration emphasizes that he fears only one thing: that delay or disarmament might deprive him of the sacrifice he has chosen. The question under the scene is whether he can still turn collapse into martyrdom. Then the moment arrives. He bows his head before an attacking Pathan in conscious imitation of earlier Sikh martyrdoms, and his head is severed from his body, completing the wedding with death that had been prepared throughout the episode.

pages.searchText: The Martyrs Receive Gurbakhsh Singh in the Heavenly Court Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The scene opens beyond the battlefield, where the martyr is welcomed by the Panth's earlier heroes. The great Singh martyr Mani Singh's spirit came himself, and Martyr Taru Singh come as well, reversing the loneliness of death by showing Gurbakhsh Singh received into a living fellowship of sacrifice. Coming near, martyrs greeted Gurbakhsh Singh with honor, while the persecutors and executioners who had tormented the Sikhs appear humbled and powerless in that higher court. The page treats martyrdom not as annihilation but as entrance into a company that already knows the cost of fidelity. Gurbakhsh Singh answers the welcome with intercession rather than self-congratulation. With folded hands did Gurbakhsh Singh pray to God for the Khalsa Panth which the Divine Guru had himself initiated, asking that the suffering community be protected and its enemies brought to ruin.

pages.snippet: Back on earth, the struggle leaves the Gilja force exhausted and shaken. When the exhausted Gilja Pathans fall asleep, the surviving Singhs harry them, seize horses where they can, and force the enemy remnants to withdraw back toward the royal camp in a state of disorder. The nar
pages.searchText: Aftermath of the Battle and the Shared Cremation of the Martyrs Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Back on earth, the struggle leaves the Gilja force exhausted and shaken. When the exhausted Gilja Pathans fall asleep, the surviving Singhs harry them, seize horses where they can, and force the enemy remnants to withdraw back toward the royal camp in a state of disorder. The narrative then turns tender and communal. Now listen to the account of the bodies of the martyred Singhs: the Singhs gather the bodies from the field, sort friend from foe as best they can, and refuse to leave their dead scattered across the ground. Their answer is an act of collective remembrance. The martyrs' bodies are piled up on a single pyre at the back of Akal Takht, and from that cremation the community begins to form the memorial tradition that will be known through Shaheed Ganj.

pages.snippet: The heavenly dialogue resumes with Gurbakhsh Singh still intent on remaining among the martyrs. Did he pray to God for an abode among the martyrs, yet the reply redirects that longing toward future service rather than permanent rest in the
pages.searchText: The Guru Decrees Gurbakhsh Singh's Return to the Panth Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The heavenly dialogue resumes with Gurbakhsh Singh still intent on remaining among the martyrs. Did he pray to God for an abode among the martyrs, yet the reply redirects that longing toward future service rather than permanent rest in the celestial assembly. The Guru's answer is decisive: That he must take birth again to be with Khalsa Panth. His martyrdom has earned him authority, so the closer he had stepped toward death in battle, the greater the host and leadership that will one day stand under his charge. The page closes by linking sacrifice to command. The martyrs acknowledge his new station, and the promise is made that his death before the Giljas has not ended his role, but prepared him to return as a leader whose courage will again serve the Panth in history.

pages.searchText: The Martyrs Petition for Gurbakhsh Singh's Future Birth Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh Episode About Nihang Gurbakhsh Singh The conclusion of the episode binds divine power, martyrdom, and future history together. For twelve years let the martyr's soul live in Divine presence becomes the request of the assembled martyrs, who ask that Gurbakhsh Singh remain in bliss for a time before returning again to earthly struggle. The Guru's assurance also defines the nature of that return. Never is the Guru distinct from his Sikhs, and The whole Khalsa Panth would abide by his command because the authority granted to Gurbakhsh Singh is presented as an extension of the Guru's own strength within the Panth. From there the narration turns toward the next historical movement. Asked in whose household he will be born, Gurbakhsh Singh is directed toward a brave warrior line, creating a hinge from this martyrdom episode into the following account of later Sikh resistance against Abdali and his allies.

pages.searchText: Jawahar Mal Appeals to the Khalsa Against Abdali Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla Episode About Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla The page answers the question raised at the end of the previous episode by linking Delhi's danger to Najib Rohilla's maneuvering and Abdali's renewed pressure. In that emergency Jawahar Mal decides to send his representatives to the Khalsa Panth so that the Sikhs may be brought openly into the struggle. The appeal stresses affinity as well as strategy. The envoys claim kinship and shared regional interests with the Khalsa and argue that this is the right moment to defend their faith and land against a devastator who threatens the whole region. Jawahar Mal also offers practical support instead of empty rhetoric. He promises plenty of ammunition and arms, abundant provisions, and an alliance that would uphold India's honour if the Singhs agree to stand with him against Abdali and Rohilla power.

pages.searchText: Abdali Is Alarmed by the Khalsa-Jat Alliance Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla Episode About Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla News of the new alliance spreads quickly through Abdali's camp. Listening about this new development, Ahmad Shah Abdali feel a sharp blow to his confidence, because he knows that any campaign against Jawahar Mal becomes far more dangerous once Sikh horsemen join the field. The political meaning is obvious to him. The young Khalsa Singhs had joined the Jat chief, and that combination threatens to snatch it from him: the prestige he had gathered after defeating other Indian powers could now be undone by a fresh coalition in the north. The page therefore emphasizes fear rather than triumph. Instead of striking at once, Abdali grows more scared and panicky, calculating not only the military risks of battle but also the humiliation that would follow if the Singhs helped Jawahar Mal throw him back.

pages.searchText: Jawahar Mal Musters a Broad Anti-Abdali Coalition Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla Episode About Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla As Abdali reaches Ambala and prepares to threaten the Jat ruler, Jawahar Mal refuses to wait passively. Calling an assembly of Rajputs, Marathas and Brars, together with Gosains, hill chiefs, and other allies, he turns the conflict into a wider regional challenge to Afghan power. The page pairs this coalition-building with military readiness. Reaching Ambala, Abdali pushes forward, but on the other side the war-drum did he order to be beaten as Jawahar Mal resolves that on the Gilja Pathan forces would he launch an attack before fear can dissolve the alliance. This display of organization deeply unsettles Rohilla calculations. Once Khalsa support, money, and war plans become visible, this Abdali's puppet came to the end of his wits and can no longer assume that the Jat ruler will be isolated or easily coerced.

pages.snippet: Confronted by a swelling coalition, Najib Rohilla abandons hopes of easy victory. A new strategy must he devise, and the page shows him searching among surrender, bribery, pressure, and negotiation for any path that might spare him from com
pages.searchText: Najib Rohilla Seeks Mediation Through Ragho Malhar Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla Episode About Ahmed Shah Abdali, Jawahar Mal of Bhara And Najib Khan Rohilla Confronted by a swelling coalition, Najib Rohilla abandons hopes of easy victory. A new strategy must he devise, and the page shows him searching among surrender, bribery, pressure, and negotiation for any path that might spare him from complete defeat. That search leads him toward mediation. Ragho Malhar is brought into the narrative as the influential Maratha intermediary through whom Rohilla hopes to send his representatives and open a back channel that can defuse Jawahar Mal's anger without forcing a public collapse. Money and persuasion become his chosen tools. He promises secretly a lot of ransom and urges the mediator to call to his camp for negotiation, trying to turn a battlefield crisis into a settlement before the combined Sikh and Jat pressure becomes irreversible.

pages.searchText: Jawahar Mal Rejects a Cash Settlement and Demands Honor Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Another Episode About Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Episode 158 opens by showing that negotiation alone cannot satisfy Jawahar Mal. Jawahar Mal did not agree to a simple monetary settlement because he is determined to never barter his family's reputation after the murder that had dishonored his house. His position is framed in terms of lineage, vengeance, and public memory. Since he has already spent heavily on the campaign and risked his standing before allies, he will not accept a compromise that looks like a purchased silence rather than justice. The page therefore sets up the symbolic terms of settlement that follow on the next readable page. Instead of cash alone, the discussion moves toward a girl in matrimony, lots of jewels and treasures, and formal gestures through which Jawahar Mal can claim that his father's murder had he avenged before the world.

pages.searchText: Najib-ud-Daula Pays Tribute and Receives Authority Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Another Episode About Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla This hinge page turns from Jawahar Mal's settlement back to Abdali's imperial arrangements. Listen further to the account about Ahmad Shah Abdali: once matters have been stabilized, Najibu-ud-Daula proceeded to pay a visit and acknowledge the ruler whose intervention preserved him. The meeting is formal and political. Najib placed his offerings before Abdali, thanks him for rescue, and is rewarded with favor that confirms his standing in the north after the recent crisis. From that audience come administrative decisions that shape the next conflict. Abdali is described as making him his deputy to rule over Delhi while also arranging that Rohilla's own troops be stationed at Sirhind, a move aimed at containing Sikh power on the Punjab frontier.

pages.snippet: The page continues Abdali's redistribution of power after the Delhi settlement. Must he turn out the Singhs from Punjab is the governing demand placed upon his dependents, for then alone would he be able to collect revenues and restore Afgh
pages.searchText: Abdali Reorders Sirhind and Misjudges the Khalsa Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Another Episode About Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla The page continues Abdali's redistribution of power after the Delhi settlement. Must he turn out the Singhs from Punjab is the governing demand placed upon his dependents, for then alone would he be able to collect revenues and restore Afghan authority in the region. To support that program, did Abdali invite Amar Singh and draw him into the circle of reward and obligation. He conferred the title of a Raja in hopes that local authority, prestige, and Sirhind's administration could be used to steady the frontier against Sikh pressure. Yet the narrative undercuts Abdali's confidence. Little did he realise the power of the Khalsa Panth, for while he distributes titles and offices, the Sikhs are already gathering strength and preparing a far more unified resistance than his camp expects.

After crossing Ropar, in the foothills did he wish to seek shelter, hoping broken terrain and guarded movement would spare him from the speed and reach of the Sikh horsemen. The opposite happens. Day and night did the Singhs keep a vigil, shadowing the Afghan movement so closely that neither rest nor confidence can return to the retreating camp. The harassment is relentless but disciplined. The Khalsa keep harassing them at night, strike at foragers and stragglers, and yet preserve moral distinction in battle, for Never would the Khalsa kill that defenceless Pathan who lay helpless and unable to fight.

pages.searchText: Abdali's Running Retreat Grows Desperate Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Another Episode About Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla The retreat hardens into a running battle in which Afghan tactics fail to restore control. Many a strategy did the Pathan soldiers adopt, but armored men and horses alike are broken by the Singh's mighty swords as the Khalsa keeps closing the distance. The page stresses how precarious Abdali's situation becomes. Impossible indeed it became for them to reach Kabul in peace, because every march segment invites another Sikh strike and every delay deepens the appearance of imperial weakness. In response Abdali looks for reinforcement and coordination. Jahan Khan is brought forward to support the battered force, but even with additional leadership and planning, in no way would the Singhs allow him a safe passage back across Punjab.

Some Singhs opined to let half of Abdali's forces cross the river so that the enemy might then be trapped and plundered in a more decisive blow. Others urge immediate attack. S. Charat Singh begged the Khalsa to take on Abdali directly, but senior judgment still weighs whether patience might yield a cleaner victory and reminds the assembly that no hasty action was in their interest. Even so, pressure mounts as Abdali's troops were crossing the river Ravi. The page follows the confusion of attack and withdrawal before the Afghans, badly shaken and eager to escape further punishment, hurry westward and hastily did they march in the direction of Multan.

pages.snippet: The episode ends with Abdali's own bitter reckoning. Much did he repent for his expedition, admitting in effect that the power he expected to crush turned out to be the force that harried and humiliated him across Punjab. His explanation is
pages.searchText: Abdali Repents the Punjab Campaign and the Khalsa Triumphs Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Another Episode About Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla The episode ends with Abdali's own bitter reckoning. Much did he repent for his expedition, admitting in effect that the power he expected to crush turned out to be the force that harried and humiliated him across Punjab. His explanation is theological as well as military. He concludes that the almighty God had supported the Singhs, and from now onwards if anyone from my progeny ever entered this region, that descendant should expect regret rather than glory. The author then seals the reversal in historical terms. On the way to Kabul did he die, and the Khalsa Panth emerges from the episode as Ahmed Shah's destroyer in reputation, the community that shattered the certainty of the invader who had once terrorized the north.

pages.title: Abdali’s Retreat Closes and the Khalsa Reclaims Punjab
pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla
pages.snippet: This closing page completes the Abdali retreat with a note of humiliation rather than triumph. The invader's remorse deepens into an admission that God had supported the Singhs, and that the very campaign meant to discipline Punjab instead
pages.searchText: Abdali’s Retreat Closes and the Khalsa Reclaims Punjab Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla Another Episode About Ahmed Shah Ata Rohilla This closing page completes the Abdali retreat with a note of humiliation rather than triumph. The invader's remorse deepens into an admission that God had supported the Singhs, and that the very campaign meant to discipline Punjab instead exposed the limits of imperial force. The narrative pushes that reversal to its personal end. Abdali is shown traveling back in grief, warning that any descendant who returned in the same spirit would meet the same regret, and then falling short of his destination to die short of Kabul. With that, the author hands the moral victory to the Panth. The Khalsa Panth occupy the territory that had been their native country from the beginning, so the episode closes not with Afghan consolidation but with Sikh endurance and recovery.

pages.snippet: This page rejects the Mughal attempt to dismiss Sikh power as a recent accident of invasion. The author insists that the Khalsa Panth existed at the time of Aurangzeb, and that such a presence could no more be concealed than the sun behind
pages.searchText: The Khalsa Predates Abdali and Holds a Legitimate Claim Additional episode: Another Episode This page rejects the Mughal attempt to dismiss Sikh power as a recent accident of invasion. The author insists that the Khalsa Panth existed at the time of Aurangzeb, and that such a presence could no more be concealed than the sun behind passing clouds. He then grounds Sikh authority in sacrifice and inheritance. The Gurus had surrendered their lives, Five provinces had been taken away through persecution and fraud, and therefore the Sikhs had a legitimate claim to the land they were now defending. The argument is presented not merely as sectarian feeling but as a case tested before an outside listener. Captain David Murray is made to hear the account in full and to accept that Perfectly legitimate was the Sikhs claim indeed.

pages.searchText: Captain Murray Accepts the Account Before the Shyam Singh Episode Additional episode: Another Episode The page returns to the moral charge sheet against Mughal rule by recalling the fate of The innocent Sahibzadas and the repeated assaults on the Guru and his household. These acts are not treated as isolated cruelties but as proof that Mughal power had forfeited any moral right to govern the Panth. From there the author resumes the courtroom-like conclusion of the previous discussion. On every count had the Mughals been proved wrong, and in both the worlds had they been discredited by the evidence of persecution, sacrifice, and survival. Captain David Murray then gives the account public weight. Fully did he believe in the narrator's version, saying it should be forwarded onward, even To the British Sovereign, the king of England, before the book turns to the opening of Shyam Singh's misl.

Sham Singhs Misi The author introduces this new cycle with a personal claim of authority, saying he heard it from my own mother because she was descended from Shyam Singh's household. That framing turns the page into a family-backed remembrance rather than a distant chronicle. It then traces the line through Mali, a Sandhu Jat at village Narla, and explains how the young Shyam Singh came under the influence of Mastan Singh and the Khalsa discipline around him. The story emphasizes initiation, inherited service, and the shaping of character in a martial but devout community. By the close of the page, Shyam Singh is no longer only a named ancestor. He stands as the worthy heir to a disciplined tradition in which hospitality, courage, and readiness to initiate into the Khalsa Panth are treated as marks of legitimacy.

After the divisions of the Panth and the rise of Kapoor Singh, the circle around Shyam Singh expands into a stronger armed following with noted chiefs, retainers, and a growing mounted force. The page therefore marks a transition from household virtue to institutional power. What begins as an account of shared food and open welcome becomes the story of a misl taking recognisable military shape under trusted leadership.

Sham Singhs Misi After news arrives that Baghel Singh is advancing, Amar Singh refuses to show anxiety and instead boasts that a determined assault will strip his rival of territory. Orders go out in every direction to reach his fort at the earliest, turning alarm into a full political and military mobilization. The page lingers over the breadth of the coalition he gathers. Allied chiefs, kinsmen, and neighboring powers are summoned, while drums, cavalry, and a visible battery of artillery guns create the spectacle of an army meant to intimidate before battle even begins. This page is about posture. Amar Singh seeks victory first by scale, display, and confident messaging, presenting himself as the stronger chief before either side has actually tested the field.

What should have been reconnaissance becomes the fuel for a boastful certainty that underestimates both Baghel Singh and the fighting reputation of the Singhs.

pages.searchText: Baghel Singh Marches On and Warnings Are Ignored S. Sham Singhs Misi Episode About S. Sham Singhs Misi Baghel Singh dismisses fearful calculations with a soldier's realism. Nobody vacated an occupied territory without a fight, he argues, so recovery can come only by marching forward and accepting battle rather than by wishful negotiation. The confrontation accordingly becomes unavoidable. Baghel Singh orders his force to march towards Patiala, while Amar Singh reacts in anger and presses his advisers toward immediate action. One voice still counsels caution, warning that the Singhs should not be treated lightly, yet hawkish chiefs brush such advice aside. The page ends with pride overpowering prudence and the clash drawing visibly nearer.

Those who had never seen the Singhs fighting a battle talk loosely of loot, horses, and easy fame, as though the Majhail veterans before them were an ordinary enemy. On the Khalsa side, however, the scale of the Malwa preparations causes unease, and practical men begin sending valuables away before the fighting closes in. Dulcha Singh argues that Now he must keep patience for five ten days, holding position and thinking carefully rather than letting pride force a rash move. The page therefore prepares the larger confrontation by showing two mentalities at once. One side mistakes noise for victory, while the other measures risk, supply, and reputation before committing fully.

pages.searchText: Dust, Noise, and the Opening Clash at Patiala S. Sham Singhs Misi Episode About S. Sham Singhs Misi The battle begins in sensory confusion and violent momentum. The sun seemed to have been eclipsed by the rising dust, while drums, musketry, and shouted commands spread panic around Patiala before either side could claim a clear advantage. Amar Singh tries to convert his numerical confidence into a decisive charge, urging his troops to kill the Singhs and seize their horses. Yet once the lines close, the Khalsa steadies itself under fire and answers with disciplined shooting that checks repeated advances. The page presents the first great testing of appearance against reality. What looked like an overwhelming host is forced to meet veteran resistance at close quarters, and the promise of a quick victory begins to fray.

Whosoever blinked and thought of retracing his steps first would yield the field, yet the Khalsa holds while the opposition begins to break under sustained attack. By the end of the page, Malwa forces got uprooted on both the battle fronts despite the deployment of additional Rohilla and hill infantry. The attempted counterstroke only confirms that Baghel Singh's side now owns the momentum of the battle.

The Fort gates did they shut behind the fugitives, while artillery thunders and surrounding villages suffer plunder in the wake of the Khalsa advance. Victory, however, does not simply become indiscriminate destruction. Chain Singh and Dulcha Singh approach Baghel Singh to argue that the lesson has already been delivered and that a negotiated settlement will better preserve both honor and the wider unity of the Panth. This page therefore turns the battle toward diplomacy. The Khalsa has shown its strength in the field, and now the question becomes how to translate that strength into terms that even defeated rivals must respect.

Sham Singhs Misi The defeated side tries to explain away the reverse and imagine new combinations of power, but Chain Singh answers with political clarity rather than anger. Both Majhail and Malwai Singhs constituted a Singh fraternity, he insists, so no ruler will prosper by setting one section of the Panth against another. He recommends negotiation through the full repertoire of statecraft rather than renewed adventurism. The familiar logic of Saam, Daam, Dand and Bhaid is invoked not to sanction treachery, but to restore balance after pride has already failed. From this counsel comes a practical settlement. Occupied lands and revenues are restored, allied chiefs receive compensation, and the field victory is converted into a political acknowledgement of Khalsa solidarity.

The reconciliation is marked through gifts, esteem, and kin-like language. Amar Singh goes so far as to offer to Baghel Singh for adoption his own son, symbolically recasting rivalry as a family alliance sealed in the idiom of Sikh fraternity. The page closes by stressing that this was not empty ceremony. In later dangers Baghel Singh repeatedly acts to uphold the family bondage he had accepted, showing loyalty to Patiala when action, not words, became necessary.

pages.searchText: A Brahmin Appeals to the Khalsa Against a Tyrant Sayyad S. Sham Singhs Misi Episode About S. Sham Singhs Misi A new narrative opens by praising the Khalsa as a power that can act where courts and governors refuse justice. The aggrieved father explains that There is a town known as Luhari Jalalabad near Delhi, where a tyrannical Sayyad has abducted his daughter and terrorized the surrounding people. The page frames his appeal as a test of Khalsa responsibility toward the weak. No official will confront the offender, so the Brahmin comes to the Sikh camp convinced that the Panth alone still acts in the cause of protection and benefaction. Warnings immediately arise about distance, danger, and the Sayyad's influence near Delhi, yet the moral pressure of the plea is stronger than caution. The episode therefore begins not with conquest but with a rescue mission grounded in justice.

pages.searchText: The Khalsa Crosses the Rivers to Fight for the Brahmin Khalsa Panth Another Episode About Khalsa Panth The Khalsa accepts the appeal and pushes eastward despite the risks of operating near Delhi's orbit. After crossing the Satluj they camp near the bank of the river Yamuna, and news of their approach sends the local Muslim authorities into hurried defensive preparation. The advance then becomes personal and symbolic at once. With the (aggrieved) Brahmin leading them from the front, the Singhs cross onward, raise their standards, and pray that they may win martyrdom while carrying out an act of welfare for others. Their charge immediately shakes the defenders. The enemy falls back toward the gates under pressure, and the page presents the coming assault as righteous intervention rather than opportunistic raiding.

The Singhs search room by room and descend even to the underground cellar where the abductor has attempted to hide from the reckoning he thought would never reach him. The Brahmin's daughter identifies the culprit, and the Singhs drag him from concealment to face exemplary punishment. The same investigation exposes the local wine-seller who had served as facilitator and procurer in the search for girls. Justice on the page is therefore both personal and public. The tyrant and his accomplice are destroyed, the daughter is recovered, and the Khalsa leaves behind a warning that predatory power will not remain safe merely because it sits close to Delhi.

The rescued Brahmin girl is questioned with care, acknowledged as a victim of coercion rather than disgrace, and publicly embraced as the daughter of the Khalsa Panth. That declaration immediately creates social obligation. The Singhs resolve to unite her with her in-laws, send messengers to her in-laws, and begin organizing communal support so that her return will be marked by dignity rather than stigma. The page is therefore as important for social repair as for martial justice. A rescue is not considered complete until the community also rebuilds the injured woman's standing, security, and future.

Because the Panth had accepted her as their own daughter, contributions are gathered for an adequate dowry and the Brahmin household leaves the camp with gratitude rather than ruin. News of the intervention then spreads far beyond the immediate family. Supporters celebrate the fact that the Sayyad was slain, while Delhi’s alarmed spokesmen report that the Khalsa has moved to the area surrounding the capital and is no longer content to remain at a distance. The page turns a single act of protection into a wider political tremor. A sense of panic gripped the inhabitants of Delhi because the Panth now appears both morally resolute and militarily near.

pages.episodeTitle: Another Episode About Khalsa Panth

pages.searchText: Begum Samru Brokers Terms With Baghel Singh Khalsa Panth Another Episode About Khalsa Panth Delhi's rulers respond to the Khalsa pressure with anxiety and debate, but no simple military answer is available. Into that uncertainty steps Begum Samru, who advises that the crisis must be handled through intelligence, diplomacy, and the older statecraft of Saam, Daam, Dand Bhed. Her reading of the situation is precise. Baghel Singh is identified as the chief under whose protection a workable settlement can be made, so envoys, gifts, and negotiations are directed toward him rather than wasted on bluster. This page therefore marks the Mughal shift from fear to bargaining. The court stops pretending that the Khalsa can simply be brushed aside and begins treating Baghel Singh as the indispensable political interlocutor.

pages.searchText: Baghel Singh Withdraws and Begins the Delhi Shrines Khalsa Panth Another Episode About Khalsa Panth Once terms are struck, the Delhi ruler sent a message to S. Baghel Singh asking that the Khalsa be drawn back from immediate plunder. Baghel Singh manages the withdrawal in an orderly way while still warning the Panth about imperial concentration and the danger of fresh alliances against them. The retreat is therefore strategic rather than submissive. After the Khalsa Dal beat a hasty retreat from the edge of Delhi, Baghel Singh put up his camp at Subzi Mandi and begins operating from a position that still commands respect. From there the narrative turns constructive. Revenues and honors are acknowledged, and Baghel Singh started construction of Sikh shrines so that political leverage in Delhi is translated into lasting sacred presence.

pages.searchText: Baghel Singh and the Delhi Memorials Khalsa Panth Another Episode About Khalsa Panth The page says that two sites connected with Guru Tegh Bahadur had mosques built upon them, and Baghel Singh said the mosques would have to be removed before memorials could be raised. This enraged the Muslims, who asked how they could live or pray without those mosques. Muslim leaders and clerics went together to the emperor, accusing him of impiety for allowing the demolition. The emperor replied that they should have objected earlier, because recanting would break trust with S. Baghel Singh and make the emperor false to his written promise. The emperor warned that Baghel Singh might ravage the country or even take Delhi if the agreement was broken. Baghel Singh saw that opposition was being organized, gathered the Khalsa around Delhi, and forced the chief objectors to submit, withdraw their protests, and give written consent.

pages.searchText: Rakab Ganj Is Reclaimed With Affidavits and Ceremony Khalsa Panth Another Episode About Khalsa Panth Resistance to Sikh claims in Delhi is broken partly by force and partly by political management. Written affidavits are gathered, pressure is applied through intermediaries such as Ram Dyal, and the necessary permissions are assembled before direct action is taken. With those papers in hand, Baghel Singh moves on the site of Rakab Ganj associated with Guru Tegh Bahadur's cremation. Demolition of the obstructing structure is ordered, the Khalsa standard is raised, and the place is publicly re-marked as Sikh sacred ground. The page closes in liturgical rather than military fashion. Sacred karah parshad is distributed and ceremony seals the reclamation, showing how legal maneuver, force, and devotion are made to work together.
